en: Nyāyadīpikā:
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is like a royal swan upon the lotus-face of Indirā, and whose form is beautiful with an abundance of intense bliss. 1.
I perpetually salute the venerable Śrī Bhagavatpāda, whose body is bliss, and who possesses supreme sovereignty over the knowledge and detachment from all phenomena. (2)
May that Padmanābha—the sun at the holy ford (tīrtha) and the leader of the herd of cows—be for my vision;
for there is no proceeding upon the path of reality without subsisting upon him. (3)
Having bowed at the pair of feet of my teachers, by the power of their grace, I shall explain the determination of the essential meaning of the Gītā according to my understanding. (4)

Now, desiring to explain the *Gītā*—which is the cause of all the goals of human life and has been otherwise interpreted by others—as it truly is, the venerable Teacher composes at the beginning of his work a salutation to his chosen deity for the purpose of ensuring its completion without obstacles and so forth; he does this as a traditional practice of the learned, and for the sake of instructing his disciples, while also announcing the commencement of the treatise. [He says: "The entire... Those who desire to avoid obstacles and the like are seen to perform salutations to other deities.

To the question, "Why then [begin] with a prostration to Nārāyaṇa?", it is said: "All... and so forth. The sense is that since Nārāyaṇa alone is complete in all qualities, is far removed from every defect, and possesses the capacity to grant all that is prayed for—whereas others possess power only through the grace obtained from Him—it is He alone to whom prostration should be made. By the word "complete" (*sampūrṇam*), he expresses the fullness of each individual quality; and by "devoid" (*vivarjitam*), he expresses the total absence of defects.

In order to indicate the preeminence of the *Bhagavadgītā* among all songs (*gītā*), it is referred to simply as "the Gītā," according to the traditional rule: "A word for the principal [subject] is used without qualification. Since he himself has already composed a commentary on the Gītā, one might ask why this new undertaking is necessary; therefore, the term "tātparya" (purport) is employed. The sense is that although the Gītā has been explained, its meaning is stated once again through the expression of its purport—rather than by mere literal repetition of words—in order to facilitate its comprehension by the disciples.

Now, one might ask: since many other texts exist, what is the special quality of the Gītā such that its specific purport alone is being stated? Furthermore, since the Gītā is situated within the Mahābhārata, why is its purport stated separately? To this we reply: because the Mahābhārata is the supreme among all scriptures, it is appropriate to state the purport specifically of the Gītā contained within it.

Anticipating the resolution that even within the *Bhārata*, because the *Gītā* is supreme, it is appropriate to state its specific purport, [the author] first establishes the *Bhārata*'s status as the best among all scriptures. Then, to the question "Why is the *Gītā* alone the most excellent even within the *Bhārata*?", he seeks to prove this by means of a citation from the Purāṇas. Regarding the phrase "Among the scriptures" (*śāstreṣu*): To the question "Why is the *Gītā* and the Thousand Names (*Nāmasahasra*) the most excellent even within the *Bhārata*?", he says: "That... (*tad*).

The sense is that since knowledge of the Gītā and similar texts is more directly a means to liberation than even knowledge of the Mahābhārata, it is appropriate that the Gītā and such works are considered superior even within the Mahābhārata.

To the objection—namely, that since knowledge of other scriptures equal to the *Gītāsāhasranāma* is also directly a cause of liberation, what distinction is there for the Gītā and the like?—the author says: "No."

Why is the *Bhārata* alone the supreme among all scriptures? To this he says: "The *Bhārata*... By the word "Veda," all scriptures are meant, in the sense that they cause [truth] to be known (*vedayanti*). Placing the *Bhārata* on a scale means placing its equivalent there. Why is this so? He says that it is understood precisely by reflecting on the meaning of the term "Mahābhārata. The meaning is: because of its greatness (*mahattvāt*), and because it is extended (*tata*) as a burden (*bhāra*), it is the *Mahābhārata*.

Furthermore, with the thought that if even the destruction of all sins occurs simply through knowing the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *Mahābhārata*, then what need is there to mention its status as the supreme among all scriptures, he says: "The etymology" (*niruktam*). "Etymology" means the derivation; [this refers] to this word *Mahābhārata*.
To show the reason why the *Bhārata* alone is the supreme among all scriptures—namely, that it was composed by the Supreme Authority—he says: "By himself" (*svayam*).

Now, one who is called an *āpta* (a reliable authority) is indeed one who perceives things as they truly are and speaks of things exactly as they have been perceived. In that regard, from what source does Vyāsa’s quality of perceiving things as they truly are arise? Since even among the incarnations (*avatāra*) of the Blessed One, such as Pṛthu and others, there is observed ignorance and so forth, it is therefore said: "Himself" (*svayam*).

Granted that Vyāsa possesses the quality of seeing things as they truly are (*yathārthadarśitva*), since—as an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa himself—he is free from ignorance, error, and doubt; but how can he be one who speaks of things exactly as he has seen them (*yathādṛṣṭārthavāditva*)? For even if he lacks the tendency to speak of what he has not seen due to negligence (*pramāda*), it is still possible for him to do so through a desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*). To this, [the author] says: "Brahma... [etc. A speaker's desire to deceive is possible only when the listeners lack the requisite fitness (*ayogyatā*).

And in the present context, since Brahmā and the others are indeed qualified listeners, there is no possibility of the Blessed One deceiving them; thus, the sense is that it is logical for him to speak of things exactly as they have been perceived. To the question, "Why might he not speak of things not as they were perceived out of mockery? he says: "But the reality... and so forth.

The sense is this: since derision (*apahāsa*) is based on the fault of being irrelevant to the context, and since the determination of truth (*tattvanirṇaya*) is what is relevant here, such derision is impossible; therefore, even by way of derision, Vyāsa cannot be accused of speaking of matters not seen as they truly are. Furthermore, since the fact of being composed by such a trustworthy person (*āpta*) is common to the *Bhāgavata* and other texts as well, one might ask: "What is the distinction of the *Mahābhārata*? To this, it is said: "Exclusively" (*kevalam*). Nothing else is stated here even for the purpose of deluding the Asuras, because that which was perceived otherwise has been spoken of through both secret vision and speech.

The sense is that it is stated otherwise in some other place for the purpose of causing delusion. Thus, the *Bhārata* is not the supreme among all scriptures merely by virtue of being rooted in the highest authority; rather, it is so because it accords with the Vedas and constitutes the fifth Veda. With this intention, he says: "the fifth."

Having thus established the propriety of explaining the purport of the Gītā, and desiring to prepare the intellect of the listener, he first shows the entire subject matter propounded by the Gītā in brief, beginning with the word "tatra" (therein).

In that regard, regarding the *Gītā*, the words "it is said" (*iti kathyate*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. One might ask: since Kṛṣṇa is no different from Arjuna, how can he be the one who brings about that awakening? To this, it is stated: "the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa. One might further ask: what purpose does the Blessed Lord, whose every desire is fulfilled, have in awakening Arjuna? To this, it is stated: "of himself" (*ātmanaḥ*). [This means] even in the absence of a personal motive...

The sense is that, due to the intensity of His affection, He spoke to awaken him, just as a father protects his child. If it is asked, "Why is Arjuna especially dear to the Blessed Lord?"—if one says it is because he possesses direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), citing the Smṛti text, "The man of knowledge is dearest to Me," then one asks, "And why does he have that? To this, He says: "Supreme... (10.41). If it is further asked, "Why is even that so? He says: "Directly... (10.42). Purandara is Indra directly; or, he is a direct incarnation and not merely one who has entered [another body]. In this context, his status as a deity must indeed be stated.

The phrase "the incarnation of Indra" is a description of his true nature. To the question, "What is the attainment [of merit] in awakening Arjuna?", he says: "Nārāyaṇa. Since the suppression of kinsmen and others is unrighteous, one might ask why this is called unrighteousness; therefore, he states by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument that this suppression is indeed righteous: "Of the Kṣatriyas. The meaning is that while such suppression of even a mere devotee (*bhāgavata*) is the supreme duty, for Kṣatriyas specifically appointed to this task, it is especially the supreme duty.

To address the question of how the suppression of kinsmen and others can be considered the supreme dharma, the text states "the hater of Nārāyaṇa and his associates" instead of simply "kinsmen and others. The underlying sense is that even though they are kinsmen and so forth, because some hate Nārāyaṇa and others are associated with him, their suppression is indeed dharma.

[Objection: "If this were indeed Dharma, it would have been taught in the scriptures; and thus, one learned in the scriptures would not suspect it to be Adharma. Yet it is so suspected. Therefore, it is not Dharma. To this he says: "Out of affection for a kinsman" (*bandhusnehāt*). The point is that this suspicion does not arise from the perspective of the scriptures, but is rather based solely on affection. [Question: How can there be a cessation of one's own supreme Dharma through a suspicion arising merely from affection on the part of a knower? To this he says: "It is almost ceased" (*nivṛttaprāyam*).

If it is argued that since Arjuna has almost desisted from battle due to such apprehensions, he should simply be instructed to engage in the fight itself—why then are the greatness of the Lord and other matters being stated? To clarify this purpose, the author says: "His own" (*sva*). The supreme duty is not merely one's own prescribed occupation, such as fighting and so forth, such that only that would need to be taught. Rather, devotion and other qualities are also included. In this context, although Arjuna harbors doubts regarding unrighteousness even within a portion of his duty, the Supreme Lord instructs him in his primary duty for the sake of benefiting the world.
The intention is that the description of the Lord’s greatness and other attributes is intended to generate devotion.

[Objection: But surely Arjuna, though withdrawn from his own prescribed duties such as war, was not withdrawn from supreme dharma, because he possessed devotion (*bhakti*) and other qualities. Therefore, what is there to be taught? To this, [the author] says: "That" (*tat*). Devotion and the rest are not each individually supreme dharma, such that by their mere presence his withdrawal from supreme dharma would not occur; rather, they must be combined. Thus, the sense is that since withdrawal from supreme dharma occurs even in the absence of any one of them, it is appropriate to teach that [combined state].

If that is so, one might ask: "Of what use is the description of *prakṛti* and the rest? To this, let it be said that the nature of *dharma* belongs to that which functions according to its own ordained rule, while the nature of *adharma* belongs to that which is contrary to it. However, one might further question: "Why is the worship of the Lord through devotion to Him *dharma*, and why is what is contrary to that *adharma*? In order to dispel such doubts and to state the reason for everything being dependent upon the Lord, [the author] says "The Lord... with the intention of providing a comprehensive definition of all things.

The sense is that since everything is dependent on the Blessed One, merit and demerit exist only as determined by the Blessed One; and it is logical that He exercises such determination only over things of that nature.

[Objection: But from where is Arjuna’s divinity and so forth known? And from where is it known that [the passage] beginning with "svavihita" (as ordained by himself) constitutes the purport of the Gītā? To this, he says: "And all... The idea is that everything—including the fact that Arjuna is a god—is understood from the Gītā itself; no other authority needs to be sought there. Furthermore, everything beginning with "svavihita" is indeed understood from the Gītā; it is not stated here by force as if it were merely for the sake of that [purport].

In this regard, it is clearly understood from the *Gītā* that the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa instructs Arjuna—who, out of affection for his kinsmen, had become almost despondent after suspecting the suppression of those who opposed him (the enemies of Nārāyaṇa) to be unrighteous—by saying: "Tell me decisively what would be for my highest good. For such a request would be inappropriate if he were already completely despondent.

To the question, "By what [authority] is it understood in the Gītā that the suppression of the enemies of Nārāyaṇa and their followers is the supreme duty of Kṣatriyas? he says: "Now (atha)," etc. The words "of the battle" and "of the aforementioned kind" are to be supplied as the remainder. The phrase "is understood" is to be connected with every instance.

The supreme duty is the worship of the Lord alone through devotion by means of one’s own prescribed mode of livelihood; that everything contrary to this is unrighteousness (adharma)—how is this understood? To this, he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). By the word "because," the necessity of performing the worship of the Lord through devotion by means of one’s own prescribed mode of livelihood is understood, since worship performed with devotion is indeed true adoration (*abhyarcana*). By the phrase "by one’s own action" (*svakarmaṇā*), it is understood that the worship of the Lord specifically by means of one’s own prescribed mode of livelihood is the primary duty.

Because the means to liberation alone constitutes the primary duty; by the word "better" (*śreyān*), it is indicated that one's own prescribed conduct is to be performed while conduct not so prescribed is to be abandoned, since that which is better is to be done and that which is not better is to be avoided. By the word "all," it is indicated that the worship of the Lord with devotion is to be performed, because that which is enjoined as the most secret of all secrets, as the means to one's welfare, and as the means to attaining the Lord, must necessarily be performed.

By the phrase "all duties" (*sarvadharma*), it is intended that through one's own prescribed mode of life and with devotion, the worship of the Lord alone is to be performed, while everything else is to be abandoned. This is because the worship of the Lord through one's own prescribed mode of life and with devotion is itself the state of seeking refuge (*śaraṇāgati*). By the term "all duties," what is intended is a semblance of dharma that is contrary to this [true dharma]. Since that which is prescribed is to be performed as the cause for the removal of all sins, and since that which is prohibited is to be abandoned for that same purpose, [the verse says] "by one's own duty" (*svadharmeṇa*).

And I would connect [the word] "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*). The sense is that the nature of being *dharma* or *adharma* is determined by whether something is to be performed or abandoned. Now, it might be argued: "Even for a knower (*jñānin*), since liberation—which consists of indirect and direct knowledge—is understood in the *Gītā* itself to depend solely on one's own prescribed mode of conduct such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, there is no need for devotion. Furthermore, it cannot be said that hearing and the rest are useless; otherwise, it would be illogical for knowledge and the like to depend upon devotion. The intended meaning is this: although hearing and the rest are indeed means to knowledge and the like, what is intended here is that devotion alone is superior to all those means, including hearing and the rest.

It is not the intention of the Gītā that one should worship the Lord through devotion while performing only those duties prescribed for oneself and abandoning what is contrary to them; for in that case, the intention would merely be the absence of anything to be done or abandoned by one possessed of devotion. To this, he says: "My work" (mat-karma).

The Gītā does not intend for a devotee (*bhakta*) to abandon all that ought to be done. The underlying sense is that even for a devotee, worship of the Lord through one's own prescribed mode of livelihood (*svavihitavṛtti*) must be performed, while that which is contrary to it must be abandoned. As it has been stated: "Action directed toward Me, consisting of one's own prescribed mode of livelihood, is *mat-karma* (My work); that alone is [true] action. Action devoid of this—meaning action that is not prescribed and is devoid of devotion to the Lord—is called *vikarma* (misdeed).
Only that action declared as the cause for attaining the Lord is to be performed; that which is prohibited for the sake of that [attainment] is to be abandoned."

Now, one might ask: if Arjuna were already a man of knowledge (jñānin), why would the Lord enjoin him to worship Him through his own prescribed duty? For it is the intention of the Gītā that such a person has no need for that. To this, He says: "Do thou perform."

It is not that the wise man lacks his own prescribed duties and so forth, as understood from the *Gītā*. For in that very text, [the Lord says], "Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action; perform action alone"—the sense being that even for the wise man, his own prescribed duties and so forth are understood as obligatory. "His own prescribed" means that which was performed by the ancients solely for the sake of the Lord; both of these are indeed "action for the Lord. Since Arjuna asked, "By what is it known that the Lord is extremely dear, a knower of direct realization (*aparokṣajñānin*), a person of the highest qualification, and a god?"—to this he replies: "Extremely difficult to see."

By the phrase "extremely difficult to see," his state of possessing immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñānitva*) is understood. From being mentioned alongside the gods, his divinity (*devatva*) is also understood. By the words "you are beloved," his being most dear is indicated. By the word "divine" (*daivī*), his divinity is shown. By the phrase "the high-souled ones," the divinity and immediate knowledge of those who worship the Blessed One with undistracted minds are understood. And for Arjuna, who possesses such devotion, that [vision] was known; this is understood from the words "he showed [himself]," which indicate immediate knowledge, as well as his extreme dearness to the Blessed One and his divinity. Through his very divinity, his status as a person of the highest qualification is also understood.

It has been stated that everything is dependent upon the Blessed Lord; by what means is this understood? If that is so, He must be perceived as distinct from all else, as all things being real, as the supreme among all, as complete in all qualities, as faultless, as independent of anything else, as the bestower of liberation, and as the subject of exposition for all scriptures. This is because the dependence of everything upon Him—whether direct or indirect—is contingent upon these very attributes. To the question, "By what is all of this understood?", he says:
No.

By the phrase "do not know Me," His fullness is understood; by "I am the origin," His supremacy over all is shown; and by "He who knows Me," His freedom from defects, the fact that everything is dependent on Him, and liberation through the knowledge of Him are indicated—since birth and other such attributes are considered defects, and since liberation consists in the destruction of all sins. By "intellect" (buddhi), it is meant that everything is dependent on Him; by "this" (etām), it is meant that liberation comes from knowing Him, because He is easily attained through unwavering yoga. By "I" (aham), it is meant that everything is dependent on Him and that liberation comes from the knowledge of Him.

Because saṃsāra consists of the darkness born of ignorance; "of them" means that liberation comes from knowledge of That. "The enjoyer" indicates that everything is dependent upon Him and that liberation comes from knowledge of Him. Since peace is liberation, "knowledge" signifies that all scriptures have that as their ultimate purpose, for it is stated that through knowledge of the Blessed Lord alone, all scriptures are known.

The phrase "I" signifies that everything is dependent upon Him; "from Me" signifies His supremacy over all; "in Me" signifies that everything is under His control; "this" signifies that liberation comes from the knowledge of Him; "the King" signifies that all scriptures have Him as their ultimate goal, because the science of the Blessed Lord is declared to be primary, and secondary matters follow the primary; "by Me" signifies both that everything is dependent on Him and His faultlessness, since the root *tan* means "to impel," and the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) indicates that He is not an effect.

"Nor am I" (*na cāham*) signifies His independence from anything else. "The sustainer of beings" (*bhūtabhṛt*) signifies that everything is dependent on Him, as well as His own independence. "Not by you" (*na tvat*) signifies His supremacy over all. "Supreme" (*param*) signifies that all scriptures have Him as their ultimate goal, because it is stated that the scripture of the Lord—designated by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it is known through this—is the best of all scriptures; for that which is not primary follows what is primary. "Mine" (*mama*) signifies that everything is dependent on Him.

"Of Brahman indeed" (*brahmaṇo hi*) refers to the fact that everything is dependent upon Him and that liberation comes from the knowledge of Him. "Two" (*dvau*) refers to the Lord's distinction from everything, His supremacy over all, the dependence of everything upon Him, the fact that all scriptures have Him as their ultimate goal, and that liberation comes from the knowledge of Him.

"Not mine, O Pārtha" (*na me pārtha*) refers to His perfection. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), passages such as "unreal and without foundation" (*asatyam apratiṣṭham tat*) are included; by the second, the reality of the world (*jagatsatyatva*) is grasped.

Regarding what was stated—that even for the knower (*jñānin*), action belongs to the Lord—the author cites a scriptural passage: "Now... The meaning is that praise and sacrifice offered with oblations are to be sought after (*arthya*) and accomplished even by the knower. To the objection, "Since liberation is certain for the knower, what is the use of ritual action?", he replies: "Even while seeing... [The word *suniyatam* means] that which is properly prescribed according to one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). The words "he would obtain through that" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Or rather, it means: because through that [action] he would obtain the excellence of bliss ordained for himself, therefore [he performs it].

Regarding what was stated—that devotion to Viṣṇu alone is the supreme among all means of realization and so forth—in order to demonstrate the scriptural authority for that, [the author] says: "By devotion."

Since there is no devotion (bhakti) without knowledge (jñāna), how can knowledge arise from devotion? To this it is said: "undisturbed" (anākula). The sense is that for one who is agitated by pride, the state of being undisturbed comes about through devotion. Because devotion is the means to liberation, [the author] incidentally wards off the doubt that it might cease immediately after that; thus he says: "even when liberated. "Abundant devotion" (bhūyasī bhaktiḥ) means excessive devotion. Since there is no duality in liberation, or because of its uniformity, it might be thought that devotion is not appropriate there; therefore he says: "under its control" (tadvaśaḥ).

In liberation, when there is the true state of devotion (*bhakti-sadbhāva*), results such as bliss may indeed arise; otherwise, they would be untenable. Furthermore, if one accepts these results, it follows that there is the attainment of growth and so forth. To this, he says: "The goal... The meaning is this: there is no existence of a result for the devotion of one already liberated, because that [liberated devotion] lacks the nature of being a means (*sādhana*). Nor is there any inconsistency on this account, because the bliss which was previously to be accomplished through devotion is the very essence (*svarūpa*) of that devotion; thus, devotion is the result [in the sense of being its own nature], and at that time, the result is experienced.

To the question, "What is that devotion to Viṣṇu like?", he says: "Brahman... [and so forth]. If it is asked, "How is it said that devotion alone is the means for knowledge (*jñāna*) and the rest, when hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices are heard of as being the means for that? he says: "All... [and so forth]. He explains that very point: "By that alone... [and so forth]. "Liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to liberation and the like. Only the yoga of devotion that has reached the state of extreme maturity is the means to liberation; the vision of the Lord is not itself the means. However, because that vision is a means to it, it is spoken of as a means to liberation.

The meaning is this: matured devotional yoga (*bhaktiyoga*) alone is the means for attaining vision (*dṛṣṭi*), and not meditation (*dhyāna*); however, because that [meditation] is a means to it, it is called a "means to vision. Matured devotional yoga alone is the means for attaining knowledge (*jñāna*), and not hearing and so forth (*śravaṇādi*); however, because those [hearing and so forth] are means to it, they are called "means to knowledge."

Regarding what was stated—that Arjuna possesses the status of a deity and thus the highest qualification, and from that, the state of one possessing immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)—the author cites scripture (*śruti*) to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between Arjuna’s divinity and his highest qualification, as well as the pervasion between having the highest qualification and possessing immediate knowledge. "Those who are inferior... [and so on]. "Martyas" refers to mortals; "middling" refers to those who are equal [to them]; and "superior" refers to the gods. To the question, "Whence does the gods possess the highest qualification? he replies: "Because of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the vision of Brahman. He states this with the words: "Not indeed... and so forth.

How, then, is their perception through hearing and so forth possible? To this he says: "It is concealed" (*tirohitam*). If it were thus, one would not need to hear it again as before, because it would have undergone further concealment; therefore he says: "By many repetitions" (*bahuvāram*). This means: through the repeated practice of that, namely, the repeated practice of hearing and so forth.

To the question, "Where has the non-obscuration of knowledge through repeated practice been observed? he says: "Just as... The word "Vyāsa" is mentioned for the purpose of illustrating such practice. To the objection, "Why could this not be the case even from the very first hearing and so forth? he says: "of the gods. The sense is that, by virtue of being gods, they certainly possess prior hearing and so forth.

Regarding that which was stated—namely, Viṣṇu’s status as the supreme among all beings such as Brahmā and Rudra—he cites the Śrutis: "Of this," etc. The meaning is: when the offering (*havis*) was presented to this Lord Viṣṇu, who showers [his devotees] with their desires and is the sovereign (*īśa*) over all, the binder (*bandhaka*), Rudra, attained his fierce majesty (*raudraṃ mahimānam*); likewise, O Aśvins, you two also obtained a share of food (*annavat-vartanam*). In the beginning of the world, there was a silent sage (*muniḥ*); he meditated thus: "Let these be born. *Viśva* is Vāyu.

"Beyond this world," [it means] "at the forefront of this universe"; the Śruti states that "supremacy" (sarvotkarṣa) is the purport of all scriptures, and that the authority for liberation lies in the knowledge of Him. "Truth" (satyam) means primary. "From Him" (tataḥ) means from Viṣṇu. O Viṣṇu, You are beyond all measurement; You are full by Your very form, and not merely by fame and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that others do not attain Your majesty.

As for the claim that even for the wise (jñānin), action must be performed and that through it there arises an excellence of bliss—that is incorrect; for it has been stated that for one who is exceedingly wise, both of those [action and its result] are absent. To this he says: "But he... (yastu). The meaning is that by this verse, the absence of action and so forth for the wise is not established; because the qualifiers such as "delighting in the Self" (ātmarati) and so on apply primarily to the liberated (mukta) alone, and according to the context of the preceding and following verses, they do not have the mere non-wise person as their object.

In this context, one who is entirely free from identification with the body and so forth is said to be liberated even while established in *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*. He states that this refers to the subject of liberation because it is designated as "recollection" (*smṛti*). [He says: "But he who... and so on.

Nevertheless, it is not proper for the knower (*jñānin*) to refrain from action, because [the scripture] speaks of the absence of action for knowers by means of the phrase "through the yoga of knowledge" (*jñānayogena*). Nor can it be said that this [absence of action] refers to one who is already liberated, because it is stated that the liberation of knowers occurs through knowledge alone. To this, he says: "Through knowledge... There is no contradiction with this statement even if one accepts that knowers perform action, because this [scriptural passage] concerns the ascetic (*yati*). Even for them, [the scripture] declares liberation through knowledge only with reference to the contraction of external actions.

The intention is not, however, that there is an absence of action [in general]. One might ask: "Could this not mean that for the knowers of reality (*jñānin*), there is simply an absence of all action? To this, he says: "For it is not so," because the Blessed Lord himself has stated that such an absence is impossible. [Objection: We do not say that what is intended here is the abandonment of action for the sake of maintaining the body of a knower, which would indeed be impossible. Rather, we mean the abandonment of actions such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and the like, because only that constitutes an obstacle to liberation (*mokṣa*). [Reply: This is not so.

He says: "Because these were spoken by the Blessed One with the intention that sacrifices and the like, when devoid of desire and so forth, do not cause bondage. [The opponent asks: "Could this injunction not be intended for the ignorant? He replies: "No, because such action is enjoined for the knower alone by the Śruti. [He explains: "Enjoined" means they are prescribed as duties in the Śruti and other scriptures; the word "etcetera" (ādi) is to be understood. [The opponent asks: "Even so, on what basis does this statement have the meaning you have stated? He replies: "On account of the designation (samākhyāna). He says: "Not so."

As for the statement that Arjuna is already a man of knowledge (*jñānin*), that is incorrect; for from the words "they will instruct," his lack of knowledge is perceived. To this, he says: "They will instruct. There is no contradiction of this statement even if Arjuna is a man of knowledge, because this instruction is stated solely for the purpose of removing the obscuration of the knowledge that had previously arisen, and not for the purpose of attaining knowledge not previously attained.
Thus, the introduction is complete.

Having thus stated the purport of the Gītā in brief, he now wishes to explain it in detail. Considering that the first chapter—consisting of a few additional verses—is not obscure and is therefore explained by the summary statement alone, he speaks of the meaning of the term *prajñāvāda* (the discourse on wisdom) while commenting on the passage beginning with "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for" (*aśocyān anvaśocas tvam*). Regarding the phrase "by excellence" (*prakarṣeṇa*), he explains the sentence-meaning with the intention that this "discourse on wisdom" is not merely indifferent to that [object], but rather is opposed to such discourse. He says: "The wise one... (*prājña...*) and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "How can those who are about to perish not be objects of grief, such that you say, 'Since you grieve for those who should not be grieved for'? And how is the statement 'I shall not fight' contrary to the view of the wise? For has it not already been established by the reasoning beginning with 'Having seen this... Thus he asks: "How? In response, he provides the second half of the verse as a refutation of the first objection: "Those whose life-force has departed... (11).

He repeats the second objection in order to resolve it: "Because of affection for kinsmen" (*bandhusnehāt*). This means: because of the fear of their destruction caused by affection for kinsmen. To the word "true" (*satyam*), he offers a deliberation based on the thought that it cannot withstand such analysis and is contrary to the view of the wise (*prājña*); thus, since the word "kinsman" (*bandhu*) is used here to refer to a sentient being qualified by a body, he deliberates upon it with the words "In that case" (*tatra*). To refute the first [alternative], he states the purport of the verse beginning with "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*) as follows: "Of the body" (*dehasya*). [The meaning is: there is no purpose for fear in that regard.

The meaning is that there is no purpose for the abandonment of one's own duty on account of the fear of the destruction of the body. (For avoidance indeed has fear as its motive; yet such [fear] is not possible here, because the body, like a clod of earth and so forth, is subject to destruction in every way. And since fear is untenable in the absence of a purpose, it is not logical to cease from one's duty on that account. If it is asked, "How can this be? For fear, being independent [of the agent], does not presuppose a prior consideration of a purpose," we reply: even if fear arises by chance, the intention to avoid it still follows from the reflection that there is no purpose [in yielding to it].

To refute the second [position], he states the purport of the verse beginning with "na tu" (but not). He says: "No. Since fear itself is impossible due to the fact that [the Self] is indestructible, it is all the more improper for one's own duty to cease because of fear; this is the meaning. Now, since the destruction of the Lord is impossible, for what purpose was it said, "But not indeed I"? To this, he explains the verse by way of an illustration: "Not, first of all... It should be understood that "and antecedent non-existence" is also implied. By the word "first of all" (tāvat), he indicates the absence of destruction in the Lord both in terms of His essential nature and His body.

The phrase "of the supreme conscious being" indicates the reason that consciousness is independent. "In this very way" means that, by virtue of being mere consciousness, there is no destruction or the like in its essential nature (*svarūpa*). From what are the supreme eternality and consciousness of the Lord established, such that He is employed as an illustrative example? Therefore, he shows their establishment through scripture with the word "eternal. In the passage "He is eternal among the eternal," it is simply stated that [the Lord] is eternal to the highest degree, but not the specific meaning intended here; therefore, he explains it by means of a traditional text (*smṛti*).

"His own body" (*svadeha*)—this is stated because even Viṣṇu possesses a connection with a body and so forth, just like the individual soul (*jīva*). It is to be construed with "in the city of liberation" (*mukteḥ pure*). Alternatively, since the Lord (*īśvara*) is also included in the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*) without being treated as a mere illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he speaks of his attainment [of that state] first: "Of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*). "That too"—meaning both kinds of immutability. Now, one might object: "In this context, it is only stated that for the Lord, unlike the individual soul, there is no destruction of essential nature (*svarūpa-nāśa*) and so forth; how then can it be said that both kinds of immutability are denied? To this, he says: "But not at all" (*na tveva*).
By the word "tu" (but), it is understood that for Īśvara there is specifically no destruction or the like; the sense is that he is exactly as previously described.

[Objection: But surely, since Arjuna is a man of knowledge (*jñānin*), even though the Blessed One was engaged in battle, there was no possibility of such a doubt; therefore, this [prohibition] would be a prohibition of what has not been attained (*aprāpta-pratiṣedha*). To this he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi*). [The word] *prāpta* means one who is fit, capable, and a virtuous person. By this very [statement], the objection that the impermanence of the Lord (*īśvara-anityatva*) is irrelevant is also removed, as this contradicts the Bhāṣya. [Question: How can this, being spoken in private (*ekānte*), benefit the world? To this he says: "In private... (*ekānte*). [He did so] by composing [it] in the form of the Gītā through the incarnation of Vyāsa. 12.

If it is enjoined here that the Lord is devoid of both kinds of destruction and so forth, then how is it that, in the verse beginning with "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*), the attainment of another body by the previously mentioned entities such as the Lord is stated? It cannot refer to those other than the Lord, because there is no mention of anything that would exclude Him. To this, he says: "My... (*mama*). In the phrase "of the embodied one," it is not the attainment of another body by the Lord that is stated, but rather by the individual souls (*jīvas*) alone. Nor is there an absence of anything that excludes the Lord [from this category].

The qualification "embodied" (*dehin*) is employed precisely to exclude the Lord (*īśvara*), the implication being that Viṣṇu lacks the status of being embodied due to the absence of a distinct body. Furthermore, because the Lord may also undergo the acquisition of another body within the realm of individual souls (*jīva*), the term "one's own" (*svakīya*) is used. If this is so, what is the meaning of the verse? To address this, he says: "Because it comes to be... (1.26). The meaning is that since even in a single body one observes change—such as its becoming a corpse and so forth—the absence of grief in that regard remains exactly the same. || 13 ||

Even when one attains youth and so forth through the loss of childhood and other stages, grief is appropriate; for it is possible for that very person to have [re]vision and so forth. However, since such vision and so forth are impossible upon attaining another body, grief [would follow]. To dispel this doubt, he introduces the verse with the word "That" (*tad*). The word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "It must be endured" means it must be overcome by means of non-identification (*anabhimāna*). To avoid the suspicion that the words "contact of the senses" (*mātrāsparśāḥ*) form a separate compound, he explains them as "objects" (*viṣaya*), etc. 14.

An objection might be raised: "Since the absence of suffering is possible even by engaging in battle, why should one abandon pride for the sake of that absence of suffering? Anticipating this, the author introduces the verse with the thought that the abandonment of suffering—which occurs through non-identification with the body and so forth—is itself a form of fruit and also a cause for the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). He says: "The fruit... The words "of the avoidance of suffering through non-identification" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

"How can immortality be attained merely by avoiding suffering?"—to resolve this doubt, which would contradict such scriptural passages as "Knowing Him thus," he introduces the word *puruṣa*. [The text says: "No. How does this remove the aforementioned doubt? Therefore, he explains it by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "Puru is Brahman. Let it be that Brahman is denoted by the word *puruṣa*; but how is it obtained that one becomes a *puruṣa* through the knowledge of That? To this he says: "Because of moving toward the Puru (*purusaraṇāt*). "Moving" (*saraṇa*) means going; the sense is that that very movement is knowledge.

[Objection: But was it not stated, in the passage beginning with "Will sin indeed take hold of us," that the suffering in the next world resulting from battle—in the form of killing kinsmen and so forth—is a cause for grief? Therefore, [the Lord] says "No" (na ca) to this doubt. Why is it not so? He explains the verse beginning with "Not of the unreal" (*nāsataḥ*) as the reason for why it is not so: "The unreal" (*asat*) refers to an evil action; this serves as an illustration. By the words "because of its being fixed" (*niyatatvāt*), the purport of the second half of the verse is expressed. The sense is that this [act of war], because it consists in the suppression of those who hate Nārāyaṇa and their associates, is indeed a virtuous action (*sat-karma*).

Now, one might object: "Just as there is no happiness from bad action (*asat-karman*), so too it should be said that there is no suffering from good action (*sat-karman*); what, then, is the use of describing the absence of both existence and non-existence? To this, he provides the authority for the words "existence" (*bhāva*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) themselves being synonymous with happiness and suffering: "In the state of existence... (*sadbhāva...*). As to why the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) denote good and bad actions, he says: "The state of existence... (*sadbhāva...*). Here, the subsequent sentence beginning with "without faith" (*aśraddhayā*) should also be understood.

He demonstrates the application of the synonymous terms *bhāva* (existence) and *abhāva* (non-existence), as well as the words *sat* (being) and *asat* (non-being), to pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, and provides the authoritative proof [for this]. "Non-existent" (*asan*): if one perceives Brahman as suffering, then that perceiver becomes suffering indeed; if one perceives Brahman as the nature of bliss, then they know the perceiver to be happy—this is the meaning. Since the word *anta* has many meanings, he states the intended meaning here: "End" (*anta*).

[The author] refutes the false interpretation that "the existence (utpatti), i.e., the arising, of the non-existent (asat)—that which was previously non-existent—is not found; and the non-existence (abhāva), i.e., the destruction, of the existent (sat)—that which is already existing—is not found. [Objection: But this violates the rule [of Pāṇini] that the word with fewer syllables comes first (Gītā 2.16). [Reply: Is there a contradiction with one perception, or a contradiction with all perceptions? It is not the first, because its status as an error is logically established. It is not the second, because the mind of another is unestablished. To this, he says: "The existent... (sann iti).

The meaning is as follows: everyone in the world conventionally asserts that an object, which is indeed designated by the term "existent" during its period of persistence, does not exist prior to its production or after its destruction. Therefore, it is possible to infer through reasoning—based on the worldly convention of production and destruction regarding what is non-existent and existent—that there is a perception (pratyakṣa) at their root. If it is objected: "By the necessity of accounting for such conventions, only the cognition that serves as their basis is established; however, there is no rule that this [basis] must be a perception," [the response is:]...

Is this knowledge of inference and so forth [valid], or is it an error? Not the first, because it is not accepted [by the opponent], and because it occurs even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the like. He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "And not... If it were an error, there ought to be a sublater (*bādhaka*); yet no such thing exists here. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the sense is that perception alone is established as the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Since the very sentence "not of the non-existent" serves as the proof for the contrary case, he says: "This... [meaning] established or accomplished.

He establishes this very point by means of the *Brahmatarka*: "In the beginning and at the end," etc. This means prior to origination and after destruction; the words "ascertained through perception" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. He states the refutation [of the opponent's view] if one does not admit non-existence in the beginning: "If," etc. If, in this effect, the specific features such as the broad base and belly do not exist previously and are produced later, then what is the object of the cognition and the linguistic usage "this effect is being produced"? The meaning is that those two would be perceived as being without an object.

To the objection that "manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is the object," he says: "In [the case of] manifestation. Even by one who asserts that manifestation is the object, the birth of what is non-existent has not been avoided; for the birth of a manifestation that was previously non-existent must be admitted. Otherwise, the occasional nature of manifestation would be untenable—this is the sense. Manifestation occurs only at some time for a manifestation that already exists previously; therefore, the occasionality of manifestation [is explained]. To this, he says: "An infinite regress (*anavasthā*)."

If there is also a manifestation (*vyakti*) of manifestation, then its birth must be admitted as occurring while it was previously non-existent; otherwise, the aforementioned fault would follow. If that [manifestation] also were manifested while already existing, then for that too it would be the same, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is the meaning. He states "In this way" (*evam*) to indicate that even if one does not admit the destruction of what exists, such a sublation (*bādhaka*) should be understood. To explain: if there were no destruction of what exists, cognitions such as "it is destroyed" would be without an object. If their object were non-manifestation, then since that [non-manifestation] existed previously, its occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) would be untenable.

If [the effect] were non-existent, it would follow that the effect is non-existent even before its production (*asatkāryatā*). If you argue that there is manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of what was previously unmanifested, then—as before—there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, the concluding statement "that which exists perishes" (*san vinaśyati*) should be understood accordingly. Now, one might object: if the birth of the non-existent is thus established, it must be the case that something absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsataḥ*) is born. What is the distinction in saying "something is born"? To this he says: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). Although the birth of the non-existent has been stated in this way, it does not refer to something absolutely non-existent; rather, the sense is that it is something existent and non-existent through a difference in form (*rūpabheda*). Why is that? To this he says: "Because of the non-difference... The connection is: "because of the experience of difference."

Because of the experience of non-difference between cause and effect—such as "the pot is indeed clay"—and because the cause exists even prior [to the effect], the prior existence of the effect is established. The meaning is that its non-existence [prior to arising] follows from the experience of difference. To the objection, "Why might the experience of non-difference not be an illusion? he says: "Without distinction. The sense is that if the experience of non-difference were an illusion, then the experience of difference would also have to be an illusion, since there is no distinguishing factor [between the two]. To the claim that "there is no such thing as an experience of non-difference," he says: "The body... [and so forth].

Therefore, the meaning is that the existence of the basis for the conventional usage of non-difference (*abheda-vyavahāra*) is inferred. To the question, "Even if such experience exists, why is this so? he says: "The powerful" (*balī*). The meaning is that uncontradicted experience is capable of establishing its own object.

As for the interpretation that this verse expresses the world's being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadvilakṣaṇatva*), he refutes that with: "And not" (*na ca*). Nothing whatsoever that is distinct from the existent and the non-existent is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*); how much less, then, the entire universe? [Objection: But surely, the existence (*bhāva*) of the non-existent—its appearance (*khyāti*)—does not exist; and the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the existent—its sublation (*bādha*)—does not exist.

Therefore, since that object of error which possesses both [aspects] is, by implication (*arthāpatti*), distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, how can it be said that "nothing whatsoever distinct from the existent and the non-existent is established by valid cognition"? To this he says: "And not... That which was stated regarding the distinction from the existent (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*) of the object of error—such as shell-silver—is indeed admitted. However, that which was stated regarding its distinction from the non-existent (*asad-vailakṣaṇya*) on the grounds of the impossibility of its manifestation (*khyāti-anupapatti*) is not tenable. For instance, when it is said that the manifestation of the non-existent is impossible, is it because of its being non-existent (*asattvena*) or because of its being non-real (*atattvena*)? He examines the first alternative:

Regarding the phrase "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*): he refutes the second [position] with "If... (*yadi*). The sense is that since the negation of an attribute is observed only when the substratum (*dharmī*) is itself perceived, it is impossible to negate the attribute of "being perceived" in that which is not perceived, namely the non-existent. He refutes the first [position] with "If... (*yadi*). Even so, the refutation of its manifestation (*khyāti*) is not possible, because it would involve a contradiction; this is the sense. Furthermore, regarding the second [position]: does the impossibility of the manifestation of the non-existent as a reality apply to an erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*) or a non-erroneous one (*abhrānti*)? The second alternative is discarded by mere admission (*aṅgīkāra*).

Stating another refutation against the former position, he refutes the first [point] with the words "na ca" (and not). He states another refutation against the former position with the words "asad" (non-existent). The sense is that it is not only the case that the negation of its attributes is untenable if the non-existent is not perceived, but no linguistic usage whatsoever is possible therein, because all linguistic usages are rooted in perception. It has been stated that there is no proof for the absence of the perception of the non-existent as being existent in error; to the question "How then is its absence [established]? he says "yat" (that which...).

The point is this: since error consists precisely in the cognition of an unreal form, such as silver, as being existent within its substrate, like mother-of-pearl; for if one does not admit the cognition of the unreal as existent in an error, it would follow that error itself is impossible, and thus such a cognition must be admitted.

This might be so if the non-existence of the form perceived in an error were universally accepted; but that is not the case, because we admit its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*). For an error is logically established as such precisely when there is a perception of something indeterminable. Therefore, how can it be said that there is a perception of the non-existent as existent within an error? To this, he says: "Because of indeterminability. Let the indeterminability of the form perceived in an error be granted; nevertheless, it cannot be denied that in an error there is a perception of the non-existent as existent.

To explain: is that indefinable silver perceived in the illusion as being indefinable itself, or as "this is real"? Not the first; for without the perception "this is real," it would be impossible for the cognition "this is indefinable" to be an illusion.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) would be an error; for a mere technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) can always be altered. As for the second [alternative], its existence must be either real (*sat*) or unreal (*asat*). Not the first, because it would contradict the very nature of being indeterminable (*anirvacanīyatva*), and because its status as an error would be untenable. In the second case, it follows that there is an appearance of the non-existent as existent—this is the intended meaning. [The opponent might argue: "The indeterminable object is neither real nor unreal, but rather merely phenomenal (*prātītika*); therefore, there is no appearance of the non-existent as existent. To this, he says: "Error... (*bhrānti*).

Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that the existence of the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) is merely phenomenal (prātītika). Even so, the appearance of the non-existent as existent remains difficult to avoid. To explain: is that phenomenal existence perceived as being merely phenomenal, or as being empirical (vyāvahārika)? Not the first, because it would entail the impossibility of purposeful activity (pravṛtti). In the second case, is its empirical nature real or unreal? Not the first, because it would contradict its being merely phenomenal. In the second case, however, how could this not be the appearance of the non-existent as existent? This is the point.

Therefore, the implication is that because the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) which establishes the difference from the non-existent does not [establish] the appearance of the non-existent as being existent, the non-existent is not what appears. Thus, he concludes that since the presumptive testimony establishing the difference from the non-existent is flawed, nothing that is the object of error can be "indescribable" (*anirvācya*): "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

[The opponent argues: "Let there be no indefinability (anirvacanīyatā) for the object of error; rather, it is said that this will apply to the universe (viśva), because its distinction from the non-existent (asat) is consistent. However, its distinction from the existent (sat) is established through the otherwise inexplicability of sublation (bādha). Therefore, [the author] says 'The universe' with the intention that it is not so, due to contradiction with scripture. [The author replies: With the intention that the universe’s being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is contradictory, he says: "The universe. [The opponent continues: "O illustrious Indra and Bṛhaspati, for you two, the universe is indeed real (satya)."

Why? The meaning is that he says this because even all the deities know the acts of you two, such as the creation of the real world. He is the conqueror who bestows desirable wealth upon Bali and others, and the giver to Indra and the rest. The meaning is that whatever the Lord created as the universe is indeed true and not false. The omniscient one, the impeller of the mind, the most excellent in every respect, the independent Supreme Lord, created all things so that they remain uncontradicted even throughout infinite time. || 16 ||

Having thus stated the absence of a reason for not engaging in battle, he will state that it ought to be performed, and that it should be done as an act of worship to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). In that regard, since both [the self and the Lord] are eternal and there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) of the Lord over [the self], one might ask: "What is the point of worshipping Him? To this, it is said: "indestructible" (*avināśī*). Even there, only the indestructibility of something is being stated; it does not mean that the Lord possesses any excellence over the individual soul (*jīva*), because no such indicative evidence is heard. Therefore, he says: "Even though... The meaning is that the word "but" (*tu*) indicates the excellence of the Lord over the individual soul.

How is destruction of many kinds, and for what reason does that [destruction] not exist in the case of Īśvara? To this he says: "Impermanence" (*anityatvam*). Impermanence is the destruction of one's own nature (*svarūpa-nāśa*). Since there is no word denoting Viṣṇu here, how can it be said "of Viṣṇu"? With the intention that the phrase "by whom all this is pervaded" (*yena sarvam idaṃ tatam*) itself denotes Him, he explains it by means of that very Śruti: "In terms of space" (*deśataḥ*). 17.

Let it be granted that Hari is indestructible in every respect; nevertheless, how is His superiority over the individual soul (*jīva*) established? To dispel this doubt, it is said: "They have an end" (*antavantaḥ*). In this context, to prevent the misconception that the mere destruction of the body is being predicated of a single embodied being, he explains: "Of the embodied beings" (*śarīriṇām*). The Lord is indestructible in every respect, whereas for embodied beings there is only mere permanence, but not indestructibility in every respect, because of the existence of bodily death and so forth. Therefore, the sense is that the Lord possesses superiority over the individual soul.

In the verse beginning with "May there be no destruction," there is the presence of a word denoting the Blessed Lord. Nevertheless, since it is stated in the form of a pervasion that "that by which all this is pervaded is indestructible," one might ask how it is determined that this refers to Viṣṇu alone. To this he says: "By which. Although this is stated in the form of a pervasion, the meaning is that because being pervaded by everything is a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Viṣṇu, the conclusion rests upon him alone; therefore, the restriction [to Viṣṇu] is appropriate.

How is this the definition of Īśvara? [One might object that] since even individual souls (*jīva*) possess such pervasiveness (*tati*) over time, the definition would be over-extended (*ativyāpti*) to them; therefore, he says: "No" (*na*). It is not only pervasiveness in terms of time that is intended here, but rather [pervasiveness] in terms of space and qualities as well. And that [threefold pervasiveness] does not belong to the individual souls—this is the sense. Here, the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which is intent on negating that the individual soul is the subject to be established and which accepts a non-primary meaning (*amukhyārtha*), is not in contradiction [with our position], because in that case [the soul's pervasiveness] is inferior even to that of the individual souls. Furthermore, it is because [the text] would otherwise involve a tautology with the words "But I am indeed... (*na tvevāham*).

One might object: "In the phrase 'they are indeed finite,' only the abandonment of the body by the individual soul (jīva) is stated, not some other kind of destruction. Therefore, how can there be an explanation by interpolating the word 'beginning'? To this he replies: "By [the soul's] unwillingness. It is true that only the abandonment of the body is mentioned here; nevertheless, since the attainment of suffering and its abandonment are undesirable, the implication is that for one who possesses such [a body], the attainment of suffering is inevitable.

Let it be so that the Lord possesses this excellence over the individual soul (*jīva*). To dispel the doubt as to what follows from this, he explains the second half of the verse: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because He possesses excellence by virtue of being indestructible in every respect. Even though He possesses excellence, why should His worship be performed? To this he says: "That" (*tat*). It is not merely because He is indestructible in every respect that His worship is said to be performed here; rather, because He is indestructible in His own nature, He alone is independent (*svatantra*).

Consequently, liberation is dependent upon that [worship]. Since the Lord, being propitiated by one's own actions such as battle and so forth, bestows liberation, the intended meaning is simply that His worship must be performed. This is the underlying sense.

Granted that the Lord possesses the power to grant liberation because He is superior [to all others], nevertheless, on what basis is it established that this is the intention of the *Gītā*—namely, that Hari grants liberation only when propitiated by one's own karma? [The author] says: "But those... [and so forth]. Even though the attainment of liberation through mere ritual action (*karman*) alone is not intended by the *Gītā*, it is indeed intended when combined with devotion (*bhakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), because it has been stated thus in the verse beginning, "But those who... [Gītā 18.56].
The sense is that such action is intended here. By the phrase "devoted to Me," knowledge of the Blessed One is expressed; "unswerving yoga" means unswerving devotion.

To the objection, "Why should [the phrase] 'of the imperishable and immeasurable' not refer to the embodied soul under discussion?", he says: "In the case of the *jīva*. This refers to the position that the *jīva* is what is expressed by the terms "imperishable" and "immeasurable. Since a clear difference in meaning arises when adopting the position of referring to the Lord (*īśvara*), it is improper to set that aside and somehow explain a different meaning; this is what is stated here. However, there is no contradiction in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), for once the primary meaning is established, another secondary meaning may also be mentioned.

It is not only because of the redundancy [if taken as referring to the individual soul] that this refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), but also because of the existence of evidence for it; thus he says: "The indestructible" (*avināśī*). It has already been established that in the passage "the indestructible," the Blessed One was indeed teaching the Lord himself. That which was stated there as "indestructibility" is recognized here in the phrase "of the imperishable" (*anāśinaḥ*). Furthermore, that which was stated there as "the essence of all" is recognized here in the phrase "of the immeasurable" (*aprameyasya*). Therefore, the sense is that the Lord alone is being spoken of here.

The interpretation that the Lord is superior to the individual soul (jīva) because the soul undergoes the destruction of the body while the body of the Lord is eternal cannot be intended by the Gītā; for there is a rule that the body is invariably non-eternal. Therefore, by the specific qualification "in the Gītā itself," even the body of the liberated soul is admitted to be eternal—how much more so the body of Hari? Otherwise, that qualification would be purposeless. With the thought that this [other] interpretation alone is thus logical, he says: "These... (ima iti).

[Objection: But how can even the body of one who is liberated be eternal? For it is a rule that a body must eventually perish. To this, he says: "Consciousness" (*cit*). The sole cause of impermanence is the state of being an insentient body; and since that [insentience] is excluded from the liberated body—which consists of consciousness and bliss—it follows that impermanence is also excluded. [Question: How can a body consist of consciousness and bliss? To this, he says: "Its own nature" (*svarūpa*). The meaning is that its very nature consists of consciousness and bliss. [Reply: For the liberated, there is no body at all.

To this, he says: "Consciousness (cit)," etc. The sense is that the scriptural passage beginning with "Indeed, being bodiless... is intended to show the absence of a material body. And with the intention that it is also intended to show the absence of a distinct body, he says: "Its own nature (svarūpa)," etc.

Now, one might ask: why is there the existence of bodies consisting of eternal consciousness and bliss for those who are liberated? To this he says: "It does not exist," and so forth. "Other defects" refers to [the liberated ones]. "Supeśasaḥ" means beautiful in form. "Unmiṣanmaṇipraveśaniṣkābharaṇāḥ" means adorned with necklaces of excellent, sparkling gems. "Suvarcasaḥ" means possessing great luster. Here, by first stating their lack of insentience (*jaḍatva*) and then describing their bodies, it is understood by implication that they possess bodies whose nature is consciousness and bliss.

But surely these statements refer only to secondary liberation (*gauṇa-mokṣa*), because they are untenable in the case of primary liberation due to the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). To this he says: "And not [so]. Why not? Because even after primary liberation, the existence of difference is established by Śruti and Smṛti. He states this with the words: "This [is so]. Here, the status of primary liberation is understood from the hearing of the scriptural declaration of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*).

He says, "He who knows," with the intention that for the liberated, there is not merely an absence of suffering due to their difference from the Lord, but rather, precisely because of that difference, they experience supreme bliss. Since these two statements occur within the context of the Supreme Brahman, they refer primarily to liberation. All those liberated ones are friends to one another; they rejoice by means of the glory known to themselves, which causes even the Lord—who presides over the assemblies of Brahmā and others—to feel a sense of awe.

How so? Because he, being a giver of divine food who competes with [the granting of] what is undesirable to these [beings], is beneficial to the senses; this is the meaning. Here too, because it takes recourse in the absence of the undesirable, its subject matter is primary liberation (*mukhya-mokṣa*). A certain Brahman remains performing the correct utterance of the *ṛc*s. And a certain Brahman, himself exceedingly well-nourished, sings the *gāyatra* Sāman upon the *śakvarī* verses which possess the meters. A certain Brahman speaks the Purāṇa-vidyā. A certain Brahman meditates on the form of Viṣṇu; such is the meaning. And of this...

Because it establishes the abundance of Brahman, its subject matter is primarily liberation (*mokṣa*). "Eating" means consuming; "laughing" means experiencing joy; and "rejoicing" means attaining delight.

Supreme equality (*paramasāmya*) means precisely having bliss as the prior limit [of gradation], and not absolute identity; with this intention, he states the proof for the gradation among the liberated: "The liberated... [etc. The *devas* are the celestial Gandharvas. The *tattvarūpas* are those presiding over the principles (*tattva-abhimānins*), such as Bṛhaspati and others. The meaning is that those other than the aforementioned—namely, the best of men—are a hundredth part less than the kings. He says, "Those with eyes... because there would be mutual contradiction if gradation were non-existent.

Having attained the fruits of their eyes and ears, free from mutual conflict, and liberated, they became unequaled in qualities such as knowledge. Among them, some were submerged in the ocean of milk; some were approaching the forest of Aśvattha trees; and some, profound like lakes fit for bathing, beheld the Blessed One—this is the meaning. This statement is explained by the scripture beginning with "having heard Viṣṇu" as referring primarily to the liberated (mukta). For this very reason, the interpretation of the verse *ṛcāṃ tvā* as referring to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is refuted.

Since there might be an insufficiency in the case of varying degrees [of desire], he says: "Of desire. The meaning is: where the objects of one's wish are sufficient, there [the priest] should say, "Make me immortal in this world."

Nevertheless, a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is not tenable, because it would contradict the scriptural texts that proclaim their non-difference. To this, he says: "And not... If it is asked why there is no contradiction, [the answer is] because another meaning is possible. If it is asked, "Why should the very meaning that is perceived not be accepted?", [the author] says: "No; because from other scriptural passages, that very other meaning is understood," namely: "The mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13) "Name... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.15.2). Thus, the meaning of the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) is established as being different from the meaning of the word "individual soul" (*jīva*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the sense of the passage is as follows: the term "Lord" (*īśvara*) denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), while the term "individual soul" (*jīva*) denotes the transmigrating self (*saṃsārin*). Since these two terms have distinct meanings, they do not contradict one another. For example, the terms "jar" and "cloth" do not contradict each other even though they refer to the same substance, because they denote different qualities such as form and color. Similarly, the terms "Lord" and "individual soul" do not contradict each other, because they denote different entities—the Supreme Self and the transmigrating self—respectively. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts that proclaim non-difference. Thus, the conclusion is that the individual soul and the Lord are indeed non-different. This is because the Supreme Self is the substratum of all attributes, whereas the transmigrating self is the substratum of limited attributes. Therefore, the Supreme Self is the Lord, and the transmigrating self is the individual soul. Hence, the Lord and the individual soul are non-different. Following Yājñavalkya’s statement, “There is no consciousness after death,” Maitreyī, not understanding his intended meaning, raised an objection: “Right here, sir, you have plunged me into utter confusion by saying that there is no consciousness after death. The meaning of this is stated as follows: [The word] *saṃjñā* [is used]. If knowledge were to perish in liberation, then it would follow that liberation is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Yet, it is indeed a human goal. Therefore, the meaning is that the statement regarding the absence of knowledge therein is merely confusing. He said: [the rest of the passage follows].

The meaning of the statement, "O Navāra, I speak of delusion," is as follows. To the question, "How is the description of the non-destruction of knowledge not itself delusive? it is said: "This Self, indeed, is indestructible, possessing the nature of non-extinction. Its purpose is to show that [the destruction] pertains to what is born of the elements (*bhūtajā*). The sense is that my statement is not delusive because its intended meaning is that elemental cognition (*bhautikajñāna*) is suspended during sleep, but innate knowledge (*nijajñāna*) is not; or else, that for those born of the elements who are not liberated, knowledge regarding this [Self] is lost.

To the question, "From where is it that one's own knowledge is not lost? he says: "And not... (*na ca*). "Destruction of the self" (*ātmanāśaḥ*) means the destruction of the knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the Self. The meaning is: if even that which is distinct from the Self does not perish, then what need is there to mention that the knowledge of the Self's own nature—the object of supreme love—does not perish? Furthermore, this serves as a resolution to the doubt as to why the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) do not perish: "For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another; there one smells another. (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.14)

The passage—"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? By what and whom should one smell? By what should one know that by which one knows all this? By what, my dear, should one know the knower?"—is now explained. Regarding the phrase "by its very nature": the meaning is that since the experience of smelling and so forth, as well as the knowledge of the Lord and the knowledge of the Self, are possible only if there exists an object of knowledge distinct from the Self—and impossible otherwise—one must admit the existence of an object of knowledge.

In a non-dualism that admits no distinction, the relationship between action and agent is contradictory; thus, even self-knowledge is not possible. As for the objection raised—that in the absence of an object of knowledge, experience and the like would be impossible—that too may be granted. To this, he says: "When... [referring to the verse]. "Anything else" refers to smell and so forth. To the question, "How is there an absence of the human goal (puruṣārtha) when there is an absence of experience and the like? he replies: "That... [referring to the verse]. For a "human goal" is that which is sought after by the person. Indeed, a person does not seek the absence of experience and the like, nor does he strive for its sake.

Therefore, the meaning is that liberation, being of the nature of the absence of enjoyment and so forth, is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The concluding statement, "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality," is now explained. The phrase "therefore" [is explained as follows]: since the consequence would be that there is no human goal in the absence of enjoyment and so forth, enjoyment and the like must be admitted. And because enjoyment and the like are possible, objects and so forth must be distinct [from the Self]. Consequently, the realization of one's own true nature [is established]—this is the underlying thought.

Regarding the meaning of the phrase, "But when he does not see this, there is no second," the word "this" (yat) refers to [the Self]. The subsequent passage, "If there were anything else distinct from him that he might see," is now being explained. As for the term "Pradhāna" and so forth: it has been stated that Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and the rest are indeed distinct from the Lord, because they are seen by the Lord as separate entities apart from His own manifestation. Furthermore, they are established as distinct because they are not seen by the omniscient Lord as non-distinct. This is supported by the statement, "Indeed, seeing, he does not see that. This sentence is now being explained.

Regarding the phrase "seeing": this explains the scriptural statement, "For there is no loss of the seer's seeing," which serves as a rebuttal to the doubt—namely, that the Lord’s perception of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other principles as inherently distinct might not be an error. The word "not" (*na hi*) [is explained]: "loss" (*viparilopa*) means "reversal" or "distortion. "Because of its indestructibility" (*avināśitvāt*): the meaning is because it is faultless by virtue of being eternal.

In order to explain the Vedic scripture, "He who knows the supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," he states what is relevant to that purpose: "brahmāṇi... and so on. Regarding the commentary on the scripture: although one knows the supreme Brahman, nevertheless, the meaning is that one "becomes Brahman itself" and does not become the supreme Brahman. Why is it interpreted in this way? One might ask: why should the meaning not simply be that by the knowledge of the supreme Brahman, one becomes the supreme Brahman? To this, he says: "yadīti... (if...).

If the individual soul (jīva) were to attain identity with the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) upon liberation, then it would likewise be so during worldly existence (saṃsāra). This is untenable because it is impossible for that which was previously separate to become non-different later; for if that were the case, suffering could not exist. To the question, "Why would it not be subject to suffering?", he says: "The sufferer. [Objection: Even one who has become the Supreme Lord may experience suffering due to the power of ignorance (ajñāna). To this he says: "Whence? [Objection: Even an omniscient being may possess ignorance through delusion (bhrānti). To this he says: "Where?"

The sense is that if one were to accept that error is rooted in the ignorance of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and that ignorance is itself rooted in error, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). He explains the two scriptural passages, "I am Brahman" and "That thou art," [by stating]: "Because it is not to be abandoned" (*ahēyatvāt*), etc. "Because it is a cognition of the non-existent" (*asanānmiteḥ*): this means because limitation within oneself has been discarded; or alternatively, because it dispels opposites and consists of valid cognition (*pramiti*). [The word] *tvam* is so called because it is light, derived from the verbal root *tviṅ* meaning "to shine."

He states that this denotability by the word "Hari" alone does not suffice, but rather that He is denotable by all words, saying: "By all. Even though He is denotable by all words, he says: "You," indicating that there is a restriction regarding specific forms [of address].

The statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) does not have non-difference as its primary purport, because it would be inconsistent with the preceding and following passages.
