With this intention, it is first explained by way of another method. Therein, the passage "Having studied all the Vedas, the high-minded one, considering himself a learned teacher, returned arrogant" is explained. Regarding the word "all": "To him his father said, 'Śvetaketu, since indeed... [and so forth].

"O gentle one, you are thus possessed of great pride; you are haughty and arrogant. Therefore, ask about that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. This is what is being explained. "One who has not performed his conduct" (*akṛtācāra*): that which is pointed out (*ādiśyate*) is the "instruction" (*ādeśa*), namely Nārāyaṇa. [This occurs] when He is known, heard, and meditated upon. "Of the unknown, the unheard, and the unthought" (*avijñāta-jñānādīnām*): the meaning is "of the knowledge, hearing, and reflection regarding that which is unknown, unheard, and unthought."

The meaning is that the fruit which belongs to the unknown knowledge of others and so forth occurs even in the absence of those [other knowledges], by the mere presence of the Lord’s knowledge and so forth. Furthermore, the fruit that arises even when the unknown knowledge of others has already arisen occurs only when the Lord’s knowledge and so forth have arisen. Alternatively, it means that when the knowledge of the Supreme Self and so forth exist, even the unknown and so forth of others become as if known and so forth.

The sense is that, because the Lord is of such a nature, it is possible for one who knows Him to realize their own absolute inferiority; thus, since an identification such as "I am Keśava" would be impossible, He was not questioned by you. In this regard, in the first two interpretations, the reason is *prādhānya* (predominance); in the third interpretation, the reason is *sādṛśya* (similarity).

To the question, "Even though the world has arisen, how is it that knowledge of the world and so forth become fruitful only when there is knowledge of the Supreme Self? he says: "Dependent on That" (*tadadhīnam*). Knowledge of the Blessed Lord and so forth occurs in this manner: [one realizes] that the Lord is the creator of the world and so forth, having brought the universe under His control. And thus, when knowledge of the Blessed Lord and so forth exists, the world is known to be dependent on Him; consequently, such knowledge becomes firm. From that, the fruit of liberation and so forth arises—this is the meaning.

To the objection that even for the world which is thus unknown, might there not be a fruit through knowledge and so forth? [The author] says: "By its own independence," etc., to show that what hope can there be for a fruit, when instead only misfortune occurs. The meaning is: in the absence of knowledge of the Lord and so forth, as described above, knowledge and so forth are obtained by the world solely through its own independence; and since that is false knowledge, it produces misfortune.

Since it is said that when there is knowledge of the Blessed One and so forth, everything else comes to be like it due to similarity—just as in the case of the knower and so on—the author explains the illustration given in the passage, "O dear one, just as by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known," with the words "And just as... Here, "the known" refers to the object of knowledge and so forth.

Because of its preeminence, even for another who is ignorant and so forth, the fruit of knowledge and the like arises merely through the knowledge and other qualities of the Blessed One; and only when the knowledge and other qualities of the Blessed One exist does the fruit of knowledge and the like arise even for another who already knows. Thus, it is stated in both cases that the example—"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real"—is explained. [He says] "Just as": because a conventional name is commenced by means of speech, therefore that modification is, for that very reason, secondary.

The meaning is that by the mere knowledge of refined words (*saṃskṛta*) such as "clay" (*mṛttikā*), even when there is ignorance regarding conventional names and so forth, the result occurs—namely, being the object of the designation "learned" (*vidvān*). Furthermore, it is only through the knowledge of refined names that ignorance regarding conventional names becomes fruitful; for by that alone, one lacks the status of being the object of the designation "learned. Regarding the phrase "that is its root": the meaning is that it has that [refined knowledge] as its primary cause.

He explains the illustrative statement, "In this way, my dear, that instruction is," with the word "evam" (in this way). The ellipsis is: "Therefore, because [Brahman] is the primary [cause], there is the fruitfulness of knowing other things and so forth through the two aforementioned modes of knowledge and so forth. It should be understood that it is "similar" in this manner. Why is the Lord alone the primary [cause]? To this, [the text] states His independent causality of the world through the passage beginning with "Being alone, my dear... He expresses that very point: "The independent one who has become the cause."

The greatness of the Lord has been stated as the reason for not conceiving the thought "I am the Lord. Now, another aspect of His greatness is stated: "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. To explain that, he says: "That is the root. Having stated another aspect of His greatness, it is said so that one should not form a notion of difference: "This subtle essence (aṇiman)—all this has that as its self; That is the Truth; That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. He explains that with the word "That."

The word *ātman* has two meanings: "pervasive" and "full. It is full of qualities. "He is not that" (*naiva so'si*)—this is another interpretation, analyzing the phrase as "not that, you are" (*atattvamasi*).

He explains the illustrative statements beginning with "Just as a bird" regarding the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). [The word] "as" (*yathā*) refers to the two passages which, though appearing to express the non-difference of the individual soul and the Lord—namely, "Having entered by means of the living self (*jīva*), let me evolve names and forms," and "This very one has pervaded [the body] by means of the living self"—are explained as being included under the phrase "contradiction with such scriptural texts" (*ityādi-śruti-virodha*). [The word] "not" (*na*) refers to the meaning of the passage, "Verily, this [body] dies when deprived of the living self;
the living self does not die," which is dependent upon that [Lord].

The scriptural passage beginning with "If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease," which appears to state that difference is false, is explained as being included under the term "etcetera" (*ādi*). Regarding the word "jīva": relying on the verbal root *vid* in the sense of "origination," the phrase "if it were to exist" (*yadi vidyeta*) is explained as "if it were to be produced. To dispel the doubt—namely, how difference can be eternal and beginningless if it is merely imagined through delusion—the meaning of the verse "This duality is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*)" is given as "of Viṣṇu."

If difference (*bheda*) were real, how could non-duality (*advaita*) be stated elsewhere? To this it is said: "Non-duality in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*). The meaning of this is "non-duality. By this, it is stated that the suffix *-tasi* in *paramārthataḥ* has the sense of the nominative case. The meaning is: "The statement of non-duality is the ultimate reality; the Blessed Lord says that non-duality [is the ultimate]. What is that state of being supreme (*paramatva*)? To this he says: "The state of being supreme. Furthermore, what is the nature of non-duality belonging to that which possesses such supremacy? To this he says:

"Thus, etc. means that this very non-existence exists within supreme non-duality (*paramadvaita*). The meaning is that this state of being non-dual belonging to that which possesses supremacy is precisely the meaning of the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*). To the question, "Why should not the meaning be the non-duality of all things (*sarvādvaita*)? he says: "They exist," etc.

The statement, "Or, because there is no sublation, difference is not imaginary; this is the meaning of the word *vikalpa*," establishes that meaning. Its sense is as follows: regarding the sentence "That is the Self, you are That" (*tat tvam asi*) and others, in order to establish that they have the purpose of conveying difference, one might attempt to conceive of another meaning for the sentence "As, my dear... (*yathā somya*) and so forth, while refusing to accept the meaning stated by [the author] himself. In such a case, contradiction with the cited scripture (*śruti*) serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*). He states another sublation as well: "A single... (*eketi*).

Just as by the knowledge of a single lump of clay all that is made of clay would be known—since that which consists of name and form is merely a verbal handle made of clay and not ultimately real, while the clay alone is the truth—so too, when there is knowledge of the Supreme Self, there arises knowledge of the world, because nothing exists apart from it; thus, any other interpretation is not tenable. "By the clay being known, all that is made of clay would be known."

The meaning is that because the modification is a mere verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇa*) and only the clay is real, the words "one," etc., would be redundant if [the text] were complete with only this much; for there is no existence of all things made of clay apart from a single lump of clay. Furthermore, since even the name is a modification.

Moreover, if in the passage concerning the "verbal handle" the intention is to state that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the Lord and the objects of his rule is superimposed upon the Supreme Self and thus has no existence apart from it, then [this contradicts] the initial proposition (*pratijñā*).

Knowledge of the world cannot arise from knowledge of the Supreme Self, because false knowledge cannot coexist with knowledge of reality; for those two types of knowledge are contradictory, as he says: "And not... [Objection: But surely, by means of the knowledge of the Supreme Self, it is indeed known that the world is false. Why, then, is it said that if the world is superimposed upon Brahman, the knowledge of Brahman cannot result in the knowledge of the world? To this he replies: "For not... If this is so, then it must be stated that through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, there arises the knowledge of the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

But it is not the case that the knowledge of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) arises through the knowledge of Brahman; the sense is that such a usage does not exist in the world. For this reason as well, he states that what is intended here is not the non-existence of the phenomenal world apart from the Supreme Self: "Nine times... [and so on]. If this is so, what follows? Since the scriptural passage concerning "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) would be logical under the view of difference, he says: "Therefore... This means: because the preceding passages have difference as their purport.

If one were to interpret the passage as being intent on difference by construing it as "you are not That," there would be a contradiction with the preceding statement, "All this has that as its self. Therefore, he causes us to remember the meaning declared by the Śruti itself: "All this has that as its self. Let it be so construed as "related to the Self. And since the relationship is one of identity (*tādātmya*), he says "That [is the Self]" with the intention that the relationship is indeed one of the nature of owner and owned.

Even while accepting the division of the words in "tat tvam asi," [the author] states another meaning established by the Śruti as being intent upon difference, because the preceding and following statements are intent upon difference: "You too... This is not merely a statement of exclusion, such as "he is not that. For this reason as well, he says "that" (tad) to show that this is a reference to "this-ness" (aitadātmya). In a reference to "this-ness," the singular gender of the word "that" (tad) would be an advantage; therefore, the meaning is that this is a reference to "this-ness. Even in the previous position, since "other than that" means "not that," there is no discrepancy in gender.

This reflection on "having this as its self" (*etadātmya*) might be suitable for you if the term *etadātmya* were used to denote that which is related to it; however, that is not certain. For it is also possible to interpret the meaning as: "the entire manifold of the Lord, the object of rule, and so forth, has the Supreme Self as its essence. If this is your position, then do you maintain here that the identity of the manifold of the Lord, the object of rule, and so forth with the Supreme Self is stated directly, or is it denied by its very nature—that the manifold of the Lord, the object of rule, and so forth does not exist apart from the Supreme Self? It cannot be the first.

Because it is impossible for the false and the real to be non-different, he refutes the second [position] with the words: "That which does not exist. If this scripture were to negate the manifold world of the Lord, the object of rule, and so forth as being distinct from the Supreme Self, then it would be invalid like the speech of a madman; for that very manifold world of the Lord, the object of rule, and so forth—which is indeed non-existent—is itself enjoined as distinct from the Supreme Self in such passages as "He thought" (*tadaikṣata*).

Nor should it be argued here that there is no fault because in passages such as "It thought" (tadaikṣata), the phenomenal world consisting of the Lord and the objects of His lordship is merely restated (anūdyate); for the meaning is that the phenomenal world of the Lord and the objects of His lordship cannot be restated, as its existence as something distinct from the Self is not established except by scripture.

For this reason as well, it is not tenable that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is being restated (*anūdyate*) in passages such as "It thought, etc. (*tadaikṣata...*) for the sake of negation. This is because [such a claim] lacks both the specific statement of the sentence—"What they say here is not tenable"—and the specific reasoning for the negation; furthermore, no instance of a restatement occurring without those two has ever been observed. Thus he says: "Even the restatement... If it is asked: "Even in the absence of such a sentence, what is the fault in accepting that there is a restatement of the phenomenal world here for the sake of negation?"—the first objection is that it involves the postulation of something never before seen (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*). He states another [objection]:

"And there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). To the question "How so?", he says: "Non-difference," etc. This is connected with the word "otherwise" (anyathā). The meaning is as follows: if, even in the absence of such sentences [as *tadaikṣata*], one were to assume that in passages like *aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*, the non-existence of the world as distinct from the Supreme Self is restated by *tadaikṣata* and so forth in order to negate it; then, since there is no distinction [in the logic applied], one could also maintain that in passages like *tadaikṣata*, having negated the non-existence of the world as distinct from the Supreme Self, the passage *aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam* restates that non-existence in order to enjoin its existence as something distinct. This is the sense.

For this reason as well, it is more logical that this [statement] is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as something distinct from the Supreme Self; thus he says: "All... etc. If it were a restatement, it would have occurred at the beginning of the section, whereas the negation occurs at its end. But that is not the case here, because it is precisely difference (*bheda*) that is stated at the ends of the sections. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no restatement in the scripture for the purpose of negating difference. To the question, "What are those statements of difference at the ends of the sections?", he says: "Not... etc.

As for the claim that there might be an instruction on difference by way of restating non-difference, that is not tenable; for non-difference is not established prior to scripture (*śruti*). Rather, it is appropriate to negate the very notion of the world-expansion consisting of the Lord (*īśa*) and the object of rule (*īśitavya*) etc., by restating it as being different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), since the difference of the world-expansion of the Lord and the object of rule etc. from the Supreme Self is already established through perception and other means of knowledge. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*). Here, by the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), the Supreme Self is meant.

It is not correct to say that because the Supreme Self (paramātman) itself is not established by perception and other means of knowledge, the difference of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—which stands in the relation of being ruled and ruler (*īśitavya-īśitṛ*) to it—is all the more easily grasped by perception and so forth. For if that were the case, it would follow that even in the Śruti, the Supreme Self must be defined as being distinct from the phenomenal world; otherwise, even perception and the other means of knowledge would be unable to apprehend that difference. Thus, the implication is that such a statement is merely the talk of a madman.

Alternatively, since the Lord himself is not established by means of perception and other sources of knowledge, and since the relationship between the Lord and the object of his lordship is likewise unestablished in that form, the difference of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form of the Lord and so forth from the Supreme Self is all the more unestablished by him.

For this reason as well, the negation of a phenomenal world (*prapañca*) distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not tenable; therefore, he says: "In that view. If the entire phenomenal world distinct from the Supreme Self were false, then all the scriptures (*śruti*) would become purposeless. To explain: are scriptural passages such as "One only, without a second" and "He who is omniscient" intended to establish attributes such as oneness and omniscience, or are they intended to establish the very nature of the Self? Even in the first case, are the attributes of oneness, omniscience, and so forth distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*), or are they the essential nature itself?

Not the first, because in that case it would follow that [the object] is false. As for the second, it is included within the third. Nor is that [third option] tenable; the point is that since the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is established by itself (*svataḥ*), its demonstration would be purposeless.

[The opponent argues: "Even though the pure nature (*svarūpa*) is not what is to be propounded, there is no futility of the Śruti because the nature characterized (*upalakṣita*) by the absence of difference, omniscience, and so forth, is indeed what is to be propounded. To this he says: "Characterized" (*lakṣita*). The meaning is that since there is no distinction between the characterized [nature] and the pure [nature], the latter is likewise not something to be propounded; therefore, it is not logical for the Śruti to have that as its object of propounding. Why is there no distinction from the pure [nature] for that which is characterized? To this he says: "Because of being devoid of attributes" (*nirviśeṣatva*).

When it was stated that [Brahman] is "characterized" (*lakṣita*), its quality of being without distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*) was already stated as well; otherwise, by the consequence of possessing distinctions, the fallacy of its falsity (*mithyātva*) would follow. Therefore, the sense is that there is no distinction between it and the pure [Brahman]. Now, one might object: "Let the attributes (*dharma*) be false; even so, what is the fault if the Scripture teaches them? To this, he says: "It is false. (*mithyeti*)

For this reason as well, it is not logical that everything other than the Self is false; thus he says: "Falsity... [and so on]. If everything other than the Self were false, would that falsity itself be real or false? Not the first [option], because that would destroy the position that "everything other than the Self is false. Therefore, the sense is that one must accept that [falsity] is indeed false. To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Therefore... Alternatively, he states that for this reason as well, there is no falsity of the specific attributes of the Self: "False... [and so on].

The specific attributes such as omniscience and so forth are not non-existent, such that the authority of the Śruti would be undermined. Nor is it said that the pure, signified object—the very nature of consciousness—is what is known through the Śruti, whereby the aforementioned defect would arise. Rather, within the one Self alone, there exist specific attributes such as omniscience, which are differentiated by the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and caused by them. If it is argued that the form of the Self, as distinguished by these adventitious attributes and differentiated by those various adjuncts, is what is propounded by the Śruti, then is this limiting adjunct false or real? Regarding the first case, he states the defect:

Regarding the term "upādhi" (limiting adjunct): If one accepts that difference and specific qualities in the Self are produced solely by limiting adjuncts, and then accepts the falsity of those adjuncts, it would follow that the essential nature distinct from them and the specific qualities caused by them must also be false. Consequently, the scripture that declares such [an essential nature] would lose its authority.

If it is argued that in passages such as "not here, not there" (*neha nānā*), even that which is false is mentioned in the Śruti for the purpose of negation, then the Śruti itself would first establish a nature differentiated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and their specific attributes—which are themselves false—and then negate them; in that case, the Śruti would be nothing more than the speech of a madman. If it is argued that they are restated (*anūdya*) for the sake of negation, we say no; for since a nature differentiated by various limiting adjuncts and its specific attributes caused by them are not established through perception or other means of valid knowledge, their restatement is logically untenable. This is the sense.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "satyeti" (if it be real). Although a *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) could be stated here, nevertheless, because that is so obvious, another defect alone has been mentioned. This is for the purpose of refuting those who, while accepting the reality (*satyatva*) of that which is distinct from Brahman, still accept a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-bheda*) within Brahman. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of what will be stated later, such as the limiting adjunct being connected to only a part [of the substrate]. By the statement "the defects are the same even in the view of a real limiting adjunct," he indicates that they likewise exist in the view of a false limiting adjunct (*mithyopādhi-pakṣa*).

[Objection: But surely, even though space is one, the experience of smoke in the kitchen-space belongs to that [specific space] alone and not to all space, due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The same would apply here as well; to this he says: "Of non-conscious things. Is it being said that, just as smoke—despite having a connection with the kitchen-space—lacks a connection with all space, so too there may be an absence of being the locus of suffering? Or is it the absence of experience, as in the case of the absence of experiencing that [suffering]? It is not the first, because we do not hold such a position as undesirable. Nor is it the second.

The sense is that because space is insentient, there is an absence of any experience [of it], and thus the illustrative example is dissimilar. Furthermore, this is an argument based on a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), since space possesses internal distinctions. He concludes with: "Therefore" (verse 18).

As for the statement that the Lord is independent because He is indestructible in every respect—that is incorrect. To dispel the doubt that the individual soul (*jīva*) is also perceived as independent—based on such notions as "He is the one who effects this soul's separation from the body" and "By him this [soul] was separated from the body"—it is said: "He who... Therein, in order to eliminate the contrary perception that the soul possesses agency in any way regarding its separation from the body and so forth, he says: "He who... (12.7).

It is explained thus: "He who perceives this living being as an independent agent of separation from the body, and he who perceives this living being as having been separated from the body by another independent living being—these two do not know. This does not mean that one who perceives the living being's agency in killing and so forth even through dependence [on a higher power] does not know. Why should there not be another meaning? To this, he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

The meaning is that if the individual soul (jīva) lacks the capacity to kill even due to its dependence on another, there would be a contradiction in the statement that the soul kills by being subject to the Lord, namely, "Kill those who have been killed by Me."

As for what was stated—that the *jīva* is eternal—that is not tenable. This very verse is intended to resolve the doubt that the conscious being (*cetana*) is understood to be non-eternal through such worldly usage as, "This man is the killer of the *jīva*," and "By this [man], this *jīva* has been killed. In that regard, according to the first position, the phrase "him who" (*ya enam*) is explained as referring to the *jīva*, and not to the Lord (*īśvara*). This is because, in that context, what is intended to be expressed is "killing" in the form of separation from the body; and while the *jīva* lacks independence in that respect, the Lord possesses it.

But in this view, since it is intended that the killing refers to the conscious [self]—as in the statement, "He who perceives this conscious one as the slayer does not know"—and because even the Lord does not perform the killing of the conscious self, just as He does not kill the individual soul (jīva), he says "the conscious one," meaning that the word "this" (enam) denotes both. || 19 ||

[Objection: "But since the eternity of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth have already been stated previously, what is the purpose of the subsequent verse? To this he says: "The soul... [and so on]. This is not a statement by the Lord (Bhagavat), such that there would be a redundancy; rather, the intention is that this Vedic mantra is cited as authoritative evidence for what was stated by Himself: namely, that both the individual soul and the Lord are devoid of birth and destruction; that the Lord possesses independence because He lacks even birth and so forth from a body; and that the individual soul, though naturally free from birth and the like, lacks independence due to the birth and so forth of its body.

Since the Lord (Īśvara) is not perceived here [in the previous verse], one might ask how this is so; therefore, with the intention that the first half-verse establishes Him—because in the phrase "this has not come to be," even arising from a body is heard to be absent, and that [absence] is a mark (liṅga) of the Lord—the author says: "This... By this, the objection—"Why [use the word 'this']? Since the negative particle can be drawn over from the preceding [verse] by the word 'or' (vā), what is the need for it?"—is refuted. Furthermore, here the absence of separation from the body is also heard in the words "it does not die."

With the intention that the word "death" (maraṇa) is well-known as signifying only the separation from the body, and since the absence of such separation from the body is a mark (liṅga) of the Lord, the first half [of the verse] establishes that [absence], he says: "Death... [He then addresses the objection: Since the word "death" is well-known not only for separation from the body but also for the destruction of one's own nature (svarūpa), why should it not have that meaning? To this, he says: "For not... [meaning that the word "death" is not at all well-known in the sense of the destruction of one's own nature].

If the meaning of the word "death" (maraṇa) were not the destruction of one's essential nature (svarūpa-nāśa), then this mantra would not be an authoritative source for the non-destruction of the Lord’s (Īśvara) essential nature, because there would be no other word to denote that [non-destruction]. Consequently, if the meaning of the word "death" were taken as the destruction of essential nature, the status of the first half-verse as referring to the Lord could not be established on the strength of this [mantra]. Therefore, he says: "The essential nature... Here, the non-destruction of the Lord’s essential nature need not be stated, such that the referent of this word [“death”] would have to be imagined as being that [destruction].

The meaning is that since even the destruction of the body does not occur for him, what need is there to mention the destruction of his true nature; this is established by the principle of "how much more so" (kaimutya).

With the intention that the statement regarding the soul's lack of birth and so forth is not heard here [in this verse], he says: "This... [referring to the second half]. To the objection, "Why could the Lord himself not be the subject taught even here?", he says: "Otherwise... [referring to the phrase "anyathā"]. [In that case] there would be tautology between "is not born" (*na jāyate*) and "unborn" (*ajaḥ*). Now, if one were to assume a difference in subject matter between the first and second halves out of fear of tautology, it would follow that the eternal one (*śāśvata*) would be someone else entirely, because of the tautology with the word "eternal" (*nitya*). To this, he says: "No."

The term "eternal" (śāśvata) does not denote permanence in such a way that it would constitute a redundancy. Rather, the intention is this: [an objection might be raised] that if the individual soul (jīva) is also unborn and eternal, then like the Lord (Īśvara), he too would possess independence (svātantrya) and other such attributes; and if that were so, one should not perform worship toward him. To dispel this doubt, it is stated that the soul does not lose its lack of independence and so forth. This is the underlying meaning.

The nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of its lack of independence and so forth, and it does not abandon that [nature]; for this reason, it is called "eternal" (*śāśvata*). To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Alpa... (small). Furthermore, to the objection that there is a redundancy in the word "ancient" (*purāṇa*), he says: "Purāṇī... (the ancient one). By this word "ancient," beginninglessness (*anāditva*) is not being expressed—by which there would be redundancy. Rather, the intention is as follows: although the soul possesses qualities such as being unborn (*aja*) like the Lord (*īśvara*), why does it not possess independence and so forth? Therefore, it is stated that due to the occurrence of the birth of the body and so on, it lacks those qualities such as being unborn, just like the Lord. || 20 ||

Regarding what was stated, "He who imagines independence in the living self (jīva) does not know," the reason for that was given as "this [self] does not kill. Now, the absence of such a conceit among the wise is also stated there as a reason: "He knows. In that context, he explains the difference in meaning between the two terms *avināśin* and *nitya* in order to avoid redundancy. He says: "*Avināśinam*" (imperishable). Since the living self (*jīva*) was mentioned immediately prior, he says "*enam*" (this) in order to dispel the impression that this word refers to the living self. He explains the entire verse by means of the Vedic text itself.

"Agency" (kartṛtvam): the ellipsis is "knowing by means of such reasons as its indestructibility. "The agent" (kartā) refers to one who identifies with agency. One might ask: "Since the individual soul (jīva) was mentioned immediately prior, why should this verse not refer to it? To this he says: "And [the Lord is] other. Since the Lord is free from the destruction of a body, if the verse is taken as referring to Him, the avoidance of redundancy is possible; but not if it refers to the individual soul, because for the soul there exists the destruction of the body. Therefore, the sense is that—due to the contradiction of redundancy—it is appropriate to set aside even the proximately mentioned individual soul and accept the Lord. || 21 ||

"Granted that there may be an absence of grief regarding the Lord (Īśvara), it might still exist regarding the individual soul (jīva). Even if it is argued that the soul is eternal and its conjunction with and separation from a body are like [the transition between] childhood and other stages of life, since birth and death are well-known to all people and one encounters them in battle, this verse is introduced as a refutation of such a doubt. Thus begins the commentary on the verse beginning with "Of the soul" (jīvasya).

If it is accepted that the conjunction and disjunction with a body are not causes for grief—just as in the case of childhood and so forth—then birth and death also cannot be causes for grief; for the meaning is that birth and death are nothing other than the conjunction and disjunction with a body. || 22 ||

The Lord possesses by his very nature an absence of destruction; nevertheless, the verse is introduced as a resolution to the doubt that grief arises because he is subject to cutting and so forth due to specific causes such as weapons encountered in battle. [The phrase] "even from a cause" refers to this. "Alteration" means cutting and the like. (23)

He introduces the verse beginning with "acchedyatve" (*acchedyatve*) in order to resolve this doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*). Now, one might ask: since it has already been stated that [the Self] is "eternal and omnipresent" (*nityaḥ sarvagataḥ*), for what purpose is eternity mentioned again? Furthermore, since this passage establishes an omnipresent entity, how can it have the individual soul as its subject? Nor can this half-verse refer to the Lord (*īśvara*), because the individual soul was mentioned immediately prior. To this he replies: "nityam" (*nityam*). The meaning is: "eternal, omnipresent, and immovable" (*nityaṃ sarvagatasthāṇuḥ*).

Who is the all-pervading one? And what is meant by "abiding in that"? To this he says: "The all-pervading. Here, neither eternity nor omnipresence is being stated, for if they were, one might suspect a redundancy or that the subject matter concerns the Lord (Īśvara). Rather, the intention is this: since the individual soul (jīva) also possesses qualities such as being indivisible just like the Lord, there would be total equality [between them]; and if that were so, what would be the purpose of its worship? Therefore, it is precisely its eternal dependence on Him and so forth that is being stated. By the mention of its being "atomic while abiding in the all-pervading," the cause of the disparity [between the two] is shown.

Now, one might object: "In this context, it would be more appropriate to say simply 'all-pervading' (*sarvagata*), and not 'abiding in the all-pervading' (*sarvagatastha*). For immobility is logically established by the term 'all-pervading' alone; it is not possible [to maintain immobility] in the case of an atom. To this, he says: "Also because of the cause" (*hetuto’pi*). Here, the word 'immovable' (*acala*) does not denote the absence of activity, which would give rise to the suspicion of a word-split as 'all-pervading'. Rather, let there be the soul's dependence on the Lord; even that might at some point perish, and consequently, there would be total equality [with the insentient].

And thus, since that worship should not be performed, the intention is that its destruction is stated precisely because it is dependent upon Him. Since this meaning is already established by the word "eternal" (*nitya*) alone, one might ask: what is the purpose of saying "by cause"? The intention is that this is not redundant, as it serves to dispel the doubt that even though it is eternal and omnipresent, it might nevertheless perish due to some specific cause such as a *vara* (boon). Even so, one might object that the term "sanātana" is a tautology; to this he says: "By sound" (*nādena*). It is not by the word "sanātana" that eternality is expressed.

However, the intention is that another reason—namely, the soul's being bound by injunctions and prohibitions—is stated due to the absence of independence; therefore, there is no tautology even though independence was mentioned prior to the presentation of the restated reason.

[Objection: Why should the verse beginning with "indestructible" (acchedya) not concern the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara) alone? What is the point of abandoning the perceived division of words and so forth? To this, he says: "eternal" (nityam). The sense is that, because of its designation in the Smṛti, this verse concerns the individual soul (jīva) alone. For this reason as well, he states that this verse does not concern the Lord: "indestructible" (acchedya).

Since it has already been stated that the Lord is indivisible and so forth in the verse beginning with "They do not cut this," if this verse were concerned with the Lord, there would be the consequence of a tautology regarding his indivisibility and other such qualities in the phrase "This is indivisible. Therefore, the meaning is that this [verse] does not have him as its subject.

Because the individual soul (*jīva*) was mentioned in proximity [to the preceding verse], he says "In whom... in order to dispel the impression that the statement "This is unmanifest" also refers to that [soul]. By stating "In whom this [world] is situated," he indicates through the term "all-pervading" that the Lord (*īśvara*) was also mentioned in proximity. If the Lord were the subject being propounded here, then the subsequent sentence beginning with "than him" would be inconsistent; for the absence of grief regarding the battle does not arise from knowledge of the Lord's unmanifest nature and so forth.

Nor, in this view, is there an object for the reflection "therefore" (*tasmāt*). If that [reflection] were to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its object, then—since it would be far removed from the context—the word "this" (*eṣa*) would be inappropriate; therefore, he says: "Thus" (*evam*). Here, it is not the grief regarding battle that is being prevented, nor is there an absence of an object for the reflection "therefore. For, since the individual soul also possesses independence due to its similarity [to the Lord] in respect to indestructibility and so forth, one might ask: "What is the use of worshipping the Lord? It is therefore stated that the Lord alone possesses independence by means of such reasons as His being eternal.

Let there be the independence of Īśvara; what follows from that? Why should He be worshipped? It is because Īśvara alone is independent, and it is therefore logical that He alone possesses the power to destroy the sorrow of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). The intended meaning is this: when He is known through His own action as being endowed with qualities such as the unmanifest (*avyakta*), He alone removes the sorrow of transmigratory existence—the destruction of all the miseries of *saṃsāra*. Thus it is said.

This would be the intended meaning here if the Gītā’s intention were that the Lord’s knowledge comes about through one's own action, such that once the Lord is known, He effects the destruction of all suffering. Why is that so? To this he says: "Of them" (*teṣām*). Here, knowledge is obtained by the very phrase "meditating on Me" (*māṃ dhyāyantaḥ*). Having thus explained this section as referring to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he now states the reasoning for its referring to both: "But not at all" (*na tveva*) and "of them" (*teṣām*). Here, knowledge is obtained by the very phrase "meditating on Me."

Having thus explained this section as referring to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he now states the reasoning for its referring to both: "But not indeed... [Sūtra 1.2.12]. Now, one might object: "Surely only one [subject] was introduced by way of the context; why could the entire section not have only that single subject? To this, he says: "Of the embodied one... [Sūtra 1.2.13], meaning that because the characteristics (liṅga) of both are present throughout, the section has both as its subject matter.

Granted that both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] are relevant to the context by virtue of the introductory statement (*upakrama*), nevertheless, one might ask: "Why does a particular passage have that specific subject as its object? To this, he says: "Because the passage is explained as having that subject as its object, and because the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of that [subject] are present therein, it is logical that it has that as its object"—this is what is meant by the words "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*).

[Objection: Let it be granted that in each of those passages the individual soul (*jīva*) is what is being taught, because qualifiers such as "being embodied" have no application elsewhere than in the individual soul. However, since qualities such as "indestructibility" are possible even in the case of the individual soul, how can it be determined that those sentences have the Lord (*īśvara*) as their subject? To this, he says: "Not indeed... [The opponent asks: How is it that the Lord also possesses those [qualities]? To this, he says: "Of the Supreme Self... Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the Bhāṣya in those various places.

And here, having accepted the primary sense itself, the removal of suspicions such as tautology is achieved without resorting to a purely secondary sense, because obstacles have been stated against accepting a mere secondary sense; whereas in the Bhāṣya, however, another meaning was stated precisely without abandoning the primary sense.

Nevertheless, it is not appropriate to maintain that these statements have the meaning already stated, because they would be incoherent. Since the coherence of the verses ending with "nāsataḥ" has been explained, [the author] now demonstrates the coherence of the verses beginning with "avināśi tu. Because a direct connection between the verse "avināśi tu" and "nāsataḥ" is impossible, he explains their connection through a sequential introduction. The word "yasmāt" (because) [is used]. The phrase "of such a nature" means that it is indestructible in every respect.

He states that this verse is also connected with what will be said later by the phrase "of the indestructible" (*anāśinaḥ*) in the manner already described: "Therefore, for that purpose. Alternatively, he has stated that the connection of "of the indestructible" (*anāśinaḥ*) is also as a supplement to "not of the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*). He further states that there is a connection with the phrase "having an end" (*antavantaḥ*): "Of others," meaning those possessing material bodies; the word "living beings" (*jīvāḥ*) is to be supplied. By this, he explains the utility of the term "embodied ones" (*śarīriṇaḥ*). By the phrase "due to eternity," he explains the term "eternal" (*nityasya*).

For this very reason, the redundancy of this [statement] with the verses "But never... (*na tvevāham*) and "Of the embodied one in this... (*dehino 'smin*) is also avoided; for it is accepted that this is a restatement of what has been introduced as the reason for the claim "This one does not kill" (*nāyaṃ hanti*). Therefore, it was said: "The [qualities] of the eternal have been stated. He states the connection of "This one does not kill" with the verse beginning "He who... (*ya enam*): "Therefore, he slays not" (*tasmād dhantā na*); by this, the statement "This one does not kill" is not a mere repetition, since the soul's lack of independence and so forth have already been explained.

And he states that there is no direct connection with the phrase "one who [knows] this," because such a connection is impossible; rather, he explains it through the sequence of the introduction, beginning with the words "since. The term "of such a nature" means "indestructible in every respect. He states that this verse is connected both by the manner already explained and also by what will be said later in the words "of the indestructible" (*anāśinaḥ*). This is expressed by the phrase "for the sake of that. Alternatively, it has been stated here that the connection of the word "of the indestructible" (*anāśinaḥ*) also serves as a supplement to the phrase "not of the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*).

Once the connection of the word "antavantaḥ" (having an end) with "anāśinaḥ" (indestructible) has been established in the manner described, he states that there is also a connection with "nāyaṃ hanti" (this [Self] does not kill). He says: "anyeṣām" (of others). This refers to those possessing material bodies; the word "jīvāḥ" (living beings) is to be supplied as the remainder. By this, he explains the utility of the term "śarīriṇaḥ" (embodied ones). By the phrase "nityatvāt" (because of eternity), he explains the term "nityasya" (of the eternal). For this very reason, since this is accepted as a restatement of what was under discussion to serve as a reason for the verse beginning with "na tvevāham," it is said: "nityasyoktāḥ" (the qualities of the eternal have been stated).

He states the connection between the phrase "this one does not kill" and the phrase "he who [kills] him": "Therefore, he kills. By this, the repetition of "this one does not kill" is removed, because the soul's lack of independence and so forth have already been stated. Furthermore, the objection that "he who [kills] him" is a mere restatement for the sake of explanation—since an explanation is impossible without the presentation of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*)—is also refuted; for it has been stated that "this one does not kill" is the subject under discussion, which proceeds in relation to the phrase "having an end."

It has been stated that the wording of the mantra establishes the eternity of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). He states that there is also a connection [for this sūtra] as establishing the basis for the phrase "he does not kill": "Because he himself... By this, the objection that if the wording of the mantra were to establish merely the eternity of the individual soul and the Lord, the mention of further qualifications would be useless, is also refuted. By the phrase "as the individual soul," he demonstrates the utility of the word "ancient" (purāṇaḥ).

Intending to show the connection between the phrase "is not slain" and the previously mentioned theme of the Supreme Lord’s very sovereignty, he states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) in order to integrate them: "But the individual soul (*jīva*)," etc. By this, the charge of redundancy (*gatārthatā*) is avoided.

Regarding the phrase "knowing it to be indestructible," since there is no direct connection with the statement "how can that person [be slain]" due to the indestructibility of the Lord and so forth, he explains that connection through the sequence of the transition [of the verse]. Thus: "ata evam" (therefore, thus). By this, the charge of tautology—that because the indestructibility of the Lord and so forth was already stated previously, this is a redundant repetition—is also refuted; for it is accepted that this is a restatement of what was said in order to establish the independence that justifies the question, "how can that person [be slain]? Furthermore, he shows the connection of the verse beginning with "vāsāṃsi" (garments) even with the context of the independence of the Lord under discussion.

Regarding the word "of the garment" (*vāsasaḥ*): he states that this [statement] is also connected with the previously mentioned independence of the Lord (*īśvara-svātantrya*). [The phrase] "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*) is to be construed with "is to be known" (*jñātavyam*).

Alternatively, even so, it is not proper for this context to have both as its subject matter, because the exposition of both would be inconsistent with the immediate topic (*prasaṅga*). Since the injunction to engage in battle is the actual subject at hand, the exposition of both is not consistent with the context. What is intended here is that battle must be performed, and since the Lord alone, by virtue of His independence, is capable of bestowing liberation, that [battle] should be performed as an act of worship toward Him.

In this context, the demonstration of the eternity of the Lord (*īśvara*) serves to dispel grief for the purpose of enjoining battle; furthermore, the demonstration of His indestructibility in every respect serves to enjoin His worship and functions as a means of establishing His sovereignty, thereby substantiating His capacity to grant liberation. Likewise, the description of the eternity of the individual soul (*jīva*) serves to dispel grief for the purpose of enjoining battle.

The description of the destruction of his body and so forth is employed for the purpose of removing grief, for establishing the absolute sovereignty of the Supreme Lord alone, and for demonstrating the lack of autonomy of the individual soul (jīva)—with this intention, he connects all the statements to their intended meaning. "Because he is of such a nature" means that he is indestructible in every respect. The phrase "because he is of such a nature" should be applied to the object of knowledge intended as "indestructibility. [The commentary] says: "Not from that which is non-existent," meaning not from the unreal.

"For that purpose" means "indestructible. "Of others" means "perishable. "Ordinary embodied beings" means "possessors of bodies. "Therefore" means "he does not kill this. "Because of its eternity" means "it is not killed. "Therefore" refers to the verse beginning with "one who [kills] him. "Since" refers to the verse beginning with "he does not die. "Through conjunction with that" refers to the verse beginning with "having been this, he is not. "The individual soul, however" refers to the verse beginning with "is not killed. "Therefore, thus" refers to the verse beginning with "knows. "Of garments" refers to the verse beginning with "garments. "Of the Lord" refers to the verse beginning with "does not kill him."

Although this is established by the very explanation already given, nevertheless, what was stated in a scattered manner does not easily enter the mind of one of dull intellect; therefore, it is stated here in a condensed form.

Regarding this, the use of the present tense in the phrase “they do not cut him” (nainaṃ chindanti) might be misunderstood as implying permission for cutting and so forth at another time; therefore, to dispel such a misconception, he says: “Not him” (nainam). The meaning is this: the use of the present tense is not intended to imply permission for cutting and so forth at another time. Rather, its purpose is to indicate—by way of reasoning—that while there may be the possibility of cutting and so forth in my body, their absence at this very moment can be demonstrated through direct perception itself. Thus, the use of the present tense serves to show that such acts are currently non-existent.

If it is said here that only the essential nature of the Lord (Īśvara) is to be accepted and not his body as well—since the state of the body is described in the words, “his skin being pierced by hundreds of arrows”—then how can it be said, “of his own body”? To this, he states the intended meaning: “By cutting,” etc. To the question, “For what purpose is this false display? he says: “The Lord,” etc. Or, to the question, “Why is it false? Why might it not be [real] from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha)? he says: “The Lord,” etc.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is untenable for [the self] to be independent. || 24 ||

It has been stated that the phrase "this is unmanifest" refers to the Lord (Īśvara). To the question of what the relevance is in describing the Lord as unmanifest and so forth, the text states "the immovable one who dwells everywhere" (*sarvagatasthāṇuḥ*) to declare the omnipresence of the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Regarding this, there may be the following doubt: Does the Lord possess a body or not? In the first case, if he were embodied and present everywhere, he would be perceived everywhere. In the second case, the refutation of the cutting of his body and so forth would be untenable. To dispel such doubts, the author introduces the first word [of the verse] with the word "sarva" (all/everywhere).

Anticipating the objection, "How is it possible for there to be unmanifestness in that which possesses a body?", he explains the term *acintya* (inconceivable) as a refutation of that: "How? [He asks]. Anticipating the objection that "if its inconceivable power were obstructed or destroyed, there would be the consequence of its being perceived," he explains the term *avikārya* (unchangeable): "And not... [He says]. Now, since the purpose is fulfilled by a single word alone, why is there the statement "not perishing" (*na enam*) instead of simply "perishing" (*prati enam*)?

To the question, "In the passage 'This one is unmanifest' (avyakto'yam), what is the purpose of the word 'this' (ayam) being used with every qualifying attribute?", he says: "yāni... and so forth. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the negative particle (nañ) is included. By this, he indicates that even for each individual attribute, there is the application of various words such as "enam" (this one) and others in the form of a distributive repetition (vīpsā). If this were the case, since the individual soul (jīva) is not manifold, the separate statement "This one is indestructible" (acchedyo'yam) would be redundant; therefore, he says: "jīve tu... (But in the case of the soul...). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the separate statement [is made] regarding the soul."

Now, one might ask: from what source do we know that the Lord possesses a body, that this body is devoid of cutting and other such injuries, and that all His forms possess these same qualities? To this, he explains the word "it is said" (*ucyate*). "All" (*sarvam*)—what are those scriptural passages (*śruti*)? To this he says: "Being" (*sat*), etc. He whose body is free from defects such as being cut is "one with a true body" (*sad-deha*). "Possessing the fragrance of bliss" means either having a pleasant scent or having a fragrance consisting of bliss. Regarding the phrase "knowledge of knowledge," etc., the meaning is that He possesses supreme knowledge and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since there are conflicting scriptural statements regarding the existence of a body for the Lord (Īśvara), there would only be doubt concerning that; how then can there be certainty of His existence? To this, [the author] shows the resolution of that matter by means of another scriptural passage: "Adeha" (without a body). [The phrase] "possessing His own nature" means possessing a body that is identical with His own nature. [The word] "consisting of bliss, knowledge, and so forth" is to be connected with the verb "exists. And from that, the phrase "is said to possess a body" is supplied as an ellipsis. [Objection: How is the identity of the body and the embodied one—never seen elsewhere—possible? To this, he says: "And He... [etc.].

[Objection: Is it not the case that [the body] has the nature of the knowledge of pleasure and so forth? This is the connection [of the sentence]. And therefore, if the body were non-different from Viṣṇu, then it would follow that it possesses the nature of qualities such as pleasure; yet that is not tenable, because in passages such as "the enjoyer of bliss," its status as an enjoyer of bliss is stated, and because one does not observe the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed in a single entity. To this, he says: "Qualities... [The objection continues: Even though they are non-different, on what basis is this observed relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed possible? To this, he says: "Even though non-different... It exists.

The ellipsis is that by this [distinction], the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is established even though [the Self] is non-different. To the question, "How can there be the existence of such a distinction? he says: "This..."

Now, is this particularity (viśeṣa) distinct from or non-distinct from that which is qualified by it? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress due to a succession of differences. In the second case, the conventional usage of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified would be lost. Furthermore, if one were to admit further particularities even in that case, there would again be an infinite regress. To this, he says: "The particularity also... Since the particularity is non-distinct from that which is qualified by it, there is no infinite regress through a succession of differences.

The meaning is as follows: just as a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) functions to establish the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed even within an undifferentiated reality, so too does that which is "particularized" (*viśeṣita*)—though devoid of internal difference—establish its own status as a particularity and the status of the particularizer as a particularizer. Thus, there is no infinite regress even through a succession of particularities. For this reason as well, it is logical that the state of being both enjoyer and enjoyed belongs to Hari alone; thus he says: "Furthermore... (*parama*...).

In order to resolve the impossibility of a single, undivided self existing in the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed, [the author] asks: "Whence is the sovereignty of Hari? To this he says: "It is logical" (*yuktā*). The ellipsis is "the logicality or illogicality of two things. In that regard, [it refers to] the Lord (*īśvara*). If that is so, then even suffering and the like might be attributed to the Lord, since there is no lack of logic; to this he says: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). The sense is: because it is understood through valid cognition, the status of being both enjoyer and enjoyed and so forth—even if contradictory—must be accepted for the one [Lord] on the strength of His sovereignty, but not anything else, because that would lack a basis in valid cognition.

Regarding the point that for the Lord alone, qualities such as being the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas defects such as suffering are not, he cites another scriptural passage: "The qualities... [etc.]. To the objection—"How is it that defects are not heard of in scripture?"—he replies, citing passages such as "Born indeed from Viṣṇu," which suggest their existence: "By the ignorant... [etc.].

Regarding the non-difference of the qualities produced by the Lord, and that all forms are of this same nature, he cites the Śruti: "One" (eka). "One" means endowed with the numerical cognition of unity. "Only" (eva) excludes distinctions such as plurality and so forth. "Without a second" (advitīya) means devoid of anything equal or superior. "Nothing manifold" (na kiñcana nānā) refers to the distinction of form, parts, qualities, and actions. [An objection: In that case, there would be both difference and non-difference. To this he says: "From death" (mṛtyoḥ). "He goes to death after death" (mṛtyuṃ tam āpnoti); that is, he enters into darkness.

To the question, "If there is indeed multiplicity, then what is the harm in perceiving difference and non-difference?", he says: "Just as... Just as rainwater that falls upon difficult mountain peaks flows downward, so too one who perceives qualities and the like as distinct—having seen them, his subsequent vision of those very things flows downward. This is the meaning.

Since these scriptural passages are devoted entirely to non-duality (*advaita*), he explains them by means of traditional authority (*smṛti*) itself: "Of mine" (*mama*). To the question, "If there is absolute non-difference, what is the cause for the distinction in worldly usage (*vyavahāra*? he says: "Even though there is non-difference" (*abhede 'pi*). If a further particularity (*viśeṣa*) is postulated among the non-different particulars such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, then one must ask whether that particularity is different from or non-different from the qualified entities, and likewise whether difference and non-difference are themselves different or non-different. In the first case, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the second case, there is no possibility of a specific worldly usage. If yet another particularity is admitted even in that case, there is simply an infinite regress. Therefore, he says: [the following].

Regarding the phrase "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣiṇām*): because there is no difference between the qualifiers and their qualification, nor between that [qualification] and its further distinctions, there is no infinite regress through a succession of differences. Nor is there an impossibility of specific linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For whatever particular distinction (*viśeṣa*) is admitted as existing, that very thing is accepted; thus, there is no infinite regress through a succession of distinctions. The meaning is this: the very same distinction that effects the differentiation of linguistic usage among non-differentiated entities such as quality and qualified, is itself accepted as the factor that effects the differentiation of linguistic usage regarding the distinction between a distinction and its locus (*viśeṣa-viśeṣin*), and so forth.

He states that even though there is no difference between [the Lord] and those such as Matsya and others, there is also no gradation (tāratamya) among them, as in the case of Indra and Arjuna, etc., by saying: "In manifestation... and so forth.

To explain what those manifestations such as the Fish and others are, he clarifies what has already been stated: "Of the Fish... Even Brahmā and others are described elsewhere as incarnations (*avatāra*) of the Lord. In response to the inquiry whether they are included here by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) or if they are not incarnations at all, he says: "Brahmā... Then [he asks]: "In that case... That is, if they are called incarnations, what is the explanation for this? To this he replies: "By Viṣṇu... The intention is that they are so designated because they possess a specific degree of divine entry (*āveśa*). [The opponent asks: Why should they not be considered direct incarnations themselves? To this he replies:

"Those who transmigrate" means: "In those very [beings]" refers to the meaning that [the Lord] was born as Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna, Bala, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Nara, Arjuna, Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, and Sahadeva among the remaining Sanatkumāra, Aniruddha, Śakra, Yama, and the two Aśvins. He states that there is not a single mode of entry into the four beginning with Arjuna by saying "very slight. Knowledge of the incarnations as non-incarnations and of the non-incarnations as incarnations is "confused knowledge" (saṅkara-jñāna). || 25 ||

Having thus stated the arguments himself, it was said that grief should not be felt. In this regard, [the fact] that the body is established [as perishable] means that for that very reason, grief should not be felt; this is expressed by the word "atha" (now/then). Therein, while refuting the existence of birth and death even for one who is liberated, he explains the verse: "tiṣṭhatu" (let it be). The meaning of "atha ca" is "tiṣṭhatu. Having restated "tathāpi," the explanation is "even by knowledge of merely that much."

Since there is no evidence that the word *nitya* signifies "restriction," how can it be explained as "by restriction" (*niyamena*)? To this, he says: "The word *nityam*. Thus, since the word *nitya* has both meanings, he asks what the reason is for adopting the sense of "restriction"; to this, he says: "But here... The meaning is that in the subsequent verse, which serves as an exposition of the meaning of this verse, the word *nitya* is explained as "constant" (*dhruva*). || 26 ||

The rule of birth and death is clearly understood here as being stated as the cause for the removal of grief; and with the intention that it is also intended as the cause for the soul's lack of independence (as previously proposed), he says: "Therefore" (tanmāt). That is, precisely because of the existence of this rule of birth and so forth. The meaning is that one should not entertain the notion of independence regarding this soul. || 27 ||

If one should not regard the living being as a wonder, then where should that [notion] be applied? If it is argued that it is said to be in the Lord (*īśvara*), that is true; however, suspecting that it might be so elsewhere as well, he introduces the verse—which serves as a conclusion to that refutation—in the form of the question: "What then? Now, an objection may be raised: "But here the 'wonder' is something else entirely, whereas the Lord is merely similar to that; since He is not Himself a wonder according to common perception, how can it be said that the Blessed Lord alone is the wonder? To this, he replies: "The wonder... [and so forth].

The meaning of the phrase "like a wonder" (*āścaryavat*) is that it is not intended to suggest that the Lord is not a wonder; rather, the sense is that he is being compared to a wonder precisely because he is one. Even so, one must admit the independence of someone other than the Blessed One, for if he alone were independent, the expression "like a wonder" would be impossible, as no likeness to himself is observed anywhere. Consequently, the restrictive determination "the Blessed One alone" would be untenable; therefore, he says: "The sky. (*gaganam iti*)

The sense here is that, by means of this statement employing a simile based on oneself (*svopamā*), the intended meaning is that anyone other than the Blessed One lacks independence; "sāgara" refers to a multitude of oceans.

Thinking, "Why should the meaning not be something already well-known?", he cites the consensus of traditional authority (*smṛti*) regarding his own stated point: "It is a marvel... By the phrase "within its scope," it is indicated that "like a marvel" is an adverbial modifier of the action. Now, if the Blessed One is indeed a marvel, then since He would be a marvel to everyone, the qualification "some" would be redundant; for a pillar is not a pillar only to some person. To this, he says: "As if not a marvel. Although the Lord is indeed a marvel to all, [the qualification is used to indicate otherwise].

Nevertheless, since most people perceive things erroneously while only a rare individual perceives them as they truly are, the intention is to describe this perception as something marvelous; thus, the qualification "someone" (kaścit) is appropriate—this is the sense. || 29 ||

It objects: "The individual soul (jīva) is eternal," so it has been said. In that regard, is it eternal by its own nature, or through the power of the Lord? Not the first, because that would contradict the accepted doctrine that everything is dependent upon the Supreme Lord. Nor the second, because that which is eternal by its very nature cannot logically be dependent on another; such is the sense. To resolve this, he explains the verse beginning with "dehī" (the embodied one), starting with the words "yasmāt" (because). He says this because if [the soul] were situated in the body merely as its protector, it would be subject to destruction at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya); therefore, he states [the following].

Regarding the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*): by the word "subtle body," both the *liṅga-śarīra* (the causal body) and the "body of consciousness" (*caitanya-śarīra*) are denoted. To the question, "Since eternity and other such qualities are inherent (*svābhāvika*), how can they be dependent upon the Lord? he says: "Substance" (*dravya*). The meaning is that even though eternity and other qualities are inherent, their dependence on the Lord is logical; for it is established by *smṛti* that even one's own nature is dependent upon the Blessed Lord. And regarding the dependence of the individual soul’s existence (*jīva-sattā*) on the Lord, this *smṛti* is the authoritative proof.

Nevertheless, one might ask: "Even so, why is there this distinction that the Lord is the protector residing within the individual soul (jīva)? To this he says: "Therein... That is, dependent upon Him; for that reason, because He is the controller thereof. This is because both existence and non-existence are not excluded from the categories of eternal and non-eternal. || 30 ||

Alternatively, regarding what was said in the words "or we may conquer," the refutation—that there is no loss in either of the two positions—is stated as "or being slain. In that context, just as in the case of "being slain, you will attain heaven," he says "having conquered" in order to dispel the contrary notion that in the phrase "or having conquered, you will enjoy the earth," it is merely the earth and not heaven [that is meant]. [An objection is raised: "Why should the very meaning already understood—not that 'only when dead in battle will you attain heaven, but having conquered, you will enjoy the earth itself'—not be accepted? To this, he replies: "He who... [and so forth].

The meaning is that this is not merely the literal sense; for it is heard in scripture that even upon victory, one attains heaven because of the deceased's prayer for heaven—praying to Yama, "May this deceased person also go to those very heroes who fight fiercely in battles, those who die therein, and those who give gifts of wealth numbering in the thousands. Thus, the intended sense is not simply what is immediately apparent. || 37 ||

Having concluded what was said, another section is commenced with the words, “This [is]... In this context, in order to dispel the notion that the terms *sāṅkhya* and *yoga* refer to specific philosophical systems (*darśana*), he states their meaning along with its authoritative basis: “Properly...”. The sense here is that since the *sāṅkhya* and *yoga* mentioned here are praised as being “joined by the intellect” (*buddhi-yukta*), while the other two [systems] are censured, these two [terms] do not refer to those [systems]. For this reason as well, he states that the term *sāṅkhya* does not intend the well-known system of Sāṅkhya: “Of the Sāṅkhya...”.

If the word *sāṅkhya* were taken here to refer to the well-known system of Sāṅkhya, it would imply that what was stated was taught by the Sāṅkhyas; yet that is not tenable. For in this context, beginning with the verse "It is not born," the Lord (Īśvara) is spoken of, whereas the Sāṅkhya system is atheistic (*nirīśvara*). Therefore, the meaning is that "Sāṅkhya" here does not refer to that specific philosophical scripture. Furthermore, he states that the words *sāṅkhya* and *yoga* here do not refer to the two well-known systems of philosophy: "By the Sāṅkhyas... [and so on]. This refers to the preceding and succeeding sections of the text.

The followers of Sāṅkhya and other schools indeed accept that violence is a cause of misfortune in the next world, but not in this one. However, [the author] further states that violence is prescribed specifically for the sake of the kingdom; therefore, there is no contradiction. To this he says: "Mokṣa... He also provides a reasoned alternative meaning for the words "Sāṅkhya" and "Yoga," saying: "Parama... This means that they serve to establish the subject matter taught in the preceding and succeeding sections. There is no contradiction here in accepting what was stated [by them]; such is the remainder of the sense. || 39 ||

[Yoga] is praised [in the verse], not [the practice of] *neha* (non-attachment). To dispel the misconception that there is neither destruction nor transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of overstepping that yoga, he explains the first half [of the verse] by means of the *Smṛti* itself: "Upon commencement... He demonstrates that very same *Viṣṇudharma* through the *Smṛti*: "By what is appropriate for oneself... The meaning is that activity consists of performing what is beneficial, while non-activity consists of abandoning what is prohibited; these are not to be practiced in relation to other objects. Regarding that *dharma*, he states the measures of time for those entitled to it: "This... He further elucidates that very point: "By one who is established in his own duty, according to his own capacity, Whether engaged in activity or remaining inactive, He does not incur sin, provided he does not neglect his own prescribed duties. The meaning is this: even if one is engaged in worldly activity or remains inactive, as long as one does not abandon the duties ordained for oneself, one incurs no sin. This is because the *Smṛti* declares that there is no transgression when one acts according to one's own capacity. Furthermore, he shows that there is no fault in the case of one who has attained perfection: "For one who has reached the ultimate goal, There is no distinction between action and inaction; For him, all activities are equal, Since he has transcended the world of duality. The meaning is that for one who has attained the supreme state, there is no longer any distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done. All actions are equal for him, because he has transcended the sphere of dualistic perception. Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no fault whatsoever in the case of one who has attained perfection. Thus, it is established that the praise of yoga is intended for the sake of attaining that state, and not for the purpose of praising mere non-attachment. Hence, the statement that there is no fault in overstepping yoga is refuted. Therefore, it is concluded that one must practice yoga until the attainment of perfection. Thus ends the commentary on the second chapter. May there be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness. May there be auspiciousness. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*): [The objection is raised that] in the Kṛta age, [the sacrifice] yields fruit, but in the Tretā and subsequent ages it does not, just as the Veda studied during forbidden days (*anadhyāya*) does not yield its fruit; to this he says, "In the Tretā... The point is that the mention of the Kṛta age there is intended to indicate its predominance. What is the fruit of this [sacrifice] such that it would be superior in the Tretā and other ages? To this he says, "Thus... [Objection: How is it that only he is liberated, since liberation exists even for those possessing the threefold knowledge (*traividya*)? Therefore, having stated the nature of the duty of those possessing the threefold knowledge, he states the absence of liberation for those who possess it.

Regarding the term *traividya*: since even the person of the three Vedas (*traividyasya*) possesses knowledge of the Lord and so forth, and since that alone is the cause of liberation, one might ask how such a person returns after having enjoyed heaven. To this he says: *samyak* ("properly"). One might then ask whether he never attains liberation at all; therefore, by explicitly stating the limit of his journey to heaven, he makes clear the point already established by implication: *krameṇa* ("in succession"). The meaning is that at the end, while offering [the fruits], the man of the three Vedas—if he offers them all individually according to the rule—[attains liberation].

One might ask: "Does one become a *traividya* (knower of the three Vedas) merely by performing the rites prescribed in the triple Veda, or is it through the knowledge that the Blessed One is supreme over all? To this, he says: "Supreme" (*param*). Since the status of being a "proponent of the Vedas" (*vedavāditva*) is common to both the *bhāgavatas* and the *traividyas*, why is this [the latter] alone mentioned? With the intention that what is intended here by "proponent of the Vedas" is not merely following the Vedas, he says: "From debate" (*vādāt*), meaning "from recitation preceded by debate" (*vivādapūrvakapaṭhanāt*).

Let it be granted that this is Vedic discourse; nevertheless, since liberation and other goals are established through that [Veda], why is it said that liberation belongs only to the Bhāgavata? To address this, with the intention that—unlike the Pāṣaṇḍas and others—it is prohibited [for the Bhāgavatas] and thus cannot be a means to liberation, he says: "The Veda... It is not only that there is an absence of being a means to liberation, but rather that it is a means to darkness (tamas). Thus he says: "From them... By the words "without beginning and without end," its state of being devoid of beginning and end is expressed, because the experience of suffering persists within darkness.

Regarding the phrase "because there is no rising at all," this refers to the non-return of those who have attained that state. To the question, "Why is there an absence of returning from darkness? he says: "Vavra. It is called *vavra* because it wards off (*vārayati*) the movement of those belonging to its own sphere, or because it always covers (*vṛṇoti*), or because it wards off bliss (*ānanda*). This has been declared in the Veda, beginning with [the passage]: "It is the Vavra... (RV 10.28.1). || 40 ||

If this Vaiṣṇava dharma is of such a nature, then why is it practiced with a single-minded consensus by only some, and not practiced by many who hold mutually contradictory views? To this he says: "The intellect" (buddhi). The meaning is that because the intellect of only some has reached a definitive conclusion, only they are devoted to Viṣṇu with a single-minded consensus; whereas because the intellects of the many have not reached such a conclusion, they do not possess devotion to Viṣṇu due to their mutual contradictions. By this, the verse beginning with "by resolve" (vyavasāya) is also explained. || 41 ||
