If the very nature of non-determinative cognition (*avyavasāyātmaka-buddhi*) is indeed the cause for the absence of Vaiṣṇava dharma, then such non-determinative cognition must be abandoned. And abandonment would occur through the renunciation of its causes. [The author] asks by what cause non-determinative cognition arises: "Non-determinative... To resolve that, he connects the verses beginning with "That which... (*yām*). Regarding "that which": in the word *samādhāne*, the firmness of certainty due to its having reality as its object is expressed.
And the ellipsis of the sentence is that in the absence of such composure, there is no performance of the duties of Viṣṇu.

He explains the verses by means of his own recollection (*smṛti*) alone. Regarding the word *yathā*: it means "in whatever manner it takes [something] as its object. Regarding *tatsāmyāt*: the meaning is "due to similarity with that. To the question, "How can the speech of the wicked be a cause of dissimilarity? he says: *svarga* etc. Regarding the phrase *na anyad asti*, he states two meanings: *na manyante* ("they do not think"). *Anugati* means "attainment" (*prāpti*). The meaning of the word *janma* ("birth") is "multitude" (*bahu*), referring to that which consists of a continuous succession of many actions. The word *anta* ("end") is used merely for the sake of emphasis (*abhiprāyamātra*).

Regarding the word *ya* (those who): the phrase "by means of doubt" (*saṃśayāt*) means "by means of doubt," with the ellipsis "they make [the objects] their domain. [Objection: If faith and the rest are present, how can there be an absence of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), given such statements as, "The man of faith attains knowledge"? To this, he says: "Of those who determine [the truth]. [Objection: If this very faith and so forth, even when devoid of knowledge of reality, bestows that fruit, then what distinction is there for those possessing knowledge of reality? To this, he says: "By whom... [And] regarding the superiority [of the latter], he says: "...not for long."

Even when committing sins greater than the killing of a Brahmin, they undergo torment for only a short time, and not for long; this is the meaning. [An objection is raised: "Since heaven is attained even by those who hate the Lord through the mere performance of sacrifices and so forth, what is the need for the desire to know (jijñāsā) and the like? To this, he says: "Of others than that. The meaning is that for those with contrary convictions, there is no heaven even through horse-sacrifices and the like. [An objection is raised: "How can this be, since we see that Duryodhana and others, despite being haters, attained heaven and so forth? To this, he says: "But those... [who...]

Nevertheless, since there is indeed the attainment of heaven for those who hate [the Lord], how can it be said that for others there is the opposite? To this he says: "Other than that. The sense is that this was stated with reference to those who hate [the Lord] while excluding the Bhāgavata teachers. By this, the phrase "this world" refers to the domain of the ignorant; "delusion" (pramūḍhatva) is simply ignorance. However, the term "more wretched" (hīnataram) refers to those who hate the Lord like non-Vaiṣṇava teachers. It is thereby stated that their "delusion" consists in false knowledge. (42–44)

The means to knowledge promised [in the previous verse] is now stated: "By transcending the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*). Regarding that, since the Vedas have as their object the realm of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), he says "by transcending the three qualities" in order to dispel the misconception that one should abandon them [the Vedas] and become free from the three qualities. He says "causing to depart" (*apagamayanti*) in order to dispel the misconception that the word "carrying away" (*yāpayanti*) means "causing to reach. [An objection: Why should the meaning not be the one commonly understood? To this, he cites the support of Smṛti for his own stated meaning: "Having resorted to... (*āśritya*).

"Sattvasthatva" means being established in *sattva* (purity), and "ātmavattva" means possessing mental composure (*manasvitva*). To dispel any other possible misconceptions regarding the meanings of the words *tattva* and *ātman*, he states [the definition] through traditional scripture (*smṛti*) itself: "Sattvam... *Santati* means complete pervasion. If *sattva* refers to Viṣṇu, then since being established in Him is His very nature, why would it need to be enjoined? To this he replies: "Santateti. The sense is that what is intended here is not merely abiding as a substratum for Him.

If the Self (*ātman*) were Viṣṇu, then that state would be its very nature and thus not something to be enjoined; therefore, he says: "The Supreme Self" (*paramātma*). The intention is that it is not merely a relationship with Him. Since this meaning is already effectively obtained by the word "situated in goodness" (*sattvastha*), why is it stated again? To this he replies: "By that" (*tena*). Even when the injunction is simply for the constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, that remembrance is attained as a single act. Therefore, the intention is that by stating the state of being the Self, [the author] sets aside that [mere remembrance] and describes the manner of remembrance as it truly is.

Yoga is the attainment of what has not been attained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been attained. To dispel the misconception that both of these should be abandoned in every respect, he says: "Contrary... It is not merely the abandonment of yoga and *kṣema* regarding objects contrary to the scriptures that is intended here; rather, it is the abandonment of the desire for them as well—this is the intention behind the mention of "desire. [An objector asks: Why should the literal meaning not be accepted? [The author replies: He says: "Otherwise... because even activities such as exertion (*utthāna*) would be considered *yoga*, since they consist in the attainment of what was not previously attained.
And thus, the implication is that there would be a contradiction with such [scriptural] passages as, "Arise and practice yoga. || 45 ||

Regarding the statement that one should take recourse to the Vedas for the purpose of transcending the three *guṇas*, the reasoning is stated as: "As much as... (*yāvān iti*). Therein, he explains by means of the traditional recollection (*smṛti*) of the word *udapāna* (well) and the word *sarvataḥ saṃplutodaka* (water overflowing everywhere). [He says: "From abundance" (*udrekat*). Since all effects are dissolved during the dissolution (*pralaya*), how can the dissolution be understood as the meaning of the term "water overflowing everywhere"? To this, he replies: "The primordial nature" (*prakṛti*).

He explains the entire verse by means of recollection: "As far as... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "is possible for the practitioner. To the question, "Why does Viṣṇu grant the fruit on account of the knowledge of the Vedas?", he says: "The Veda... Let it be that the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is indeed the knowledge of Viṣṇu; nevertheless, to the question, "How then does the Blessed Lord grant the fruit?", he says: "From knowledge..."

He shows the meaning of the verse by unifying the two statements established [in the preceding verses]: "From all sides," etc. Now, one might ask: "In this context, certain qualities such as 'exaltedness' (udrikta) are heard; how is it that Viṣṇu alone is meant? Why could it not be someone else? To this he says: "For all," etc. Furthermore, one might ask: "Since the liberated souls (muktas) and Lakṣmī are also exalted, how can Viṣṇu be determined to be the one on the basis of exaltedness alone? To this he says: "And those who," etc. The point is that although the liberated souls are exalted, because they lack the status of being protectors (pālaka), it is impossible for them to be the "well" (udapāna).

He states another reason for the impossibility of the liberated souls being the source of the well (*udapāna*): "And not... Because Lakṣmī (Ramā) is the beloved of all, she is the instigator of time and other factors; therefore, they are not included [among the liberated]. Furthermore, while their superiority is indeed admitted, it does not exist in a primary sense; thus, he says they do not possess the status of being the source of the well: "And not... By this, it is understood that even Lakṣmī’s role as an instigator is indeed accepted. To the question, "Even if superiority and so forth are impossible elsewhere [than in the Lord], why [is it so here]? he replies: "Therefore..."

Moreover, even such excellence as this is not possible elsewhere; how much less so in the case of one who has been submerged in water everywhere? For this reason also, he says that the well is Viṣṇu alone: "At the time of dissolution... etc.

One might argue: "Let there be no well for others because it is impossible; even when water has overflowed everywhere, how could there be a well for Viṣṇu as well? To this we reply: "Because of the method of elimination (pariśeṣa). He states this based on the Śrutis: "It breathed" (ānīt). That one Brahman, without the impulsion of Vāyu, impelled time and the other factors by its own power alone. Therefore, there was nothing else whatsoever superior to it; rather, that alone existed in its fullness.

Furthermore, in this entire region, there was the nature of darkness (tamas), which existed as unperceived water; by that water, everything was concealed during the dissolution—this is the meaning. Following this, the Blessed One remained within the water on all sides, devoid of any protector; he was non-dual and transcendent over all. || 46 ||

The reason why one should not practice the contemplation of identity is stated here with the words, "In action. It is simply said that Arjuna possesses some capacity for performing action, but not for bringing about its fruit. To the question, "How then is the absence of non-difference from the Lord established for all living beings by this? he says: "In action... Here, the word "they" does not refer to Arjuna alone, but rather to all living beings. Having stated their incapacity for bringing about the fruit, the Lord's capacity for it is intended.

The sense is that, for this reason, the very reasoning stated here [in the previous verse] serves as the proof for the absence of non-difference. Now, one might object: "Granted that this much is intended; nevertheless, since there is no formal proposition (pratijñā), how is it known that this reasoning is stated for the sake of proving the absence of non-difference? To this, he says: "Mā karma... The meaning is: "May the Lord, who is the cause of the fruit, not be [the agent] through the mind. And regarding this, he cites scripture: "Eṣa... [referring to] the individual soul (jīva) himself. 47.

It has been stated that there should be no attachment to the non-performance of action. To the question "What then [should one do]?", it is said: "Established in yoga. Since it might seem contradictory to say "abandoning attachment to action, perform actions," he says: "Attachment. The meaning is that by the word "attachment" (saṅga), the mere connection with action is not denoted—which would cause the contradiction—but rather attachment to the fruit alone. || 48 ||

It has been stated that action is inferior to knowledge (*jñāna*). One might then raise the objection: "Since knowledge is superior, it is logical to contemplate oneness with the Lord (*īśvaraikya-bhāvanā*) while in the state of knowledge. To dispel this doubt, it is said: "In the intellect" (*buddhau*). To the question, "How is the resolution of this doubt expressed therein?", he says: "In the intellect" (*buddhau*). Demonstrating the agreement of traditional scripture (*smṛti*) regarding this very point, he explains the second quarter-verse (*uttara-pāda*) by means of that same authority: "Of the ignorant" (*ajñānām*). The explanation of the words "fruit" (*phala*) and "cause" (*hetu*)—namely, "those who [worship Him] as one with themselves" (*taṃ ye svaikyena*), etc.—is as before.
"Miserable" (*kṛpaṇāḥ*) means objects of pity. He states the reason for this: "In darkness" (*tamasīti*). (Verse 49)

Granted that there may be a superiority in knowledge; but what follows from that? To this, he says, "Therefore," meaning that the means to knowledge must be established. In that regard, let the establishment of the means to knowledge be granted. However, one might raise the doubt: "What is the use of performing actions devoid of attachment to results? In response to this, it must be stated that action itself, when free from attachment to results, is the means to knowledge. To the question, "Why is skill in action (*karmakauśala*) here said to be a means to knowledge?", he speaks with the intention that it is precisely action endowed with qualities such as freedom from attachment to results that is expressed by the term "skill in action."

Regarding the phrase *yathāvat* ("as it truly is"): since the knowledge of the Blessed One (*bhagavaj-jñāna*) was not included in the expression "established in yoga" (*yogasthaḥ*), one might wonder whether it is intended here as well. To this he says: *bhagavat-* ("of the Blessed One"). The sense is that because the knowledge of the Blessed One is accepted as the means for attaining immediate realization (*aparokṣa-jñāna*) in the subsequent verse—which serves as an exposition of the meaning of this verse in the words "endowed with wisdom" (*buddhiyuktaḥ*)—it is therefore intended here as well as in the preceding context. (50, 51)

To the question of how far these actions must necessarily be performed by one desiring liberation, it is said: "When... (yadā). In that context, he says "detachment" (nirveda) to dispel the misconception that the word *nirveda* signifies mere world-weariness (*vairāgya*). He explains these two verses precisely according to the *Smṛti*: "Buddhi... and so on. The phrase "that which is to be heard and has been heard" is an indicator for all ritual actions. Through "concentration"—the steadiness of the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures—there arises immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).

By this, it is explained that through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) described as "immovable in the name" (*namādhāvacalā*), there arises direct, immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Viṣṇu, who is himself immovable. Regarding the phrase "union with Him" (*tadyoga*), which means union with the Blessed Lord (*bhagavadyoga*), one might ask: "Since union with the Blessed Lord exists for all [devotees], what is its distinction? To explain this, he says: "Liberation" (*mukti*). The meaning is that one attains Brahman. Here too, the words "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*) are to be connected. Now, an objection is raised: "In this context, 'contrary to the Vedas' (*śrutivipratipannā*) is stated, which implies a contradiction with the Vedas."
To explain how she has entered the path of hearing, he says: "In the Śruti," etc. (vv. 52–53).

The question regarding the characteristics and so forth of the knower (jñānin) under discussion is now posed. Therein, he explains the phrase "What is his speech? (*kā bhāṣā*) in order to dispel a possible misconception. He asks: "By whom? (*kaiḥ*). Now, one might object: since it is already established that he is called a "knower," what is the purpose of this question? To this he replies: "By whom. He states: "Of one established in samādhi" (*samādhisthasya*), in order to dispel the misconception that he is asking about the characteristics and so forth of a knower who is currently performing samādhi; rather, [the term] refers to one who is established in samādhi. || 54 ||

The characteristic of the knower is stated as "he abandons. In this context, to dispel the misconception that the abandonment of all desires by the knower refers merely to the abandonment of both prohibited and non-prohibited desires, [the author] explains it precisely according to that traditional teaching (smṛti), beginning with the word "all" (*sarva*). Why is there not a cessation of all desires for the knower, such that a restriction on the meaning of the word "all" would have to be made? To this he says: "immediate" (*aparokṣa*). For the knower, there is never even the non-cessation of prohibited mental states; how much less, then, could there be the cessation of all desires? This is the meaning.

In that case, since the characteristics of a knower would be absent at the time knowledge is suppressed, it follows that the state of being a knower would cease to exist; therefore, he says "it is true" [in response], meaning: because the absence of prohibited desires exists only at the time when knowledge is not suppressed. Now, if the Seer (the Self) were ever suppressed, then it could not be the means to liberation, as it would be weak due to its occasional nature; to this he says: "even so. It is capable [of being the means] when its own reflection is its object.

Regarding the two occurrences of the word *ātman* in the phrase “in the self by the self,” he says “in the self” (*ātmani*) in order to dispel the misconception that they refer to something other than the individual soul (*jīva*) and the mind (*manas*). To the question, “Why are they not [referring] to the individual soul and so forth? he replies, “satisfied” (*tuṣṭa*). The point is that since satisfaction is mentioned here through the abiding of the Self and so on, whereas such satisfaction is impossible through the abiding of the individual soul and so on, the two words *ātman* do not refer to those [latter]. || 55 ||

If such knowledge is indeed required, why do not all people achieve it? To this, it is said that the conquest of the senses comes through fasting, and by that alone is knowledge attained; thus, the extreme difficulty of attaining knowledge is expressed in the verse beginning with "viṣayāḥ. In that context, he explains the unprecedented meaning of the word *rasa*. *Rasa*... [59]

By the words beginning with "one free from passion" (*vītarāga*), the characteristic of a knower (*jñānin*)—namely, the absence of passion and the like—is stated. This is to be accomplished by one who desires to know (*jijñāsu*). Furthermore, when there is thorough knowledge of the cause and its fruit, the abandonment of passion and so forth occurs. Therefore, for the sake of abandoning passion and the rest, their cause and fruit are described by the words "meditating" (*dhyāyataḥ*). In that context, by the two terms "delusion" (*saṃmoha*) and "confusion of memory" (*smṛtivibhrama*), erroneous cognition itself is expressed. To the question, "In that case, how does the relationship of cause and effect [between delusion and confusion] arise?", he says: "From delusion" (*saṃmohāt*).

In this context, by the term "delusion" (*saṃmoha*), false knowledge is expressed—such as the notion that what is unrighteous, like the theft of another's wealth, is righteous. And by the term "confusion of memory" (*smṛtivibhrama*), the erroneous recollection of the meaning of the Vedas and other scriptures—which previously were known by oneself as declaring that the theft of another's wealth and so forth are unrighteous—is expressed. The point is that a relationship of cause and effect between these two is possible. [Objection: It is difficult to maintain that "from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect."

Since consciousness is invariably concomitant with cognition, it is impossible for cognition to perish [without the former]; therefore, explaining this, he says: "By the sentence" (*vākya*). The meaning is that it is "ascertained" (*nirṇītam*), determined even without dependence on a mere sentence alone; it is not merely knowledge (*jñāna-mātra*). || 63 ||

It has been stated that when mastery over the senses has arisen, liberation is attained through the natural clarity of the mind, characterized by the non-attachment to sense objects; therefore, this [mastery] is something to be achieved. It is now said that there is no fault in its not being achieved. In that regard, since tranquility (*śānti*) is to be accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one might ask: how can it be said that "there is no tranquility for one who does not cultivate"? To this, the word "tranquility" here does not refer to the cessation of the mind. Rather, it refers to the state of having the intellect fixed on the Blessed Lord. Since that state is achievable through cultivation, the author states the meaning of the word "tranquility" along with its authoritative basis: "Tranquility... (Verse 66)

The verse beginning with “That which is called Night” is stated having summarized the previously mentioned characteristics. In that regard, since even the gods—who are the impellers of all—are knowers, if knowers were unable to perceive anything other than the Supreme Self, the worldly course of life would come to an end; therefore, he explains that statement by means of Smṛti itself, as referring to knowers other than the gods: “From the gods... By the phrase “as by others,” the purport of the first half-verse is expressed: the meaning is that Brahman is not known by those who are ignorant. “Like the sun... [is the second half].
The meaning is that just as the sun illuminates everything by its own radiance, so too do they encompass everything through their own knowledge. || 69 ||

If the knower is thus indifferent toward everything, how can he be an enjoyer of sense-objects? To this it is said: "being filled... He explains this by means of that very [scriptural] tradition: "enjoying... [The phrase] "consisting of dharma" means that which is called dharma. As for the question, "How can he be called an enjoyer of objects if he is not one who desires?"—the meaning of what was stated, "not desiring objects of desire," is expressed as "he is not such a one."

Now, one might object: since the enjoyment of sense objects is impossible in the absence of desire, how can it be said that the absence of desire in the knower is for the sake of achieving liberation? To this, he says that by the word *kāma* (desire) here, only prohibited longing is intended; for only that is opposed to liberation, whereas mere desire in general is not opposed to liberation. He explains this with the words: "What is it? The meaning is that desire (*kāma*) is that longing which has as its object something considered contemptible (*kutsita*). Furthermore, he states that in the passage "one who desires desires" (*na kāmakāmī*), there is no prohibition of mere desire in general, saying: "And not... [referring to the subsequent verse].

Now, one might object: since the word *śānti* (peace) denotes devotion to the Blessed One (*bhagavanniṣṭhā*), how can it be explained as "he is liberated"? To this, [the author] says, "Peace," by means of a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) itself, indicating that liberation too is denoted by the word *śānti* precisely because of its connection with devotion to the Blessed One. || 70 ||

The statement made in the preceding verse is elaborated upon by the word "vihāya" (having abandoned). In that context, if the word "kāma" (desire) is taken to mean longing, then there is a tautology with the term "niḥspṛhaḥ" (free from longing). If, however, it refers to sense objects, then [the meaning is] the abandonment of sense objects.

What does he eat? And how is his state of desirelessness (niḥspṛhatva) possible, given the contradiction with the statement that there is "cessation of all desires" (sarvakāmanivṛtti), as well as the consequence that there would be an absence of life-sustaining activities and so forth? To this, he says: "Prohibited" (niṣiddha). Since the word "all desires" (sarvakāma) refers to sense objects (viṣaya), there is no fault of tautology. Nor is there an impossibility of [the sage's] conduct; for here, by the term "desireless," what is intended is abandonment through the mere absence of longing, rather than the abandonment of sense objects in their very nature. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the statements of the Smṛtis and other authorities.

The sense is that by "free from desire" (*niḥspṛha*), what is intended is the absence of longing for prohibited objects. Now, one might object: since even the wise are seen to employ such notions as "I" and "mine," how can it be said of him that he is "free from egoism" (*nirahaṅkāra*) and so forth? To this, with the intention that egoism and the like consist not merely in the cognition "I am" and so on, but rather in the underlying sense of the words "egoism" and so forth, he states the meaning of those terms by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "Not his own nature" (*asvarūpa*). "Possessiveness" (*mamatā*) is the mental state of thinking, "This is under my control. (71)

The aforementioned definition is summarized by the word *eṣā*. Regarding that, he says *brāhmī* in order to dispel the notion that it is merely a quality (*dharma*) of Brahman. Now, since all actions are destroyed by mere knowledge—as stated in such passages as "And his actions perish when He, the higher and the lower, is seen"—and since liberation exists immediately after such knowledge, why is the injunction for the recollection of the Lord at the time of death, expressed in the words "having stood in this [state]," prescribed for the sake of attaining Brahman? To this, he replies: *of the knowers*.

Even for the wise, if there is no remembrance of the Lord at the time of death, then another birth certainly occurs; there is no attainment of Brahman. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to enjoin such remembrance at the time of death for that purpose. Nor is another birth impossible for the wise simply because their karma has been exhausted; the point is that although uncommenced karma (*aprārabdha-karma*) is destroyed by knowledge alone, those who do not have remembrance of the Lord even at the time of death possess commenced karma (*prārabdha-karma*).

If it were the case that for the sake of liberation one must directly depend upon the death of the Lord at the very moment of death, then, because that would be difficult to accomplish, no one at all would attain liberation. Therefore, he states [the following] to show that what is intended by the Lord here is direct remembrance at the time of death: "Prārabdha... [etc.]. There is no contingency of everyone attaining liberation merely by requiring remembrance at the time of death for the sake of liberation; for since the *prārabdha* karma itself acts as an obstacle to remembrance at the time of death, there is a rule that remembrance occurs at the time of death only when that [karma] has been destroyed.

The sense is that liberation is certain when that [recollection] exists. Now, one might object: if there were a certainty that the Blessed One intended liberation occurs only through recollection at the time of death and not otherwise, then such an interpretation of the meaning would be possible. Why is this not the case? To this he says: *yaṃ yaṃ...* (whichever... etc.). Since the word *nirvāṇa* is well-known even in the sense of liberation—as seen in such passages as "peace, liberation, and then *nirvāṇa*"—how could the compound *brahma-nirvāṇam* be a locative tatpuruṣa (meaning "the extinction in Brahman")? Nor can the construction be "Brahman and *nirvāṇa*."

Since liberation cannot be defined as anything other than the attainment of Brahman, he says: "The arrow" (*bāṇam*). Because the word *bāṇa* denotes a body, by means of the term *nirvāṇa*, the bodilessness of Brahman is expressed precisely for the purpose of excluding the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahma*); the sense is that it is not [merely] liberation. Now, one might object: how can Brahman be bodiless? This would contradict [scriptures such as] "Thousand-headed," and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of Smṛti itself: "Because of non-existence" (*abhāvāt*). 72.

Thus ends the second chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 2 ||

In order to demonstrate the subject matter of this chapter as being connected to the preceding chapter, he states what was expounded in that previous chapter: "Knowledge" (jñāna). By the passage ending with "This knowledge has been declared to you," the nature of the Lord and so forth is known—that is, it has been defined. Then, up until the conclusion of the chapter, the means for attaining knowledge of that nature were explained; such is the meaning of the previous chapter. To state the subject matter of this chapter as being connected to that, he says: "Therein" (tatra). Between those two—knowledge and yoga—yoga also is of two kinds.

This is because of the distinction between *karma-yoga* and *dhyāna-yoga*. The meaning is that the Blessed One elaborates upon *karma-yoga*, which was previously mentioned, by means of this chapter. Now, one might object: since *karma-yoga* has already been elaborated upon earlier in such passages as, "For those endowed with wisdom, having abandoned the fruit born of action," why is there a need for this chapter? To this, he says: "In particular."

But surely, since knowledge has also been mentioned here in the passage beginning with "The senses are superior," how can it be said that [the Lord] is expounding *karmayoga*? To address this, he says: "In particular" (*viśeṣataḥ*). This means "predominantly.

Now, where was it previously stated that the intellect is superior to action, such that Arjuna’s question—"If the intellect is indeed superior to action"—serves as its seed? To this, he says: "By far" (*dūreṇa*) [in verse 1.2].

In the response, "In this world," the author says "Jñāna... [and so on] to dispel the misconception that for some qualified persons only knowledge is to be practiced, while for others only action is to be performed. Here, by the term *jñānayoga*, mere knowledge is not intended, nor is mere action expressed by the term *karmayoga*; rather, both are present in each case. Indeed, both should be called *jñānakarmayoga*. If it is asked, "How then can one be called *jñānayoga* and another *karmayoga*?"—[the answer follows].

The point is that the usage [of the term "knowledge" or "action"] is justified because it is intended to refer to the predominance of either knowledge or action in each case, just as the word "milk" is applied even to milk mixed with a small amount of water.

If it is asked, "Why should the meaning not be accepted as it is well-known—that for the Sāṅkhyas there is knowledge alone, and for the Yogins action alone?"—the author says [the verse] beginning with "The Sāṅkhyas... with the intention that such an acceptance would contradict the Smṛti. To the question, "Since the gods possess many actions, how can they be considered primarily Sāṅkhyas?", he says, "Though possessing much... (bahv-). Then, in response to the inquiry, "Is there action alone even for householders and others?", he says, "Even for the knowers of truth" (jñāninām api). If so, why are they called "Yogins of Action"? To this he says:

[The opponent] says: "It is not so. [The author] replies: "Neither one nor the other. For it is heard in the Śruti and other scriptures that for the Sāṅkhyas, the human goal is attained through knowledge alone, while for the Yogins, it is attained through action alone. Yet, it is not logical that the human goal should be achieved by either one individually. Therefore, the sense is that it is not proper to grasp them as being separate.

If it is asked, "In the absence of action, how can there be the goal of man (puruṣārtha)?", does the word "action" intend merely action in general, or specifically actions such as sacrifice? He refutes the first [position] with: "Not indeed. He refutes the second with: "Nor... The sense is that knowledge alone, even if it were a means for the cessation of saṃsāra without action, would not effect the complete goal of man. Then, if it is argued that let action alone be the producer of the goal of man, he says: "Nor..."

The sense is that this is because it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "Not by action, nor by progeny," and so forth. By this, the intended meaning of [the verse] beginning with "Not by non-commencement of actions" is also stated. One might suppose here a combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action if the means to the human goal were being stated for Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and so on; however, since what is stated here is the absence of each one's being a means to the human goal, he says: "The culmination... (*niṣṭhā*).

The term *niṣṭhā* is derived from the root *sthā* in the sense of "cessation of motion" (*gati-nivṛtti*). The word "of motion" (*gateḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. To the question, "How does this resolve the objection? he says: "Liberation" (*muktiḥ*). Here, by the word *niṣṭhā*, which denotes the cessation of motion, the intended meaning is that liberation is the final end of the course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-gati-paryavasāna*). Now, if it is thus accepted that liberation results from both knowledge and action, would there not be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "Not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality"? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the wise" (*jñānin*): even if one accepts that liberation is accomplished through both knowledge and action, there is no contradiction with this Śruti, because [the scripture] declares that knowledge alone, devoid of action, is the means to liberation—a point we also accept. As for action, since liberation is already established by knowledge alone, we accept action only as a cause for an increase in bliss. If one asks, "From what [source] is it known that liberation comes from knowledge alone and the increase of bliss comes from action? the intended meaning is: "Precisely from the Śruti text beginning with 'of the wise'."

For this reason as well, in the phrase "by means of the yoga of knowledge" (*jñānayogena*), action (*karman*) must also be connected; it is not knowledge alone that is intended. He says: "Otherwise. That is to say, if one were to accept the human goal through knowledge alone; since practitioners of action (*karmayogins*) are also under discussion, why would this statement—which declares the impossibility of the human goal in the absence of the commencement of action—not apply to them as well? To this he replies: "Both. (This indicates that both are required.)

The meaning is that this [teaching] does not concern only the practitioner of *karmayoga*, but rather concerns both [the practitioner of action and the practitioner of knowledge]. Why is its applicability to both known? To this he says: “And equality. It is incorrect to say that through action there is an increase in bliss in liberation, because the scripture stating “There is no other path” (*nānyaḥ panthā*) excludes the very connection of action with liberation; therefore, he says: “No other. This scriptural statement excludes only the impossibility of attaining [liberation] through knowledge, but it does not negate the connection with action.
The meaning is that if this were so, it would contradict the Vedic scripture stating, "For the knower, there is the certainty of liberation. || 3 || 4 ||

Regarding the phrase "by way of being an effect" (*kāryataḥ*), since no agent other than [the Supreme Being] is perceived as independent, one might otherwise understand that the qualities of *prakṛti* themselves possess independent agency. To dispel such a misconception, he says: "Agency" (*kartṛtvam*). Here, what is stated is merely that the qualities are the agents of transformation; their agency is not independent. This is because Viṣṇu’s status as the independent agent is declared by the word "unwilling" (*avaśaḥ*). If it is asked: "Why not take the word 'unwilling' to mean dependence on another, and thereby conclude that the qualities themselves possess independent agency?"—the answer is: No.

The sense is that [the opponent's view] contradicts the Śruti statement, "He is the agent" (*kartṛtvam*). There is a variant reading "Śruti" (instead of "Bhāva"). In that case, in order to dispel a contrary impression, it was explained by the Śruti itself; since Viṣṇu’s independent agency is not perceived here, it is said: "Not subject to another's will" (*avaśaḥ*). To the question, "How does the word *avaśa* express subordination to Viṣṇu?", he says: "Aḥ. (5–8)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since it is said that 'a living being is bound by action,' and since action is thus a cause of bondage, why is it enjoined that 'one should perform action'? To resolve this doubt, he introduces the verse with the words "By action... (karmaṇā). Here, it is understood that action not intended for sacrifice (*ayajñārtha*) is what binds; it is not meant that non-Viṣṇuite action is the binder. Therefore, he states the meaning of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) according to the scripture itself with the word "the Knower" (*jña*). Here, the term "sacrifice" does not refer to the well-known ritual sacrifice.

Rather, the meaning is that the Blessed One is the knower because he has made [the object] his domain by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness; the construction is "that very thing which is this domain. || 9 ||

Regarding the statement that "action must be performed," another reason is stated: "from food" (*annāt*). Here, one might ask: how is it that food originates from *parjanya*, a specific deity? And how does that [food] originate from sacrifice (*yajña*)? Furthermore, since the sequence has been described as starting from "from food," how can it be called a "wheel"? To resolve these doubts and to refute the interpretation of the words *brahman* and *akṣara* in any other sense, he explains by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "because of producing" (*jananāt*). That which has the supreme as its produced effect is thus described.

"From sacrifice" (yajñāt) means that [the Lord] comes into being through a deity propitiated by sacrifice. Sacrifice (*yajña*) is the relinquishing of a substance for the sake of a deity; ritual action (*karman*) is any other activity. "Arises from the Vedic statement" means how it arises eternally—it is understood, comprehended, and realized. The sense is that the Lord, being correctly understood through the Veda, causes one to perform virtuous deeds. Since He is thus manifested through sacrifice via this traditional succession, therefore...

The sense is that because the Lord is established in sacrifice, when the wheel is set in motion by the performance of sacrifice, it becomes a meritorious act for the purpose of manifesting the Lord; it is not merely for the sake of being the cause of the sustenance of beings. "He does not turn the wheel" means he does not perform [worldly] action.

If the destruction of the universe were to result from the non-activation of the wheel due to the non-performance of action—since the universe is contained within that wheel—it would follow as a consequence that those in other stages of life (*āśrama*) besides the householder's stage (*gārhasthya*) would be destroyers of the universe; for there is an absence of sacrifices and the like in those other stages, such as those of the three Vedas (*traividyā*), where action takes the form of sacrifice, charity, and austerity. To this, he says: "Vocal" (*vācika*). Vocal [action] consists of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) and so forth; mental [action] consists of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*): although these are common to all, the meaning is that while others may have different [actions], for these [householders], it is precisely this.

He states another sacrifice for others [beginning with] "of one dwelling in the forest" (*vanasthasya*). "Without a ritual" (*akratuḥ*) means devoid of the immolation of animals. "Consisting of service and so forth" (*śuśrūṣādyātmaka*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the worship of the sacred fire is included. "The giving of knowledge, fearlessness, and so forth" (*vidyābhayādītyādi*): by the word "and so forth," the giving of food that one may eat oneself is intended. The giving of knowledge, fearlessness, and so forth, preceded by the giving of food, is what is intended here; specifically, the giving of food exceeding what one would consume oneself. "Food" (*anna*) refers to roots, fruits, and the like.

Regarding the phrase "originating from the imperishable Brahman" (*brahmākṣarasamudbhavam*), the author refutes the erroneous interpretation that the word "Brahman" refers to the Veda and the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to Brahman, by providing another reason: "Brahman... [The text continues: If, in this context, the word "Brahman" referred to the Veda and the word "imperishable" referred to Brahman, then there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of Brahman through the word "Brahman" in the subsequent passage, "Therefore, Brahman is all-pervading."

The meaning is that there is no reference by means of the word *tat* to anything not previously introduced by the word *yat*, except when there is a specific reason; nor is there a reference to the Veda in that context, because the statement that it is "established in sacrifice" would otherwise be useless. He states another defect as well: "And [the word] *cakra*... Since rituals do not originate from the Veda, since the Brahman (as the source) does not originate from the Veda, and since the Brahman is not born from the elements, if one were to postulate a different meaning [for the passage], the Veda and so forth would fail to enter into the cycle (*cakra*).
The sense is that if one accepts [the view] that [words] denote individuals, it would follow that many words would have non-primary (secondary) meanings. || 14 || 15 || 16 ||

Another argument for the necessity of performing action is stated here: "But he who... In this context, since the words *tṛpti* (satisfaction) and *saṃtoṣa* (contentment) have the same meaning—as seen in such expressions as "satisfaction, contentment, and fulfillment"—one who is "satisfied with the Self" (*ātmatṛpta*)...

Because it has already been stated [in the previous verse], the phrase "and being content in the Self alone" (*ātmanyeva ca santuṣṭaḥ*) would be a tautology; therefore, he says: "Contentment" (*tṛpti*). The word "the meaning is a distinction" (*viśeṣo'rthaḥ*) is the ellipsis. If one asks, "On what basis is this interpretation of the meaning made? he explains by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*), namely the verse beginning with "Viṣṇu": "Viṣṇu... and so forth. Thus, having accepted that the words *tṛpti* and *santoṣa* have the same meaning, the difference in meaning was stated through a difference in grammatical analysis (*vigraha*). Now, with the intention that there is no tautology because there is indeed a difference in the meanings of the words *tṛpti* and *santoṣa*, he states the authoritative evidence for their difference in meaning.

Regarding the term *rati*: bliss (*ānanda*) is that which constitutes one's essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas that born of action (*karmaja*) arises from assistance and the like. [An objection is raised: "If the words *rati*, *tṛpti*, and *prīti* have distinct meanings, what follows regarding the difference in meaning between the words *tṛpti* and *santoṣa*? To this, with the intention that since the words *prīti* and *santoṣa* are synonyms, the difference in meaning between the words *tṛpti* and *prīti* necessarily establishes the difference in meaning between the words *tṛpti* and *santoṣa*, he states the proof for their synonymy: "Santoṣa" [is a synonym]. Synonyms are those which denote [the same thing] through various synonymous terms. (17)

Now, having stated that "there is no duty for one who is liberated," it is said, "Therefore, he is unattached. Since the reason for performing action has not been stated therein, what is referred to by the word "therefore"? To this, he says: "Because... Just as there is an absence of duty for the liberated because of the absence of any purpose, why should there not likewise be an absence of duty for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) due to the absence of any purpose through action? To this, it is replied: "He is unattached."

In this regard, he explains that [verse]—beginning with "unattached"—in order to dispel the misconception that liberation is attained through action alone. The meaning is "while performing action," and not "only while performing action"; this is the intended sense. Therefore, the remainder of the sentence is: "Since there is indeed the existence of a fruit for one who is not yet liberated through action, there certainly remains a duty for him."

[Objection: Since it has not been stated that there is an effect for one who is not liberated, how can there be a reference to him by the word "from that" (*tasmāt*)? [Response: This is not so; for by stating that "there is no effect for the liberated one alone," it follows as a matter of course that there is an effect for the non-liberated one. [Objection: But since the particle *eva* (alone) is absent in the phrase "for the liberated one alone there is no effect," how is the existence of an effect for the non-liberated one established? To this, he says: "For the liberated one alone... (*muktasyaiva*).

The sense is that even in the absence of the particle *eva*, the restriction of its meaning is understood through the word *tu*; therefore, by that [word], the existence of duties for one who is not liberated is established. However, some explain the sentence "But he who... as referring exclusively to the knower (*jñānin*). That is not correct, because it is understood from such Smṛti texts as "But he who is delighted in the Self is liberated" and "He who possesses delight through the grace of Viṣṇu" that it refers to the state of liberation, and because the existence of duties for knowers has already been stated. With this in mind, he states another objection: "Therefore... [tasmād iti].

If the intended meaning here were the absence of duty for one who possesses knowledge alone, then the injunction to perform action in the concluding statement, "Therefore, unattached," addressed to Arjuna, would be contradictory; for he too is a possessor of knowledge—this is the sense.

Since there is no evidence for Arjuna’s state of being a knower (*jñānin*), he is indeed ignorant and thus qualified for ritual action; therefore, the injunction of action directed toward him is not contradictory. To this, [the author] says: "Brahman... [The phrase] "of those who" (*ye teṣām*) should be supplied. Even if this [passage] refers to liberated beings (*mukta*), the injunction of action toward Arjuna would still be contradictory, because by the force of these words, the Pāṇḍavas possess the characteristics of the liberated—such as being devoted to Brahman—and are thus equal to the liberated. To this, [the author] says: "Self... There is no absolute equality between the Pāṇḍavas and the liberated.
By the word "only" in the phrase "delighting in the Self alone," the absence of discontent among the liberated ones is distinguished from that of the Pāṇḍavas; therefore, he says: "Of these... (19).

Now, an objection is raised: "Since liberation is established through knowledge alone, how can it be said that one attains the Supreme only by performing action without attachment? To this, it is replied: "By action alone. Here, in order to dispel the misconception that liberation is said to be attained by action alone [to the exclusion of knowledge], he explains it by connecting it with that very [preceding] context: "Together indeed. The word "kāryam" (to be performed) implies that action must be performed even by the knowers of Truth. Another reason for the necessity of performing action is stated: "The world... [referring to the verse beginning with *lokasaṅgrahamevāpi*].

In this regard, although the gathering of people (*loka-saṅgraha*) is possible, since there is no purpose for it [for the Knower], how can it be said that action is enjoined for the Knower for the sake of gathering people? Therefore, he explains [the passage] by recalling the verses beginning with "The world" (*loka*), starting with the words "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*): "But that is contentment. (20, 21)

Furthermore, even though I am devoid of any personal motive, I perform action solely out of compassion for the sake of maintaining the world; therefore, what need is there to say that it must be performed by the knower who possesses the purpose of increasing bliss in liberation? This is expressed in the words, "Not for Me, O Pārtha. The meaning of this is: "It is for My own [sake]. [Objection: But is it not improper to say that the Lord performs the protection of the world and so forth even in the absence of a motive?

The [author] dispels the doubt that "activity is impossible in the absence of a purpose" by means of the Scripture itself: "By way of protection. The meaning is that even in the absence of a purpose, it is logical for the Lord to perform acts such as protection because He possesses the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of being an agent. An objection is raised: "Indeed, activity due to such an inherent nature is observed only in insentient things; for example, fire, wind, and so forth engage in burning, moving, and so on solely by their own nature, without any purpose."
Since one does not observe the activity of volition to be devoid of a purpose, how can even the Lord act without aiming at a purpose? To this he says: "From Me" (22–26).

If action were to be performed by the wise even with the same obstinacy as the ignorant, it would follow that there is no distinction between the actions of the learned and the unlearned; therefore, the specific distinction based on attachment and non-attachment is stated in the words "the attached," and this is further elaborated in the words "from nature. Having thus explained the distinction between the actions of the learned and the unlearned, the performance of action by the wise is enjoined in the words "in Me. Since the statement "having renounced all actions, fight" appears contradictory, he explains it by means of that very [scriptural] tradition: "I am not... etc.

"I am not the doer"—this is freedom from possessiveness (*nirmamatva*). "Hari is the doer, and the entire act is His worship"—this is the surrender of agency (*karmanyāsa*) to Hari. To the objection that if Hari alone is the doer, how can it be appropriate to define [the practice] as "His worship" and so forth, he says: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The sense is this: although Hari alone is the doer, nevertheless, because my own agency exists only through His impulsion, it is appropriate to define it as "His worship" and so forth. "Devotion to Him" (*tadbhakti*) is freedom from desire (*nirāśīstva*). "Its fruit" (*tatphalam*) is the fruit of worship.

By the statement that the renunciation of action (*karmanyāsa*), when joined with selflessness (*nirmamatva*) and other qualities, brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu, the purport of such passages as “Those who [offer] to Me” is expressed. To the question, “How does the renunciation of action in Hari, performed by one endowed with selflessness and so forth, bring satisfaction to Viṣṇu?”, he says: “Because. Since the state of reality is thus, therefore such contemplation indeed brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu; the sense is that Viṣṇu is fond of knowledge according to the actual state of things.

Agency consists solely in independent agency; therefore, how can agency be attributed to the individual soul (*jīva*) and others? To this end, he demonstrates the use of the word "agent" even for one who is dependent on another. [He says: "The person... Now, it is said in some places that the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is the agent, not the individual soul and so forth; in other places, that the individual soul alone is the agent, not the Lord and so forth; and in yet other places, that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone is the agent, not the Lord and so forth.

Therefore, one might ask: how is it that the Lord alone is the agent and not I, while I am merely an agent dependent upon Him, such that the renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*) is logically established? To this, he says: "Thus" (*iti*). Where the agency of the Lord and others is mentioned, there it must be understood through such a distinction as: "the Lord possesses independent agency," and so forth.

Where it is stated that Īśvara and others lack agency, it must be understood through such distinctions as that Īśvara possesses no independent agency of his own; however, where agency is stated, it does not mean that everyone therein possesses independent agency. Where non-agency is stated, it should be understood that everyone therein is entirely devoid of agency. This is because of statements such as "independent agency belongs to Viṣṇu alone. This is the meaning.

Intending to explain the passage beginning with "prakṛteḥ" and so forth, and to interpret the words such as "prakṛti" occurring therein as referring to "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature) and the like, he first states the authoritative evidence for that meaning: "kvacid" (in some places). The word "svabhāva" refers to the individual soul (jīva). This is because the Smṛti passage beginning with "yasmātsvatantrakartṛtvam," which serves as an explanation of the statement "mayīti" and so forth, is useful for explaining the passage "prakṛteḥ" and so forth; therefore, the explanation is provided by way of transposition.

In the passage beginning with "of Prakṛti," since the agency of the triad beginning with Īśvara has been asserted, and since the non-agency of the individual soul (jīva) is subsequently asserted, and since the distinction between agency and so forth is stated in the Smṛti, [the author] explains by means of that very Smṛti in order to dispel any contrary impression regarding the passage beginning with "of Prakṛti": "By nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). Here, the composition of the *Pīṭhikā* serves as a direct commentary on the phrase "by nature" and so forth. To the objection—"Since there exists a transformation of gods and others into other states, how can godhood and so forth be their 'nature'?"—he replies: "Not of these... (*naiṣām*).

Since we observe that victory and other such states are subject to change, how can it be said that they do not exist? To this, he says: "The body... Even if divinity and so forth were inherent, why is it that gods alone are superior and so on? To this, he says: "Superior... The sense is that the superiority of the gods and others is established by the superiority of their respective fruits. Why then do the gods and others remain in saṃsāra if they are fit for liberation and the like? To this, he says: "Attainment... The words "of their own appropriate fruit" are to be supplied as the remainder.

The phrase "due to the non-completion of the means" (*sādhanasya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the reason]. If attainment were to occur through the completion of the means, then there would never be a continuous succession of *saṃsāra*, because since *saṃsāra* is beginningless, it would have been possible to complete the means even prior to this point, resulting in the final liberation of all sentient beings. Therefore, he says: "Not at all" (*naiva*). Although *saṃsāra* may continue eternally by the will of Hari, [this is so] because it is beginningless—this is the ellipsis. If it be asked, "If living beings (*jīvas*) are by nature of three kinds, what follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is that because divinity and so forth are innate (*svābhāvika*), the qualities that follow them are also innate; thus, the phrase "mixed innate [qualities]" and so on should be applied accordingly. To the question "And what follows from this?", he says: "By way of their effects" (*kāryataḥ*). "Helplessly" means under the control of Viṣṇu. "By the material" means by the innate [qualities]. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Innate... By this, the meaning of the word "prakṛteḥ" (of nature), which denotes the karma of the ignorant, is explained. [The phrase] "making the innate qualities the cause."

"He causes them to perform virtuous deeds by taking into account their superior qualities," and so forth. By the phrase "by Viṣṇu through the qualities such as the will of Viṣṇu," two meanings of the expression "by the qualities of Prakṛti" are stated here. The qualities of Prakṛti intended here are Sattva and the others, insofar as they serve as the material cause (upādāna). The agent acts with independence; this is the implied sense.

To the question, "If the ignorant person acts in this way, how does the wise person act?", he says: "But the knower of reality... By this, the meaning of the term *tattvavit* (knower of reality) is explained. To the question, "What is the cause for the egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) of the ignorant?", he says: "By their own nature... This should be construed as follows: when the qualities (*guṇas*) are predominant, those who are deluded believe that these [qualities] act without being prompted by another; when they are mixed and so forth, they are deluded by them; and when knowledge and other qualities are present, they claim, out of independence, to possess superior knowledge and other such qualities.

In the case of their non-existence, that same fault [of ignorance] would persist. Regarding those qualities which are dependent on Viṣṇu, they do not know them in their true existence; it should be understood that they do not know them as "they do not exist" when they are absent. To show that these [qualities] should be made known to the wise, he says: "In them... The sense is: if they are unworthy, one should not reveal them; otherwise, one should reveal them after examination. "Making unmanifest" means: so that his own statement does not fail to make the reality manifest. By this, the phrase "of Prakṛti" is explained.

The meaning of "to the dull-witted" (*mandān*) is "toward those who are unfit. To the question, "Why should the truth not be spoken to those who are unfit? he says: "Having understood" (*buddhvā*). Since the restraint of the mind would lead to the cessation of activities that follow one's own nature, he says: "One's own nature" (*svabhāvam*). By this, the explanation of the word "similar" (*sadṛśam*) is provided. || 35 ||

When it was stated, "One should not fall under their power," the word "atha" (then) is asked. Since the Lord's role as the impeller has been mentioned in the passage beginning with "prakṛteḥ" (from primordial nature), and since He Himself has been described as a deity among the gods, this question might be considered redundant; therefore, he says: "From the Supreme Lord. The phrase "a powerful one belonging to the lower order" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This is not stated in the actual question; hence he says: "atha" (then).
The sense is that by the word "atha," which denotes immediate succession, it is understood that [the teaching] follows immediately after the Supreme Lord and the gods. || 36 ||

The explanatory statement beginning with "kāma eṣaḥ" (this is desire) explains the stated meaning by means of a corroborating Smṛti text itself: "akhila... and so on. Therein, "kāmaḥ" is the explanation of [the word] "kāmaḥ"; it should be construed as "desire is powerful. By the very phrase "aśubheṣu," the word "vairiṇam" (the enemy) is explained. To the question, "How is desire powerful among those who incite one toward the inauspicious? he says: "sarvam... The meaning is that just as smoke and the like envelop fire, mirrors, and infants, so does it [envelop the mind].

"Gradually," etc.: it should be understood that just as smoke slightly veils fire, so does [passion] slightly veil the virtuous person, and so forth. And since desire must be conquered by giving it what it requires, he says: "Of the great eater. To the objection that even a large amount might be given, he says: "Of that [desire]. By this, the passage beginning with "by smoke" is explained. If so, how is it to be conquered? First, he states its locus: "While eating. By this, the meaning of the word "senses" is stated.

"Let this be the basis; but what is the weapon for its destruction? To this he says: "By knowledge," etc. By this, the purport of the passage beginning with "the senses" has been stated. Now, since it was already stated that desire is the veil of all by the words "by smoke," why is it said again that it is "veiled"? To this he says: "By knowledge," etc.

Previously, desire was described as an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) because it acts as an obstacle to the arising of knowledge; now, however, its status as an obscuration is stated in terms of its acting as an obstacle to the means for attaining immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of knowledge that has already arisen. Thus, the intention is that there is no tautology. To address the objection that the phrase "by the fire which is difficult to satiate" is redundant, he says: "Not merely... [and so on]. As for the question, "Why is it considered that desire is not sufficient?", he says: "Of fire... (37–41).

To dispel the misconception that the senses, mind, and intellect mentioned in the passage beginning with "the senses, mind, and intellect" are being elaborated here, he explains by recalling that very [scriptural] tradition: "From all... This means from all those who identify with objects and so forth. As for the passage beginning with "From that, Brahmā," it refers to: "The Great Self is higher than the intellect; the Unmanifest is higher than the Great; from the Unmanifest, the Puruṣa."

"Beyond [him]"; this is an explanation of the Śruti text: "There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa. Although here it is stated merely that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is superior to the intellect (buddhi), this example is cited to indicate that what has been taught elsewhere should also be applied here.

As for what was said—that those presiding over the sense objects (*artha*) are superior to those presiding over the senses (*indriya*)—that is not correct, because it contradicts the Śruti text: "The sense objects are indeed higher than the senses. Nor is it appropriate for Rudra to be the presider over the mind (*manas*), because that contradicts the statement: "Rudra has the form of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Likewise, it is not appropriate for Sarasvatī to be the presider over the intellect (*buddhi*), because it contradicts the declaration that she is the presider over discernment (*vijñāna*). To this, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). Why is there no contradiction? To this, he says: "All... (*sarva...*).

If that is so, one might ask: why do the scriptures speak of separate abodes for Lakṣmī and others, stating that "Śrī belongs to the Unmanifest (avyakta)" and "Brahmā belongs to the Great Principle (mahat)," and so forth? To this, he says: "Because of the subsequent... The meaning is that since the Unmanifest and the others increase in degree sequentially, their respective presiding deities (abhimānins) are also indicated to increase in degree accordingly; thus, separate abodes for those presiding deities are mentioned. Why should this progressive increase be made known? To this, he says: "Because of the superiority... [of the subsequent ones].

He states an exception to the previously mentioned principle that "all [deities] possess pride in all [their respective domains]" with the words: "In their respective stations" (*sthāneṣu*). The meaning is this: while the superior deities exist as possessors of pride within the stations already mentioned for the inferior ones, the inferior deities do not exist as possessors of pride within the stations mentioned for the superior ones. If this is so, then how is it stated in the Purāṇas and other texts that Sarasvatī and the others possess pride in the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)? To this he replies: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "it is used figuratively (*upacaryate*), because... [of the following reasons].

And he cites the *Atirātra-śruti*: "In whatever [matter]... This means that when there is an objection (*codya*)—namely, that the son has ownership over a certain object while the father also has ownership over that same object, and conversely, that the son has ownership over an object while the father also has ownership over it—the resolution (*samādhāna*) stated therein is as follows: in that case, the father's ownership exists in the primary sense (*mukhyataḥ*), whereas the son's ownership exists only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*). This is the intended meaning.

By this [statement], since Indra and others preside over the sense organs (*indriya-abhimānin*), while the lower and higher beings such as Suparṇī and others preside over objects (*artha-abhimānin*), the Śruti declares that objects are superior to the sense organs with the intention of referring to Suparṇī and the rest. However, this sentence speaks of the superiority of the sense organs over objects with the intention of referring to Śiva’s sons; thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because Rudra and the others preside over the mind, ego, and so forth, it is stated that there is no contradiction between these two declarations.

[Objection: "But if all [words] were to denote everything, then the determination of the meaning of words such as 'the unmanifest' (avyakta) would not be possible; for since everything would be the referent, the exclusion of one thing over another would be untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of Smṛti itself: "bahviti" (much...). Furthermore, anticipating the doubt—"In cases where there is equality of gender, context, and so forth, how is the determination made?"—he refutes it by means of Smṛti itself: "liṅgeti" (gender...). 42.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Gītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable Ānandatīrtha, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 3 ||

He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter by way of its connection with what has already been stated: "Of the two that have been mentioned" (*uktayoḥ*). To dispel the notion that it refers to only one of the two—namely knowledge or action—he says "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*). Since action was explained in the preceding chapter, one might ask, "What is the purpose of this [chapter]? To this he says "the distinction" (*viśeṣa*). To generate an inclination toward the yoga of action already described, it is said, "This is the dharma previously practiced," using the words "this" (*imam*); recollecting the purport of that, he says "Brahman" (*brahma*).

If the Gītā were merely an abridgment of the Pañcarātra, then its status as the supreme among all scriptures would be lost; therefore, he states that it is an abridgment in terms of its words alone, but not in terms of its meaning, with the words "Just as... (yathā). One might argue: "Even if the Gītā contains the entire meaning of the Pañcarātra, let there be no inferiority of the Gītā to the Pañcarātra; however, how does this establish its status as the best of all scriptures? To this, he replies: "The Veda... (veda).

The sense is that it is logical for the Gītā to be the supreme among all scriptures, as it fulfills the meaning of the Vedas to an even greater degree than all other treatises by encompassing the entirety of the Pañcarātra teachings. || 1 || 3 ||

One might ask: "Since the Blessed One Vivasvat is recent and [this teaching] is ancient, how can he be its instructor? Thus he asks, "The other [time]. In this regard, since Arjuna appears to be ignorant of the Blessed One, the previously mentioned inconsistency arises; therefore, he says, "Even though they know. The point is that one should not infer from this question that Arjuna does not know the Blessed One to be beginningless and eternal, because the statement "even though they know" shows that the purpose of the question is to seek specific knowledge and so forth. [This is for] the sake of establishing—that is, for the sake of strengthening what is already known. (4–5)

If there were other past births, then you would not be free from birth and death; and thus, there would be a contradiction with what was stated in the verse, "But it is indestructible" (2.17). To this, it is said: "Though unborn... (2.24). In that context, the phrase "by means of his own *māyā*" is explained as follows to dispel the misconception that it refers to the power of ignorance (*ajñāna*): "The Self... [and so on]. Here, the expression "by means of his own *māyā*" does not mean "by the power of ignorance," because that would contradict all authoritative scriptures.

Rather, the meaning is that by the words "Mahāmāyā" and so forth, it is stated that [the descent] is based solely on His own will, as indicated by the term *māyā*, in order to prevent interference from others during the incarnation. Having cited the phrase "presiding over His own *prakṛti*" (*prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya*) in order to dispel the misconception that it refers to the acquisition of a material body, he explains the word *prakṛti*: "The *prakṛti*... Here, the acquisition of a material body is not being asserted, because contradictions with the Śrutis and other authorities have already been stated. Rather, [the point is]: "If You descend, there must be a purpose."

The sense is this: in order to resolve the doubt that there would be a contradiction with the statement "there is nothing unattained," it is simply asserted that even in the absence of a specific purpose, the descent (avatāra) and so forth are appropriate because they are of such a nature. This point would hold if it were established that Hari’s descents and so forth occur by His very nature without any external purpose; but from what is that established? To this he says: "Of the Lord" (devasya). And this nature is the Lord Himself, not something distinct from Him—this is the meaning.

Let it be granted that the activity [of the Lord] arises from the very nature of Viṣṇu; nevertheless, why is the word *prakṛti* used here in the sense of "nature"? To this he says: "For this very reason. Since the word *prakṛti* here denotes nature, for that very reason the qualification "His own" (*sva*) is employed. The meaning is that if it were intended only in another sense (as "material cause"), then—without the expression of dependence on oneself through the unique term "mine" (*mama*)—this [usage] would not be common to both meanings. He extends this same logic to the present case as well: "The material cause," etc.

And in such passages as these, the meaning is that there is a qualification by its own specific term; therefore, if the word *prakṛti* signifies "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), then one might ask: in the verses "by me, the supervisor, *prakṛti*" and "know *prakṛti*," does it also signify intrinsic nature? In response to this expectation, he says: "By me. The ellipsis is: "therefore, in those [other] cases, *prakṛti* is indeed something other than intrinsic nature. He states another reason for its being different: "Know *prakṛti*... (referring to the verse beginning with *prakṛtim*).

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the term "by me" (*mayā*) is included. This is because in the phrase "by me as the supervisor" (*mayādhyakṣeṇa*), there is the perception of a relationship through subordination, and in the phrase "my nature" (*prakṛtiṃ me*), there is the perception of a relationship through the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). [Objection: If [the relationship] were perceived as something other than a relationship of ownership, then here too, since it is perceived as a relationship of ownership, it would have to be something other [than ownership]. To this, he says: "Here... This [objection] would hold true if the word *sva* (own/self) denoted only a relationship of ownership; but it is not so.

In this context, because the word *sva* primarily denotes its own nature (*svarūpa*), the intention is that it denotes only the nature itself and not a relationship, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). To the question, "Where is the denotation of the word *sva* as 'own nature' observed? he says, "Own nature" (*svabhāva*), with the thought that such usage is observed in the word *sva* within the term *svabhāva*. Regarding the word *sva* in the term *svabhāva*, there is no undesirable consequence in establishing it as merely "otherness" (*anyatvamātra*), because two meanings are accepted [in the case of the word *sva*]. However, to establish it as "only other" (*anyaiva*) is improper.

The sense is that since the word *sva* can also denote its own form (*svarūpa*), it would not exclude others—just as in the case of the word *me* (my)—and thus [the term *bhāva*] would be redundant. To this he says: "The word *bhāva*... The point is that if the word *sva* occurring in the compound *svabhāva* were to denote its own form, then that alone would suffice; therefore, the word *bhāva* would be useless. He says: "The word *bhāva*... If only the word *sva* were employed, then because *sva* can also mean "one's own," there might be such a doubt. To ward off that [doubt], the word *bhāva* is employed, because the word *sva* joined with the word *bhāva* generates the cognition of the form itself. This is the sense.

Now, if the word *prakṛti* here denotes "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), then by saying "the *prakṛti*," it would mean "one's own intrinsic nature. Furthermore, it has been stated that the two instances of the word *sva* denote "essential form" (*svarūpa*). In that case, there would be a redundancy; therefore, he says: "In the phrase *svasvarūpam*... Just as the term "essential form" (*svarūpa*) is applied even to what is not the essential form through metaphorical usage, [the author] uses the expression "one's own essential form" (*svasvarūpam*) to avoid that [misunderstanding]. And in that case, even though both instances of the word *sva* denoting "essential form" are present, there is no fault of redundancy.

Thus, even though there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the term "intrinsic nature" is employed through figurative usage; therefore, to prevent that misconception, it is stated as "one's own intrinsic nature. The meaning is that, for this reason, there is no fault of tautology. He explains the three verses beginning with "Though unborn... by means of the Śruti itself. 6, 7, 8.

Having thus described the activities such as entering [the womb] as arising from the very nature [of the Lord], the fruit of that knowledge is now stated: "Birth," etc. Therein, he refutes the misconception that liberation occurs through mere knowledge of the birth and actions of the Lord. The phrase "of those who... implies that it should be understood that [liberation] arises only from their combination. It should be understood that knowledge arises only from the combination of tranquility (*śama*) and the other [means]. This means that even though each has been stated to be a means for knowledge individually, [they must be combined]. The word "stated" implies that it is to be grasped [as the truth]. || 9 ||

To the question, "Why is this knowledge the means to liberation? it is said: "vīta... (in the verse). Therein, in order to dispel any contrary understanding regarding the phrases "consisting of Me" (*manmayāḥ*) and "having attained My state" (*madbhāvam āgatāḥ*), he explains them precisely according to the *Smṛti*: "Mayam iti. Although the direct meaning is that those for whom the Blessed Lord is the foremost are "consisting of the Blessed Lord" (*bhagavanmayāḥ*), even so, the Blessed Lord is the foremost of all. To the question, "What is the distinction of the knowers [of truth]? it is therefore stated: "by whom the preeminence of Hari is understood."

The meaning of the phrase "having attained My state" (madbhāvamāgatāḥ) is "they are liberated. To the question of how the term "My state" (madbhāva) denotes liberation, He says: "In Me" (mayi). "State in Me" (mayi bhāvaḥ) refers to union (sāyujya) and so forth. || 10 ||

Since liberation exists even for those who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividyā*), one might ask: "What is the distinction for those who have taken refuge in You? To this it is said: "Thus... Therein, he says "tathaiva" (in that very same way) in order to dispel the misconception that "he bows down to him who is bowing," and so forth. The meaning is this: there is no equality of fruit between the knowers (*jñānin*) and those possessing the threefold knowledge; for I bestow fruits only in accordance with their service (*sevā*), and because there is a disparity in that service.

Since those who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividyāḥ*) do not worship other deities, how can it be said that they "take refuge in her"? To this [it is replied]: if, while worshipping deities, they desire the accomplishment of their ritual acts (*karman*), then they are indeed following my path; otherwise, there would be no fruit for their actions—this is what is meant by the word "my" (*mama*). In that case, if even those possessing the threefold knowledge follow the path of the Blessed One, there would be no distinction between a devotee of the Lord (*bhāgavata*) and one possessing the threefold knowledge; therefore, he explains the verse with the words "any... (others).
"By surrendering to Me"—the word "end" is to be understood as the ellipsis here. In this regard, he cites the support of the Smṛti: "Any... (verses 11 and 12).

To the question, "Why is there no fruit without the worship of the Blessed One? it is said that his status as a father and so forth is appropriate; this is stated in the verse beginning with "The fourfold order" (*cāturvarṇyam*). Here, one might raise the objection: since there are only three *guṇas*, how can there be a division of the four orders (*cāturvarṇya*) according to the *guṇas*? He dispels this doubt by means of the traditional scripture (*smṛti*) itself: "Sattva... [and so on]. Because he shines (*rājate*) through *sattva*, the Brāhmaṇa is *sāttvika*. Since he possesses more *sattva* than *rajas*, he is the Kṣatriya. One who possesses equal *sattva* and *rajas* is the Vaiśya.

The meaning is that a Śūdra is one who possesses even more tamas along with rajas. By this, it is stated that Brāhmaṇas and the others have sattva as their predominant quality. He states an exception to that: "Only Vaiṣṇavas are sāttvika. Only Vaiṣṇavas are sāttvika, meaning they have sattva as their predominant quality; it is not the state of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth that causes one to be sāttvika and so on.

To the question, "What is the classification of karma like?", he says: "Karma... [and so on]. If only Vaiṣṇavas are *sāttvika*, then what is the basis for such statements as "Brāhmaṇas are *sāttvika*"? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of traditional scripture (*smṛti*) itself: "Vaiṣṇavas... [and so on]. Others are hostile [to this view].
