Since Vaiṣṇavas are rare among Śūdras and others, the meaning is that the various degrees of *sāttvikatva* (sattvic-ness) and so forth are described as being distinct according to the divisions of caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*), in the form of statements such as "only Brāhmaṇas are *sāttvika*."

Just as being *sāttvika* and so forth is not characterized by caste alone, so too tranquility (*śama*) and the rest are not characterized by caste alone; rather, they are characterized by innate caste. To this effect, he cites a Smṛti: "Innate... [The opponent objects: "But what is non-innate Brahminhood and the like? To this he replies: "By birth... This refers to what is well-known.

It has been stated that tranquility (*śama*) and so forth belong only to the natural-born Brahmin, while valor (*śaurya*) and so forth belong only to the natural-born Kṣatriya, and so on. Regarding this, he states an exception: "Viṣṇu... etc. The meaning is that devotion to Viṣṇu, which is denoted by the word *śama*, does not belong to the Brahmin alone; rather, it is present in all social classes (*varṇas*). This is merely an illustration; self-restraint (*dama*) and the other qualities should be understood in the same way. Furthermore, this [usual] tranquility is not what is intended here, for if a Kṣatriya were possessed of such tranquility, there would be a collapse of the kingdom. Thus, this is not the commonly known form of *śama*.

However, although one should have said "devotion to Viṣṇu" or "tranquility," he has stated that which serves the same purpose. To the objection—given that tranquility and the other qualities exist even among Kṣatriyas and others, how can there be the knowledge of the natural distinction between castes such as "this one is a Brāhmaṇa and this one is not"—he says: "The Lord of the Universe. The meaning is that because tranquility and the other qualities abound in a Brāhmaṇa, whereas they exist in decreasing measure among Kṣatriyas and the rest, the natural distinction between castes is to be understood by the abundance or scarcity of these qualities. Thus, "this one is a Brāhmaṇa and this one is not."

In response to the inquiry, "Just as you are the creator of all, is there likewise another creator of you?", it is said: "Of Him" (*tasya*). Regarding that, he explains by means of a *smṛti* (traditional text) in order to dispel the misconception that He is otherwise, stating: "Know Him to be both the agent and the non-agent," because His agency is illusory (*māyika*). If one objects that the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "know Him to be the agent also as the non-agent" is redundant—since such agency and non-agency are not contradictory—he replies: "The word 'also'... and demonstrates its purpose.
"The agent" (kartā) || 13 ||

It might be argued that if the Blessed One were the creator of all, He would be subject to the taint of karma; therefore, it is said: "Not me" (*na mām*). Since the word "me" (*mām*) is already established there, for what purpose is the pronoun "me" (*mām*) used again in the phrase "thus me" (*iti mām*)? To this he says: "The individual soul" (*jīva*). If one were to understand the passage as "He who knows 'actions do not taint me,'" etc., with the intention of identifying oneself with the Lord, a misconception would arise—that it refers to one's own self. To dispel that, the qualification "me" is employed with the sense that "he who fully knows me [the Lord], not his own self. This is the meaning. (13–16)

Having made the promise, "I shall declare that action to you," he speaks the words "of action. He explains them because they serve as the means for attaining the group of letters (varṇas). Regarding the word "action": it should be understood that it arises from Me alone. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following a *r*, even when not within the same word, is observed in such instances as "brahma ṇa indra upayāhi vidvān" and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he indicates that the previous method of interpretation should also be applied to the phrase "and it should be understood" and the rest. || 17 ||

This awakening is praised with the words, "In action" (*karmaṇi*). Therein, he explains the first half [of the verse], because its meaning is difficult to grasp: "In action" (*karmaṇi*). Because of the absence of both ritual action (*karman*) and its fruit, and because of the presence of that [absence] through the term "non-action" (*akarma*), it is indicated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is "action. To the question, "How is it that the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*) are denoted by the terms 'action' and 'non-action' through such etymologies? he says: "The hand" (*kara*). The meaning is: because of being immeasurable (*amita*), that is, because of not being made an object (*aviṣayīkṛta*). To the question, "What is this so-called 'hand' (*kara*)? he says: "The hand" (*kara*).

Since the word *kara* is observed to denote only the hand and so forth, and not the sacrificial ladle (*agṛṣṭi*) and so forth, it is stated: "ending in the letter *s*" (*sakārānta*). The sense is that this [word] ending in *s*, denoting the sacrificer (*hantṛ*) and so forth, is indeed different [from the word for hand]. It should also be understood as denoting the injunction of action (*karmavidhi*). For this very reason, it was stated: "in the injunction of action," and so on. By this word "injunction" (*vidhi*), the objection—namely, how non-agency (*akartṛtva*) is expressed by the word "non-action" (*akarma*)—is refuted. To the question, "How is the *kara* (the agent) measured in the living being (*jīva*), who is not an agent? he says: "That" (*tat*).

The observation of action in one who is not the agent is not contradictory; the point is that even though he is a non-agent by virtue of his independence, he possesses agency dependent upon the Lord. For this very reason, it was stated previously [in the Sūtra] "because of lack of independence," and so forth. Furthermore, he shows that the word *karman* has a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) among the learned to refer to the individual soul (*jīva*). [He says: "And it is well-known. Now, since a person of knowledge does not perform all actions either independently or dependently, how can he be said to be a "performer of all actions"? To this, he says: "All... [and so on].
The meaning is that liberation from the fruits of all one's own appropriate karma is certain. || 18 ||

It is stated that one must not only abandon the conceit of agency, but also abandon desire and the like, by means of the five verses beginning with "Of whom... (*yasya*). In that context, in order to dispel the possibility of perceiving the word division as *nir-āśrayaḥ* (without support) instead of *an-irāśrayaḥ* (not without support), he says: "anirāśrayaḥ. To the question, "Why should the word division not be understood according to the way it is commonly perceived? he replies: "bhagavad-... (of the Blessed One).

The meaning is that even for the knower (*jñānin*), because he has the Lord as his refuge—as stated in passages such as "and for those who are ignorant" (*ajñānāṃ caiva*)—it is untenable for him to be without a refuge; therefore, the division of words is not according to the [literal] understanding [of the compound]. Now, one might ask: since the knower still possesses a connection with a body here, how can he be said to be liberated? To this, he says: "Of the liberated" (*muktasya*). (19–23)

Now, one might ask: where is the abandonment of the conceit of independence intended to occur? Furthermore, he asks "How? regarding the state of being for the sake of sacrifice (*yajñarthatva*). To resolve that, he introduces the subsequent section with the word "Brahman. Here, the oneness of Brahman is stated regarding the ladle (*arpaṇa*) and so forth; in order to dispel the misconception that this refers to the manner of abandoning conceit, he says "in Brahman. [An objector asks: Why should the literal meaning not be accepted? To this, he provides the support of *smṛti* for his own stated position with the words "One... (referring to the *Mahābhārata*).

By this, it is meant that in the case of the oblation and other such acts, one performs the oblation and so forth after realizing that one’s own independence regarding them is not established and that they are dependent upon Brahman; thus, there is the abandonment of the conceit of independence. It is stated that "offering unto Brahman" (brahmārpaṇam) means being for the sake of the sacrifice. || 24 ||

That is elaborated upon by the verse beginning with "The divine" (*daivam*). In that regard, in the first half [of the verse], only the worship of a certain deity is mentioned, and not a sacrifice performed with the realization that Brahman is the goal. Therefore, one might object that this half-verse is not consistent with what preceded; to this, he says: "The divine. By the statement, "They worship the Blessed Lord as the sacrifice," it is expressed that the Blessed Lord himself is the sacrifice, and that such worship of Him is indeed the performance of sacrifice.

How is the Blessed Lord the sacrifice (*yajña*), by virtue of which such worship would constitute the performance of a sacrifice? To this he says: "His own" (*sva*). His very own nature, consisting of bliss and so forth, is the oblation; the Blessed Lord Himself is the fire and He consumes it. Therefore, the meaning is that this [worship] is a sacrifice. Regarding the phrase "in the fire of Brahman," because its meaning is difficult to grasp, he explains it in connection with what precedes: "Brahman. The meaning of the phrase "by that called sacrifice" is: having known that everything is dependent upon Him. || 25 ||

[Objection: But in passages such as "The ear and so forth," it is stated that the oblation consisting of the ear and other senses is indeed offered into the fire called restraint (saṃyama), and not its offering into Brahman. Therefore, this [verse] is not connected with what precedes it. To this, he says: "That... The point is that even here, since it is understood from a consideration of what will be said later in the verse "Thus manifold... that the offering into Brahman is intended, there is no lack of connection. || 26 ||

"Restraint of the senses and so forth" means the restraint of the organs of action (karmendriyas) and of the vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna. Now, one might ask: since it was stated here that "by sacrifice alone" refers to the renunciation of the conceit [of being the agent] within the sacrifice of action itself, how is this consistent with the previous context regarding the "divine" [sacrifices] and so on? To this he says: "By sacrifice alone. Why is this statement—"one is himself the sacrifice," and so forth—considered a novel meaning (apūrvārtha)? To this he says: "By that very [means]," etc. (27–31).

Regarding the phrase “in the mouth of Brahmā,” he says “śrotra-” (in the ear) to dispel the misconception that it means “at the beginning of the Veda. The ellipsis is “such a doubt might arise”; [the author asks] why the meaning as it is commonly understood should not be accepted. To this, he cites the support of Smṛti for the stated meaning: “sarva-” (all). || 32 ||

The reason for the superiority of the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) over sacrifices consisting of material substances (*dravyamaya-yajña*) is stated in the verse beginning with “all” (*sarvam*). Since the words *sarva* and *akhila* are understood to have the same meaning there, and because it might otherwise be perceived that there is no action subsequent to knowledge, he says “all” (*sarvam*) in order to dispel that notion. The intention is that [knowledge] is filled—that is, it becomes fruitful. As for the question of how the word *samāpti* can here mean “filled” when it is not seen to signify completion, he says: “completed” (*samāpta*).

Regarding the science of archery, the statement of the five sages joined by Kṛṣṇa and Sātyaki implies that they were masters of all branches of knowledge. One might argue: "Granted that the word 'completion' (pūrti) may be used even when a task is finished, how can it here denote completion [of study]? Why not simply accept its conventional meaning? To this, he says: "Knowledge," etc. Because yoga is mentioned again, and because the performance of action is taught even after the attainment of knowledge. (33)

Having stated the superiority of knowledge over action, its attainment is now enjoined with the words "That [knowledge]. One might ask: since He has Himself set out for the very purpose of imparting knowledge, and since knowledge has already been taught in the passage beginning with "But never indeed I...", how can it be said that "They will teach you knowledge"? To this he replies: "Knowledge... This is said with the intention of certainty—that they *will* teach it—because it is being spoken of as something to be taught through indirect means (parokṣatayā); thus, there is no contradiction with His having previously set out for the purpose of imparting knowledge.

Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that knowledge has already been taught, for the intention is that even though it was taught in brief, it will be taught again through such statements as "I shall impart knowledge to you. || 34 ||

Knowledge is praised with the words "that which... In that context, he says "in the Self" (*ātmani*) in order to dispel any misconception that it might reside elsewhere than in Himself or in Me. The meaning is that since the status of being the substratum of all beings is impossible for anyone other than the Lord, this is not merely a matter of conventional perception. If this is so, one might ask why the word "and also" (*atho*), which expresses a conjunction, is used; to this he replies: "And also" (*atho*). (35–40)

The fruit of knowledge is called "yoga. In that context, regarding the phrase "one who possesses the Self" (*ātmavantam*): if "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), then the mention of its own connection [to the body] would be both illogical and useless. If, on the other hand, it refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then since all beings equally possess that [Supreme Self], what is the distinction for the knower? To this, he says: "The Self... (verses 41–43).

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 4 ||

Hari Oṃ. This verse demonstrates the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter. [The word] "Yoga" [is explained as follows]: previously, Karma-yoga was described in its integrated form; that [Karma-yoga], moreover, is twofold according to the distinction between Yoga and Saṃnyāsa. And the nature of these two types was briefly stated in such passages as "Perform action" and "Having abandoned attachment. The meaning is that he clarifies that very point with this chapter.

He introduces the question with its underlying intention: "In [the verse] beginning with 'one who has renounced actions through yoga' (6.1), the word *nyāsa* (renunciation) is understood as referring to the stage of life of a wandering ascetic (*yati-āśrama*); whereas the word *yoga* heard in [the verse] beginning with 'practice yoga' (2.48) is taken as referring to the stage of life of a householder (*gṛhastha-āśrama*). Having made this distinction, [the opponent argues that] because ascetics, by abandoning all action, have eligibility for knowledge alone, while householders, by abandoning knowledge, have eligibility for action alone, it is not logical for both to be established in a single goal. This is the intended sense.

He asks which is superior between yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa). The sense is that since both are enjoined as duties to be performed, yet it is impossible to practice both simultaneously, one must choose one over the other; therefore, it is necessary to grasp whichever is the better. || 1 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that this question concerns merely which of the two—yoga and renunciation—is superior, and not with the intention of pointing out a contradiction as previously stated? For if that were so, there would be no resolution. Therefore, [the author] states the intention of the answer: "One... The meaning is as follows: Since both are suitable for a single person and both lead to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), they must both be practiced; thus, if one were superior, the question would be entirely redundant. Furthermore, if the question is intended merely to ascertain their essential nature, then yoga alone is distinguished as superior.

Since no word is heard here that declares yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to be suitable for a single person, [the author] reads and explains that [word]: "Both" (ubhau). The meaning is that both are individually conducive to the highest good. To the question, "Why might this not be so?", he says: "But renunciation... (saṃnyāsastu...). The sense is that because it is stated that renunciation devoid of yoga brings about misfortune, and because yoga devoid of renunciation is impossible, it is only the two combined that are said to bring about the supreme good, not each one individually. || 2 ||

How is the conjunction of yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) appropriate? To resolve the doubt that this might be so because of the difference in qualification between the ascetic (yati) and the householder (gṛhastha), he introduces the verse with the words "dveṣādīti" (beginning with "hatred," etc.). Here, in passages such as "one who has renounced action" (saṃnyastakarmāṇam), and likewise in "practice yoga" (yogamātiṣṭha), it should be understood that what is intended is yoga consisting of dedication to the Lord and so forth, and not the stage of life (āśrama) of a householder.

[Objection: But how can the avoidance of hatred and so forth be called renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) here? This would contradict the statement that defines renunciation as the abandonment of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*): "The wise know renunciation to be the relinquishing of optional rites. To this, he says: "And not... [This objection does not apply. There would be such a contradiction if, in this context, the mere avoidance of hatred and so forth were intended to be designated as renunciation. But that is not the case.

The meaning is that even when accompanied by the abandonment of desire-driven actions (*kāmyakarman*), the avoidance of hatred and the like is intended to be *saṃnyāsa*. How, then, is the avoidance of longing and so forth called *saṃnyāsa* here? Because it has been described as *tyāga* (renunciation) in the verse: "The wise declare the renunciation of the fruits of all actions to be *tyāga*" (Gītā 18.2). Nor is there a lack of contradiction because *saṃnyāsa* and *tyāga* are identical; for in the verse beginning with "Of desire-driven [actions]," *tyāga* is mentioned as distinct from *nyāsa* (formal renunciation), and thus there would be a contradiction [if they were the same]. To this, he says: "Nor... [and so on].

The avoidance of longing and the like is indeed renunciation (*nyāsa*). Nor is there any contradiction in describing it as abandonment (*tyāga*), because renunciation and abandonment are one and the same. Nor is there a contradiction in their being mentioned separately.

Just as, for instance, although the Pāṇḍavas are Kurus, the separate statement "the seed of the lineage of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas" is appropriate—since the Pāṇḍavas are a sub-division of the Kurus and thus the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas do not possess direct identity—so too, although abandonment is renunciation, because abandonment is a sub-division of renunciation, there is no direct identity between abandonment and renunciation; therefore, the sense is that their separate mention is justified.

The objection raised—that because the words "renunciation" (nyāsa) and so forth refer to the stages of life (āśrama) such as that of the ascetic (yati), there can be no coexistence [of these stages] due to the difference in their respective qualifications—is refuted by not accepting that those words have such a meaning. || 3 ||

Now, it is stated that even this distinction of qualification is not tenable, beginning with the word "Sāṅkhya. Because its meaning is difficult to grasp, he explains the verse [beginning] with "The ignorant" (bālāḥ). The meaning is: only one who is properly established in the path of knowledge attains the fruit of knowledge; and only one who is properly established in the path of action attains the fruit of action.

Having stated that householders possess the qualification for knowledge because of the existence of attaining the state reachable only by ascetics through knowledge alone, the conclusion is drawn with the word "yat" (which). In that regard, one might ask why the identity of knowledge and action is asserted in the concluding sentence, "The Sāṅkhya is one"; therefore, he explains it correctly with the words "Therefore... The phrase "of the knowers, the ascetics" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Even if a performer of action attains the fruit of action solely through the proper performance of action, [the opponent asks] from where does his knowledge come? To this, he says:

"Not indeed" (na hi). Even if one attains the fruit of knowledge solely through the practice of the path of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), how can there be action for the knower? To this doubt, the resolution should be seen as follows: for one established on the path of knowledge, the correct practice [of that path] does not occur without action, because it lacks the means for achieving the complete fruit. In this regard, he cites the agreement of the *Smṛti*: "Free from desire" (*niṣkāma*). By this, knowledge is said to belong to those who perform action. With the word "by the intellect" (*buddhyā*), he states another reason for the existence of knowledge.

"From this" refers to both [the paths] called "liberation. The meaning is that for those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*), [liberation occurs] precisely because of the existence of knowledge (*jñāna*). By this, the verse beginning with "that which by the Sāṅkhyas" is explained. To the question, "If both possess the existence of both knowledge and action, how can there be a distinction between the stages of life (*āśrama*)?", he says: "Therefore. The sense is that the existence of both in both cases is established through reasoning and other means. There is the possibility of contraction and expansion. 4, 5.

It has been stated that only the combination of *yoga* and *saṃnyāsa* brings about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). An objection is raised against their non-combination in the verse beginning with "But renunciation... (*saṃnyāsastu*). He explains this by recalling that very [scriptural] tradition: "Liberation... and "Yoga..."; the word "is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The connection is that [the path] is of the nature of that [liberation] because it is offered to Viṣṇu. The first three quarters [of the verse] have been explained; now he explains the first half of the verse beginning with "There is no other" (*nānyaḥ*). He clarifies this with: "To Viṣṇu... and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), it should be understood that an action performed with the thought that one's own appropriate duties—such as offering them to Viṣṇu—need not be performed, results in hell. Why is it said "due to non-yoga" (ayogataḥ) instead of simply "without yoga" (yogaṃ vinā)? To this he says: "That [renunciation]" (yam). Since the identity of yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) will be stated later, the meaning is that renunciation must indeed be understood as having the nature of yoga.

Since yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) are one and the same, how is it that they are mentioned separately in the phrase "renunciation and karma-yoga"? To this he says: "Yoga... etc. Yoga and renunciation have one and the same meaning; however, renunciation is a specific sub-division of yoga. Therefore, their separate mention is justified, just as in the case of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas. || 6 ||

Having stated that renunciation (*nyāsa*) without the form of yoga serves as a means to achieve misfortune, the fact that renunciation in the form of yoga—spoken of by the phrase "yogayuktaḥ"—is a means to liberation is now elaborated upon. Regarding the term "yogayuktaḥ": since it is precisely yoga and renunciation that must be discussed there, and since those two have already been expressed by the words "yogayukta" and so forth, one might ask why the phrase "sarvabhūtātmabhūtātmā" is used. To this he says: "sarva... (all). By this too, yoga alone is being expressed; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Nor is there any redundancy because yoga has already been mentioned by the word *yogayukta*; for the meaning is that *karmayoga* was expressed by the term *yogayukta*, whereas by this [present] term, *dhyānayoga* is expressed.

Here, the identity of all beings is stated regarding the qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*). To the question, "How then can this be called an exposition of *dhyānayoga*? he explains it precisely through a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "From taking up... [and so on]. "With mind fixed on the elements" means with mind established [in them]. (7)

It has been stated that renunciation in the form of yoga is the cause of liberation. To this end, he introduces two verses as a refutation of the question: "In what manner does renunciation take the form of yoga? He explains [the verse] by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*) in order to dispel the misconception that the sense organs themselves possess independent agency. [He says: "By Viṣṇu... (8–9).

With the intention that liberation occurs for one who has performed renunciation through yoga and is not merely figurative, the fruit is stated again in the words, “In Brahman. Therein, to dispel the misconception that the dedication of actions to Brahman means their non-performance, he says, “That is worship. The phrase “the dedication of actions” is to be supplied as the ellipsis; the sense is that otherwise, it would contradict the statement that one “performs” them. Furthermore, even in your own position, if actions were performed by the Lord, then the individual soul (jīva) would be rendered a non-agent.

And in that case, the statement "he acts" would be contradicted; furthermore, the phrase "for my auspicious purpose" would be impossible. Therefore, he says: "By [His] sovereignty. It is indeed true that if actions were performed by the Lord, the individual soul (jīva) would be a non-agent. However, this does not entail an impossibility regarding the soul's agency or its connection with the fruit of action. The point is that since non-agency is accepted only in the sense of a lack of independence, agency is established through dependence on the Lord.

Furthermore, if the individual soul (jīva) were not independent, its status as the performer of worship to the Lord and its connection with auspicious yoga would be untenable; for we do not observe the use of the term "agent" (kartṛ) nor a connection with results in the case of one who is not independent. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by means of a traditional authority (smṛti): "It is his own salutation. The words "caused to be performed by the child" are to be supplied. The connection is that it would be performed by the child as the agent. (10–12)

Furthermore, what is called the "placing of actions in Brahman" is simply the relinquishing of the conceit of one's own independence regarding them; it is not the abandonment of their essential nature. Thus he says: "Therefore. For by the words "having placed all actions in Brahman," renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is indeed expressed, and its definition is elaborated by the phrase "all actions. In that context, because there is no abandonment of the essential nature of the actions, their renunciation is stated to be by means of the mind alone.

Therefore, the sense is that even here, the meaning is not the abandonment of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of actions. To the question, "If renunciation is designated as being by the mind alone, how can there be no abandonment of their essential nature? he says: "Because of lack of independence" (*asvātantrya*). Renunciation of action by the mind alone consists precisely in the abandonment of the conceit of independence; it is not the abandonment of the essential nature. For if it were so, the qualification "by the mind" would be redundant—this is the sense. (10–13)

As for the claim that the soul’s lack of agency is due solely to its absence of independence, whereas dependent agency does indeed exist, that is not tenable; for it contradicts the subsequent statement, “There is no agency. To this, he says: “Just as... Even though souls lack independent agency and so forth by their own nature, such agency exists when granted by the Supreme Self. Therefore, he dispels here the very doubt as to how it can be said that [agency] is grounded in Brahman.

The intended meaning is that [the text] does not, however, state the total absence of agency in living beings (jīvas). Furthermore, the phrase "independence regarding the connection with the fruits of action" should also be supplied. By this, the charge of redundancy regarding the statement "neither agency nor actions" is also removed. Now, one might object: "In this [verse], only the absence of agency and so forth is stated, and not the lack of independence therein; therefore, how is this doubt dispelled by this? To this, he says: "In action... [and] "does not create agency and so forth" refers to that [state].

The meaning is simply that [the Lord] does not create independence; therefore, this serves as the resolution of that doubt—this is the sense. Now, one might ask: why could it not be the case that here the absence of agency and so forth is being predicated of the Lord alone? To this he says: "Otherwise. The meaning is that if it were here stated that the Lord alone lacks agency and so forth, then the statement "he does not create the agency of the world" would be redundant.

As for what was said—that the individual soul possesses agency and so forth by virtue of its dependence—that is not tenable. For it has been stated that the Lord does not create the world's agency and other such qualities. Nor does the phrase "does not create" mean that He lacks independence; rather, it is used in the sense that although agency and the rest do exist, He does not bestow independence upon them. Since no such usage is observed where one says "He does not create agency," etc., while intending to convey the non-bestowal of independence, [the author] says: "In the case of a country... (janapade).

If the agency of both the individual souls (*jīvas*) and the Lord of all (*sarvātman īśvara*) were not negated here, then the statement that activity proceeds from "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) alone would be untenable; therefore, he says: "By Himself" (*svayam eva*). Here, the term "intrinsic nature" does not denote the well-known *svabhāva* (as a fixed essence), for that would involve the aforementioned contradiction. Rather, the meaning is that the Blessed Lord alone [is the agent], because He is independent of anything else in His own abiding as well as in His acting upon others.

With the intention that the use of an unfamiliar term instead of a well-known one is for the purpose of indicating the reason (*hetu*), he states the meaning of the sentence: "Because it is its very nature" (*svabhāvatvāt*).

Now, why should one postulate such a different meaning? Why could it not be the case that agency and so forth belong neither to the individual soul (*jīva*) nor to the Lord (*īśvara*), and that the activity of the universe proceeds solely from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*)? This is because the phrase "of the world" can reasonably be understood as "with reference to the world. To this, he provides support for his own position through a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "On account of independence," etc. The ellipsis is: "He does not create this [world], but rather it proceeds by itself. He says the following because if the Lord alone were the agent, there would be the taint of *karma* (moral action).

"Simply by virtue of His autonomy. By this, the meaning of the phrase "He does not take [anything]" is also explained. If the Lord exists as the agent who remains present within all things through His autonomy, why is He not perceived? To this he says: "Due to ignorance. By this, the term "ignorance" is explained.

As for the claim that "the Lord himself brings [all things] into being," that is not tenable, because He lacks agency (*kartṛtva*). Even if agency were to exist in Him, it would not be inherent (*asvābhāvika*)—to this he says: "I am... and so forth. The two statements, "I am all" and "He is the cause," are the proof for the existence of His agency; "He is the cause of this" and so forth are for the sake of establishing that His agency is inherent. The meaning is: "Apart from You, nothing whatsoever is done by anyone, whether far or near."

Here, by stating that there is no agency other than the Blessed Lord, and by the possibility of God’s agency being independent of others, it is precisely His naturalness (*svābhāvikatvam*) that is expressed. In the phrase "as in the world" (*lokavat*) as well, by stating His agency in the absence of any expectation for results and the like, it is precisely His naturalness that is expressed. Furthermore, he says [the following] to show that for God, non-agency is not unnatural, and agency is indeed natural: "On the contrary... (*viparīta*). Now, one might object: "By the term 'unnatural,' we intend to mean that God’s agency is indeterminable (*anirvācya*)."

But [the Lord's agency] is neither dependent on a fruit nor dependent on another; therefore, there is no contradiction with the cited statement. To this he says: "It is indeterminable" (*anirvācya*). The position that the Lord's agency is indeterminable has already been refuted in the second chapter precisely because indeterminable entities have been refuted there. Thus, the sense is that it need not be refuted again here.

Now, one might object: "Since Brahman is devoid of all distinctions, how can it possess agency in the ultimate sense? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca). The agency of Brahman would be non-ultimate only if it were devoid of all distinctions; however, that is not tenable. The underlying point is that if such were the case, Brahman would lapse into a state of voidness, and those who accept it [as such] would consequently fall into the position of being Nihilists (Śūnyavādins).

Even though Brahman is devoid of all specific attributes (*viśeṣa*), it does not follow that Brahman is a void (*śūnya*), because of its existence. To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). There would not be the consequence of Brahman being a void if its existence were established. But that establishment does not occur, because [Brahman] is admitted to be devoid of all specific attributes; this is the sense. Why, even if it is devoid of all specific attributes, is existence not established? To this, he says: "In terms of being expressible" (*vācyatva*). If Brahman exists, its existence must either be existence itself or be the state of being expressible by the word "exists."
And because that [entity] possesses specific qualities, it is not logical for it to be devoid of all specific qualities; this is the intended meaning.

If existence (*astitva*) were accepted as a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*) of Brahman, then in the case of non-distinction (*nirviśeṣatva*), its existence would be unestablished. This is not so, because that [existence] is merely the very nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman; therefore, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). If existence and so forth were merely the nature of Brahman and not its specific attributes, then terms such as "Brahman exists" would be synonyms, just like the word "Brahman" itself. Consequently, the co-occurrence [of these terms] in such passages as "If one knows that Brahman exists" would be untenable.

The sense is that, in that case, the Upaniṣads would be as unworthy of respect as the ravings of a madman due to the fault of tautology. Even though there is no specific attribute such as existence (astitva) in Brahman, words like "is" (asti) indicate it by means of excluding superimposed attributes such as non-existence; therefore, there is no synonymy among these words. To this, he says: "By way of exclusion" (vyāvartya). There would be non-synonymy for words like "is" if those words excluded non-existence and other such attributes from Brahman; however, that is not tenable.

The meaning is this: because the exclusion of non-existence and other such attributes must be based on the specific qualities—such as existence—that are admitted to reside in Brahman, which has been accepted as being excluded [from those attributes]; and because those [qualities] are not admitted [in the case of the non-existent]; for even if existence and other specific qualities were present in Brahman, it would follow that non-existence (asat) would also possess that exclusion [of non-existence]. Just as the word "Gaṅgā" refers to its bank by secondary indication (lakṣya), even though the quality of being the Gaṅgā itself is absent there, it would follow that the exclusion of "non-Gaṅgā-ness" would also apply [to the non-existent].

He states that it is not correct to say that words such as "is" (*asti*) and so forth do not convey specific qualities such as existence (*astitva*) and the like; [he says this] with the words "Otherwise... (*anyathā*). If words such as "is" did not convey specific qualities of Brahman such as existence, then they would be utterly useless. This is because, for one who desires to know Brahman, the statement of Brahman itself must be purposeful, and because Brahman is already understood from the word "Brahman" alone. Nor can the exclusion of non-existence (*asattva*) and so forth be the purpose, since it has been stated that such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, [the inquiry] "from what is Brahman excluded? is not desired to be known. If it is argued that even though it is not desired to be known, the delusion regarding the non-existence and so forth of Brahman is being prevented, we say no, because this position cannot withstand analysis. Does the delusion occur with respect to a perceived or an unperceived Brahman? Not the first, because if Brahman is perceived, its mere nature—including existence and so forth—is also perceived, leaving no room for delusion; moreover, if existence and so forth are not perceived even when Brahman is perceived, its status as a mere entity (tanmātratva) would be untenable. Nor is the second, because it would entail the postulation of something never before observed—this is the sense.

Furthermore, Brahman is not indicated by words such as "exists" (*asti*) through the exclusion of non-existence and so forth; for it is accepted that [Brahman] is inexpressible by any word. He states this, saying "And not," because it is established that only that which is expressible by a word can be indicated. It was previously stated that if existence were admitted for Brahman, it would follow that it possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatva*), and thus its [true] nature would not be established. For this reason as well, the existence of Brahman is not established, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it. Since the establishment of an object is never seen to occur without a means of valid knowledge, and if one were to mention a means of valid knowledge, the admission that Brahman is beyond the scope of all means of valid knowledge would be violated—this is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that [Brahman] is not established because there is a lack of evidence for its existence, then the non-existence of Brahman is likewise not established, since there too there is a lack of evidence. Thus, it is not appropriate to claim that the doctrine of Brahman is identical to the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda); therefore, he says: "Non-existence... [The meaning is: we need not state a separate proof for the non-existence of Brahman, because its non-existence is established simply by the absence of any proof for its existence.

The meaning is that just as non-existence is established in the case of the seventh taste and so forth due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence, so it is exactly the same here. By this, an inference based on the mark of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-liṅgaka-anumāna*) is indicated.

[Objection: "Surely, even if Brahman is not known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its non-existence cannot be asserted, because it is established precisely by way of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*). [Reply: This is not so, because the alternatives are untenable. To explain: regarding the self-luminosity of Brahman, does a means of valid cognition exist or not? It cannot be the second [alternative], for in the absence of a cognition, that [self-luminosity] would not be established; thus he says: "And as for self-luminosity... In the first case, is this self-luminosity something distinct from Brahman, or is it its very nature (*svarūpa*)? He refutes the first [position] with: "Self-luminosity..."

The meaning is that if the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of Brahman were established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) as something distinct from Brahman itself, then it would follow that Brahman possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). He refutes the second alternative with the words "If not" (*na cet*): if self-luminosity is not distinct from Brahman, but is rather its very nature (*svarūpa*), then by accepting the existence of a means of knowledge regarding self-luminosity, one would effectively have accepted that Brahman itself is accessible through a means of knowledge. Consequently, the doctrine of its being beyond the reach of any means of knowledge (*aprameyatva*) would be destroyed.

By the term *svaprakāśa* (self-luminous), it is not meant that [Brahman] possesses the quality of illuminating its own object; for if that were so, Brahman would be distinct from itself, and thus Brahman would possess attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). Rather, it means simply the absence of being illuminated by another. Therefore, he says: "by another" (*parā*). If, by the term *svaprakāśa*, one intends merely the negation of being illuminated by another, then Brahman would be devoid of illumination altogether, since being illuminated by another is not admitted.

The meaning is that this self-luminosity, known as the illumination of its own object, has been refuted by the aforementioned method through the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and even if it were to exist, it would be discarded because it would entail the possession of specific qualities (*saviśeṣatva*) and the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*).

Even so, it cannot be said that Brahman is non-existent; for, since Brahman is indicated by such scriptural passages as "Brahman exists" through the exclusion of non-existence and the like, its existence is established by implication (*arthataḥ*). If this is argued, we say no, because it has already been refuted. Even granting it for the sake of argument, he says: "by implication. [The phrase] "by that means of knowledge" (*tat-pramāṇataḥ*) means by the authority of the scripture stating "Brahman exists. Furthermore, he states that the claim that Brahman is established through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is contradicted: "self-luminous," etc.

By the term "self-luminous" (svaprakāśa), it is not admitted that Brahman possesses the quality of illuminating its own object; rather, it is merely the non-admission of its being illuminated by another. Therefore, the meaning is that because Brahman is devoid of both self-illumination and illumination by another, it cannot be established as self-luminous at all, and certainly not established by that very term.

Furthermore, Brahman could possess self-luminosity only if luminosity itself were possible; yet that is not possible. This is because the luminosity called "Brahman" is devoid of anything to be illumined. First of all, it cannot be self-illumined, as that is not admitted [by you]. Nor can it be illumined by another, because no such other exists. Nor should it be said that Brahman is of the nature of luminosity devoid of anything to be illumined; for luminosity is never observed to exist without something to be illumined, whether that be itself or another.

"Just as food is not seen without that which is to be eaten, so it is exactly thus," he says: "The illumination. Now, one might object: in a single action, it is contradictory for one and the same thing to possess both agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*). Therefore, how can it be said that illumination is not seen without that which is illuminated? For this would entail that a single entity possesses both agency and objecthood—since it is said that it is illuminated by itself, it illuminates itself, and it is illuminated. To this, he replies: "Agency and objecthood..."
The sense is that it is contradictory for a single entity to think "I know myself" with respect to itself.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Light is indeed a substance; therefore, how can it require an object, like eating and so forth? Dispelling this doubt, he states an additional defect: "And knowledge... [and so on]. It is accepted that Brahman's being light consists in its being knowledge. However, it is not logical for Brahman to possess the nature of knowledge, because it is devoid of both a knower and an object of knowledge; the meaning is that knowledge devoid of these has never been observed. He concludes: "Therefore... [and so on].

The meaning is that because Brahman is devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) and is immeasurable (*aprameya*), its existence cannot be established; this is the sense. He concludes the refutation of the Lord’s lack of agency and so forth with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Because [the position] is faulty, the view that "agency does not exist, or if it exists, it is not inherent" is rejected. Furthermore, he cites scripture regarding the Lord’s agency by nature with the verse beginning "Hari" (verse 14).

By the word "by knowledge" (*jñānena*), another means for the aforementioned knowledge is stated as "learning" (*vidyā*). In this context, what is intended is not equanimity toward objects such as Brahmins and the like; rather, it refers specifically to the Supreme Brahman residing within them. This is because Brahmins and others are inherently unequal, whereas the Brahman residing within them is equal, and because contrary knowledge is not a means to [true] knowledge. With this intention, he cites the authoritative evidence regarding the inequality of individual souls and the equality of Brahman: "In those who are unequal... (*viṣameṣu*) and so forth.
By this, the statement "Brahman is indeed faultless and equal" is also explained. || 18-20 ||

That which was stated—that the renunciation consisting of yoga (yogarūpasaṃnyāsa) brings about the supreme good—is now established by the verse beginning with "bāhya. Because its meaning is difficult to grasp, he explains it as follows: when even a renunciant who is engaged in only a small measure of yoga through the remembrance of the Supreme Self and so forth finds happiness even within saṃsāra, then what need is there to mention that one who is engaged in the great yoga of meditation and so forth will find the supreme good such as liberation? This is the sense of the passage. (21–23)

The characteristic of the knower (*jñānin*) is stated as: "He who is inwardly happy" (*yo'ntaḥsukhaḥ*). Regarding that, the phrase "become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*) is explained as "merged with Brahman" (*brahmaṇaikībhūta*) in order to dispel any other possible misconception. [The commentary says: "In Brahman. The word "with the mind" (*manasā*) is to be supplied. If it is asked, "Why should the meaning not be exactly as it appears [in the literal sense]?"—the answer is no; for even in the case of a knower, the difference from Brahman has been established. Furthermore, he states another defect: "Otherwise. If, in this context, the state of being Brahman were predicated of the knower, then [the statement] "he attains Brahman" would be contradictory.

The meaning is that no one indeed goes to their own self. Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that having internal happiness and so forth is a characteristic of the knower; however, how can 'having an internal light' (*antarjyotiṣṭva*) be a characteristic of the seer of Brahman? For that [internal light] is simply the state of being a seer of Brahman. To this, he says: "Having internal happiness and so forth" (*antaḥsukhatvādikam*). Here, it is not "having an internal light" that is stated to be the characteristic of the knower; rather, it is precisely "having internal happiness" and so on. The intention is that "having an internal light" is mentioned there as the cause for those qualities. (24–27)

By the phrase beginning with "brahmayoga," the mode of ordinary meditation is described in the verse starting with "sparśān. There, one might raise the objection: how can one who is meditating but not yet liberated be said to be "liberated indeed"? Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it by means of a traditional authority (smṛti): "He is not liberated [but is as if liberated]. This refers to a resemblance to the liberated state, consisting in the abandonment of egoism and other such traits. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "he is called 'liberated indeed'. Since such a result occurs through the power of knowledge alone, therefore... [28-29]

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 5 ||

Hari Oṃ. He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words, "Dhyānam" (Meditation). It was promised [in the previous chapter] with the words, "But regarding Yoga, hear this. And Yoga is twofold: Karma-yoga and Dhyāna-yoga. Among these, Karma-yoga has been defined both briefly and in detail. The method of Dhyāna-yoga was defined briefly at the end of the fifth chapter; its detailed exposition is what is stated in this chapter—this is the sense.

The doubt that the meditation under discussion belongs only to one who has moved on by abandoning the sacred fires and so forth due to a state of detachment is dispelled by the word "anāśrita" (unattached). In that regard, it would be untenable to say that there is no status as a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) or a yogi for one who is without the sacred fire; for if that were the case, it would follow that the stage of life of the ascetic (*yati*) is not to be practiced, since the ascetic would lack both yoga and renunciation by virtue of being without the sacred fire. Since those two alone are the means to the highest good, the author says: "He... (referring to the verse).

The consequence would arise that the stage of life of the ascetic (*yati*) is not to be practiced if the ascetic were without fire; however, that is not the case. The sense is that he is "established in Brahman" (*brahmaniṣṭha*), for there is scriptural mention of fire even for him. Furthermore, he states that the ascetic does not lack fire: "The Self" (*ātma*). The meaning is that because the fire previously accepted during the stage of life was deposited within the Self at the time of entering the ascetic stage, the ascetic is not without fire. By this, it is shown that the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and the yogi are not merely one who is without fire and without ritual action (*akriya*).
However, by this [statement], the false interpretation that "he who performs the action which is his duty does so without depending on the fruit of the action" is also refuted. || 1 ||

By the statement "He is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi," the doubt that renunciation and yoga are distinct is dispelled by the words "renunciation" [and so forth]. To the question, "In that case, since renunciation and yoga are one and the same, why are they mentioned separately? he says: "Yoga... [2]

Among the various forms of *karmayoga*, what kind of yoga is necessarily required by one who seeks knowledge? To this, it is said: "of one desiring to ascend" (*ārurukṣoḥ*). Since the word *yogarūḍha* has a difficult meaning, its sense is explained as "one who has fully ascended. Here, having stated that action is required for one seeking knowledge, it is now stated that the cessation of action is required for the knower. Thus, there is no contradiction with such statements as "neither without the sacred fires nor without ritual acts. To this, he says: "of various people," meaning of those who are high, low, and middling.

"Like the king's [servant]" means that service is established as necessary, just as it is for a king and others. To the question, "If service must be performed even by one established in yoga (*yogastha*), what is the distinction between one seeking yoga (*yogarthin*) and one established in yoga? he says: "By him also. This refers to other seekers of yoga. When the distinction between the seeker of yoga and the one established in yoga ought to be stated, why is the distinction between the unaccomplished and the accomplished mentioned? To this he says: "Having attained... and so forth.

[The author asks: "How is service to various people a means to knowledge? To this he says: "Through the grace of the Blessed Lord," beginning with the words "tasya" (of that). [Objection: Since even the ignorant abide in Hari, why is it said that one established in yoga must abide in Hari? To this he explains what was stated: "siddha" (perfected), etc. "Anything else" refers to service to various people and so forth. [Objection: Since liberation is certain for the knower, what is the need for meditation and the like? To this he says: "tasya" (of that). And thus, the sense is that there is a fulfillment of bliss in liberation.

Here, by the word *karman*, service to various people alone is meant, and not the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth. And by the word *śama*, the cessation of service to various people is meant, as well as meditation on the Lord (*bhagavad-dhyāna*) and so forth; it does not mean the cessation of rituals such as the twilight prayers. This is because of the designation (*samākhyā*) in the Smṛti [which specifies] "of various people. Therefore, the sense is that there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. To clarify that the word *śama* denotes meditation on Viṣṇu and so forth, he cites the Smṛti for the sake of clarity: "Śama... (Verse 3).

The definition of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-lexical) is stated by the words "For when... (*yadā hi*). Regarding this, since it is said that for the knower there is an absence of action—by stating that he is not attached to actions—there might appear to be a contradiction with such statements as "nor is he inactive" (*na cākriyaḥ*). To address this, he asks: "How so? (*katham*). The point is that here the attachment to action is not being predicated of the knower in terms of his essential nature; rather, it refers only to the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding all actions. This is because [the Lord] has already explained it in that very way.

If the renunciation of *saṅkalpa* (volition) applies to all actions, then it would follow that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the action must be renounced; for as long as the nature [of the action] is not abandoned, the renunciation of *saṅkalpa* is impossible. To this, he says: "In Me" (*mayi*). This consequence of abandoning the nature of the action would arise only if the abandonment of the nature of *saṅkalpa* itself were intended. But that is not the case, because by the term "renunciation of *saṅkalpa*" what is intended is precisely the knowledge that *saṅkalpa* and so forth are dependent upon the Lord.

The sense is that, in the passage "having renounced all actions in Me" (mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasya), it has been established that the word *saṃnyāsa* means the knowledge of dependence upon the Lord. He states another method as well: "dependent on Me" (madadhīnam). || 4 ||

It is said that divine grace (*bhagavat-prasāda*) is the primary means for ascending in yoga, expressed by the word "should uplift" (*uddharet*). In this context, to dispel the misconception that the term "self" (*ātman*) refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he explains it precisely by recollecting the traditional teaching: "He should uplift. To clarify what kind of persons are "good" and what kind are "bad," he explains the phrase beginning with "that": "of another person"—that is, of one who has not brought the Supreme Self under control through devotion.

For this reason as well, he states that it is appropriate to understand the term *ātman* here as referring to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). [He says: "The Supreme Self. The sense is this: when the question arises—"What does He do for one by whom the self has been brought under control?"—the supplementary portion of the text (vākyaśeṣa) states that "that Supreme Self, having been brought under control, becomes perfectly established in his heart. Therefore, it is understood that even previously, by the word *ātman*, the Supreme Self alone was intended. || 5 || 6 ||

The characteristics of one who has ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*) are elaborated upon in the verse beginning with "cold and heat. In that context, he states [the following] while keeping in mind the distinction between the meanings of the words *jñāna* and *vijñāna*: "In all cases" (*sarvatra*), meaning in the Vedas and so forth. (7–8)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since friends and the others are unequal, how can it be said that the man of knowledge possesses an equal mind toward them? Anticipating this doubt, he dispels it by means of a traditional authority (smṛti). Regarding the verse beginning with "yasya" (of whom): in order to refute the notion that the pairs of words *suhṛt* (friend) and *mitra* (ally), as well as *ari* (enemy) and *dveṣya* (hated one), and *udāsīna* (neutral) and *madhyastha* (indifferent), have the same meaning, he states their respective meanings through tradition. [The commentary explains: "*Animitta*" (without cause) means one who performs a service having first recognized [the recipient] as such; "*upakārakṛt*" (one who does good) means one who performs a service after personally determining that the other person is in a state of distress. (9–19)

The nature of the perfection of yoga is stated by the passage beginning with "When," and so forth. In that context, he says "the Self" (ātmānam) in order to dispel the impression that the two occurrences of the word "Self" (ātman) refer to the individual soul (jīva) and such; for otherwise, satisfaction would be impossible—this is the sense. (20–26)

The fruit of yoga is stated as "tranquil" (*praśānta*). In that regard, he states the meaning of the term *brahmabhūta* in order to dispel the perception of any other [literal] sense: "in Brahman," etc. The implication is that otherwise there would be contradiction with many authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By this, the previously mentioned term *matsaṃstha* is also explained. (27–28)

The object of meditation is stated as "dwelling in all beings. To dispel the misconception that the word "Self" (ātman) there refers to the individual soul (jīva), he says: "all... The intention is that since the brief statement "the enjoyer" specifies that the Supreme Self alone is the object of meditation, and because of the subsequent reference in the words "who [knows] Me," this is the meaning. (29–30)

The fruit of meditation on the Supreme Self is stated as "all. In that context, he explains the phrase "established in the state of a knower" (*ṇakatvamāsthitaḥ*) in order to dispel any other possible misconception: "abiding in all" (*sarvavrate*). The sense is that otherwise, there would be a contradiction with his own statement that [the Self] "dwells in all beings" (*sarvabhūtasthitam*). || 31 ||

The term "Self" (ātman) is used to describe a particular state of the yogi himself. To dispel the misconception that this [Self] pertains to all living beings, he explains [the verse] with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). Here, affection toward those belonging to the Lord (bhagavadīya) alone is enjoined, as if toward oneself, and not toward non-Vaiṣṇavas. This is because it has been stated that for Vaiṣṇavas alone the Lord is dear ("the Self is a kinsman"), whereas it has been stated that for non-Vaiṣṇavas the Lord is not dear ("of the non-Self"). (32–36)

He states the meaning of the word *ayati* found in Arjuna’s question in order to dispel the misconception that it refers to a householder (*gṛhastha*) and so forth: "The word *ayati*... [means] the householder and others. To the objection, "Why should it not have that very meaning? he says: "Because of effort... The intention is that the rebuttal would involve the possibility of one becoming a member of the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramin*) through the power of faith in that [state of being a householder].

[Objection: Since the word *yoga* signifies a means to knowledge (*jñānopāya*), and since [the Lord has said] "The man of faith attains knowledge" (*śraddhāvān labhate jñānam*) and so forth, faith (*śraddhā*) is also a means to knowledge; therefore, there is a mutual contradiction between these two statements, namely, "endowed with faith" (*śraddhayopetaḥ*) and "whose mind has wavered from yoga" (*yogāccalitamānasaḥ*). To this, he says: "Yoga... The meaning is as follows: This contradiction would exist if the word *yoga* here were used in a general sense to denote any means to knowledge. But that is not the case, because what is intended here is specifically *dhyāna* (meditation). Nor is there a contradiction in the word *yoga* denoting a means to knowledge, because *dhyāna* itself is a particular kind of means to knowledge. This is the intended sense.

For one whose mind has wavered from yoga, the fruit described in such passages as "having attained the worlds of the merit-makers" is established for the seeker (*jijñāsu*). In that context, he explains [the verse] by means of that very Smṛti in order to dispel the notion that there is an absence of injunctions and prohibitions for the seeker of yoga: "Mokṣa... and so on. "Established therein" (*tadāsthita*) means one who possesses only slight engagement in that [yoga]. (44–45)

Yoga is praised in the verse beginning with “tapasvibhyaḥ. Since yoga has knowledge as its purpose, one might ask how it can be said to be superior to knowledge; therefore, he explains this by means of that very traditional authority (smṛti): “Of austerity,” and “by the meditation of the ignorant. For one who does not know the method of correct meditation, the mere knowledge of the method of meditation is superior to meditation itself. The meaning is that meditation accompanied by knowledge of the method of meditation is more excellent than knowledge of the method of meditation alone. He also states the gradation even among meditators: “Even there,” and so forth.

To explain what kind of person is a non-devotee (*abhakta*), he says: "Other" (*anya*). Those in whom there is no devotion are "non-devotees. By the phrase "knowing others to be dependent on me," the worship of others is described as being by way of [my] retinue. "Pure-minded even among my worshippers" means that one who is free from desire (*niṣkāma*) is superior; by this, the verse beginning with "among yogins" (*yoginām*) is explained. For instance: among all yogins, he alone who possesses devotion to me—expressed by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*)—is considered disciplined (*yukta*).
Even among those, he who worships me alone is considered more disciplined; and even among them, he who worships me without desire for fruit is considered the most disciplined. (46-47)

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 6 ||

Hari Oṃ. [The author] shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words "bhagavad-... etc. The meditation previously mentioned is a means to knowledge only when preceded by devotion, and not otherwise; therefore, the meaning is that the greatness of the Blessed Lord is described in this chapter for the sake of devotion. To the objection—"Since the greatness of the Blessed Lord has already been described previously in the passage beginning with 'na tvevāham' (7.19), what is the purpose of this?"—it is said: "viśeṣataḥ" (in detail). The meaning is that what was previously stated in brief is here stated in detail.

The word "rare" (*durlabha*) has not been stated [in the previous verse] because even the subsequent chapters describe the greatness of the Lord. To generate a desire for the knowledge that has been promised, its rarity is stated in the verse beginning with "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*). He explains this through the traditional commentaries (*smṛtis*): "Of the infinite... (*anantānām*). If only a few truly know [the Lord], then how can there be liberation for others? To this he says: "Of others... (*anyeṣām*). By this, it is explained that even among those who strive, only some become perfected (*siddhas*). For all those liberated while living (*jīvanmuktas*), liberation denoted by the term "perfection" (*siddhi*) occurs.

All those who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa have attained perfection because they possess knowledge of Him and other such qualities; however, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa is extremely rare—this is the meaning. "The mass of living beings" (jīvaghana) refers to the essence of all souls. By this, it is stated that not only are those of great knowledge rare, but even one possessed of great devotion and so forth is difficult to find. || 3 ||

The knowledge that was promised is stated by the words beginning with “the ground” (*bhūmi*). He explains that very point as follows: “The insentient,” etc. By the phrase “consciousness is Śrī,” it is explained that she is the *jīvabhūtā* (the individual soul). By the phrase “those two,” the meaning of “my *prakṛti*” is expressed. The meaning of “having this as their womb” is “of the world. Since Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world, one might ask how this is so; therefore, he says: “As the father. The meaning is that Viṣṇu is the cause precisely by virtue of being the father.
By this, the statement “I [am the cause] of the whole” is explained. In that case, regarding the two *prakṛtis*...

To the question, "What kind of causality is this?", he says: "The Mother. It is stated that even the power of the insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) to act as the material cause is dependent upon the Lord. "By the strength of Viṣṇu" (4.6).

Since it is possible for even those who are superior to you to possess the status of father and so forth, one might ask how it is that [the Lord] says, "of the whole," and so on; therefore, He says, "from Me. To dispel the misconception that only things distinct from Himself are being negated there, He says: "from Me. Herein, there is no negation of anything distinct from Himself; rather, there is no entity other than Me that is more supreme. On the contrary, I alone am the most supreme. Therefore, the sense is that it is entirely appropriate for Him to say, "I am the whole," and so forth.

To the question, "Why might this not be a negation of anything other than oneself? he says: "Otherwise. The meaning is: if there were a negation of anything other than oneself here, then since that which is other than oneself would already have been expressed by the word *paratara* (higher), the word *anya* (other) would be redundant; conversely, if the word *anya* were accepted as meaning "other than oneself," then the word *paratara* would be redundant. Furthermore, if Viṣṇu alone is the *paratara*, then there ought to be [mention of] the *para* (highest) and *avara* (lower) as well. To address why this is so, he cites a Smṛti text regarding the stated point: "The lower ones... and so forth.

He is not "other" (para) because he is connected with suffering, nor is he "lower" (avara) because he is not properly afflicted by suffering; therefore, the meaning is that he is "intermediate" (madhyama). If Viṣṇu is the "higher than other" (paratara), then who is the "highest" (paratama)? To this he says: "Because of non-existence. Here, by the two terms *paratara* and *paratama*, Viṣṇu alone is being spoken of. However, he is not merely the "highest" (*paratama*), because there is no other entity intermediate between the *paratara* Śrītattva and the *paratama* Viṣṇu. Nor is Viṣṇu merely the "higher than other" (*paratara*).

The sense is that there is no other entity superior to her. Now, one might object: since even inert *prakṛti* is eternally free from suffering, why is Śrī alone the supreme? To this he says: "Of whom... Even though she is free from suffering, because *prakṛti* is the cause of suffering, it is undoubtedly inferior; such is the meaning.

Regarding what was stated—that the individual souls (jīvas) are inferior—he states an exception to that: "Now" (atha). Here too, the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* have the same meaning. [Objection: Since the conscious being is superior even to the unconscious, how can primordial nature (prakṛti) be inferior when those who are averse to the Lord are themselves the most inferior? To this he says: "For not... [The sense is: the connection of the individual souls with suffering has been stated; if so, how can there be liberation? To this he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ); the meaning is: "in the manner already described."

[Objection: If liberation from suffering occurs through the knowledge of the Blessed One, then the liberated one would be distinct [from Him]. And if that were so, it would be incorrect to say that Śrī alone is the Supreme; therefore, he says: "The liberated one... Even though there is no inferiority due to His enjoyment of eternal bliss, and even though there was previously equality regarding the absence of suffering, he states "even in that case" to show that there is no equality even with respect to bliss and the like. [Objection: Since liberation is taught in the Śrutis and other texts as resulting from both knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), how can it be said here that liberation is attained through the knowledge of Viṣṇu’s supremacy? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of Viṣṇu": it is stated that the word "by the Śruti" is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, by means of the knowledge of the supremacy and other attributes of Śrī and the others, the meaning of the statement "I shall give you knowledge along with realization (vijñāna)" is also explained. He speaks of the rarity of both knowledge and realization in order to generate a desire for them. Or, by this, the cause for the gradation among the liberated ones is stated. By this, the verse beginning with "Of men" is also explained. || 7 ||

Because everything is dependent upon Viṣṇu, He is the Supreme; thus he says "He" (saḥ) to demonstrate that [the world] is under His control. By this, the passage beginning with "I am the essence" (raso 'ham), which demonstrates His consciousness, is explained. He tastes, He takes up the essence, and He impels the essence. Because He shines forth by Himself (*svayaṃ prabhāsamānatvāt*) and because He impels light (*prabhā-preraṇāt*), [He is the Light]. He praises (*praṇauti*), meaning He lauds and impels the act of praising. He causes sound (*śabdayati*), meaning He speaks and impels sound. (8)

He impels fragrance by means of both the fragrant and the non-fragrant, and he himself is fragrant; thus he is the "Meritorious Fragrance" (puṇyagandha), because he himself bestows meritorious fragrance. He is radiant and he impels radiance; thus he is "Radiance" (tejaḥ). He is the giver of life, and from him comes life; thus he is "Life" (jīvana). He heats, performs austerity, and impels austerity; thus he is "Austerity" (tapaḥ). || 9 ||

Because it is a manifestation (*vyañjana*), because it is that which manifests (*vyañjaka*), and because it impels (*preraka*); because it awakens (*bodhana*), because it is the awakener (*boddhṛ*), and because it impels the intellect (*buddhi*). || 10 ||

Because it is eternally full by virtue of being independent of the enjoyment of sense objects, its power is devoid of desire; because it is not applied inappropriately, its splendor is devoid of passion; [for one who is] passionate...

They employ their power even in inappropriate places; or, they possess the state of strength free from sensual desire (*kāmarāga*). Another meaning is stated: "of such a kind" (*etādṛśa*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) that his self consists of such power; and another meaning is also stated. "Or" (*vā*) is used because he possesses full delight (*pūrṇarati*) in that [state]. Here too, the absence of sensual desire is as before; it should be understood that this is also because he impels desires that are not contrary to the Dharma (*dharmāviruddhecchā*). By the rule beginning with "taste in water" (*apsu rasa*), he is the giver of all tastes and so forth to all things, such as water; therefore, the meaning is that he is the name-giver (*nāmadheya*) for taste and the rest.

To the objection that [the Self] might not bear those names because it is non-different from taste and so forth, he says: "From all sides" (*sarvataḥ*). In this regard, independence (*svātantrya*) is the reason. The point is that the lack of independence of taste and so forth is well-known. || 11 ||

He states that [the Lord] is not only the impeller of qualities such as taste, but indeed the impeller of fire and the rest as well: "And those which... [He asks: "Just as this world is dependent upon the Blessed One, so let the Blessed One be dependent upon this world, like the earth, mountains, and so forth. To this he replies: "Dependent upon that. The sense is that this world alone is dependent upon Him, but He is not dependent upon this world. By this, the meaning of the verse "But I am not in them; they are in Me" is stated by way of its converse. || 12 ||

To the question, "Why is the Supreme Self, who is thus the impeller of all, not known by the world?", he says: "By the insentient," with "by Prakṛti" being the understood remainder. "Because He is to be measured by Him": because He is fully known only by Viṣṇu; that is to say, by Lakṣmī. By this, the meaning of the passage beginning with "by the three" is explained. The meaning of "mine" is "under my control."

By the phrase "by Viṣṇu alone," the meaning of the verse "I am not manifest" is explained; this serves to dispel the doubt as to why the Blessed Lord does not ward off the delusion regarding His own nature that is produced by the insentient *prakṛti* and other factors. If the world were deluded by the direct power of the Blessed Lord, then no one would possess knowledge; therefore, he says: "But those... By this, the phrase "Me alone" is explained. To the question of how crossing over *māyā* occurs through surrender to the Blessed Lord, he says: "Lakṣmī..."

Now, one might object: since it was previously stated that Lakṣmī alone is under the control of the Lord, how can it be said that both are under the control of Viṣṇu? To this, it is said: "Lakṣmī is that goddess who is inert Māyā. Thus, Lakṣmī’s subordination to the Lord exists because the insentient Prakṛti is under Lakṣmī’s control. Therefore, since both deluding forms of Prakṛti are under the Lord's control, it is entirely appropriate that one crosses over Māyā by taking refuge in Him; hence the meaning is that one should take refuge in Him. By this, the phrase "composed of the qualities" (guṇamayī) is explained.

By the phrase "through exclusive devotion" (*ananyabhaktyā*), the intended meaning of "single-minded devotion" (*ekabhakti*) and so forth is expressed. To the question, "What is this so-called 'exclusive devotion' like?", he says: "Of such a kind" (*yādṛśī*). In that context regarding devotion, this indicates the analytical etymology (*vigraha*): "one whose devotion is toward a single [object]. By this, the objection that if grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) were accepted, the word *bhakti*—being a member of the *priyādi* group—would not undergo masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is also resolved.

To the question, "What is the fruit for those who, knowing Viṣṇu’s supremacy over all and the subordination of others to Him, practice devotion? he says: "Thus" (evam). "Knowing thus" means knowing and then worshipping. By this, the meaning of such statements as "The man of knowledge, however, is My very Self; that is My view" is established. The word "tu" (however) has the sense of emphasis, meaning "it is not otherwise. To the question, "Why is liberation for the knowers of the Lord alone and not for others? he says: "Complete" (pūrṇam).

The meaning is that the power to grant liberation belongs to the Blessed Lord alone through His fullness, and not to others. By this, the meaning of the term *Vāsudeva* has been stated. If liberation comes through the knowledge of the Blessed Lord, then it would follow that it should belong to everyone; therefore, he says: "Thus [He is] known. Even though liberation exists through the knowledge of Vāsudeva, those who possess that knowledge are not all [people]; thus, liberation does not belong to everyone. By this, the word *saḥ* (He) is explained.

Since many who possess knowledge of the Blessed One are seen in the world, how can [the Lord] be said to be difficult to find? To this he says: "That which... Regarding the term *miśrayājinaḥ*, it means those who sacrifice in a contrary manner. By this, the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "by desires" (*kāmaiḥ*) has been stated. As for what their fruit is, he says: "Viṣṇu... That is supreme, being higher than Lakṣmī and the others; [this applies] both to those who do not know Him and to those who know Him contrarily.

To the question, "What would be the result for one devoid of knowledge, who—due to a specific cause—is free from erroneous cognition yet performs the propitiation of another deity? he says: "Of the ignorant. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); other causes, such as the absence of a definitive guide, are also to be understood. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the worship must be performed. "Separate service" means the worship of another deity without [regard for] being part of the retinue; it refers to the practice of *vidyā* and so forth, the knowledge concerning that [deity], and acts such as hymns of praise.

And this fruit does not belong to one who is merely ignorant; rather, it belongs only to him who, immediately after [attaining] knowledge, abandons the previous path and engages solely in the worship of the Lord.
