With the thought that for some who are fit for *tamas* (ignorance), ignorance may occasionally occur, he says: "If... This [statement] is merely for the purpose of excluding those fit for *tamas*, since the fruit exists even for those who are eternally learned (*nityavedin*), because of the presence of past offenses. To the question, "How can there be a fruit in view of what follows if there is ignorance? he says: "By not knowing..."

If one were to know the reality of Viṣṇu from the Blessed Lord himself, yet—due to some specific cause—does not abandon the previous path, what would happen to him? To this he says: "atyāga" (non-abandonment). The ellipsis is "he makes [him] understand that he must abandon [it]. The phrase "in another birth" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). If the connection is "if his own," then certain [authorities], taking the guru and others as the instrumental cause, and not directly [by the Lord], state the subject matter of the verse beginning with "anena labhate ca."

Thus, by means of scriptural testimony (*pramāṇavacana*), it is stated that Viṣṇu’s designation as *rasa* (taste) and so forth is due to His being the cause of taste and so forth, not because of non-difference. Furthermore, since the dependence of everything upon the Blessed Lord is declared in both the introduction and the conclusion, that [non-difference] is understood; thus he says: "From Me alone" (*matta eva*). This is explained by the scriptural statement: "But the man of knowledge is My very Self—that is My view," and "Knowing thus, he attains Him. Moreover, he says "He attains" (*āpnoti*) in order to establish through reasoning that the meaning is precisely as stated there, and not that it signifies non-difference.

From what does the word *ātman* derive its meaning of "attainment"? To this he says: "And that which... This is a statement from the *Mahābhārata*: "Because it attains (*āpnoti*), because it takes up (*ādatte*), because it eats (*atti*) objects here, and because its state is continuous (*santato bhāvaḥ*), therefore it is called *ātman*. Why is this word *ātman* taken to mean "attainment" rather than "essential nature" (*svarūpa*)? To this he says: "Established... (*āsthita*).

The meaning is that, since in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśe�ṣa*) which explains this very point, it is stated that the knower who worships the Blessed One with the supreme goal in view attains that [goal], here too the word *ātman* has the sense of the object to be attained, not the sense of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, an objection is raised: since liberation follows immediately after knowledge and is limited merely to the exhaustion of karma, how can the necessity of many births be asserted in the words "of many births" (*bahūnāṃ janmanām*)? To this, he says: "Of many... (*bahūnām iti*).
The term "Vāsudeva" has been explained by the authoritative statement that it is the perfect reality; and in order to establish this meaning through reasoning, he says: "Vāsudeva."

The meaning here is that only the perfection (*pūrṇatva*) of Vāsudeva is being stated, and not the non-difference (*abheda*) from everything. This [verse] is applied specifically as a statement of the reason why those who know the Lord alone attain the supreme goal, according to authoritative scripture. Now, it also indicates an alternative interpretation: that at the end of many names, one becomes a knower of the truth that "Vāsudeva is everything. Regarding the word "knowing" (*jānan*): one might ask, "Why should this sentence not be intended to express non-difference? To this, he says: "They take refuge" (*prapadyante*).
The statement, "Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods," has been explained by the passage beginning with, "Having known that supreme Viṣṇu. (21-22)

He explains this further with another sentence: "Having known... Does darkness consist merely in ignorance? No, he says: "Even so... The meaning is: even though it is said thus, nevertheless (*tathāpi*). The word *tāvat* should be supplied [to complete the sense]. There are some persons who are devotees of the Lord (*bhāgavata*), and there are some who are versed in the three Vedas (*traividyā*). And it has been stated that for them, liberation and other such fruits [result from their knowledge]. (23)

Now, it is said that there are even some who are hostile [to Him], namely those referred to as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*). For that reason—as in the previous case, because no specific fruit has been mentioned for them—the fruit is stated by means of a traditional recollection (*smṛti*): "The unmanifest... Thus, since the Blessed Lord possesses such majesty as being the impeller of all, how is it that some consider the Blessed One to be non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this end, it is said: the individual soul and the Lord possess the states of being manifest and unmanifest respectively, due to their being knowable and unknowable in every respect. (24–25)

If, by the power of *māyā*, there is ignorance regarding the Blessed Lord for someone, then does such [ignorance] regarding the world exist for you as well—like two people situated on opposite sides of a wall who cannot see one another? To this, it is said: "I know... In that regard, if there were an absence of knowledge of the Blessed Lord in anyone at all, it would follow that the Vedas and other scriptures are rendered useless; how then can it be said, "But no one knows Me"? Therefore, he explains this by means of that very traditional teaching (*smṛti*), beginning with "Just as... (verse 26).

It has been stated that even the non-dual knowledge (*advaita-jñāna*) held by some arises from My will, as expressed in the words, "I am not manifest. That is incorrect, because in passages such as, "That which some unskilled persons call 'oneness' (*aikātmya*) is due to being overcome by desire and anger, having fallen into the power of egoism," it is stated that desire, hatred, and so forth are themselves the causes of non-dual knowledge. Therefore, it is said: "Will" (*iccheti*). In that context, in order to demonstrate the difference in meaning between the two words *moha* and *saṃmoha*, [the author] restates the compound term *dvandva-moha* and explains the meaning of the word *moha*.

Regarding the phrase "dvandva": from what source does the word *moha* have the meaning of "false knowledge"? To this he says: "*tamaḥ*" (darkness). The meaning is that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is an obscurer, like the darkness associated with the night. Let it be that *moha* is false knowledge; but what is this so-called "delusion regarding pairs" (*dvandvamoha*)? To this he says: "*jīva*" (the individual soul), etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of its attributes such as omniscience and limited knowledge. He explains the word *saṃmoha*, which has not been covered by the word *moha*: "*saṃmoha*" means "clinging to that" (*tad-āgraha*).

The meaning is the strengthening of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). To the question, "From what does this meaning of the word 'delusion' (*saṃmoha*) arise? he says: "In the non-apprehension of that" (*tadagrahe*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the "error" (*viparyaya*) under discussion is referred to, according to the statement: "And delusion is indeed error. Anger [is directed] toward those who possess knowledge of reality as it is. In order to remove the aforementioned doubt, the word "creation" (*sarga*) was stated; he explains that word so that it may serve to remove that very doubt: "Creation" (*sarga*). Indeed, false knowledge arises through desire, aversion, and so forth.

Nevertheless, that [desire] is indeed an intermediate cause, because it functions as a cause only starting from the time of creation; for in the absence of a body, desire and the like do not exist. However, since Viṣṇu is the cause at all times, the statement [regarding Him] is appropriate—this is the sense. Now, one might object: here, the state of being an intermediate cause for desire and so forth is attributed to the delusion regarding the duality of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), and not to the knowledge of the non-difference between the jīva and the Lord. Indeed, there is no restrictive rule that the knowledge of the identity of the substantive alone constitutes "delusion regarding duality. To this, he says: "jīva... (verse 27).

To the question, "What happens through the knowledge of the Blessed One?", it is said: "Old age," etc. In that regard, although the Blessed One has stated that "it is Brahman," one should not suspect that Brahman is anything other than the Blessed One. With the intention of dispelling that very suspicion—since he said "Me" when it could have been said that "Brahman, together with the elemental and the divine [principles]"—he says: "That," etc. When this was said, the word "arose" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 30 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 7 ||

He demonstrates the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter by way of its connection with the preceding chapter: "It has been said. First, an explanation is provided here for what was stated in such passages as, "They know that Brahman. In connection with the explanation of what was said in, "And at the time of departure, [remember] Me," the fruit of remembering at the time of death, the method for that [remembrance], and the path to the attainment of Brahman are stated; such is the meaning.
It should be understood that the term "attainment of Brahman" (*brahmaprāpti*) applies to the remembrance at the time of death and so forth, because through these means Brahman is attained.

But surely, because Arjuna is a man of knowledge, he already knows that the Blessed One himself is Brahman; therefore, how can the question "What is that Brahman? be appropriate, given the absence of a cause for such doubt? To this, he says: "That [is Brahman]. Even though Arjuna is a man of knowledge, this question is justified. In the phrase "that Brahman," because the Blessed One has spoken of Brahman using the remote demonstrative pronoun "that," there arises the perception that the Brahman mentioned here might be a deity other than the Blessed One.

From such passages as "Brahman has Vāsudeva as its essence," it is understood that the Blessed Lord is Brahman. The sense is that there exists a cause for the question, namely the doubt produced by this twofold perception. Now, one might object: since the word *brahman* refers exclusively to the Blessed Lord, how can there be a perception of something else even when it is specified as "that" (*tat*)? To this, it is said: "In the primordial matter... (*prakṛti*).

The sense is this: although the word *brahman* has its primary meaning in the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), since Prakṛti, the Vedas, and so forth also possess that meaning in a secondary sense, there arises the understanding—justified by the specific qualification *tat* (that)—that even if the primary meaning is impossible here, some secondary meaning among Prakṛti and the others might be intended. Now, an objection may be raised: the doubt that Brahman might be something other than the Blessed Lord, which was suggested by the qualification *tat*, has already been resolved by the Blessed Lord himself in the subsequent passage, "Know Me as the one who presides over the elements and the divine."

Since it was said "me" (*mām*) when one ought to have said "Brahman" (*brahma*), how can there be the perception that Brahman is distinct from the Blessed Lord? To this, it is said: "Above" (*upari*). Although this perception has been refuted in the subsequent passage, it nevertheless arises once again. In that context, regarding the phrase "and [Me] with regard to sacrifice" (*sādhiyajñaṃ ca*), the word "and" (*ca*) implies "and Me with regard to the elements and with regard to sacrifice" (*sādhibhūtādhiyajñaṃ mām ca*).

The sense is that because it is accompanied by the overcoming of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, the knowledge of Viṣṇu is said to be something other than the knowledge of Brahman; this is understood precisely from the qualifying term "that" (*tat*). In the phrases "whatever it may be" (*yat kiṃcit*) and "something other" (*anyat eva*), the word "arisen" (*jātaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the thought, based on the understanding of the particle "iti."

[Objection: Since the Blessed One himself has stated that he is Brahman in the words, “Me, together with the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva,” one should have replied “I am Brahman” to the question, “What is that Brahman? Why, then, is it said, “The Imperishable (akṣara) is the supreme Brahman”? To this, he says: “Supreme. That is precisely how it is: the supreme Imperishable is indeed Brahman. [Objection: Let it be so that the supreme Imperishable is called Brahman; what is the purpose of saying this, given that the word “supreme Imperishable” is well-known to refer to Viṣṇu?

Nevertheless, since he did not state it directly as "I am," what is the reason for speaking in this way? To this he says: "Of the ignorant" (*ajñānām*). This refers even to his own status as the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣaratva*). Now, one might object: for those who do not know that Viṣṇu is the supreme imperishable, it was not said "I am Brahman"; rather, it was simply said "the imperishable is Brahman. Therefore, there would only be the suspicion that Brahman and the imperishable are indeed different from the Blessed Lord, and not the knowledge that the supreme imperishable and Brahman are the Blessed Lord. To this he says: "Furthermore" (*punar*).

It is true that doubt arises; and that doubt is resolved by the subsequent statement, "He is called the unmanifest, the imperishable," which describes the imperishable as unmanifest. This is because the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is applied to the Blessed Lord in the verse, "They think of Me, the unmanifest, as having attained manifestation. Therefore, the sense is that since the resolution "the imperishable is the supreme Brahman" can also yield the understanding of "I" (aham), such a resolution is appropriate.

If the word *akṣara* is primary (*mukhya*) in denoting Viṣṇu, then in the passages "And those who [worship] the unmanifest *akṣara*" and "The immutable (*kūṭastha*) is called *akṣara*," Viṣṇu would have to be the referent of the word *akṣara*. To this, he says: "And those... Even though the word *akṣara* is primary in denoting Viṣṇu, in the passage "And those who [worship] the unmanifest *akṣara*," it is determined that the referent of the word *akṣara* is indeed something other than Viṣṇu.

This is because, by stating "those devotees who worship You" and "and those who [worship] the Imperishable," the Lord has questioned the relative gradation between the two types of worshippers—those of the Lord and those of the Imperishable—as distinct entities. Furthermore, through passages such as "those who [meditate on] the Imperishable, the indefinable" and "but those who [perform] all actions," the difference in the results for the worshippers of the Imperishable and the worshippers of the Lord is explicitly stated. Likewise, in the passage "the Immutable (Kūṭastha) is called the Imperishable," it is determined that this very Imperishable is Viṣṇu.

The sense is this: because it is stated that Viṣṇu is "higher even than the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), and since it is improper to accept a figurative meaning when the primary meaning is possible, the subject here must indeed concern Viṣṇu, as there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) to the contrary.

Surely, if Viṣṇu is also the Brahman who presides over sacrifice (*adhiyajña-brahman*), why is it said that he is "I alone am the *adhiyajña*," rather than "I alone am the Brahman"? Since a distinction in expression cannot occur without a specific reason, one might conclude that Viṣṇu is only the *adhiyajña* and not the Brahman; to this, the Lord says: "As the *adhiyajña*. Even though both the Brahman and the *adhiyajña* are Viṣṇu, it is appropriate to state "I alone am the *adhiyajña*" rather than "I alone am the Brahman," because the Blessed One has spoken of himself as being associated with the *adhiyajña* in the words, "Me, along with the sacrifice" (*sādhiyajñaṃ mām*). Therefore, he is the *adhiyajña*.

The doubt that [the Self] is indeed different from the Blessed Lord arises; however, the statement "I alone" is intended to remove that [doubt]. Although by the use of the word "That" (tat) the doubt that Brahman is distinct from the Blessed Lord might arise, that doubt is dispelled—relative to the understanding of an enlightened person—by the use of the word "Me" (mām), and thus there is no need for the statement "I alone. By this, the objection that because it was stated, "In this way, many kinds of sacrifices are spread out in the mouth of Brahman," the questions regarding the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*) and their answers are devoid of any meaningful attainment, is also refuted.

If the Blessed Lord alone is the presiding deity of sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), how was his association with others previously mentioned? To this he says: "Of him alone" (*tasyaiva*). Even though the Blessed Lord alone is the presiding deity of sacrifice, his association [with others] is appropriate; the sense is that the presiding deity of sacrifice exists as an internal form within the bodies of all living beings. By this, the intended meaning of the word "body" (*deha*) is explained.

Demonstrating the authority for this and dispelling the doubt as to how the Lord alone can be designated by the term "That" (*tad*)—even though He is Brahman—he explains [the passage] by means of two verses from the *Smṛti*: "Of living beings... (*prāṇinām*). The sense is that the designation "That" is appropriate because Brahman exists as the internal form within all-pervading things. Because He is the object of sacrifice (*yajña*) superior to all those various living beings, He is "the Sacrifice" (*adhiyajña*); and because He is expanded (*bṛṃhita*), He is "Brahman"—this is the meaning. In the phrase "due to being superior to the elements" (*bhūtādhikatvataḥ*), the word "elements" (*bhūta*) refers to earth and the other [gross elements].

"Having many lives," from which it follows that [He] is called "Purusha"—this is the remainder [of the sense], according to the Śruti: "The letter *ṣa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the Self (*ātman*). Now, one might ask: why was the question, "Who is the Adhiyajña here, and how? not answered by the inquiry, "In what form is the Adhiyajña, and how is He Pūṣan? To this he says: "In what form? [The answer is given] "by stating His characteristics. This means: by stating the characteristics of the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān) through the words "the ancient Seer" (*kaviṃ purāṇam*). One might further ask: how does the statement of the Blessed Lord's characteristics answer the question regarding the essential nature of the Adhiyajña? To this he says: [as follows].
"I alone. The meaning is that because the Lord of Sacrifice (adhiyajña) has been stated to be non-different from the Blessed One in the words, "I alone am the Lord of Sacrifice. || 4 ||

And regarding the question, "How are You to be known at the time of departure?"—the meaning is: for what purpose, as being of what nature, and in what manner are You to be remembered? In that regard, the answer to the question "For what purpose are You to be remembered? is stated as "at the end" (*ante*). Therein, he states the meaning of the term *madbhāva* (my state of being) in order to dispel any other possible misconception; namely, [the meaning is] "my state of being. The sense is that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the remainder of the sentence: "he goes to that very one."

One might ask: "Since that [attainment] is achieved simply by remembering at the time of death, for what purpose is it said that one must always be permeated by that state? To this, he says: "Always" (*sadā*). It is not for the sake of attaining that [state] that constant permeation by that state is enjoined; rather, the meaning is that although it was stated that "remembering, he departs," such direct remembrance at the time of death occurs only for those who are always permeated by that state. Thus, it is precisely the means for direct remembrance at the time of death that is being described.

Now, one might object: since it is possible to practice the remembrance of the Lord with great effort precisely at the time of death, what is the use of being constantly permeated by His nature? To this, he says: "If not. In the absence of constant permeation by His nature, even for one who remembers with great effort, the memory—due to the power of *prārabdha* karma—occurs only regarding other objects. And consequently, attainment of Him does not occur.

Indeed, just as for one who practices *samādhi* with great effort, a lapse may still occur due to the force of *prārabdha-karma*, the sense is that one must therefore always remain permeated by that state [of Brahman]. If, due to the force of *prārabdha-karma*, the remembrance of Brahman does not occur at the time of death, then it would follow—absurdly—that even for the wise (*jñānin*), there could be no liberation at the time of death because of the absence of such remembrance, owing to the presence of *prārabdha-karma*.

To this he says: "Immediate [knowledge]... The point is as follows: although it was stated that those possessing immediate knowledge (aparokṣajñānin) remember [the Lord] and thus depart, there is indeed direct remembrance at the time of death; therefore, liberation does not fail to occur for them. This is because, while there exists the destruction of previously accumulated karma and the non-clinging of future karma, the karma already set in motion (prārabdha-karma) is finite and can reach its conclusion through experience.

In explaining this, he states the agreement with the words of the Blessed One: "At the time of departure," etc. Now, if this is so, it follows that the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) alone is the cause for recollection at the time of death, and that immediate realization (*aparokṣa-jñāna*) is also a cause by virtue of being its cause. Thus, one might ask: what is the use of being constantly permeated by that [realization]? To this, he says: "The disciplined," etc. It is true that the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma* is the direct cause of recollection at the time of death, and that immediate realization is also a cause by virtue of being its cause.

Nevertheless, the state of being constantly permeated by that [object] certainly becomes the cause for recollection at the time of death, because it is a means to direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*). The point is that since constant permeation by that object is a means to direct perception, it is said, "by one whose mind is disciplined" (*yuktacetas*). By this, the construction is indicated: "Those who, having taken refuge in Me with a disciplined mind, strive—they know That Brahman. He states through the *smṛti* that the aforementioned constant recollection, which is a means to the direct perception of the Lord, is effective only when conjoined with devotion (*bhakti*) and so forth, and not by itself: "By devotion" (5).

The answer to the question "In what manner are you to be remembered? is stated as "the Seer" (kavi). In that regard, if [the Lord] were of the nature of the sun, there would be the contingency of birth and so forth due to possessing a body; therefore, it is said, "beyond darkness" (tamasaḥ parastāt). Having restated that, he explains it: "Of darkness. For the Śruti says, "Darkness is indeed the unmanifest" (avyaktam). || 9 ||

The answer to the question, "In what manner are You to be remembered? is stated as: "That which is imperishable" (1.2.11). In that regard, having previously stated that the means for remembering at the time of death is "being constantly permeated by that state," the word *brahmacarya* is now explained with reference to how that is so. [The commentary says: "Of the mind and so forth. The meaning of the statement, "I shall declare that goal to you in brief," is: "I shall declare the method of remembering That. || 11 ||

To dispel the notion that the phrase "the single-syllabled Brahman" (*ekākṣaraṃ brahma*) refers to the single syllable as the *śabdabrahman* (Brahman as sound), he explains it [as follows]: "The single... etc. The meaning is: that which has the single syllable "Oṃ" as its designator is "single-syllabled. Since the word "Brahman" has its primary application only to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), it does not have the [merely] perceived meaning [of sound]. || 13 ||

Since even those who have reached the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) and the other higher realms are subject to rebirth, why is it specifically stated that "having attained Me, they do not undergo rebirth"? To this, it is said: "Up to Brahman" (ābrahma). There, because of the statement "birth occurs until [the world of] Janaloka," there is no birth or the like for those residing in Janaloka and the worlds above it. Anticipating the doubt—how can it be said that there is a return starting from the abode of Brahmā—it is refuted by means of Smṛti itself: "They do not return" (niyamīd iti). Here, the word "birth" (janman) is also indicative of "death. "With their bodies dissolved" (aṃsalayau iti).

The meaning is that there is birth on earth as a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*), and birth at the end of the dissolution (*layānta*), as well as death at the beginning of that [dissolution]. He states that there is also death for the partial incarnation by saying, "Even there. Even though he has descended as a partial incarnation, this is not improper; for it has been stated that birth and so forth do not exist primarily for one who is already liberated, and because there is only a slight degree of birth and so forth at the beginning of creation, this statement has that very sense as its purpose. || 16 ||

In order to establish that there is no returning [to saṃsāra] only upon attaining Me—as previously stated—the Lord’s agency over the entire creation, dissolution, and so forth, is declared in the verse beginning with “A thousand. Therein, the word *sahasra* (thousand) might be misunderstood as referring to one thousand; therefore, he explains it to dispel such a misconception: “*Sahasram* means... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: “much more than what is commonly known as a thousand. Now, [one might object]: “There are thousands of four-yuga cycles...”

To the objection—"Since it is stated in passages such as 'the day of Brahmā is said [to consist of] a thousand yugas,' that the thousand-year period constitutes the day of Viriñca, how can the word 'thousand' have a meaning even greater than that?"—he replies: "Of Brahmā. The intention here is that the day and night of the four-faced one (Caturmukha) are not what is being described, for if they were, the word 'thousand' would not have a meaning greater than that; rather, it refers to the day and night consisting of two parārdhas belonging to the Supreme Brahman (Parabrahman).

Why is it asserted that the term "Brahma" refers to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*) and that its day and night are intended here, rather than the day and night of Viriñca? To this he says: "From the Unmanifest" (*avyaktāt*). Even though such supplementary statements exist, why should this not refer to the day and night of Viriñca? To this he says: "For not... (*na hi*). "At the end of the days" (*āhanīti*); the meaning is "at the conclusion of those [days]. In this way, it should also be understood that at the arrival of the day, there is the manifestation of all manifested beings. Now, one might ask: how can there be the existence of day and night for the Blessed Lord?

[The author] refutes the objection—namely, that because there is no modification caused by time, and because in passages such as "at the end of the closing of the eye of the Supreme" (paranāmanimeṣakānte), a period of two *parārdhas* is spoken of as a "closing of the eye" (*nimeṣa*)—by means of the very [scriptural] tradition (*smṛti*). "Of the eternal" (*nityasya*) means "of the changeless" (*nirvikārasya*). Regarding the basis for the metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), he says: "because of non-activity. The meaning is that the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) and so forth is metaphorically designated as "night" and so on, because there is an absence of activity during the time of dissolution, just as there is at night, whereas there is the presence of activity at other times, just as there is during the day. (Verses 17–22)

It has been stated that for those who have reached the Blessed One there is no return, whereas for others there is a return. To the question of by which path those who are subject to return and those who are not arrive [there], it is said: "Where. He explains this to dispel any other possible understanding, stating: "Where" means at which time those who die go to non-return, and at which time they go to return; he says, "I shall declare that time. Thus he speaks. "Where" (yatreti).

[Objection: But since fire (*agni*), light (*jyotis*), and smoke (*dhūma*)—even though they are presiding deities of time—are to be described as destinations on the path, how can it be said in the declarative sentence, "at which time" (*yatra kāle*)? To this he says: "Fire," etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "of fire, light, and smoke, which are to be described as destinations. The sense is that because the presiding deities of time are numerous among those to be described as destinations, the word "time" (*kāla*) functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the others, just as the word "water" (*payaḥ*) indicates "saline water" when referring to water mixed with a small amount of salt.

Now, an objection may be raised: since in passages such as "They attain the light" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*) and "Because of its renown through the path beginning with light" (*arcirādinā tat-prathiteḥ*), light is stated to be the first thing reached, how can it be said here that fire is reached first? Furthermore, on what basis is it claimed that the words "day" and so forth refer to deities? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of *smṛti* itself: "Fire... (*agnir iti*). Thus, by the designation of *smṛti*, it is established that the aforementioned meaning—that those who die during the time of the day and so forth do not return—is indeed correct. He states the subverting argument for the contrary view: "At that time... (*tatkāla iti*).

If the intention here were that death at times such as the day [of the new moon] leads to non-return and so forth, then what would be the purpose of mentioning fire, light, and smoke? For the point is that there is no such thing as "death" in fire, light, or smoke as there is in the case of the day and so on. Furthermore, he states that the meaning is not thus understood: "Now (atha)..."

In the Śruti passage beginning, "He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course [of the sun], having gone to the majesty of the gods, attains union with the Sun; and he who dies during the southern course," it is stated that a knower who dies during the northern course attains Brahman without returning, whereas a ritualist who dies during the southern course attains the moon and returns. Subsequently, it is declared that for a knower who dies either during the northern or the southern course, there is attainment of Brahman without returning.

Therefore, the sense is that there is no other meaning [to the passage], because there is no restrictive rule stating that those who die during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) return, while those who die during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) do not return.

*Mahimānam* means worship (*pūjā*), based on the verbal root *maha* in the sense of worship. Since the Śruti states, "From the sun [he goes] to the moon," and because both the sun and the moon exist even on the path of Brahman, it is logical that one attains the majesty (*mahimānam*) of the sun and the moon. It should be understood here that the statement regarding the attainment of Brahman by the knower who dies during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) is intended to indicate a preponderance of results. Regarding this, he cites the Smṛti: "The wise man... The phrase "wherever" (*yatra tatra*) means either during the day and so forth, or during the night and so forth.

The purpose of describing the path is stated as "These [are not... (naite). Therein, in order to dispel the misconception that this fruit results merely from indirect knowledge of the journey, he explains it precisely according to the Smṛti: "The two paths... (mārgāv iti). The meaning of the word "yogī" is "he should behold Brahman.
The meaning of the phrase "in the Vedas" is: "Transcending all merit, he goes to that supreme Brahman" (sarvapuṇyātigo yātyasau brahma tatparam). || 27-28 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha.

He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter [with the words] "In the seventh," etc. The words "the majesty of the Blessed One" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Nor should it be argued that this [chapter] ought to be the eighth; for it is separated [from the seventh] by the resolution of Arjuna’s question.

The knowledge that was promised is stated as "by me. Regarding this, one might raise the objection that the statements "all beings abide in me" and "beings do not abide in me" are contradictory; the Lord dispels this doubt by means of a traditional authority (smṛti) itself: "Viṣṇu-gāni. The meaning is that because Viṣṇu is devoid of touch, there is no contradiction, as he does not abide in them by having physically touched them.

[Objection: But since it was stated, "All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them," the statement "My Self sustains beings but does not dwell in beings" is a mere repetition. To this, He says: "My... [and so on]. The intention is that previously His being the support of beings was stated; now, however, it is stated that His own body is such, and thus there is no tautology. [Objection: How can characteristics of the Blessed One, such as being the support of beings, be possible in that body? To this, He says: "That... [and so on].

The meaning is that because the body is non-different from the Blessed Lord, it is appropriate for the characteristics of the Blessed Lord to apply to it. Now, one might object: "If there is thus non-difference between the Blessed Lord and His body, does this not result in a mere repetition? To this he says: "Of the body. Having admitted the difference between the Blessed Lord and His body, there may arise in people a suspicion—based on the fact that it is a body—that even the bodies of the Blessed Lord are insentient; to remove that, their sentience is asserted here through their identity [with the Lord] by virtue of being endowed with the characteristics of the Blessed Lord.

The intended meaning is that, therefore, there is no tautology. Alternatively, he says "of the body" (*dehasya*) because if the body were intended here, then what would be the purpose of employing the word "self" (*ātman*) instead of the well-known expression "my body"? For if it were simply said "my body," one might suspect how the characteristics of the Blessed One could belong to an insentient body. To avoid that objection, its sentience would have to be stated separately; however, by using the word "self," both points are expressed.
For this word "self" (ātman) has two meanings: the meaning of the body and the meaning of its animation. Therefore, the sense is that it was said, "my self. || 4.9 ||

If you [the Lord] are indifferent while the world is under the sway of *prakṛti*, then independence would accrue to *prakṛti* alone; therefore, it is said, "by me. Even there, the word "presiding" (*adhyakṣa*) expresses indifference itself; thus, to dispel any contrary impression, he explains it by recalling that very [traditional] definition: "Presiding" (*adhyakṣa*). The meaning is: he whose senses are presided over by him is the "presider" (*adhyakṣa*). || 10 ||

If you are of such a nature, then why do some despise you, and what is their opinion? To this it is said: "They despise. In that regard, since the Blessed One has spoken of a human body, there might appear to be a contradiction with the statement, "The sustainer of beings, yet not abiding in beings"; therefore, he says: "A human form. Here, it is not the humanity of the Blessed One's body that is being asserted, which would cause a contradiction.

However, the meaning is that [the Lord] is perceived as having human likeness solely because He is the cause of the contempt of the ignorant. Nevertheless, one might raise the objection that there is a contradiction with what was stated previously, since in this passage the distinction between the Blessed One and His body is expressed by the phrase "having resorted to a body" (*tanumāśritam*). Anticipating this, he resolves the doubt by means of the very same traditional authority (*smṛti*): "But the body... (*tanvā*). Just as Devadatta’s body is dependent upon him, so too the body of the Blessed One is dependent upon Him; therefore, the expression that the Blessed One has "resorted to" that body is figurative (*gauṇa*). This is the meaning.

And he explains the verse by recalling it with the thought that ignorance (*avajñāna*) is not merely knowledge of [the Lord] as inferior, but includes other forms as well: "Brahman," etc. The word "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is to be supplied here with the terms "non-difference" (*ananyatā*) and "incompleteness" (*apūrṇatā*). "Confusion" (*saṅkara*) regarding the incarnations (*avatāra*) means knowing those who are not incarnations as incarnations, and knowing incarnations as non-incarnations. Furthermore, He is to be known as distinct from all, the supreme among all, devoid of internal differentiation, and exactly as He is. (11–14)

One might ask: "Could it not be that the gods despise [the Lord] simply because they have found fault with Him? To this it is said: "If that were the case, even those who are by nature divine would show contempt; yet such is not the case," as expressed by the word "mahātmānaḥ" (high-souled ones). Therein, the phrase "by way of oneness" (*ekatvena*) is explained precisely through *smṛti* in order to dispel any contrary understanding. Regarding the four terms beginning with "ekena," the explanation follows their respective order as "of one form" (*ekamūrtiḥ*), and so forth. || 15 ||

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is declared to be what was promised as "I am the sacrifice" (*ahaṃ kratuḥ*). To dispel the misconception that Hari’s nature consists merely of being the sacrifice and so forth, he explains it by means of a *smṛti* [verse] itself: "Because of being worthy of worship" (*arcyatvāt*). The verbal root is *ṛg-añcana*. "He is always equal; therefore, he is the *sāman*"—this is his own nature (*svadhā*). Because he protects through measurement (*māna*), he is the *mantra*; the meaning is that he protects once he is known. From the roots *uṣ* and *pluṣ* meaning "to burn," those who are burnt by the three-fold affliction (*tāpa*) are the *uṣṭas*.

The word *darbha* is etymologically explained as "that which bears (*bibharti*) distress (*daram*)," with the implication that it is used in sacrifices and the like because it has been invoked. For the world (*jagat*), which lacks movement—that is, which is unable to move by its own power—[the darbha serves as a support].

He states another traditional text (*smṛti*) here to show that Hari, though distinct from *kratu* and the others, possesses those respective names through the function of metaphorical application (*yogavṛtti*). [The verse begins with] "tat-tat... The word "evam" (thus) indicates that this very meaning has already been stated previously in this *smṛti*. The reasons for His being distinct from each of those objects are His independence and His status as the creator of all. If He is distinct, how can He be denoted by those respective names? The meaning is: solely because He possesses infinite qualities which serve as the grounds for the application of those various words.

By the maxim "because it depends on that, it is meaningful," independence and other such qualities are the causes for being denoted by their respective words. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Oṃkāra" through another Smṛti: "Omiti. It is *ākriyate*, meaning it is invoked; it *pāti*, meaning it protects; from *māna*, meaning from knowledge. "Greater than the Father": the meaning is that he is greater even than Viriñca, the father of the world. Because he is the *nidhātṛ*, meaning the sustainer; because of his *vyāñjana*, meaning his manifestation of the universe.

He states the difference in meaning between the words *pralaya* (dissolution) and *mṛtyu* (death) based on authoritative evidence: "Pralaya... [and so forth]. The meaning is that He is the destroyer even at times other than the cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). Because, by abiding in the senses, He prevents their death through the maintenance of the body, He is therefore called *amṛta* (the Immortal). The word *pralaya* implies "causing dissolution," as is understood from the context. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "I am the sacrifice" (*ahaṃ kratuḥ*), the meaning is His being the enjoyer of all sacrifices and the like without exception. (Verses 16–19)

In this regard, having raised the objection that there would be no difference in the results for the Traividyas and the Bhāgavatas if the Blessed Lord were the enjoyer of all sacrifices and so forth, it is resolved by the words "The Traividyas. That very point is elaborated upon with the words "Even those who... In that context, although there is equality between the Traividyas and the Bhāgavatas in terms of both being worshippers of the Blessed Lord, a difference in their results is stated along with its reason. Since that [reason] is not clearly perceived, he explains it by means of a traditional Smṛti verse: "Ananya-... (those whose mind is not directed elsewhere).

It has been stated that those who possess the three Vedas (*traividyāḥ*) worship other deities, as expressed in the words, "those devoted to other deities sacrifice. The meaning of the term "ananyaḥ" (non-dual), which is stated as the opposite of that [group] for the Bhāgavatas, is "because they do not sacrifice to other deities. Furthermore, the absence of both superior devotion and knowledge of reality in the possessor of the three Vedas is stated in the words, "but they do not know Me in truth. This is because there is an absence of devotion when there is an absence of knowledge of reality. The meaning of the term "paryupāsate" (they worship), which is stated as the opposite of that [Vedic group], is "due to the intensity of their devotion."

Because worship itself becomes a form of constant attendance through an abundance of devotion. The desire of those possessing the threefold knowledge is stated in the words, "Those who desire objects seek the path to heaven. The meaning of the phrase "meditating upon Me," which is spoken as the opposite of that, is expressed by the term "without desire"; that is, meditating upon Me alone and not upon any object of desire. The final dedication of those possessing the threefold knowledge is stated in the words, "Having sacrificed to Me, they sacrifice to Me alone."

The meaning of the phrase "those who are constantly engaged" (*nityābhiyuktānām*), which was stated as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to that [the Lord], is expressed by the words "due to constant yoga" (*sadāyogāt*). This means due to being constantly engaged in recollection, directing [the mind toward Him], and so forth. "Distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭyam*) refers to superiority by virtue of the fruit. This is because it has been stated [by the Lord Himself] in the words "I carry their welfare and security" (*yogakṣemaṃ vahāmi*) that He grants the human goal of non-return. The phrase "even though he is a worshiper of Viṣṇu" (*vaiṣṇavād api*) means even though he is one who sacrifices to the Blessed One. To this, [the author] says [the following] in response to the fact that in passages such as "He turned the animals away from the deities" (*paśūn devatābhyaḥ pratyauhat*), even Brahmā and others are heard to be worshippers of other deities.

"Vaiṣṇavas" means [they worship Me] as such, but not as a deity; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: by the phrase "but they do not recognize Me," which occurs in the context of explaining that the followers of the three Vedas act without prior knowledge of the injunctions, the absence of knowledge regarding the reality (tattva) has been stated. Why, then, is the Bhāgavata's lack of knowledge regarding the reality not mentioned as its counterpart? To this, the author explains by recalling that very point, with the intention that it has already been expressed by the word "paryupāsana" (worshiping). (Verses 20–23)

Regarding the statement, "But they do not know Me in truth; therefore they fall," since the qualification "in truth" is used for those who do not know the Blessed One, there might arise the misconception that this refers to the downfall of those "ignorant of the three Vedas" (avidvāṃsaḥ) who possess contrary knowledge after their enjoyment of heavenly rewards. To dispel such a misunderstanding, he says: "Having sacrificed to Me... (māmiṣṭvā).

Nor should it be assumed here that the falling from heaven of the Traividyas—who either do not know the Blessed One or possess false knowledge—is being described because of the statement, "But they do not know Me in essence. This is because the meaning of "But they do not know Me in essence" is logically consistent with the sense that even though they know Him as the best among all gods, they do not correctly understand His status as the master of Brahmā, Rudra, and the rest, who are His attendants.

From what source is this meaning inferred? It is because, at the conclusion of the passage concerning those "versed in the three Vedas" (*traividya*), it is stated that they sacrifice to the Lord by surrendering everything and praying for His worship—namely, "The knowers of the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having sacrificed with rituals, pray for the path to heaven"—and because such [a prayer] would be impossible if they did not know Him to be the supreme among all deities; and this is also the sense conveyed by the force of the word *abhi*.

Furthermore, he states that falling from heaven after the enjoyment of its pleasures is taught here not only for those with mere ignorance (*kevalājñāna*) and those with false knowledge (*mithyājñānin*): "Of all... and so forth. Because it has been stated that for those with mere ignorance, sacrifices and other rituals become fruitless, while for those with false knowledge, they yield contrary results—"Falling from [heaven] after the enjoyment [of its fruits] is taught here for one with mere ignorance or one with false knowledge"—the meaning is as follows. And regarding the one with false knowledge: "If he goes, he certainly goes to blind darkness.
Explaining what was thus stated, he concludes: 24–28.

By the statement, "I eat what is offered with devotion," it is said that He is fond of His devotees. If this were so, there would be a lack of affection toward those who are not devotees; consequently, the Lord would appear to be partial. To address this, it is said: "I am equal. Because the meaning of that [previous statement] might seem unclear, he explains it by means of a traditional verse (smṛti): "Not of Him... The meaning is: there is no one among the gods who is not a devotee of Him, nor is there anyone who is dear to Him who is not a devotee.

By this, it is implied that even in the verse, "To Me there is none hateful and none dear," one should supply the words "the devotee" and "the non-devotee. The meaning is that I bestow fruit according to devotion; thus, I show affection only toward devotees and lack affection toward non-devotees. If I were to harbor hatred toward devotees or affection toward non-devotees, only then would I be partial. But such is not the case; therefore, the sense is that I am indeed equal. However, it must be stated that I show affection toward those who worship Me with devotion.

To the question, "Why is it said that 'these [qualities] of theirs are not common to those who are not devotees toward Me'? and so forth, he says: "Out of love," etc.; "they abide," etc., is the remainder. The sense is that this very point is being stated. (29–31)

[Objection: Surely all those who have taken refuge in the Blessed One are indeed meritorious, based on such statements as: "Even a Pulkasa who is always devoted to the Lord is superior in *sattva*. Therefore, how can the Lord say, "But those born of sinful wombs, O Pārtha" (*māṃ hi pārtha*), thereby characterizing women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras as being of sinful origin, while characterizing Brāhmaṇas and royal sages as being meritorious? To this, he says: "Sinful, etc. (*pāpādi*). By nature, the fact that those of the highest castes, such as Brāhmaṇas, belong to lower castes, such as Kṣatriyas, is caused by sin.

The meaning is that for those of lower castes, such as Śūdras, attaining the status of higher castes, such as Vaiśyas, is brought about by merit (*puṇya*). Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), desire (*kāma*) is also included. The meaning is that innate Brāhmaṇahood and the like are said to be meritorious. He states its definition: "Those that persist in liberation. The meaning is that innate Brāhmaṇahood and the like, which remain even in liberation, are [the ones referred to].

Just as Brāhmaṇas and others might naturally become Kṣatriyas and others, and Kṣatriyas and others might naturally become Brāhmaṇas and others, one might raise the doubt: why should natural males not become females, and natural females not become males? To this, he says: "They go... He explains that through sin, as in the case of Sudyumna becoming Ilā, and through desire, as in the case of the sons of Agni becoming Apsarases. Since we see Ilā becoming Sudyumna, how can it be said that "women do not attain manhood"? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "from its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*): because it was observed by Sthūṇākarṇavara that the woman Ambā’s state of being Śikhaṇḍin was due to her very own nature, he says "by a man" (*puṃsā*). The meaning is this: for Ambā, through Sthūṇākarṇavara, there was merely an existence together with him in that body during that birth; however, she did not possess a male body independently. The intention is that only that much [of his presence] is admitted.

In response to the inquiry as to which among women are superior—given that men [become] women due to their own nature and sin, while for those [women] it is due to their inherent nature—the text says: "The excellent ones. By the phrase "from those born of sin," it is indicated that those born of desire are inferior. If women were superior by nature to those born of sin, it would follow that the *āsurī* women are superior to those born of *ilā* and so forth; to preclude this, it is stated: "virtuous women" (*satstriyaḥ*). Here, inferiority is intended to be conditional (*aupādhika*).

He states the duration for one who possesses no remaining natural [karma]: "of all," meaning that the final body follows its own nature. He states the duration by way of reiterating what preceded: "but in liberation. The meaning is that this qualification is appropriate because it can be explained as non-contradictory in accordance with the scriptural statement. By this, the following is explained:

Even those born of sinful wombs—women, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even Brāhmaṇas who are royal sages (rājarṣis)—attain the supreme goal; how much more so these meritorious ones, such as women and Vaiśyas, who are born of their own nature? Here, although one might expect the mention of "men" just as there is the mention of "women" among those of sinful wombs, men are not mentioned because there are no men who have been caused to fall by sin. (32–33)

Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 9 ||

Hari Om. In the sixth chapter, meditation (dhyāna) was described. Since the subject matter of this chapter—the forms of the Lord’s manifestations as objects of meditation—is already evident there, it is not explicitly stated here.

Having promised, "Listen further to My greatness," it is said: "They do not know Me. Since it was stated there that "the hosts of gods and the great sages do not know My greatness," the author says, "for the sake of indication" (*upalakṣaṇārtham*), in order to dispel the misconception that the Gandharvas and others do know [it]. The two terms "hosts of gods" and "great sages" are indicative of all [beings]. The sense is that if even the hosts of gods and the great sages do not know [it], then for others, that [ignorance] is all the more certain. (1-2)

The greatness known as liberation arises here from one's own knowledge, as expressed in the words "He who [knows] me. Since it was already stated there that [the Self] is "unborn" (*aja*), the repetition of "beginningless" (*anādi*) might seem redundant; therefore, he says: "Of the cart" (*anasya*). Here, "cart" (*ana*) refers to the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*). ||3||

The greatness known as liberation is said to arise from one's own knowledge, which is referred to by the term "buddhi. Since the words *buddhi* and *jñāna* have the same meaning in that context, the author provides a traditional definition (*smṛti*) to show that the word *buddhi* has a different referent [from knowledge itself]: "Buddhi... [The verse says: *bhūta bodhaḥ*. Because it is the substratum of that [knowledge], the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is the locus of that knowledge—is called *buddhi*, just as the ocean (*jaladhi*) is so named because it is the locus of water. This is the meaning. || 4 ||

If it is asked, "Are the intellect and so forth of the beings alone [produced] from Me at every Manvantara, given that there is mention of different groups of Seven Sages (Saptarṣis)?"—the answer is: those who resided in the previous Manvantara. This is because of the qualification "previous. To clarify who those residing in the previous Manvantara were, he shows them by means of traditional recollection (smṛti): "Marīci," and so on. If it is asked, "Which four among the fourteen Manus are intended here?", the answer is: not only the well-known Manus indicated by the word "Manu" here, but all the gods as well.

He cites the Smṛti to show that their fourfold nature is intended with reference to the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. Regarding the term "Manus": since the root *man* means "to understand," they are called Manus because they possess understanding. However, since understanding is common to all living beings, one might ask: what is the distinction of the gods and others? Therefore—

It was stated that this is due to the distinction in their realization (*bodhavaiśeṣyāt*). Now, one might ask: why abandon the well-known usage of the term *devāḥ* (gods) or *brahmādyāḥ* (those headed by Brahmā), and instead employ an unfamiliar term? To this he says: "Because of wretchedness" (*dīnatvāt*). The intention is that since terms such as *deva* and so forth are common to the Asuras as well, whereas the word *manu* alone is unique to the gods, only that [word] is employed. Regarding where these two types of gods are assigned, he says: "Non-Viṣṇuite," etc.
By this very [statement], the intended meaning of the passage "Of these, this world consists of these creatures" (*eṣāṃ leka imāḥ prajāḥ*) is also explained. || 6 ||

The fruit of knowing the majesty [of the Lord] as described has been stated with the words, "This [Vibhūti]. In that regard, since neither *karma-yoga* nor *samādhi-yoga* has been mentioned here, one might ask: how can this be called "this yoga"? With the intention that *karma-yoga* and the like are not intended here, he shows another meaning of the word "yoga" through a traditional authority (*smṛti*). "It is joined" (*yujyate*): the meaning is that the goal (*upeya*) is attained or made possible. Furthermore, it is a "capacity" (*śakti*); the meaning is that it is "yoga" because by means of it, something is capable of being joined. Now, one might object: since the sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and so forth has not been mentioned here, how can this be called "this Vibhūti" (manifestation)? To this, he says:

"Exalted" (*viśiṣṭā*)—he states the intended meaning. Regarding "greatness" (*mahattvam*): the sense is that greatness has been described as being such that it is unknowable even by the hosts of gods and others. Since greatness was not explicitly mentioned when [Arjuna] asked, "For Your divine self-manifestations (*ātmavibhūtayaḥ*) ought to be told in their entirety," how can the word *vibhūti* mean "greatness"? To this he replies: "various" (*vividha*). The sense is that in this context, the word *vibhūti* is intended to mean "the manifestation of various forms."

Granted that the word *yoga* may denote a means (*upāya*) and so forth, nevertheless, since no such means has been mentioned here, the meaning in this context must be "power" (*śakti*) alone. With the intention of stating that this [power] has indeed been mentioned, he says: "Yoga... (verse 7).

In order to generate confidence regarding the meaning already stated—that there are indeed those who worship Me in such a manner—it is said, "I [am the one they worship]. In that regard, since the sense of "Me" is already established by the statement "I am the source of all," why is it further said, "they worship Me"? To this he replies: "They worship Me. If "Me" were not mentioned, there might arise the impression that, with the intention of asserting the identity of the individual soul and the Lord, they worship their own self, thinking, "I alone am the source of all," and so forth.
It is for the purpose of removing that [misconception] that "Me" is stated. (8)
To the question of how it is that the vital breaths have gone to the Blessed One, he says: "Madgatā" (9.20).

In this context, regarding the inquiry into the nature of His manifestations (*vibhūti*), it is stated: "I am the sun among the luminaries," and so forth. Therein, He prevents the misconception that the objects qualified by their own respective classes and so on are themselves the forms of the Lord’s manifestations, by means of the word "yeṣām" (of whom). The phrase "of their own class" (*svajāteḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a portion of their own class and the like. He elaborates upon that very point with the word "brahma" (the Brahman). In the passage beginning with "the cause of excellence" (*ādhikyahetuḥ*), the words "of the Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*) and so on are to be supplied as the remainder.

For this reason as well, the Sun and so forth are not merely the forms of the Lord’s manifestation (*vibhūti*), but rather [the Lord] resides within them; thus he says: "In which? The sense is that if the Sun and so forth were the forms of the manifestation here, and not what is contained within them, then the response would be inconsistent with the question, "In which and which entities are You to be meditated upon? The term *jīva* (living being) is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for insentient matter (*jaḍa*).

If the form of manifestation (*vibhūti-rūpa*) were merely inherent in each respective object, then one might raise the objection that Kapila and others mentioned in such statements as "Among the perfected ones, I am the sage Kapila," "Among the sages, I am Vyāsa," "Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva," "Among those who bear weapons, I am Rāma," and "Among the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu"—would also lack the nature of being the Lord (*bhagavat*). Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by means of traditional authority (*smṛti*) itself: "It is twofold. The form of manifestation is the form of glory (*vaibhava-rūpa*).
Here too, the term "its own genus" (*svajāti*) is indicative of other [genuses] as well. The sense is that the question "in which ones? concerns those whose forms are concealed.

It has been stated that each respective name refers to a specific manifestation (*vibhūti*) inherent in that particular object. In this regard, since there is no identity between the Lord and those various objects, how can they bear those names? Therefore, he demonstrates that the manifestations possess those names precisely through *yoga-vṛtti* (etymological derivation). "Ātmā" [is explained as follows]: He is "Ravi" because he is known (*īyate*) by means of sound (*raveṇa*), that is, the Vedic word. The verbal root is *iṇ*, meaning "to go. A cloud containing water denoted by the word *mara* is *marī*. He who moves (*cālayati*) that is *marīci*. "Sukha" [is explained as]: from happiness (*sukhāt*) to happiness (*sukham*), that is, exceeding happiness (*atisukham*), is *śaśam*.

The moon is "tadvān" (possessing that). "Sāma" is so called because of its equanimity (*sāmyataḥ*); "Veda" is so called because of its knowledge (*vedanataḥ*). By this, the statement "I am the Sāmaveda" is explained. "Vāsaḥ" means all space; he who exists therein is "Vāsava. "Pāḥ" means protectors; because he is desirable and worthy of worship by them, he is "Pavana. The verbal root *vana* (in the sense of *ṣaṇa*) means "to share in" or "to enjoy. From the verbal root *pava* (in the sense of "purification"), he is "Pāvaka" because of his purifying nature. "Meraḥ" means one for whom there is no lord (*īśaḥ*) or impeller; because he possesses that character, he is "Meru."

This is because of the statement "so too from the sense of habitual action" (*tācchīlyārthād*). The meaning is: because of devouring—that is, being the enjoyer—of the essence, which is the object of the essence. "Skandana" means removal by oneself. "From the roasting of adversaries"—this is the ellipsis. "Jāḥ" means those that have been born. "Pād" is the recitation; because it is an object of sacrifice (*yajyatvāt*), it is a sacrifice, thus a "recitation-sacrifice" (*japayajña*). Because its state is like that of a horse, it is "aśvattha. From such passages as "That lake of mine is *aira*," *aira* means prosperity (*śrī*). It protects that [prosperity], thus it is "airāvata."

That which is required by men (*nara*) is *nāra*; he who gives that is *Nārada*. One who possesses modesty (*hrī*) is *Hrīmat*; his abode (*ālaya*) is *Himālaya*. Those who are bowed down (*natāḥ*) in an exceptional manner are *Vinatāḥ*; because he is their refuge or is connected to them, he is *Vānateya*. The happiness (*kaṃ*) of dwelling (*vāsa*) is *vāsaka*; because it is preeminent (*adhika*) in its excellence, it is *vāsaka*; thus, one who possesses it as a giver is *Vāsuki*. The caves (*darāḥ*) are the various divisions (*prabhedāḥ*) of happiness (*ka*); he who drinks from (*pibati*), that is, experiences (*anubhavati*), them is *Kandarpa*. The verbal root is *pā*, meaning "to drink."

The meaning of the verbal root *ṛ* (to go) should be understood [here]. He measures and knows that; thus he is Aryaman. From the verbal root *kala* (to know), *ākalana* means knowledge. He for whom *vara* (excellent) is *ṇa* (bliss)—as it is said, " *ṇa* indeed denotes bliss"—is Varuṇa. Or, he is Varuṇa because he covers (*vṛṇoti*). From the verbal root *māṅ* (to measure), *mā* means knowledge. Since the prefix *ūna-* is intended here in the sense of "little," he makes the world's measure small; thus he is Makara. His devotees seek their own Self; they are the *mṛgas* (deer). Because he is their lord, he is Mṛgendra (Lord of Deer).

She is called Jāhnavī because she causes one who abandons *saṃsāra* due to its lack of essence (*asāratā*) to choose [liberation]. "Place" (*sthāna*) means a support (*āśraya*). She is called *adhyātma* because she exists as the mistress (*patnī*) with reference to the Self (*ātman*). She is called *kīrti* because she is renowned. She is called *vāk* because she speaks. She is called *śrī* because she is resorted to (*śrayate*). Likewise, she is called *medhā* because she is understood; and *kṣamā* because she is endured. She is called *dyūta* because of her devotion to play (*krīḍā*), derived from the verbal root *div* meaning "to play" and so forth. Regarding the word "singers," the word "her own" (*svasya*) is to be supplied. She is *bṛhatsā* because her essence (*sāra*) is great (*bṛhat*). She is *ama* because she is immeasurable (*ameyatva*); thus she is *bṛhatsām*. She is *uśatī* because she possesses the desire for heaven and other such goals.

From the verbal root *uś* meaning "desire": he is *kusumākara* because he produces knowledge for the world that makes me—who was previously base—become well-praised (*suṣṭubh*). He is *mauna* because of his connection with the sages (*muni*) by virtue of being worthy of praise (*īḍya*), according to the Vedic scripture: "He reaches the end of the path; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. He is *mārga* because he is the head of all paths due to his expansiveness. He is *kapila* because he playfully drinks (*pibati*) or experiences (*anubhavati*) bliss (*kaṃ*). He is *vyāsa* because his abiding state (*sthiti*) is distinguished (*viśiṣṭā āsā*) within him;
this is based on the Vedic scripture stating "the letter *ṣa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," and because the sound *ṇa* denotes cessation (*nirvṛti*).

He is Viṣṇu because his nature consists of distinguished blissful activities. He is the giver of sovereignty over dissimilar beings such as the moon and so forth, because the constellations and other such entities are of a different genus. In passages such as "I am the *sattva* among those possessing *sattva*," he is described as being the essence of *sattva* and the like among the substrates (*dharmin*). In passages such as "among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara," he is described as being the excellence among those of the same genus for Śaṅkara and others.

"I am Vāsava among the gods, Uśanas among the poets, Dhanañjaya among the Pāṇḍavas, the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) among sacrifices, the thunderbolt (vajra) among weapons, and the Sāmaveda among the Vedas"—in such passages, the superiority of Vāsava and the others is stated by way of being a single instance of their respective classes.

To the question, "How is it that Vāsava and the others possess superiority only as a single instance of their class? he says: "Among the gods," etc. The meaning is that since Brahmā and others alone are superior among the gods and so forth, Vāsava and the others possess superiority only as a single instance of their class.

As for the statement that, because the *Ṛgveda* is superior, the *Sāmaveda* is superior only by virtue of being a single part belonging to the same class, that is incorrect; for in some places, the superiority of the *Sāmaveda* over even the *Ṛgveda* is stated. To this, he says: "In some places. The meaning is: where the superiority of the *Sāmaveda* over the *Ṛgveda* is mentioned, it is stated there with the intention of expressing the superiority of the presiding deity of the *Sāmaveda* over the presiding deity of the *Ṛgveda*, and not with the intention of referring to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Vedas themselves. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

This might be so if the presiding deity of the Ṛgveda were distinct from the presiding deities of the Sāmaveda; but why is that so? To this he says: "The Ṛc... [etc.]. Now, one might object: since there is no superiority of Prāṇa, Śiva, and others—the presiding deities of the Sāmaveda—over Lakṣmī and others—the presiding deities of the Ṛgveda—how can the statement of the Sāmaveda’s superiority over the Ṛgveda be justified even with respect to their respective presiding deities? To this he says: "Even there... [etc.]. The meaning is that even among the presiding deities, superiority should be understood according to what is possible.

When it is stated that the Sāmaveda has superiority over the Ṛgveda, then, when there is an intention to speak of Prāṇa—the presiding deity of the Sāmaveda—one should understand the superiority of Sarasvatī and others who preside over the Ṛgveda. When there is an intention to speak of Śiva, then the superiority of Umā and others should be understood; such is what has been stated. (20–40)

Having stated the summary of the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), the detailed explanation is now given with the words "Whatever... and so forth. In that context, one might ask: why does the Lord state that "whatever possesses such manifestations and so on is presided over by Me," instead of saying "it is born from a portion of My splendor" (*tejoṃśasambhava*)—that is, being produced from a part of Himself? To this He replies: "Of Me... The meaning is that it becomes conjoined with a portion of His luminous nature; thus, it is "born from a portion of His splendor" (*tejoṃśasambhava*), but not something whose birth is *from* a portion of His splendor (*tejoṃśāt sambhavaḥ*). The intention is that [the latter formulation] would entail an inconsistency. (41)

The expansion of that manifestation is then stated with the words, "Or rather. Therein, he says [the question] "What? in order to dispel the misconception that there is no fruit whatsoever from the extensive knowledge already described. The statement "What is the use of knowing? is intended solely to indicate that the knowledge about to be described possesses a superior fruit compared to the knowledge already mentioned; it does not, however, indicate that the previously mentioned knowledge is fruitless. To the objection, "Why should it not indeed indicate that the previously mentioned knowledge is fruitless? he replies with the word "Otherwise."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that even if the previously mentioned knowledge is fruitful, one must simply state that the knowledge about to be described is superior in its fruit? Therefore, is the objection raised by saying 'What is the use of knowledge? not improper? In response to this, [the author] cites a Smṛti verse to establish that even while making known the superiority of what is about to be described, the aforementioned objection regarding auspiciousness remains possible: "Anyat... The remainder of the sense is that "being censurable" means "it is to be abandoned. The meaning is: "However, it should be understood that something other than this is indeed superior. If there is something else superior, then that which was objected to is indeed to be abandoned.

Because the attainment of the superior makes the inferior useless, he says: "Both. This means that when both are attained, there is no need to discard the inferior, since one has obtained that which is more excellent. || 42 ||

Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 10 ||

In this context, the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) is described for the purpose of meditation; thus, because the subject matter of the chapter is clearly perceived, it is not explicitly stated [here]. To dispel the doubt that the Lord might have created the universal form at that very moment by taking some primary matter (*pradhāna*) or other material cause as a substrate—since the universal form had not been seen previously or subsequently—he says: "Himself" (*ātmānam*).

Since it was stated that after the request to "show yourself, the imperishable" (*darśayātmānam avyayam*), [the Lord] "showed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form" (*darśayāmāsa pārthāya paramaṃ rūpamaiśvaram*), it is established that the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) is the very nature of the Lord himself; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the manifestation would not correspond to the request. This is also established directly by the use of the word "divine" (*devam*). It is imperishable, supreme, consisting of all wonders, infinite, and facing in all directions.

Since Viśvarūpa is described as being endowed with such attributes of the Lord (Īśvara) as these, it is established that he is the very nature of the Lord himself. And since he is the very nature of the Lord, his eternity and his essential character of being consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*), etc., are established. Because the Blessed One is eternal and consists of consciousness, bliss, and so forth, the statement that he "created" the Viśvarūpa by means of non-conscious material causes is, therefore, incorrect; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the "Universal Form" (*viśvarūpa*) is simply the entire universe, as indicated by [the description] beginning with "having the moon and sun as eyes"? Therefore, how could it be the direct essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Lord? To this, he says: "Mine" (*mama*). Since it has been stated—in the passage beginning with "Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts, O Guḍākeśa, within my body"—that the universe rests upon the Universal Form, it follows that their difference is established; thus, it is logical that the Universal Form is the direct essential nature of the Lord. This is the intended meaning.

The meaning of the phrase "having the moon and sun as eyes" (*śaśisūryanetra*) is that its eyes have the moon and sun as their substratum. Now, one might object: since the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) is a collection of infinite forms, it is not logical for it to be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Blessed Lord, because the identity of one thing with many distinct parts is contradictory. To this, he says: "My forms" (*me rūpāṇi*). It is not the case that the Universal Form cannot be the form of the Lord simply because it is a collection of infinite forms.

"Behold my forms, O Pārtha, by the hundreds and thousands," and from such statements as "I see you on all sides, of infinite form," it is understood that infinite forms have been displayed; and since it is understood from "I wish to see your form" and so forth that only the display of a single form was requested, the state of being a single entity possessing infinite forms is not established. Nor is this contradictory, because the sense is that even those infinite forms are mutually non-different.

The objection that “the infinite forms are non-different” is untenable, because if the forms were one, their infinitude would be impossible; he dispels this doubt with a statement from the *Brahmatarka*: “One. Another supporting argument is given: “Only due to specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*). To the question, “In the absence of difference, how can there be a distinction in worldly usage based on mere specific distinctions? he says: “Absence. Where...

The absence of difference in the underlying reality is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); in that case, what is called "distinction" is merely that which brings about specific conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, the sense is that because there is an absence of difference as determined by *pramāṇa*, it is logical that specific conventional usage applies to the forms of the Blessed One precisely on account of their distinctions. Even though there is no difference [in essence], specific conventional usage regarding the forms of the Blessed One arises from distinction alone.

If it were so, then even in the case of cows, horses, and the like, there would have to be a specific conventional usage based solely on a "particular" (*viśeṣa*); therefore, he says: "Non-existence. The point is this: only where the absence of difference is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a "particular" accepted as the basis for establishing a specific conventional usage. However, since in the case of cows, horses, and so forth, difference itself is established by valid means of knowledge, [the particular] is not the cause of the specific conventional usage.

Now, is this particularity (*viśeṣa*) different from or non-different from the qualified entity (*viśeṣin*)? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress of differences. In the second case, the conventional usage of "particularity" and "qualified entity" would not be possible. Nor can the specific conventional usage be established there by means of another particularity alone, for that would entail an infinite regress of particularities. To this, he says: "The particularity also... Since the particularity is also the very nature of the qualified entity, there is no infinite regress of differences. Even in the absence of difference, the establishment of the conventional usage of "particularity" is achieved through the particularity itself.

The point is that since a particular (*viśeṣa*) itself serves to establish its own specific conventional usage within itself, there is no infinite regress of particulars (*viśeṣānavasthā*), as one need not admit further particulars.

He analyzes and defines that very particularity (*viśeṣa*) [as follows]: "Substance," etc. This statement, which applies to both sentient and insentient entities, is to be construed respectively. In the case of a sentient being, a particularity arises; some are eternal—thus the particularity is of two kinds. Nor should it be argued that because a particularity is of the nature of substance, it is eternal and therefore cannot be produced. For even though it is eternal by virtue of being of the nature of a sentient substance, the mention of its production is possible when one intends to refer to a specific individual manifestation.

In the case of non-conscious [substances], since a specific substance itself is the material cause of a particularity, there arises a two-fold distinction: some particularity, though existing as long as the substance endures, exists in the form of the effect through the nature of its material cause—the specific substance; while another exists as long as the substance endures. This is the sense. He provides examples of these two types of particularities for both conscious and non-conscious entities in their respective places, beginning with the word "vastu" (the object).

In the statement "the nature of consciousness exists," the specific attributes of being conscious, being a substance, having a nature, and existing are eternally manifest. In the statement "the conscious one acts, enjoys, and moves," the specific attributes of acting, moving, and enjoying are associated with manifestation and non-manifestation. Both of these types of attributes are absolutely non-different from the qualified substrate (*viśeṣin*). Likewise, in the statement "the nature of the mango fruit exists," the specific attributes such as being a mango and being a fruit exist as long as the substance endures and are absolutely non-different from the qualified substrate.
