In the expression "the mango fruit is yellow," the sense is that particular qualities such as yellowness are occasional and are both non-different and different from the qualified object.

To the question, "What is the proof for the existence of such a distinction (*viśeṣa*)?", he says: "The distinction. He clarifies that very point: "And not... [and so on]. Now, an objection is raised: since whatever specific form exists in an object is distinct from the nature of the substratum (*viśeṣya*), and since the nature of the substratum is itself devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), how can it be said that a distinction is known in all objects? To this, he says: "Of the qualified (*viśiṣṭasya*). This would be the case if the qualified were something other than the nature of the substratum; but this is not so.

If the qualified (viśiṣṭa) were distinct from the nature of the qualificand (viśeṣya), it would follow that the nature of the qualificand itself is not an object of knowledge (*aprameyatva*). This is because it has already been stated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies only to that which possesses the particularity (*viśeṣavat*). Furthermore, it follows that there can be no knowledge of the qualified if there is no knowledge of the qualificand; for as long as the differentiator (*vyāvartaka*) is unknown, it is impossible to correctly know that which is to be differentiated (*vyāvartya*), since the nature of the qualificand is what differentiates the qualified. This is the intended meaning. He states another objection regarding the non-objectivity of the nature of the qualificand: "māna... [etc.].

The point is that since the establishment of an entity depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if the essential nature of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) were not an object of cognition, that very nature would be non-existent. For this reason as well, he states "itself" (*svayam*) to show that the essential nature of the substantive is not devoid of distinctions. The meaning is as follows: regarding that which is the essential nature of a substantive, one must necessarily admit the distinction consisting in its being the "essential nature of a substantive. This is because it is impossible to know or to employ in linguistic usage [the term] "the essential nature of a substantive" for something that is devoid of the distinction of being the essential nature of a substantive. Therefore, even the essential nature of a substantive is not devoid of distinctions.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the nature of the substantive (*viśeṣya-svarūpa*) as qualified by the specific attribute (*viśeṣa*) is indeed different from that same nature of the substantive when it is already qualified? Therefore, [the ultimate] is simply without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). To this, he says: "That" (*tad*). The meaning is: although the nature of the substantive within that qualified entity is different from the qualified entity itself, it is nevertheless accompanied by the specific attribute consisting in being the nature of the substantive; therefore, it is not without attributes. Even in that qualified entity, the nature of the substantive is indeed different from the qualified entity itself.

He states the infinite regress involved in accepting that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is non-distinct [from the qualified] (*nirviśeṣa*). Regarding the word "thus" (*iti*): just as an infinite regress is asserted when one accepts a difference between the nature of the qualified and the qualifier, so too, upon reaching that same conclusion even when accepting their non-difference, that position must likewise be abandoned. Furthermore, if there were non-difference between the nature of the qualified and the qualifier, then with the knowledge of the nature of the qualified, the qualified form would also necessarily be known; consequently, a question regarding the qualified form after restating the nature of the qualified would be untenable. Therefore, he says:

Regarding the term “non-difference” (*abheda*): A single entity is restated; while it is known in its generic form (*ākara*), it is unknown in the specific form being inquired about. Since every entity is thus both known and unknown in respect to each [form], there is no logical inconsistency in the question. Furthermore, because the qualified form (*viśiṣṭākāra*) is non-different from the nature of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no infinite regress dependent on difference—this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase “because that which is non-different is qualified”: the meaning is that whatever is non-different from the qualificand is the very nature of that [qualificand] itself, and as such, it is qualified.

Dispelling the doubt as to how there can be both "knownness" and "unknownness" even through a difference in form when there is absolute non-difference between the qualified (viśiṣṭa) and the qualificand (viśeṣya), he explains what was stated [in the previous verse] with the words: "In oneness... The meaning is: since the experience of the identity of the qualified and the qualificand is established, there is no fault of infinite regress; and since, despite this non-difference, there is an experience of specific distinctions, and by the force of that [distinction] there is the experience of knownness and unknownness belonging to the very same single entity, there is also no fault of the impossibility of the question.

[Objection: "But why should there not be both difference and non-difference between the qualified (viśiṣṭa) and the qualifier (viśeṣya)? For if that were the case, the impossibility of the question [regarding their identity] could be resolved by means of their difference, and the infinite regress [of qualifiers] could be resolved by means of their non-difference. [Reply: Do you accept difference and non-difference between the qualified and the qualifier in some instances, or everywhere? In the first case, we have agreement, because we do accept difference and non-difference of the qualified—characterized by a qualifier that exists as long as the substance—with respect to the qualifier itself. He refutes the second position:

"Regarding 'difference and non-difference': these two are accepted by the opponent. The phrase 'in all cases' implies 'in the case of the qualified and the qualifier. Regarding 'the qualified [entity] having agency and enjoyership as its qualifiers': the meaning is that it refers to that qualified entity for which agency and enjoyership are the qualifiers. This is because, with respect to an object qualified by such qualifiers as agency and enjoyership—which persist as long as the substance exists—there is no experience of difference and non-difference characterized by the specific thought, 'I am an agent and an enjoyer, distinct from [the Self]. "

This is the state of being (*bhāva*). By this very demonstration of the non-difference between the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣin*)—characterized as agent, enjoyer, and so forth—that which was stated, namely that the agency and other attributes of specific conscious beings (*cetana-viśeṣa*) who undergo manifestation and disappearance are non-different from the qualified entity itself, is also established. Now, he establishes the non-difference of eternally manifest qualities such as essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so on. [The verse begins with] "Difference" (*bheda*). The words "of that which is eternally manifest" are to be supplied. [The phrase] "internal" (*āntara*) means existing in consciousness independently of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body.

In passages such as "the pure nature" (*śuddhasvarūpa*), since there is seen to be non-difference alone through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "the pure-natured one is liberated"—between the pure nature, reality, and so forth, which are eternally manifested particulars, the sense is that when the qualifier and the qualificand are non-different, the non-difference of the qualifier is necessarily established. Thus, he establishes the identity of the qualified [consciousness] even with those particulars characterized by manifestation and concealment, such as agency, as well as with particulars such as knowledge, which consist in the unity of consciousness. [He does this by stating: "not separate" (*apṛthak*).

The meaning is that there is a rule that no perception occurs as something separate [from consciousness]. Now, an objection is raised: just as it is said that [the self] is of a pure nature and so forth, and just as it is said to be the agent, the enjoyer, powerful, and wise, so too it is said that Kṛṣṇa is stout and so forth. Therefore, there should be oneness of consciousness even for specific qualities such as blackness, which are caused by the body. To this, he says: "External," etc. We do not assert the oneness of consciousness with the specific qualities merely because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two kinds of qualifiers and the qualified; rather, we do so when, in the absence of the perception of difference, there is coreferentiality.

Furthermore, there is no non-perception of the difference between Kṛṣṇa and Devadatta here, by which blackness would constitute the very nature of Devadatta; for the meaning is that their difference is indeed perceived.

Some, however, maintain that there is identity with consciousness only for those specific attributes such as pure nature (*śuddhasvarūpatva*) which are eternally manifest, but not for [attributes] such as agency (*kartṛtva*). [The author] refutes this with the word "viśeṣa" (specific). Is this twofold distinction—that identity with consciousness belongs only to pure nature and so forth, but not to agency and so forth—postulated on the strength of some reason, or without it? Not the first, because no such [reason] is observed. Not the second.

Since even agency and the other attributes can be established as being one, it is futile to postulate a duality, as that would entail the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Furthermore, it would lead to the necessity of postulating something that is neither supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor contradicted by them. If, disregarding such faults as conceptual over-elaboration, one were to assert the distinctness of agency and the rest, then there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that even the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) such as pure nature (*śuddha-svarūpatva*) must likewise be distinct; this is because the opponent has no fear of such faults. Thus, the absolute non-difference of the specific qualities and so forth from the conscious principle (*cetana*) has been established.

By that same principle, it should be understood that even in the case of an insentient entity, there is absolute non-difference between the particularity (*viśeṣa*) and its possessor (*viśeṣin*), provided that the particularity exists as long as the substance itself does.

He now supports the two [positions of] difference and non-difference regarding the particularity that does not exist as long as the substance: "There is no unity... If it were stated merely that "there is neither unity nor plurality," a suspicion might arise that [the nature of reality] is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*). To refute that, he says "due to the necessity" (*niyamāt*). Thus, the sense is that because each one is absent. The connection is as follows: due to experience and because there is no other way, there is neither unity nor plurality.

[Objection: "But since even in the conscious [self] there exists both difference and non-difference, and because the conscious and the unconscious thus share a single mode of being, why is it specifically designated as 'unconscious'? To this he says: "One" (*eka*). In the case of the conscious self, difference and non-difference are experienced only with respect to distinct counter-correlates, such as "I am different from the pot" and "I am non-different from myself. In the case of the unconscious, however, they have only a single counter-correlate. Therefore, the conscious and the unconscious do not share a single mode of being; this is the meaning.

Thinking that by describing the experience of the existence of both difference and non-difference between the cloth and its constituent parts, such as the threads, one has already demonstrated the experience of the existence of both difference and non-difference between the threads and their specific qualities, such as "cloth-ness," [the author] says: "One... Because of the experience of the oneness of the threads in the form of the cloth and their mutual difference, both difference and non-difference are experienced between each individual thread and the cloth.

The sense is that if the cloth were absolutely non-different from each individual thread, it would be impossible for their mutual difference to be experienced. He states the absence of any other alternative [in the words]: "From the threads. If the cloth were absolutely different from each individual thread, then the cloth would be seen separately from each individual thread; but this is not the case. Nor is the cloth absolutely non-different from each individual thread, because if the cloth were non-different from each individual thread as it exists in its own particular configuration, it would follow that the cloth does not exist when those individual threads are present—this is the sense.

Since the collection of all parts is not itself manifold, and since the whole would be non-existent in the absence of those [parts], and because parts are defined as those existing in a specific configuration, the absolute non-difference of the whole from its parts must be understood. To the objection—"Just as there is absolute non-difference of the single self despite the multiplicity of attributes such as agency residing within it, why should there not likewise be absolute non-difference of the single cloth despite the multiplicity of threads?"—he says: "And not... (na ca).

Is it being argued that there is an inconsistency in what was stated, or is it merely an attempt to prove ultimate non-difference even in the insentient by means of an example based on specific attributes residing in the Self? It is not the first, because here there is no multiplicity of agency and so forth; for it has already been stated that a particular empirical usage is accounted for simply by a specific attribute that sustains itself. Nor is it the second, because through the experience of difference in the Self as qualified by each individual attribute—such as "I am the agent" and "I am the enjoyer"—there is likewise an experience of absolute non-difference in each individual attribute.

The sense is that there is no cognition of a cloth in each individual thread. Is it the case that difference and non-difference between part and whole exist only in the final insentient composite, such as a cloth? No, he says: "In this case. The meaning is that in the case of an insentient cloth and so forth, there would be difference and non-difference with its own parts, and for those parts as well, there would be difference and non-difference with their own parts; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*aparyavasāna*). One might ask: since the atom is eternal, how can there be an infinite regress when a finality is possible there? To this, he says:

"Not [so]," he says. It is not only because there is a lack of evidence for partlessness that there is an infinite regress; rather, he says "not" to indicate that the atom possesses parts. Not only is there a lack of evidence for its being partless, but also because it is understood to have parts through the distinction between its eastern, western, and other spatial divisions; thus he says "eastern," etc.

If it is argued that although there are no parts in the atom *per se*, the cognition of such [parts] arises because parts exist as conditioned by spatial directions such as "east" and so forth—then what? Would the condition (*upādhi*) be connected to a single part of the atom? If so, since that single part already exists prior [to the conditioning], it follows that it must make known the distinction of parts that already existed previously; this is the meaning. He refutes the second alternative with the word "akhilam" ("the whole").
Now, one might object: since qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are partless (*niravayava*), how can it be said that "there is nowhere any entity that is without parts"? To this he says:

"Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because parts are perceived through the distinction between prior, posterior, and other spatial divisions, and because any part that is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) has already been refuted.

Thus, by establishing both difference and non-difference between the parts and the whole, the difference and non-difference of particularities such as "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*)—which do not persist for the entire duration of the substance—and which qualify the threads and so forth, have been established. Now, he establishes the difference and non-difference of particularities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth—which are accepted by opponents as being qualities (*guṇa*) and the like, and which do not persist for the entire duration of the substance—and which qualify the threads and so forth. [He says: "In existence... [and] "in the insentient."

In a given entity, difference and non-difference are indeed logical for qualities, actions, and so forth—those specific attributes that exist as long as the substance exists—during the state of their own existence. This is because, in cases such as "the fruit is blue," one must accept non-difference due to the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, even while the entity exists, since there is at times the linguistic usage of its absence—as in "the fruit is not blue"—one must also accept difference.

The meaning is that when there is absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*) in a thing, its destruction is impossible. However, it should be understood that after destruction, there is indeed difference, because it is illogical for that which is itself non-existent to possess non-difference. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of the conscious self (*cetana*), there is absolute non-difference even regarding strength, knowledge, and so forth, which are non-existent during states such as deep sleep, why should it not be the same here? To this, he says: "In the conscious self... (*cetane*).

The meaning is as follows: because it is established—even during states such as deep sleep—that strength and other qualities persist in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), by virtue of worldly usage such as "this person is sleeping, yet he is strong"; thus, absolute non-difference is logical [in this case], but not for qualities like blackness and the like, because those are utterly destroyed. To the question, "Why should blackness and the like not also persist in the form of potentiality?", he says: "And not... The implication is: we would accept the persistence of blueness and so forth in the form of potentiality if there were worldly usage regarding them with the intention that they exist as potentialities, just as there is for strength and the like;
however, there is no such usage as "the mango fruit is blue" when it is actually yellow.

As for what was stated—that by the power of its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), a single sacrificial cake (*pūpa*) becomes the object of manifold transactions—that would only be possible if a non-difference of form were established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since it has been stated, "Where there is absence [of difference]," and no such proof is found, he says: "It is one only. Furthermore, the claim that this [multiplicity] is possible even though it is difficult to reconcile due to the possession of inconceivable sovereignty is incorrect. For if that were so, then by the power of supreme sovereignty, even the identity with the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such things would logically follow. Therefore, he says:

"Parama" (supreme) means as follows: whatever consists of auspicious qualities, even if all that is difficult to accomplish through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), is accepted as being possible in Hari due to His possession of supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*); however, [this does not apply] to such things as identity with the individual soul (*jīvaikya*). For if that were the case, the very notion of supreme sovereignty would be untenable—this is the intended meaning. (1.14)

Having seen the universal form, [the Lord] praises it under the guise of repeating what has been seen, saying, "I see. In that context, regarding the phrase "Brahmā seated upon a lotus-throne," he explains the term "seated upon a lotus-throne" (*kamalāsanastha*) in order to dispel the impression that it refers to a limited meaning. As for how Brahmā can be situated within Brahman, he says, "Rudra," with the intention that this is a specific qualification of Rudra, who is denoted by the word "Lord" (*īśa*).

This explanation would be valid if Rudra were established in Brahman; but why is that so? To this he says: "Viṣṇum" (verse 15–18). Regarding the phrase "of heaven and earth," since it is already established by the use of the word "by you" (*tvayā*) that [the agent] is singular, for what purpose is "by one" (*ekena*) stated again? To explain its significance, he says: "Of heaven and earth."

Since there is the possibility of a misunderstanding—that the phrase "without beginning, middle, or end" refers to infinity of magnitude—[the author] asks, "For what purpose is this said? and then replies, "Because [people] are generally afraid. This is stated because most people are afraid. Thus he says: "From Arjuna."

The sense is that, by the force of these words, the term "the three worlds" refers here to those devotees who are free from obstacles and are capable of seeing the universal form (viśvarūpa) residing therein; since the Lord possesses a certain degree of majesty, fear may also arise upon seeing Him, and thus the statement beginning with "having seen the wonder" is justified. Because it was said, "I see the gods in Your body," the liberated ones—referred to indirectly in the verse "for these hosts of gods"—are distinct from the non-liberated ones mentioned there, and thus there is no tautology.

There would be no tautology if this [verse] referred to liberated beings. Why is that? If it is argued that it is not so because the use of the third person (parokṣanirdeśa) is possible even for those who are not liberated, we say no; for the intention is expressed by the statement, "They enter You," which describes entry into the Lord by their own will alone. Thus he says: "They enter" (viśanti). Even so, why does this refer to liberated beings? To this he says: "Entry" (praveśa). (21–25)

[Objection: But since the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others lack any activity directed toward entering the mouth of the Blessed One, how can it be said, "And these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [enter You]," and so forth? To this, he says: "Others... Even for those whose activities are not directed toward entering the mouth of the Blessed One, because they enter there by means of the very activity of the Blessed One's mouth, the usage "they enter" is appropriate as a figurative expression (*upacāra*).

The meaning is that, just as in the expression "the people entered the water," the entry of the subjects occurs there through their very activity directed toward entering the waters of dissolution (*pralaya*), so too here [the entry into the mouth occurs through the Lord's activity]. If the entry were caused solely by the Lord’s facial activity, it would apply only to the army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, because the faces of the Lord are turned toward them. Therefore, the phrase "together with my own" (*sahāsmadīyaiḥ*) would be inappropriate; hence he says: "The army" (*senā*).

Now, one might object: since they were crushed at the very start of the battle, others did not see them; how then could Arjuna and I see them in such a manner? To this, he says: "But those... Since only those who were about to die at that very moment are being referred to here, such a statement is appropriate for the commencement of the battle. Furthermore, because [the bodies] fell in a shattered state, they came within the range of subtle vision, and thus it is logical that others saw them in that way as well.

The meaning is that because Arjuna has been granted divine vision by the words "I give you divine sight" and so forth, it is logical that he perceives what cannot be seen by others. He provides an illustration for the fact that others do not see this, beginning with the word "Just as. He gives an illustration for Arjuna's perception of what is invisible to other eyes due to his possession of divine vision, beginning with "Just as. This has been explained in detail in the *Viṣṇudharma*. (26–30)

Regarding the phrase "Tell me, who are you?", he says "viśeṣa... (concerning specific qualities) in order to dispel the misconception that the questioner is asking, "Which deity are you? Since the qualities and so forth have already been stated by [the Lord] himself, one might ask why there is a further question; hence he says "viśeṣa," meaning "concerning a subject already known to himself. One might then ask why it could not concern his essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone; to this he replies: since [the Lord] was already known previously as Viṣṇu, this question concerns only his specific qualities, actions, and so forth, and not his essential nature alone. || 31 ||

Since qualities and so forth were not mentioned in the context of exclusion (parihāra), this [definition] does not have them as its object; therefore, with the intention that the word "time" (kāla) itself denotes qualities and so forth, he explains it by means of a traditional authority (smṛti): "Time," etc.

"Bound" (*kalitāḥ*) means connected with oneself. The roots *kala* are listed as meaning "to bind," "to destroy," "to know," and "to cause to flee. To answer the question "For what purpose is he of such fierce form? it is said, "the destroyer of the world," and so forth. That is appropriate because of the phrase "even without [you]. Since Yudhiṣṭhira and the others are also spared there, how can it be said that "all will die without you"? To this, he says: "Even (*api*). It is not being said here that all will die without Arjuna alone.
However, with the exception of Arjuna’s brothers, Aśvatthāman, and others—the sense being that they are included by the word "even" (api)—32-33.

Since I myself have set out here to annihilate the worlds, there is no room for hesitation regarding the destruction of the enemy; therefore, it is said, "Therefore, fight. In that context, [the phrase] "Droṇa and Bhīṣma" [is used].

How is there a specific mention of Jayadratha [as being killed] by Droṇa and others? Since he lacked the necessary capability, the author says: "Of Jayadratha... The meaning is that this specific mention of him is due to a most powerful boon granted by his father—"May his head be split asunder if anyone should cut off his head and let it fall on the ground"—and not because of any special capability like that of Droṇa and the others. Now, one might ask: how can it be said that they were "slain by me alone" while they were still alive?

If this were the case, how could it be said, "You shall be the conqueror"? To this he says: "They are slain. Being "as good as slain" means being close to death because their life-span has been taken away. If they were not actually slain, then one should have said, "Become the slayer. Why, then, is it said, "Be merely the instrumental cause"? To this he says: "Afterwards."

The sense is that because he lacks independent agency as a slayer, he is said to be merely an instrument (*nimittamātra*). Or, [the Lord] says this because it is impossible to kill one who is already dead: "How can it be said, 'Kill those who have been killed by Me'? Therefore, He says: "Afterwards" (*paścāt*). The meaning is that since Arjuna himself is the actual slayer, the Blessed One intends only to say: "Standing in [his] place, you too become the object of the worldly convention that 'you are the slayer' regarding those killed by Me. (34–38)

In the passage of Arjuna’s praise beginning with "Vāyu, Yama, Agni," etc., he demonstrates that the words *vāyu* and so forth refer to the Blessed Lord through their etymological function (*yogavṛtti*), based on traditional authority (*smṛti*). Regarding *vāyu*: because there is no distinction between the letters *va* and *ba*, the word *va* signifies strength (*bala*). From the verbal root *aya-paya gatau* (to go), the word *āyu* signifies knowledge (*jñāna*). The verbal root *idi* signifies supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). (39–41)

Regarding the verse, "Whether you have been treated with disrespect in matters of recreation, bedding, seating, or food, or even if alone," although I am indeed one and the same as you, the Lord says "even though alone" (*eka*) to dispel the misconception that He might mean something else—such as "forgive me in accordance with worldly convention. He then provides the connection (*anvaya*) by saying "even" (*api*). The meaning is this: although He is unworthy of disrespect because He is the Supreme of all, He simply says "you have been treated with disrespect"; nothing else is intended, for there is no evidence for Arjuna’s identity with the Blessed Lord.

To the question of how the word *eka* (one) can signify "the most excellent of all," he says: *eka iti*. The meaning is that he is *eka* because he is *e* (the supreme), and he is *ka* because he acts (*karoti*). For indeed, an agent who is independent of anything else is the most excellent of all. (42–45)

In the statement of Arjuna’s prayer, “Be [present] in that very form,” it is said, “Abandon the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) and assume your former one. To dispel the misconception that this implies a total relinquishment of the Universal Form, he says: “In that very form” (*tenaiva*). The point is: when another form is perceived, why should there not be an abandonment of the Universal Form? Why then conceal it? To answer this, he says: “The five-faced one” (*pañcānana*). Since it is stated that even in the Narasimha form the Universal Form remains concealed, the implication is that the perception of another form does not entail the abandonment of the Universal Form. (46)

The rarity of the vision of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), which is intended to generate an excess of devotion, is expressed by the word "by me. In that context, since the phrase "the universe consisting of light" might be misunderstood as stating that the Lord’s form is identical with the universe, he explains the word "universe" (*viśva*) by recalling its traditional definition in order to dispel such a misconception. [He says: "The universe... Furthermore, since the statement "that which has never been seen before by anyone other than me" might be misunderstood as implying that the universal form was not seen by others besides Arjuna, he says "by you" (*tvat*) to dispel that misconception. [He says: "By you..."

It is not stated here that the Universal Form was not seen by anyone other than Arjuna. On the contrary, since it was not said that "it had never been seen by anyone before this," but rather stated as "by someone other than you," the meaning is simply that it had been seen by him [Indra] previously while in his body as Indra. In that case, one should not even suspect that it was not seen by Brahmā and others either; for the phrase "other than you" was spoken with the intention of referring to those inferior to Arjuna. He says: "tvad" (than you). It should not be imagined on this basis that it was not seen by those inferior to Arjuna.

He says "by them" because the state of not being seen was stated with the very intention that it was not seen even by those inferior to Arjuna. This interpretation would indeed be valid if the universal form had been seen by Brahmā and others, as well as by Indra—who is inferior to Arjuna—and if it were established that while Indra saw it just as Arjuna did, those inferior to Arjuna did not see it in that way. To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "The universal form..."

Whether Indra’s vision is superior or inferior, it is not possible for you to state specifically that he must be seen by means of Indra’s body; for if his vision were superior, it would not have been mentioned, and if it were inferior, no prohibition against it is observed. (47)

If the vision of the universal form by others were also intended here, then there would be a contradiction with the subsequent statement, "Not by Vedic study, nor by sacrifices, nor by gifts. Therefore, he says: "Not [in the subsequent statement]. It is not being said in the subsequent statement that others besides Arjuna lack the vision of the universal form.

However, when it is said that those inferior to you have not seen it as you have, the intention is this: although He is not seen by them in that way through their own power, one might suspect they could see Him in that way through means such as the Vedas; therefore, it is stated that even by means such as the Vedas, those inferior to you cannot see Him as you do. If it is asked, "Could it not be that the meaning is simply that the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) was not seen by anyone other than Arjuna?"—we say no, because that would contradict the cited Smṛti.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the preceding statements here, such as "having seen the wondrous form" and "the worlds were seen. Therefore, he says: "Otherwise... (verses 48–49).

Regarding the statement, "He showed his own form," since it specifically declares that the form of Kṛṣṇa is His own, one might argue that the previously stated fact—that the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) is the very nature of the Lord—is incorrect. To this, he says: "As His own" (*svavat*). Here, by the word *svaka*, the belonging of Kṛṣṇa’s form to Himself is not being asserted in such a way that the Universal Form would not also belong to Him. Rather, the meaning is simply that it is to be shown as His own, according to the etymology: "it is made [or shown] like His own" (*svavat* = *svakīyavat*). Thus, it means it is to be manifested as belonging to Himself.

Now, since both are shown to belong to the Blessed Lord, why is there a specific mention of the form of Kṛṣṇa alone? To this he says: "The universal form. It is true that both forms are shown to belong to the Blessed Lord.

Thus, [this vision] belongs only to the wise; however, for the ignorant, it is only the form of Kṛṣṇa that is manifested as belonging to the Lord, and not the Universal Form (viśvarūpa). Therefore, the intention is that a specific statement is appropriate with reference to the ignorant. For this very reason, it was said "as by himself" with reference to those of limited knowledge. Why must it be explained in this way? Might the Universal Form not also belong to the Lord? To this he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

In the context of refuting the perception of the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Viśvarūpa as being respectively one's own and not one's own, [the author] refutes the subordination of the form of Kṛṣṇa by recalling the statement that "He showed the supreme form," which declares Viśvarūpa to be supreme. [The text says: "Supreme" (para). Otherwise, [if it were not so], [it would be] by its very nature. Then, [one might ask: "If Viśvarūpa alone is supreme, how is supremacy seen even by the wise in [the case of] the incarnate forms? To this, he says: "Manifestation" (vyakti). The manifestation of supremacy resides in Viśvarūpa, not in the forms of the incarnations.

Therefore, the sense is that such a view is logical. Furthermore, this manifestation is stated with reference to those of limited knowledge; it is not stated with reference to great knowers of Brahman, such as Brahmā and others, because for them, even Kṛṣṇa and the like are perceived as supreme. Thus he says: "The ignorant... (50). Now, one might object: since it is said, "Having seen this human form," that the form of Kṛṣṇa is human, how can it not be inferior? To this he says: "In some respect... (51). The meaning is that otherwise there would be a contradiction with the cited scriptural statement.

Now, one might object: since it was stated in the verse, "This form is very difficult to see," that even those who constantly long to behold this form do not actually see it, how can it be said that the universal form (viśvarūpa) was seen by those superior to Arjuna as well as by those inferior to him? To this, he correctly applies that statement [beginning with] "Those who... [The text continues: "Those who... [are devoted to me alone, etc.]"—this refers to those who, having abandoned all other duties, worship me alone with single-minded devotion; they, being purified by the yoga of knowledge, behold my supreme form. But those others, who are not so, do not behold it. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word "eternal" (nityam) is used here in the sense of "always" (sarvadā), meaning that while they always desire to see it, they do not see it at all times. Thus, there is no inconsistency. Moreover, the Lord’s intention is this: "I am exceedingly difficult to behold even for those who possess the power of yoga, such as Brahmā and the rest; therefore, it is not surprising that you do not see me. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word "eternal" is intended to indicate that the vision of the Lord's form is extremely rare, occurring only once in a great while. It is not meant to imply that the vision is impossible even for those who possess the power of yoga. Otherwise, the statement "I am exceedingly difficult to behold" would be redundant, as it would have already been established by the word "eternal. Therefore, the meaning is simply that the vision is rare. Alternatively, the word "eternal" may be taken as qualifying the word "desire" (kāṅkṣiṇaḥ), meaning that their longing for the vision is constant. In this case, the meaning is that although they always desire to see it, they do not see it because they lack the power of yoga. Thus, there is no contradiction. The construction [of the verse] is indicated as follows: "That form of mine which you have seen by means of this [vision], even those gods who constantly long to behold this very form—what they see is this [form], which is extremely difficult to perceive. The sense is that otherwise, there would be a contradiction with what has been stated. || 52 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Oṃ. He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter [with the verse beginning] "sādhana... The meaning is that in this chapter, a determination is made regarding the superiority of the previously mentioned worship of the Lord over the two means to liberation—namely, the worship of the Unmanifest and the worship of the Lord. Now, one might object: if the worship of the Unmanifest were also stated anywhere to be a means to liberation, just like the worship of the Lord, then the question arising from the doubt expressed in the words "Thus, those who are ever-united... would be appropriate.

And since that [object] does not exist, how can there be a question? To this he says: "Of Śrī. The man who is born for the sake of propitiating Śrī goes forth from his home for that very purpose; he bestows his own age upon the teachers and gurus who instruct him in Śrī. Thus, men who worship Śrī attain immortality. The meaning is that in that couple known as teacher and disciple, all desired things become real.

Is the worship of Śrī itself an independent means for attaining liberation? To address this, the author cites a traditional verse (smṛti) with the intention that one must first generate the grace of Śrī, and through that, by means of the grace of the Lord alone [liberation is attained]. He says: "Śrī... [and so on]. Why is it that the grace of Śrī generates the grace of the Lord? To answer this, he speaks of the supreme majesty of Śrī: "The Unmanifest... [and so on].

If prosperity (*śrī*) is of such a nature, why should its grace itself not be the cause for the attainment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)? For what purpose, then, is it said that it is a means for attaining the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*)? To this he says: "Of her" (*tasyāḥ*). Since even Śrī is subordinate to Viṣṇu, the grace of her is not a means for the goals of human life independently; rather, it is only by being the grace of Viṣṇu. He states the reason why Viṣṇu is superior to Śrī, who has become the Great Brahman (*mahadbrahma*): "He who... (*yaḥ*).

Thus, the meaning is that, having raised the doubt based on the words of the Śruti and Purāṇas that the meditation on the Unmanifest (avyakta) is a means to liberation just like the meditation on Viṣṇu, he asks about the supreme means.

If the worship of Śrī were understood to be a means to liberation just like the worship of the Blessed Lord, then a question regarding that very subject should have been asked. To the question, "Why is this done regarding the worship of the Unmanifest (Avyakta)? he says: "The Immutable (Kūṭastha). Since the words *kūṭastha* and *akṣara*, which are employed for the conscious primordial nature (*cit-prakṛti*) in the subsequent passage—"The Immutable is called the Indestructible"—are used here as well for the Unmanifest, the Unmanifest is indeed the conscious primordial nature.

Therefore, the sense is that since the worship of the conscious nature (*citprakṛti*) is understood to be a means to liberation, the question regarding the worship of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is indeed appropriate. By this, the faultlessness of the statements "from such scriptural passages as... and "from the worship of the unmanifest" is also established. Now, one might object: "Since words such as 'unmanifest' have their primary meaning in the Supreme Brahman, why should that not be what is intended here? To this, he says: "Otherwise..."

The meaning is this: if the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) here were used to denote the Supreme Brahman, then Arjuna’s question—asking which among his own worshippers of the Unmanifest and the worshippers of the Blessed One is superior—would be illogical, as it would imply a distinction between the Blessed One and the Unmanifest. Why is it illogical? To this he says: "Because the Blessed One’s status as the Supreme Brahman has already been stated by Arjuna himself," namely in the verse beginning with "the Supreme."

Others, however, thinking that here the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the qualityless Brahman—which is otherwise called the Void—imagine that the meaning of the question is: "Between one who worships that [Brahman] and one who worships the Lord, who is superior? They then state that the answer in the refutation declares the superiority of those who worship the unmanifest. To them, he says: "But as for those... etc.

Having stated that His own devotees possess the highest status with the words, "They are considered by Me to be the most disciplined," and having clearly declared that only those who worship Him are supreme through the phrase "in Me alone," [the Lord] has effectively refuted those who claim the superiority of worshippers of the Unmanifest (Avyakta). Consequently, because of their audacity, they are merely objects of grief—[the Lord's thought being], "Alas, these are ruined!"—and not opponents against whom a rebuttal could be formulated; such is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: since Śrī possesses activity, how can she be described as "immovable and fixed" (*acalaṃ dhruvam*)? To this, he reconciles the two by means of the *Smṛti* itself. [The objection is: "They worship that which is indefinable, unmanifest, and inconceivable"—this is contradictory, because worship is impossible for that which is indefinable, unmanifest, and inconceivable. Therefore, he reconciles the indefinability and other attributes with the fact of being an object of worship by means of the *Smṛti* itself, stating: "Because of her subtlety" (*sūkṣmatvāt*).

"Only My devotees are said to be the best" (in the verse beginning with) "In Me. [Objection: Since liberation exists even for those who worship the Unmanifest (avyakta), just as it does for Your devotees, how can they be considered superior? To this, while acknowledging that the Unmanifest-worshippers do indeed attain liberation, the superiority of His own devotees is stated with its underlying reason in the verse beginning with "But those who [worship] the Imperishable. There, the attainment of the Lord being described is not intended for the Śāktas alone; with this intention, He explains the passage beginning with "In Me" by means of the scripture itself: "By those who do not know Viṣṇu."

In this context, by the phrase ending with "one should meditate constantly" (*dhyāyīta nityadā*), the intended meaning of the prefix *pari* has been stated. By the phrase "pleased by that" (*tena tuṣṭā*), the intended meaning of "they attain Me alone" (*te prāpnuvanti māmeva*) has been stated. With the thought that, although meditation on the Unmanifest is a means to liberation, it should not be considered the highest [path], He says: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). The words "along with Śrī" (*śriyā saha*) are to be supplied [to complete the sense]. By this, the meaning already expressed in the verse "having fixed [the mind] on Me" (*mayyāveśya*) is established.

If liberation exists even for those who worship the Unmanifest (avyakta), how can it be said that those who worship the Blessed Lord are superior? To this, he says: "Because... By this, the word "affliction" (kleśa) is explained. In this manner, "service" (paryupāsana) consists of the extreme restraint of the collection of senses and equanimity toward all things.

Since there can be no grace from the Unmanifest (the Lord) without good conduct such as being devoted to the welfare of all beings, it should be understood that for those endowed with mere supreme faith—even if they possess other forms of good conduct—the abundance of afflictions remains, because the grace of the Blessed One is possible even in their absence. For this reason as well, he says that the worship of the Blessed One alone is supreme: "By Viṣṇu. When one worships the Blessed One together with Śrī, since the supreme grace of both is possible, liberation occurs without delay.

However, in the view that there is a separate meditation on the Unmanifest (avyakta), one must first perform some meditation on the Lord, then meditate on Śrī separately for a long time, and subsequently perform uninterrupted meditation on the Lord together with Śrī; since liberation occurs only after such a long duration, the implication is that meditation on the Lord alone is superior. By this, the meaning of the verse beginning with "But those who [offer all actions]" is explained. He concludes the stated superiority of the worship of Viṣṇu by means of two reasons with the words: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
And the remainder is that there is a predominance of these.

"It is incorrect to say that those who are constantly engaged are the most perfectly engaged, because [this would imply] the same meaning. To this, he says: "Engaged" (*yukta*). It should be understood that the term *nityayukta* (constantly engaged) has the sense of *nityodyukta* (perpetually striving). Now, one might object: "In the verse beginning with 'But those who... (*ye tu sarvāṇi*), the superiority of worshipping the Lord through *ananya-yoga* (exclusive yoga) is stated. Therefore, how can this [verse] be explained as being intended to state the excellence of worshipping the Lord together with Śrī? He dispels this doubt by means of an authoritative scriptural statement itself: "Of Viṣṇu... (*viṣṇoḥ*).

By the phrase "non-association with others" (*ananyayoga*), the connection with the worship of another deity is not prohibited; rather, it prohibits the worship of another [deity] independently, without acknowledging its subordination to and inclusion within the retinue of the Lord. Therefore, the interpretation provided by Prājña is correct—this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might raise the following objection: "If a question is asked regarding which is superior among the meditations on the Unmanifest (avyakta) because liberation is heard of for those who meditate upon it just as it is for the worshippers of the Blessed Lord, then why is no such question asked regarding the meditation on other deities? For it is also heard that meditation on other deities is a cause of liberation, as in the passages: 'Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace,' and 'Having known Hari, Hara, and Viriñca, one is released from transmigratory existence. Thus, why is no question asked in that regard? He dispels this doubt by means of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana) maxim: "It is finite," etc. (Antavat iti).

The sense is this: since the status of the worship of other deities as a means to liberation has already been refuted, even though such [worship] is mentioned in the Śrutis and other texts, one must assume that those passages have a different purpose; thus, the question was raised regarding the worship of the Unmanifest (avyakta) alone, and not regarding the worship of other deities. If that is so, then since the status of the worship of anyone other than the Lord as a means to liberation has already been refuted elsewhere, it follows that the worship of the Unmanifest also lacks that status. Why, then, is a question asked concerning it without assuming a different purpose for those statements? To this, it is said: "Of Lakṣmī. [This implies that the worship of the Unmanifest is actually the worship of Lakṣmī.]

The sense is this: although the worship of anyone other than the Blessed Lord is generally prohibited as a means to liberation, since Lakṣmī is exceedingly dear to the Blessed Lord, there exists a distinction between her and others; thus, it is possible for her worship to be a means to liberation. Consequently, rather than formulating the prohibition as referring to the worship of anyone other than her, Arjuna—without posing a question regarding the worship of others—instead asked a question specifically concerning the worship of the Unmanifest (Avyakta). This is the underlying intention.

"Because my worship is superior, perform that alone. If that is unavailable, know me [through the name]. In its absence, know me through the yoga of practice (*abhyāsa-yoga*). And in its absence, be intent on my work (*mat-karma*). And if you are unable to do even that, it is said: 'In me' (*mayi*), meaning resort to my yoga (*madyoga*) and renounce the fruits of action. In this context, "resorting to my yoga" is simply being a performer of my work (*mat-karmakṛt*). To explain how this is so, he clarifies it by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*): "The Vaiṣṇavas... The construction is: one performs all actions as Vaiṣṇava acts.

The meaning is that one performs [the action] with Viṣṇu as its object. "Worship" (arcā) refers to cleansing and bathing the image; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), meditation (dhyāna) is also to be included. "Possessing merely the connection with that" means possessing merely the means for performing those actions. By this, the phrase "my connection" is explained as "the connection with my being the object of the action. The sense is that if one desires the state of having the Blessed One as the object of one's action, only then does that connection arise; it does not arise through other means such as optional (kāmya) worship and the like. By this, the meaning of the previously stated term "all actions" (sarvakarma) is established.

He states that there is also a gradation even in the worship of the Blessed Lord: "Not perfectly," etc. That knowledge arises when meditation is not attained, and practice arises when even that is not attained—this is established by the words, "For [the latter] is better. By this, the following is explained: even regarding meditation preceded by knowledge, the desireless alone is superior to the desirous; thus he says, "Therefore," etc. He states the reason for that: "Therefore," etc. By this, the word "from meditation" is explained. Now, one might object: here it is said that peace is the fruit resulting from renunciation.

Therefore, how can it be said that "liberation arises from that"? To this he says: "Peace" (śāntiḥ). Now, one might ask: why not accept that here only the abandonment of the fruits of action is being described as having meditation as its excellence? Why is the accompaniment of meditation preceded by knowledge being stated? To address this, he says: "Peace. Here, it is intended that the abandonment [of action] is the cause of liberation, which is expressed by the word "peace. And that is not tenable if one understands abandonment as mere renunciation, because it has been said: "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga. [This refers to] abandonment accompanied by meditation preceded by knowledge.
The sense is that, because it is possible for that [to exist], it is precisely that which is intended here. || 4.15 ||

The passage beginning with "But those who [perform] all actions," and so forth, is elaborated as "one who is free from hatred" (*adveṣṭā*). Therein, the phrase "one who has renounced all undertakings" (*sarvārambhaparityāgī*) is explained in four ways in order to dispel any other possible misconceptions. [The commentary begins with: "Not non-Vaiṣṇava... This establishes the stated meaning. [It continues: "All... By the expression "renunciation of the fruits of all actions," it is established that one is called "one who has renounced all undertakings" through the renunciation of the fruits of all undertakings.

By the word "in me" (*mayi*), it is established that he is one who has renounced all undertakings through the abandonment of pride regarding all actions and the dedication of all undertakings to the Blessed Lord; for this is how the phrase "in me" is explained by the *Smṛti* itself. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the phrase "having renounced all duties" (*sarvadharmān parityajya*) under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is established that he is one who has renounced all undertakings through the renunciation of undertakings not belonging to Viṣṇu; for that will be explained with supporting reasoning later on.

Now, since the phrase "one who has renounced all undertakings" (*sarvārambhaparityāgī*) is explained as "one who has renounced the auspicious and the inauspicious" (*śubhāśubhaparityāgī*), why is it specifically stated that he is "one who has renounced the undertakings of non-Vaiṣṇavas" and so forth? To this, [the author] explains it in a way that does not contradict what was previously said, by recalling that very [explanation]: "Devotion... This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that this also includes the undertakings of Vaiṣṇavas as means to that [devotion].

Regarding the phrases "equal in pain and pleasure" and "free from joy, impatience, fear, and agitation," he explains them by means of traditional authority (*smṛti*) itself in order to dispel any misconception regarding their restrictive meaning. He says: "For the most part" (*prāyaḥ*). Thus it is said that one is called "equal" with respect to pleasure and so forth, and "devoid of joy" and so forth. If this is so, then since some slight inequality and the like still exist, how can there be a statement of their total absence? To this he replies: "As [it is said]" (*yathā*). Why should the primary sense not be accepted? To this he replies: "For not... (*na hi*).

[Objection: Since joy (*harṣa*) is a quality (*guṇa*), why is its renunciation said to be required? To this, [the author] shows that the word *harṣa* has the sense of something to be abandoned (*heya*) by means of a traditional authority (*smṛti*). He says: "The drawing away" (*hṛtiḥ*). The word "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the compound]. [Objection: In passages such as "one who is without hatred," only the state of being dear is mentioned for those possessing non-hatred and so forth; however, in the verse beginning with "But those who [follow] the nectar of dharma," those possessing faith and so forth are described as being exceedingly dear.

To the question "For what reason is this said?", he replies: "By the individual [means]. In passages such as "one who is not hateful" (*adveṣṭā*), it was stated that dearness is attained by each of those means individually. In the verse beginning with "But those who," however, there is extreme dearness through the totality of the previously mentioned means, such as "not being hateful. The sense is that the collective is superior to the individual.

[Objection: Is it not possible that in passages such as "one who is free from hatred" (adveṣṭā), dearness is expressed by means of qualities like non-hatred, whereas in the passage "But those... (ye tu), extreme dearness is expressed by means of devotion (bhakti), since devotion is the highest of all means? To this, he says: "Devotion" (bhaktiḥ). The sense is that since devotion has already been mentioned even in the description of non-hatred and so forth, this distinction [between them] is not logical. [Objection: Since devotion was not mentioned in the description of the individual means in the verse beginning with "He whom the world does not fear" (yanmāṃ nodvijate lokaḥ), how can it be said that devotion is inappropriate for the individual [means]? To this, he says: "Because" (yasmāt). (17–19)
Because the meaning of the phrase "the immortal state of Dharma" is difficult to comprehend, he explains its meaning: "Dharma... (verse 20).

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words "All," etc. The meaning is as follows: that which was primarily taught in the first hexad as the means to knowledge, that which was described in the second [hexad] as the nature of the Lord in passages such as "But I am not...", that which was shown as the nature of the individual soul (jīva) in "The earth, water, fire...", and that which was declared as the field (kṣetra) in "The earth, water, fire...", all of that which was stated in a scattered manner is presented here in this chapter in a condensed form for the sake of easy comprehension.

The term *sarvārthasaṅkṣepa* (the summary of all meanings) refers to the fact that he summarizes the meanings of all the chapters and presents them in brief. In this regard, the objection is raised: "Since the knowledge of the Lord alone is the cause of liberation, for what purpose are both the field (*kṣetra*) and the essential nature of the Lord stated? This doubt is first resolved by the word "this" (*idam*). Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to how the body—described as a modification of the field in the passage "an aggregate, consciousness..."—can be called the entire field, the scripture explains this as follows: "For [it is] injury... (*hiṃsā* etc.).

Because the *jīva* is eternal by its very nature, it is said that the *jīva* is "injured" only through the injury to this [body] which has transformed into the form of the body and so forth. Indeed, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and other elements become the cause of injury to the *jīva*. From the verbal root *śṛ* in the sense of "injuring," because it is the cause of injury, it is *śara*; and because it is impelled (*īrya*) by another, it is *īra*; thus the meaning is *śarīra* (body). From the verbal root *kṣi* in the senses of "dwelling" and "going," the meaning of the term "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) is expressed by the phrase "the unmanifest and so forth. Their modifications are the modifications of the field (*kṣetra*).

By this, the meaning of what was stated as "desire and aversion" is established. With the intention that mutability does not belong to desire and the rest when they are of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), he says: "of the nature of consciousness. By this, it is understood that [desire and so forth] are themselves non-conscious (*acid-rūpa*) by nature; the word "exist" (*vartante*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. To the question, "Do these always exist in a state of mixture?", he says: "only in *saṃsāra*, not at all times," with the intention that [this is not the case during liberation]. To the objection, "Since aversion and suffering are absent in liberation, how could a liberated one be joined with desire and the rest which are merely consciousness?", he says: "and liberation... The remainder [of the classification] is "demonic" (āsurī) and "divine" (daivī). If that were so, there would be an even greater predicament, since in divine liberation there is no possibility of hatred and the like, while in demonic liberation there is no possibility of happiness and the like; therefore, although it is impossible for the entirety of desire and so forth to exist in each [state], there is no contradiction because they are possible through their respective divisions. With this intention, he says: "Pure consciousness alone" (cinmātra). The word "where" (yatra), which follows, is connected to what comes later as well. Although devotion to Viṣṇu is not explicitly mentioned among desire and the rest, it is understood as the counter-correlative to hatred because hatred has been mentioned.

In order to dispel the notion that the phrase "he who knows this" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), he explains it by means of another statement: "The Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*). [Objection: Since everyone who knows the field is a "Knower of the Field," why is Viṣṇu specifically designated as such? To this he says: "For not... [etc.]. [Objection: One might ask, "Is he himself included within the field while knowing it? In response to this expectation, he says: "He... By this, the verse "not being" (*na sat tat*) is explained. [Objection: How can there be omniscience if he is not present in all things?

To this he says: "He" (*saḥ*). By this, the statement "outside and within" (*bahirantaśca*) is explained. Since Viṣṇu is non-different from all living beings, how can there be His abiding in them? To this he says: "And distinct" (*vilakṣaṇaśca*). How is there distinction? To this he says: "Everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*). Since it might be argued that the possession of powers such as hands and so forth in hair and the like contradicts reason, he says: "Kṛṣṇa," with the intention that because it is perceived, it does not contradict reason.

By this, the meaning of the term "from all sides" (sarvataḥ) is explained. To the question, "What indeed is the power of the Lord's hands and so forth?", he says: "All... (sarva...). The word "knows" (vetti) is also indicative of [the capacity for] action. By this, the phrase "possessing the qualities of all the senses" (sarvendriyaguṇa) is explained; that is, by means of which all the qualities of the senses are manifested and sustained. To the question, "If the Lord possesses hands and so forth, how can there be statements in the Śrutis and other texts regarding His being without sense organs (anindriya)?", he says: "He... (saḥ).

By this, the meaning of the statement "devoid of all sense organs" is established. To the question, "If qualities such as knowledge exist, how can there be a declaration that He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)?", he says: "By qualities... [etc.]. Why is an alternative meaning imagined for the scriptural teaching of being "devoid of qualities," rather than simply accepting total absence of qualities? To this, he says: "All... [etc.], because His embodiment of all auspicious qualities is established by authoritative means of knowledge. By this, the meaning of the statement "nirguṇa" is established.

To the question, "If Hari possesses hands, feet, and so forth, how can He be described as 'non-moving' (acara)? he says: "Otherwise" (anyathā). To the question, "Since He is sometimes described as 'moving' (cara), how can there be an absence of changeability (vikāritva)? he says: "Moving" (cara). By this, the verse "the non-moving and indeed the moving" is explained. To the question, "How can there be movement for one who is all-pervading? he says: "Pervaded" (vyāpta); for His nature is not merely all-pervasiveness, but He also possesses atomicity (aṇutva) and intermediate size (madhyamatva).

By this, the intended meaning of such statements as "It stands pervading everything" and "It is seated in the heart of all" is established. To the objection—namely, that since contradictory attributes are stated in passages such as "That is far, That is near," and because the Lord is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva), how could what has been said be logical?—the author reconciles this by stating: "Because of omnipresence. By this, the phrase "standing afar" is explained.

[Objection: Since qualities such as all-pervasiveness (*vyāptatva*) and atomicity (*aṇutva*) cannot coexist in another entity, how can they reside together in Hari? To this, he says: "Ananta... [meaning *ananta-śakti*]. [Objection: Even if He possesses infinite and inexhaustible powers, how can those [contradictory qualities] exist in Him? To this, he says: "Nor... (*na ca*). Furthermore, because the name "Kṣetrajña" is not well-known in the sense of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is not that [the soul] which is meant here; thus he says: "Nor... (*na ca*). Even if it exists in some places, its presence [is not intended here]. Nor should it be said that the name "Kṣetrajña" is not well-known even for Viṣṇu, because it is well-known in the very scripture already cited, and also in other scriptural passages.

He demonstrates its well-known usage: "the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*). "Mental manifestations" (*manaso vibhūtīḥ*) means the transformations of the mind. "Fashioned by *māyā*" means fashioned by one's own will, which serves as the instrumental cause.

For this reason as well, he states that the phrase "he who knows this" does not refer to the individual soul (jīva). [The word] "therefore" [means]: since the individual soul is not intended here, it is for this very reason that, according to the Lord's intention, it says "he who knows this. Because the term *kṣetrajña* has been explained in a general sense, and because the individual soul also possesses some degree of knowledge of the field (*kṣetra*), it would follow that the soul itself attains the status of *kṣetrajña*; therefore, in order to exclude that possibility, it is said, "Me, the *kṣetrajña*"—this is the meaning.

If it is asked, "Why is it said that 'Know Me as the Knower of the Field' (kṣetrajña) was stated for the purpose of refuting the individual soul's (jīva) status as the Knower of the Field?"—is this said while accepting that the statement "He who knows this" refers to the Lord (Īśvara), or does it have the individual soul as its subject? [The author] refutes both positions with the words: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

If one accepts that the phrase "He who knows this" refers to the Lord (Īśvara) but does not accept that the phrase "Me, the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajñaṃ mām) serves to distinguish Him from the individual soul (jīva), then since the supreme Lord's status as the Knower of the Field would already be established by the former phrase alone, the repetition of that statement in "Me, the Knower of the Field" would be redundant. Alternatively, if one accepts that "He who knows this" refers to the individual soul but does not accept that "Me, the Knower of the Field" distinguishes Him from the soul, then the very fact of the soul being the Knower of the Field—which ought to be stated—would be [implied] by the former...
The sense is that by the mere statement "he knows," the matter is complete; therefore, the phrase "me, the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajñaṃ mām) would be redundant and even contradictory.

Even if the phrase "he who knows this" refers to the individual soul (jīva), the subsequent sentence is not purposeless. For, having stated the soul's status as the Knower of the Field, the status of the Lord is also stated; thus, it is established that the soul—described as the Knower of the Field—and the Field are one with the Lord. This makes the passage meaningful. On the contrary, if this were not accepted, the status of the Lord alone as the Knower of the Field would be established [as the sole conclusion]. To this, he says: "bhedeti" (regarding difference).

The meaning is as follows: having stated that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the status of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), one might think that the difference between that [soul] and the Lord (īśvara) is now being declared; however, even if one accepts that the Lord himself is the Knower of the Field, the phrase "he who knows this" remains meaningful. This is because it serves the purpose of etymologically defining the name "Knower of the Field. Since the etymology of the name "Knower of the Field"—namely, "one who knows the field (kṣetra)"—is well known, one might ask: "Is it not sufficient to say 'and Me, the Knower of the Field' alone? Why provide the etymology? To this, he says: "All... (sarva...).

When it is stated, "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi*), there might arise the impression that, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of *kṣetra* (the field) and *jña* (the knower), the Lord Himself is being described as consisting of both the insentient and the individual soul (*jīvātman*). To refute this, even the well-known etymology is stated. Nor should it be argued that, by abandoning the well-known etymology, such a doubt could not possibly arise; for the point is that such an impression is possible for those who accept the non-difference of everything—consisting of both the insentient and the individual soul—from the Lord.

Since it is possible to state—by inserting the term denoting the Lord (*īśvara*)—in the very sentence beginning with "He who knows all this, from the etymology of the name *kṣetrajña* for the Lord and the absence thereof in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), they call him the *kṣetrajña*," there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in postulating a separate sentence for that purpose; therefore, he says: "The *kṣetrajña*. It is not the case that in the subsequent sentence his status as *kṣetrajña* is mentioned merely to exclude the *jīva*, such that there would be prolixity.

However, the meaning is that while the Lord's indistinct statement regarding His exclusion from living beings is set aside here by the phrase "by the Lord," one's own abiding in the field is mentioned to indicate the sense of the term *kṣetra* (field), derived from the root *kṣi* (to destroy/perish).

Regarding the argument that after stating the individual soul's (*jīva*) status as the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) in the passage "he who knows this," the Lord's (*īśvara*) status as such is also stated in the words "and also the knower of the field," and therefore there is no redundancy—this is refuted [by the author] with the phrase "in that view. The sense is as follows: if the position is taken that "he who knows this" refers to the individual soul, then since the etymology of *kṣetrajña* is "one who knows the field" (*kṣetraṃ jānāti*), the status of being the knower of the field is established for the Lord just as much as for the individual soul by the very statement "he who knows this. Consequently, the sentence "and also the knower of the field" would be entirely redundant. This applies to the individual soul described as the knower of the field and to the field itself.

He refutes the argument that the statement "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi) is meaningful for the purpose of expressing non-difference from the Lord. [The author says: "All," etc. If it were intended here in the phrase "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" that there is non-difference between the entire field and the Knower of the Field, then one ought to have said, "Know all fields and the Knower of the Field to be Me."

The intention is that the use of the locative case in the phrase "in all fields" (*sarvakṣetreṣu*) would otherwise be untenable. One might then argue: "In that case, let it be stated here that the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed non-different from the Lord; for if that were so, there would be no contradiction. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*). If only the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*), described as the knower of the field, and the Lord were intended to be expressed, then one should have said, "I and the knower of the field are one and the same. It is not logical, however, to first refer to the knower of the field and then enjoin its status as the Lord.

The sense is that, since even this Lord—whom [the text] intends to enjoin by saying "Know me" after having referred to the individual soul (jīva)—is, like the individual soul, merely imagined, there is no distinction between them. || 3 ||

Since it has already been stated that "that field is [the body]," the phrase "and from which" would be redundant; therefore, he says: "And from which. If one objects, "In that case, it should have been said 'and she who is,'" he says: "And she," with the intention that this is a different proposition. To the question, "What is this 'consent' (anumati)? he says: "Conforming" (anusāriṇī). The words "of the production of the effect" are to be supplied. By this, the meaning of the word "consenter" (anumantṛ) is also explained. He states the authority for this: "Impulsion," etc.

If it is argued that since [the Lord] is "that from which" and "that which," these two propositions must be stated, and yet the statement of both is not heard [in the text], he says: "The witness" (*upadraṣṭā*). Here he provides the authority by saying "the witness, the permitter," and so on; the sense is that because the "permitter" has been mentioned, permission itself is also mentioned as his attribute. To the question of where the proposition "and whose power" was promised is stated, he says: "That which is to be known" (*jñeyam*).

Now, one might ask: since consciousness (*caitanya*) is immutable, how can it be taught as being present within modifications (*vikāra*)? To this, he says: "Consciousness" (*cetanā*). Furthermore, one might raise the objection: since the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) of the elements mentioned in the passage beginning with "the great elements" constitutes the field (*kṣetra*), how can it be said to be an effect (*kārya*)? Dispelling this doubt, he states the authoritative proof for the aforementioned point: "The aggregate" (*saṅghāta*). (7)

Knowledge is said to be that which enables one to speak of the knowable; thus, "humility" (amānitva) and so forth are called knowledge. Since the phrase "the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality" (tattvajñānārthadarśana) therein has an unclear meaning, he states its meaning: "The reality... [and so on]. Now, an objection may be raised: having stated the means to knowledge through "humility" and so forth, and having stated knowledge itself as "the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality," why is it said at the conclusion, "this is called knowledge"? To this he replies: "It is known" (jñāyate). The ellipsis to be supplied in the word "proktam" (is called) is "by the word 'knowledge'" (jñāna-śabdena), or rather, "it is said to be declared. || 12 ||

Now, one might ask: since the expression "the beginningless supreme Brahman" (*anādimatparam brahma*) is complete with the word "beginningless" (*anādi*) alone, for what purpose is "possessing no beginning" (*anādimat*) stated? To this, he says: "Beginningless" (*anādi*). And here...

There would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya, because a fault was stated in the Bhāṣya regarding the non-acceptance of the primary meaning of the suffix *matup* mentioned therein. Here, however, having accepted that very [primary meaning], he states another purpose for the suffix *matup*: "he gathers" (*cinoti*). He explains the statement, "The Supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being," by means of the authoritative scriptural text itself, using the words "primarily" (*mukhyataḥ*). [Objection: How can the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) be denoted by the words "being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*), and how can the Lord be distinct from them? To this, he says: "The formed... (*mūrtam iti*).
But it is formless. || 17 ||

To dispel the misconception that the phrase "to be reached by knowledge" (*jñānagamyam*) merely expresses being an object of knowledge, he says: "By himself" (*svayameva*). Here, it is precisely his state of being known by himself that is expressed, and not the state of being known by another. Nor is there an absence of the Blessed One being known by himself; for it has been stated that he is "by himself. To the question, "Why could the meaning not be 'known by another'? he says: "By another" (*anya*...).

The sense is this: in order to refute the position of those disputants who claim that the Lord cannot be an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) because of the contradiction between agent and object within a single action—arguing that "knowledge" and "the knowable" imply such a contradiction when the word "knowable" is used—it is stated here that He is indeed His own object of knowledge, and not the object of knowledge for another. Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy, since His being the object of knowledge was already stated in the introductory sentence: "I shall declare that which is the knowable. To the question, "If the purpose is to show that He is His own object of knowledge, how can this be called a statement of His majesty? he replies: "Because of [the absence of] agent and object... [and so forth].

The meaning is this: with the intention that "the Lord effects within himself the state of being an agent—even that which is unjoined—in a single act of knowledge and action," this is said; therefore, this is an expression of His sovereign power (*prabhāva*).

He states another means of knowledge regarding the knowability of the Lord: "The knower of Himself, the knower of the independent. And His knowing is independent. To the question "Of what is He the knower?", he says: "By Himself. Furthermore, that knowing of His which was described as independent is not distinct from Him; thus he says: "And consciousness. To the question "Is He known by Himself alone?", he says: "And [He is] the object of knowledge. Why is it said "in some respects"? For one might ask: why could He not be known by others in every way? To this he says: "That..."
