Just as others depend upon the grace of the Lord for His knowledge, so too the Lord has no dependence on another regarding His own self-awareness; thus, he explains His sovereignty with the word "sva" (own). By that—namely, by being the knower of Himself and so forth—it is as follows: He whose nature is light (*prakāśa*) and who is independent (*svatantra*) is "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*). To say that He could be both the knower and the known of another is not the definition of the term "self-luminous."

Since the individual souls (jīvas) are also self-luminous, how can it be said that [the Lord] alone is so? To this he says: "Of the individual souls. The sense is that because the individual souls lack independence and the status of being enjoyers, it is logical that He alone is [so described]. || 18 ||

Having concluded what was said, that knowledge is now praised with the words "iti" (thus). In this regard, he explains the phrase "madbhāvapada" (the state of being Me) in order to dispel any other possible misconception: "madbhāvāya" (for the sake of attaining My state of being). || 19 ||

Since it was promised that "that which [arises] from what, and what it is," the nature of *prakṛti* and so forth is now stated in the verse beginning with "prakṛtim. There, the words "prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ ca" (both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*) are to be understood as the remainder of the statement. The reversal of word order is for the sake of connecting the word "ubhau" (both), which was mentioned earlier, with the masculine gender. By this, it is indicated that "ubhau" constitutes a separate sentence; furthermore, the phrase "ubhe api" (both indeed) serves as a summary.

Regarding the phrase "and the modifications and the qualities" (*vikārāṃśca guṇāṃśca*), [the author] refutes the misconception that the *prakṛti* is an independent cause of the modifications and so forth by explaining the very meaning of the word "qualities" (*guṇa*), since it has been stated that "desire and the rest are modifications. The phrase "of the modifications" (*vikārāṇām*) means that because the independence of the Lord alone will be declared in the passage "the witness, the permitter," there is no independence for the *prakṛti*; rather, its role is solely that of the material cause (*upādānatva*). Now, one might ask: since the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are also modifications—just like desire and the rest—what is the purpose of mentioning them separately in the phrase "and the modifications and the qualities"? To this, [the author replies]:

He says: "And of the qualities (*guṇānām*). Even though the qualities such as *sattva* are themselves modifications (*vikāra*), the separate mention of both "modifications" and "qualities" is appropriate because it is intended to show that while *sattva* and the others undergo relatively few modifications, desire (*icchā*) and the rest undergo a greater number of modifications than those. This is the meaning.

In order to refute the impression that the verse beginning with "kāryakāraṇakartṛtve" refers to the non-conscious *prakṛti* and the individual soul (*jīva*), he explains it—by means of authoritative evidence itself—as referring to the conscious *prakṛti* and the Lord (*īśvara*). [He says: "By his own body... and "having veiled the reality of Viṣṇu. The meaning is: "without knowing the true state of Viṣṇu. Since bondage through karma is possible only for one who is ignorant of the reality of Viṣṇu, and since [karma] is the cause of the body and senses, the conscious *prakṛti*—which is the cause of ignorance—is the cause of the body and senses for the individual soul (*jīva*).

He explains the second half [of the verse] with reference to the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*): since the Lord is the agent of everything, why is His agency regarding the power of experience (*bhoga-śakti*) stated as something distinct? To this he says: "Of all... Just as Viṣṇu, though the protector of all, is specifically called the "Protector of Vaikuṇṭha" because there is no other protector for Vaikuṇṭha as there is for other places, so too Hari, though the agent of everything, is specifically called the "agent of the experience and so forth of certain [beings]."

The meaning is that, as in the case of other effects, there is an absence of activity by others regarding [the soul's] being an enjoyer and so forth. "Specifically by its own action" means solely by its own action. By this it is indicated that although the Blessed One is the cause of the agency of both the effect and the cause, the conscious primordial nature (*cit-prakṛti*) requires its own activity for the granting of the state of being an enjoyer; thus, while the Lord is the cause of the agency of the effect and the cause, His activity is more predominant in the agency of the cause, and this is what is meant by calling Him the "cause" of the agency of the effect and the cause.

He states that both of these points are indicated in the *Gītā* itself: "Of the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvarasya*). Even though the Supreme Lord alone is the cause of the agency of both the effect and the cause, it is appropriate to speak of the conscious nature (*cit-prakṛti*) in that regard; for while its activity is slight in the granting of the status of enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), it possesses greater activity in terms of agency when compared to that [conscious nature]. Likewise, even though the Supreme Lord is the agent of everything, it is appropriate to speak specifically of His granting the status of enjoyer.

The meaning is that, in order to indicate that the Lord alone possesses greater activity than the conscious principle (*cit*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), and so forth—on the grounds that their activity is minor when compared to the activity required for the bestowal of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) elsewhere—it is stated "is said" regarding the first and second halves of this verse. To the question, "How is this indicated by this [verse]? he says: "Even in the case of agency," and "in comparison with the state of being an enjoyer. This means "in comparison with the activity [of others] in the bestowal of the state of being an enjoyer upon themselves. The phrase "greater activity" refers to the remaining part [of the verse]: "agency over the cause and effect. The reason for the state of being an enjoyer is stated; the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

To dispel the misconception that the term "Lord" (Īśvara) is being referred to in the verse "For the Person (Puruṣa) abides in Nature," he says: "The Person. Since the Lord was introduced by the word "Person" in the passage "The Person [is the witness] of pleasures and pains," one might ask how the word "Person" can here refer to the individual soul (jīva). To this, he says: "Of both. Although the Lord was introduced here by the word "Person," it is nevertheless appropriate to understand the word "Person" in this context as referring to the individual soul.

In the verse "both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*," the word *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) just as it does to the Lord (*īśvara*), because both are equally derived from the source material (*prakṛta*). Otherwise, the term "both" (*ubhau*) would be redundant; this is the intended meaning. One might object: "Granted that the *jīva* is the subject under discussion, nevertheless, it is not logical to abandon what is proximately mentioned and instead grasp what is remotely mentioned. To this, he says: "Just as... Even though the Lord is proximately mentioned, the abandonment of Him and the grasping of the *jīva*, who is remotely mentioned, is justified.
This is because this *puruṣa* is perceived as the enjoyer of the qualities of *prakṛti* and the world.

The meaning is that since that [state] is impossible for the Lord (Īśvara) and possible for the individual soul (jīva), it is logical to rely on the object [of the text] according to what is appropriate. Or, he says "yathā" (as follows) to address the question: "If both are under discussion, why is only the jīva mentioned? || 21 ||

If the word "puruṣa" here were intended to mean the individual soul (jīva), there would be a redundancy; for the relationship between the soul and its effects and causes has already been stated by the phrase "in the state of being the agent of effects and causes," and the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth has already been stated by the phrase "it experiences the qualities born of nature. Therefore, he says: "The effects... [and so on].

The intention is that although the relationship between cause and effect and the experience of pleasure and so forth have been mentioned previously, there is no fault of redundancy because the statement "the Puruṣa, indeed, abides in Prakṛti" was made for the purpose of refuting those who maintain their falsity. To the objection—"Since the establishment of [the Puruṣa's] non-agency depends upon valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), how can it be refuted merely by stating what has not been said before?"—he replies with the word "hi" (indeed).

The meaning is that because the relationship between cause and effect and the experience of pleasure and so forth are stated here as being established by experience through the use of the word "hi" (for/indeed), the contradiction with experience on the part of those who maintain their falsity has been demonstrated; thus, this is not merely a matter of verbal assertion.

Since the experience "I am happy" or "I am miserable" may be erroneous, one might ask: if the enjoyment of pleasure and so forth is admitted to be false, how can there be any contradiction [with our experience]? To this, he says: "For not... The meaning is that the experience whose object is pleasure and so forth is not an error, because it is an experience of an internal object; for no error is ever observed in the case of an experience of an internal object. Furthermore, he says: "Nor is it... because there is an absence of any subverting cognition (bādhaka) to show that this experience is an error.

[The author] addresses the objection: "Since the Jains and others perceive the self and so forth as having a medium size (*madhyama-parimāṇa*), their cognition is seen to be erroneous; how then can it be said that [our cognition] is non-erroneous on the grounds that it is an experience of an internal object? Dispelling this doubt, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*): "The body... etc. Here, the mere fact of being an internal experience is not the reason (*hetu*), for if that were so, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Rather, it is [the experience] qualified by immediacy (*aparokṣatva*). Since error is observed only in the case of external immediate experience, the absence of such error in internal experience is established.

The sense is that for the Jainas and others, the delusion regarding [the soul's] being of medium size and so forth arises solely from inference and other such means. To the objection—"Even in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), why might the experience of pleasure and so on not be a delusion?"—he says: "In that case too" (*tatrāpi*). Wherever there is a delusory nature to the experience of external objects, it is postulated precisely because of contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since there is no subverting factor for the experience whose object is pleasure and so forth, its non-delusory nature is logical; this is the sense.

For this reason as well, one should not claim that pleasure and so forth are false because the experience of objects such as pleasure is an error; thus he says: "The Witness" (sākṣī). The sense is that if pleasure and so forth—though established by the experience of the Witness—were merely imagined through delusion, then the entire distinction that "everything is false, while the Self is true" would fail to be established, since even this very distinction would itself be subject to falsity, being established by the experience of the Witness. [This refers to] "delusiveness" and "non-delusiveness."
The meaning is: "imagined by delusion" versus "not imagined by delusion.

The distinction that "everything is false while the Self is true" exists only from the standpoint of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), but not from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, its non-establishment is not undesirable; to this he says: "From conventional usage. Even this established rule—that it exists only from the standpoint of conventional usage—is not proven. The sense is that if the Witness (*sākṣin*) lacks validity, there would be no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for it. Furthermore, if the experience of the Witness were invalid, then the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) regarding a post and so forth in relation to a pillar and so forth would be a delusion (*bhrānti*).

The claim that mental states such as the perception of a pillar and so forth are non-erroneous is not established, because it is the Witness-consciousness alone (*sākṣin*) that apprehends whether a cognition is erroneous or non-erroneous. And if that [Witness] is not established, even mere worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established; with this intention, he says: "Error. By this, the position that the distinction—namely, that "everything is false" while "the Self is true"—exists from the standpoint of worldly transaction, and that this is established through scripture and other means, is also refuted. This is because the validity of scripture and the like is also apprehended by the Witness.

One should understand that the passage beginning with "of that which is established by perception" (*sākṣisiddhasya*) is a single textual unit; thus, the phrase "it is an error" (*bhrāntiḥ*) must be understood as being supplementary to that [preceding statement], insofar as it serves to state the probandum (*sādhya*).

As for the statement that the direct experience of objects such as pleasure is not an error because there is no sublater (*bādhaka*), that is incorrect; for there exist authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as the scriptural text, "And he who is already liberated is liberated again. To this, he says: "Experience" (*anubhava*). By this [statement], the erroneous nature of the experience of objects such as pleasure is not established, because its own essential nature and its validity (*prāmāṇya*) have not been proven. The point is that it is the very experience of the Witness (*sākṣin*) that establishes those [objects], and yet that [experience of the Witness] is asserted to be erroneous.

Nor is it reasonable to hold that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) is erroneous only with respect to objects such as pleasure, while it is non-erroneous regarding the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; for there would be a lack of confidence due to the absence of any specific means of valid cognition [to establish that distinction]. Anticipating the objection that even if the witness-consciousness is erroneous, the validity of the nature of the means of valid cognition will be established through worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), he says: "From transaction" (*vyavahārataḥ*). The nature of the means of valid cognition and so forth is not established by worldly transaction, because neither the world nor its transaction is established.

The meaning is that the witness (*sākṣin*) alone is the grasper of that [object], and it is admitted that this [witness] is illusory (*bhrānti*). Anticipating the objection that "even if the witness is illusory, the establishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and the transactor will occur through mere cognition (*pratīti*)," he refutes it with the words: "Through cognition. The sense is: the establishment of worldly transaction and so forth might indeed occur through cognition alone, provided that cognition itself were established; however, it cannot be said that there is any means to establish that [cognition].

Raising the objection, "Since the witness (sākṣin) himself is established through cognition, how can there be an absence of a means of proving him? he offers the following rebuttal: "By itself" (svataḥ). The meaning is this: the witness is not established by cognition; for since [the opponent] admits that [cognition] regarding pleasure and so forth is erroneous, the power [of the witness] is blunted by the doubt that "this cognition exists even in the absence of actual perception," and thus [the witness] cannot be proven by it.

For this reason as well, he states that the experience of objects such as pleasure is not an error: "sva... (one's own). The sense is that if the experience of objects such as pleasure were admitted to be an error, then even the self would be non-existent, because there would be no means of establishing it. [Objection: But the self is perceived directly through the very cognition "I"; therefore, how can there be an absence of a means of establishing it? To this, he says: "svayam" (by itself).

The point is this: the self is not established by the experience "I am," because since that experience is admitted to be erroneous with respect to pleasure and so forth, there is no means to rule out the possibility of it being an error with respect to the self as well. [The opponent might argue: "Since an error without a substratum is impossible, the self, as the substratum, is established through the otherwise inexplicability of errors such as pleasure. To this, he says: "without a basis" (*nirālambana*). The self is not established by this reasoning either; for the point is that the suspicion of error would still apply to the experience of this reasoning itself, just as it does to the experience of pleasure.

Since it is said that scripture (*śruti*) is the means of valid knowledge regarding the Self, he says: "That" (*tad*). The point is this: since it can be argued that scripture is not a means of valid knowledge because there is no proof for its validity as a means of knowledge regarding the Self, the Self cannot be established by it. To the objection—"How can scripture be invalid when its validity is experienced?"—he says: "Validity... [etc.]. The validity of scripture is not established by experience.

The point is that, just as with the experience of pleasure, if this [experience] were also invalid, there would be the possibility of mistaking it for a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "established by the witness" (*sākṣisiddhasya*) with the word "iti. The meaning is that if the experience of the witness were an error in the manner described above, then not even a single thing—such as the established rule that "everything is false, but the Self is true"—would be proven.

It has been stated that because the authority of the scripture establishing the [proposition] "the experience of pleasure and so forth is an error" is not established, the status of that experience of pleasure and so forth as an error cannot be proven by it. Now, since the status of even that scriptural experience as an error is possible, the experience of pleasure and so forth remains non-erroneous; its status as an error is not established by that [scripture]. With the intention that the negation of one of two mutually contradictory things is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other, he says: "Error."

For this reason as well, he states that the experience of pleasure and so forth is not an error: "Sukha... (pleasure...). If the experience of pleasure and so forth were an error, then that hidden doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*) which has been accepted would be exposed. This is because the experience of objects such as pleasure is, according to your view, the very nature of the Self (*ātman*). [The opponent objects: "The experience of objects such as pleasure being of the nature of the Self is only in your own system, not in ours; rather, in our view, it is merely a modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*). To show that this constitutes a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), he says: "Na hi... (not indeed...).

[Objection: Let it be granted that the experience of pleasure and so forth is an error (*bhrama*) and that it constitutes the very nature of the Self (*ātman*). Even so, how does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of the Self? To this, he says: "Of the error... The meaning is as follows: If the experience of objects such as pleasure were an error, it would have to be an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is accepted that an error is an effect of ignorance. And if that were the case, the Self too would be an effect of ignorance, since the experience of objects like pleasure is [according to you] the very nature of the Self. Furthermore, if the Self were an effect of ignorance, its falsity (*mithyātva*) would be unavoidable.

Let it be that the self is difficult to establish through reasoning; nevertheless, that does not constitute a refutation [of the self], because the self is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating the objection that "there can be no sublation of what is established by *pramāṇa* merely on the grounds that it is difficult to establish through reasoning," he offers a rebuttal: "As for being difficult to establish... If it is argued that even the difficulty of establishing the self through reasoning does not constitute a refutation because it is supported by *pramāṇa*, then let pleasure and so forth also be either difficult or easy to establish.

The meaning is that one must state: "That [objection] is not a sublater [of our position], because it is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). To the question, "Granted that there may be an impossibility [of its occurrence] through reasoning (yukti), why is it not a sublater? he says: "For not... This was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's point]. He then says: "Impossibility... to show that if one accepts its non-sublativeness without resolving the impossibility through reasoning, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The meaning is this: if the existence of the self is accepted on the grounds that its difficulty of establishment (*durghaṭatva*) is not a subverting factor when analyzed through reasoning, then let the ignorance of the self also be accepted, for there is no difference between the two cases. It is only for that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) that its difficulty of establishment is not [a subverting factor] when analyzed through reasoning.

It is called a subverting [objection]. Nor is the self's nature as ignorance established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), such that its logical difficulty would not constitute a subversion; therefore, he says: "Ati... (The meaning is: It is not the case that the self's nature as ignorance is unestablished by valid means of knowledge. For, if one were to accept that some things are conscious and some are unconscious, the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) would result. The sense is that it is established by logic that it is superior simply to accept that everything is unconscious. Not only is logical difficulty non-subverting when something is established by valid means of knowledge...

However, [the objection applies] only where there is no contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since the nature of the self as ignorance (*avidyātva*) is contradicted by valid means of knowledge, the contradiction established through reasoning (*yukti*) serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) precisely in that case; therefore, he says: "And not... The sense is that for the opponents who assert the nature of the self as ignorance, there is no contradiction with any valid means of knowledge in the manner described above.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the Blessed Lord, by the force of experience, asserts the reality of the causal relationship and the enjoyment of pleasure, pain, and so forth, why does He not likewise refute the view of those who maintain that experience is an illusion? Anticipating this doubt, he concludes what has been said with the words, "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The sense is that the Blessed Lord did not personally refute that view because it was already clearly understood, according to the method previously stated, that the theory of the illusoriness of experience is tainted by infinite defects.

It was stated that "the Puruṣa resides in Prakṛti. In that regard, since the individual soul (jīva) is inherently pure, what is the cause for its residence in Prakṛti? To this, it is said: "The cause. Therein, when the connection of the Supreme Self with a body through the state of being an individual soul is mentioned, one might ask what the cause is for such a connection with a body for that which is pure. Therefore, in order to dispel the misconception that the possession of qualities (saguṇatva) is the cause of that [connection], he says: "Of this... (verse 22).

In this context, attachment to the qualities such as *sattva* is stated to be the cause of the individual soul’s (*jīva*) connection with a body, but it is not intended that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) possesses qualities therein; for that is logically untenable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since the falsity of such [qualities] has already been refuted—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, is the soul’s attachment to the qualities such as *sattva* the independent cause for births in good and evil wombs, or merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta-mātra*)? It cannot be the first, because being insentient (*jaḍa*), such [attachment] is incapable of being an independent cause.

He introduces the verse as a response to the doubt that "in the second [case], an independent cause must be stated," with the words: "svatantra" (independent). To the question, "How is Hari's status as an independent cause expressed by this? he explains the verse by means of an authoritative scriptural statement: "sarvebhyaḥ" (from all). "Uparyupari vartamānaḥ" means existing higher and higher; that is to say, supreme. "Svānukūlyena" means by way of being favorable to himself, through not causing distraction to his own self. "Matyā" means intentionally, with prior deliberation. His independence is stated precisely as the reason for that [supremacy].

By the term "supreme" (*parama*), the meaning of "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) is expressed. In the passage beginning with "the witness" (*upadraṣṭṛ*), the connection of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) should be understood; it is not to be seen as stating a reason for the status of being the non-permitter (*anumantṛ*). By the phrase "other than the embodied one," the word "supreme" (*para*) is explained. Now, one might ask: since it was not previously stated that the non-permitter resides within the body, how can it be said here, "in this body"? To this, he says: "Me. (*mām iti*)

The sense is that the statement "in this body" is appropriate because, in the verse, "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata," the one who permits (anumantṛ) was previously described as being situated within the body. Now, one might object: let the status of being a witness (upadraṣṭṛ) and so forth be stated as the reason for being the one who permits; why is it stated that the one who permits is situated in the body? To this, he says: "By that... Since it might be asked who this one who permits is, he shows by the phrase "stated even in the body" that it is none other than "I" who am the one who permits.
The sense is that this is because the Self has been described as residing within the body. || 23 ||

In order to generate an intense desire to know the meaning already stated in the verse beginning with “prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva,” the fruit of that knowledge is declared by the words “ya enam. He explains this by means of an authoritative statement itself: “dvividham” (twofold). “Having known [it] indirectly” (parokṣataḥ). Regarding the phrase “existing in every way” (sarvathā vartamānaḥ), the meaning is that even one who exists through negligence or unrighteousness is certain to attain liberation. To the question, “What is the means for the vision of the Supreme Person and so forth? he says: “anādī” (beginningless).

To explain how there is diversity, he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). "By themselves" (*svayam*) means by their own intuition (*svapratibhayā*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means by the two aforementioned methods. By this, it is stated that [the sages] possess meditation (*dhyāna*). By the expression "some" (*kiñcit*), it is implied that although other means besides meditation exist for them, they are not mentioned here because those means are insignificant. As for the statement "some" (*kecana*)—given that the rule of internal vision has been declared for sages in passages such as "The sages are internally luminous"—he asks: for what purpose is this expression used? To which he replies: "Some" (*kecit*).

The meaning is that the scripture has as its subject matter other sages (*ṛṣi*). By the word "gods" (*devāḥ*), the sense of what was stated in the phrase "others by means of Sāṅkhya" is conveyed. "Gradually" means in the course of time.

If the gods possess vision even in the absence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), then for what purpose do they practice meditation, which is opposed to such vision? To this he says: "Of those... Those for whom *sāṅkhya* is their intuition (*pratibhā*) and *yoga* is the means of vision are called *sāṅkhyayogāḥ*. It has been stated that "intuition [arises] from clarity through gradual stages. Among the gods, who possesses the highest intuition? To this he says: "Brahmā... By the word "some," the term "action" (*karma*) is explained.
Here too, the meagerness of both hearing and realization is to be understood. By the word "others" (anya), the meaning of what was stated as "but others" (anye tu) is conveyed.

He is the recipient of the intuitive inspiration (*pratibhā*) of the sages and the kings of the gods. In this regard, when the question arises whether these possess only a single kind of intuition or whether it exists in varying degrees, he says: "Of the sages. He states the measure of Brahmā’s intuition with the words: "Of Brahmā. Then, one might ask: for what purpose does he hear [the Veda] from Hari? To this he replies: "Of Viṣṇu. It is solely for the sake of pleasure, and not for the sake of knowledge. For whom, then, is the hearing for the sake of knowledge? To this he replies: "Of others. [The term] "superhuman" (*mānuṣettara*) [is used].

The meaning is that for humans, knowledge generally arises from hearing alone. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how is it stated in some places that even among yogins who practice meditation and the like, there is the state of being 'one who has heard and known' (śrutaveditva) provided hearing and other means are present? To this he says: "Atyalpa... (extremely small). Having thus described the various means for the realization [of Brahman], he returns to the subject at hand with the words: "Sarve... (all).

As for the statement that even those engaged in meditation (*dhyāna*) and other practices possess hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, that is incorrect; for if that were the case, it would be impossible to specify for some that they "having heard from others" (*śrutvānyebhyaḥ*). To this he says: "Of others" (*anyeṣām*). The meaning is that although hearing and the rest exist for those engaged in meditation and so forth, the specific mention that "human beings worship having heard from others" is appropriate, because due to their extremely limited intellectual capacity, there is an abundance of hearing [required] for them.

By this, it is explained that [the capacity] is extremely limited. How is even an extremely limited flash of intuition (pratibhā) possible for human beings? Since it was stated that they are "devoted to sacred revelation" (śrutiparāyaṇāḥ), which implies their exclusive reliance on hearing, he says: "Of human beings."

The qualification "devoted to the Vedas" (*śrutiparāyaṇāḥ*) is appropriate even though the manifestation of intuition (*pratibhā*) among human beings is extremely limited; for that intuition lacks independence because it depends upon a foundational means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*), and because it is generally incorrect. The underlying sense is that the term "non-existent" (*asat*) is seen to be applied to that which is dependent and not authoritative.

Regarding the statement that the intuition (*pratibhā*) of humans is generally not properly produced because it depends upon the measure of its source (*mūla-pramāṇa*), and that it is moreover meager—that is incorrect. He dispels this doubt by means of authoritative evidence itself, on the grounds that among humans such as the Pāṇḍavas and others, intuition is observed to be both extensive and correct even with respect to matters never heard before. [He says: "Even unheard... The meaning is that it is "renowned" (*viśrutā*), which is to say, pervasive (*vyāptā*) and abundant (*bahulā*). And he states other characteristics of that [intuition]: "And he who... and so forth.

The meaning is that one should know those two supreme deities to be such that the man possesses a lower body nine times the measure of his own face, and the woman possesses a lower body eight times the measure of her own face; furthermore, by the measure of their respective fingers they are ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) tall, by the measure of their respective palms they are ten palm-lengths (tāla) tall, and by the measure of their respective feet they are seven foot-lengths (pāda) tall. In this context, what is called a "tāla" refers to the length of the hand from the tip of the middle finger to the wrist.

Having described the characteristics of the supreme gods, he states the characteristics of gods in general: "As far as... This means that the measurement of the gods, ranging from the highest to the lowest, decreases sequentially from ninety-six *aṅgulas* down to eighty-nine *aṅgulas*. In this context, the measure of the seven steps likewise decreases sequentially by one *aṅgula* at a time. He then states the characteristics of the *Gandharvas* and others: "Less than that..."

Thus, from ninety-one finger-breadths down to seventy-eight finger-breadths, there is a gradual decrease in the dimensions of the Gandharvas and others. Here too, the meaning is that the dimension of the Asuras decreases gradually by one finger-breadth at a time until it reaches seventy-seven finger-breadths. He states the characteristic of humans: "to that extent" (tāvat). This means the dimension of humans is seventy-eight finger-breadths. He states the characteristic of the Asuras: "from that" (tataḥ). This means the dimension of the Asuras is below seventy-eight [finger-breadths].

The meaning is that the measurement of the *devopadevas* (secondary gods) should be understood as being eight finger-breadths below the measurement of the supreme gods (*devottama*), which is ninety-six finger-breadths above the height of the *māna* (the central deity). He states the characteristics of the *ṛṣis* and others: "Among the gods," etc. The meaning is that the measurement of those such as Cyavana and Pṛthu should be understood to be like that of the lower-ranking gods. He states the reason for this gradation of characteristics: "As far as," etc. By this, it is also stated that this [gradation] is natural.

That which was stated—that Hari alone is the independent cause for all living beings in their births within good and evil wombs—is now elaborated upon by the words "as long as" (*yāvat*). In that context, in order to dispel the misconception that the association of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) with Hari is merely an association with a material body (*jaḍadeha*), he says: "The Field... (*kṣetra*).

The sense is that since the statement in the subsequent chapter, "My womb" (*mama yoniḥ*), which serves as an explanation for the phrase "as far as [anything] is born," declares that the origin of all beings arises from the union of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, it follows that here too, by the word *kṣetra*, Śrī alone is intended.

Since it may be asked why the word *kṣetra*—well-known in the context of the unmanifest (*avyakta-tattva*)—is here said to denote Śrī, [the author] demonstrates by means of authoritative evidence that Śrī is denoted by the word *kṣetra*, and incidentally that the words *mahābhūtāni* and so forth, as well as *ahaṅkāra* and others, denote deities. He says: "The Unmanifest. Since Sarasvatī and others are also denoted by the word *Śrī*, he says "always" (*sadā*) in order to exclude them. To the question, "Is she denoted by that word because of her non-difference from the insentient unmanifest? he replies: "Flawless" (*nirdoṣā*).

How, then, is it denoted by such terms as "the unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth? To this he says: "For she... etc. It is called "unmanifest" (avyakta) because it is not manifested. It is called "field" (kṣetra) because Viṣṇu dwells within it. By the term "possessing great qualities" (mahāguṇā), the Great Principle (mahat-brahman) is meant; by "the best of souls" (jīvottamā), the Primal Matter (pradhāna) is expressed—this is the meaning. Although the Great Principle is not explicitly mentioned here, it must certainly be understood because it is the first effect. [The text speaks] with reference to the functions. He explains what was stated: "The soul... etc. The meaning is that the intellect (buddhi) is so called because it makes known sound and the other sense objects. His son, Aniruddha, is also included.

It is called *sparśa* because it touches (*sparśayati*). From the root *hṛ*, meaning "to take," it means the tongue (*jihvā*) because it is the cause for taking up tastes (*rasa*). It is [called *ghrāṇa*] from the root *āghrāti* because it is the cause for smelling odors (*gandha*). It is [called *vāk*] from the root *vac* because it sets speech into motion. It is [called *sana*] because it is the instrumental cause for loss and gain; the root is *san*, meaning "to gain. In some places, because it is stated that Viṣṇu is the deity of the feet, it is said "by Viṣṇu. And it is stated that the two who produce sacrifice are not Hari and Hara. Regarding *śacī*: it is so called because she sets movement into motion (*padanāt*); the root is *pada*, meaning "to go."

"By being unobstructed" means by the absence of impediment. It is called *vāyu* (wind) because it blows (*vāti*). It is *agni* (fire) because of consuming (*adanāt*). It is *pṛthivī* (earth) because of its expansion (*prathana*), that is, its vastness. It is *jala* (water) because it is the cause of birth and dissolution; this is the meaning. The verbal root is *pṛthu*, meaning "expansion. Since it is observed that both origination and dissolution are dependent upon water, it is established that the presiding deity of that [element] is likewise [dependent]. Regarding the phrase "because of sounding," the meaning is "because of being the initiator of sound and so forth. The primary wind is *sukha* (pleasure) because it brings pleasure (*sukhanāt*); such [etymologies] are to be understood. She is indeed Śrī herself. Thus, the meaning is that Vidyutī is the wife of Vāyu, just as Sarasvatī is [the wife of Brahmā].

It has been stated that Śrī alone is *icchā* (will). He establishes this as follows: "She is *icchā*. If deities such as Lakṣmī are denoted by words such as *avyakta*, *cetana*, and *icchā*, then, having in some places spoken of the *avyakta*, [he proceeds].

Furthermore, as to how [the Lord] is described by terms such as "consciousness" (cetanā) and so forth, he says: "By place," etc. It is appropriate that there be a repetition [of the description] using terms like "consciousness" for the Śrī who was previously denoted by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta); the meaning is that there is a difference in form due to the difference between the locus of the presiding deity (abhimānin) and the object of that presiding (māna). This should be understood similarly regarding other deities as well. If so, how is it that words such as "unmanifest" are applied to insentient objects? To this he says: "By these," etc.

The sense is that insentient things are denoted by words such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) because they are presided over by deities named "the Unmanifest" and so forth. It "wastes away" means it destroys. Having made [the earth] its "abode" (kṣiti), it "protects" (trāti) by means of providing its own dwelling. "Kṣīṇa" means inferior. Regarding the phrase "existing as specific modifications": the meaning is that they exist as being more intensely subject to transformation than [the principles] beginning with Mahat. He states that this very same ground for the application of the word "modification" applies even to objects such as a jar: "from the specific" (viśeṣāt).

Regarding the passage beginning with "vigatam" (passed away), the meaning here is that in the final effect, there is no production of another effect except through destruction. To the question, "Since even those who possess ego (abhimānin) are denoted by words such as 'desire' (icchā) and so forth, how can they be considered modifications (vikāra)?", he says: "That... The relationship is the state of being the governed and the governor.

As for what was stated—that all that is conscious and unconscious is the field—that has been said [correctly]. For it is impossible for the conscious entity to have the aforementioned body, since such a definition as "the cause of injury" and so forth cannot apply to it; therefore, he says: "Of whom... Even though the conscious entity is the field, there is no impossibility of its having the aforementioned body, because it has been stated: "Whose self is the body."

The sense is that even if the etymological derivation [of "body"] as previously stated is impossible, its status as a body is still established because it is dependent upon the Lord. In the verse, "Whatever being is born," the word *sattva* denotes the individual soul (*jīva*); this was already indicated by the citation of the statement, "My womb. Regarding that, he states the authority for the word *sattva* denoting the individual soul: "It is *sattva*. That which is referred to in the phrase "one of the two" ought to be called the *jīva*, yet in the Śruti it is called *sattva*.

If the word *sattva* were taken to mean the individual soul (*jīva*), then because that soul is beginningless, the birth mentioned in the phrase "is born" would be untenable; therefore, he says: "The root *jan* [means] manifestation. (27)

It has been stated that the Supreme Lord resides within the bodies of all. In that case, one might argue that due to the gradations of those substrates, He would also possess gradations; furthermore, because of His co-existence with those who suffer, He Himself would experience suffering. To this, it is said: "He is equal" (*samam*). In that context, the phrase "not perishing while they perish" (*vinaśyatsu avinaśyantam*) would be inappropriate, since there is no destruction of individual souls (*jīvas*). Nor can it refer to insentient objects, as there is an absence of the word "and" (*ca*) or similar indicators. Therefore, he says: "Among the souls" (*jīveṣu*). It is stated that one who knows in this very way is a "knower" (*jñānī*).

The fruit of that knowledge is called "unequalled. He explains this by means of two verses, recollecting them as follows: "Suffering... and "He himself... The meaning of the phrase "he does not harm" is expressed by the words "he himself. (28–29)

If Īśvara were the cause of births in good and evil wombs without depending upon karma, then he would be subject to partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and other such faults. If he depends upon karma, his sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is lost. Furthermore, since he too would possess a body (*deha*), he would lack sovereignty; therefore, it is said: "By means of *prakṛti*. In that context, this is stated to dispel the misconception that *prakṛti* alone is the agent and not the Supreme Self: "By means of *prakṛti*" [means] "having himself initiated [the process]."

The meaning is: "having himself awakened [the soul] to its prior karma and so forth. He states the underlying intention: "Of Viṣṇu," etc. Even though [Viṣṇu] is dependent on karma, there is no loss of the Lord’s independence; for he himself awakens the prior karma and so forth, and depending upon that, causes the [soul] to perform actions now. The point is that it is not the case that karma and so forth are the awakeners of Viṣṇu. To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Previously," etc.

"Let it be that Hari awakens karma and so forth, but He does not awaken Himself; nevertheless, because Hari is dependent upon them, He lacks independence. To this [the author] replies with the intention that since even the existence of karma and so forth is subject to the Lord, there is no lack of independence even when He depends upon them. Thus, he states the authority for the fact that the existence of karma and so forth is dependent on the Lord: "The substance... [He asks], "On what basis is this meaning conceived? and therefore he shows the traditional scriptural testimony (*smṛti*) regarding this point: "By Himself... [and so on].

Now, one might ask: "Since the word 'by the Lord' (īśvareṇa) is not heard here, how can this meaning be established? To this he says: "By him" (tena). Since the Lord has been introduced in the passage, "For seeing the Lord equally established everywhere," the meaning is established even though it is not explicitly stated as "by that Lord. If it is asked, "What is the point of this interpretation? Why could it not simply mean that agency belongs to primordial nature (prakṛti) alone and not to the Lord? he shows the contradiction with the Smṛti and the contradiction with other scriptural passages by citing the verse beginning with "I" (aham).

He says "by *prakṛtyā*" because it was indicated there by the phrase "by that Lord" (*teneśvareṇa*). With the word "and" (*ca*), he addresses the question of how this is established, and thus says "by the subject matter at hand" (*prakṛtena*). The meaning is that it should convey the agency of the subject matter at hand for the action being expressed.

It has been stated that it is not reasonable to postulate another meaning [for the scripture] because it would contradict the scriptural statements declaring God to be the agent. Furthermore, he says that such a postulation is not reasonable because the agency of *prakṛti* (primordial matter) is contradicted by the Śrutis and other authorities: "Of *prakṛti*... The meaning is: apart from You, nothing whatsoever is created by anyone, even at a distance. For this reason as well, he says that it is not reasonable to postulate another meaning: "Kevala... (the absolute).

The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction with Īśvara; therefore, the word "alone" (*kevala*) was used [to exclude him]. The intention is that in the phrase "the Self as non-agent," since the opponent accepts that Īśvara is not the agent, the word "and" does not have the sense of conjunction with him. For this reason as well, one cannot maintain that Īśvara is not the agent; to this effect he says: "From that very [source]. Furthermore, he says: "I... to show that it is not reasonable to assume any other meaning than this.

In this context, since the statement "as far as it is produced" establishes that the Lord is the creator of all, an explanation asserting that the Lord is not the agent is also contradictory. Nor should it be argued that even in the preceding verse, agency belongs to *prakṛti* alone, while the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) possesses agency only figuratively through its conjunction with it; for the meaning of this very passage will be stated differently in the subsequent chapter by the words "My womb is the Great Brahman," and so forth. Furthermore, he states that the meaning of this [verse] is that agency does not belong to *prakṛti* alone.

Regarding the phrase "insentient" (*acetana*): how is there a contradiction with one's own statement? To this he says: "Desire," etc. For agency consists in the acceptance of activity preceded by desire; such is the Vedic revelation. "Insentient" means devoid of desire. Therefore, the point is that there is a contradiction in saying that something is both insentient and acts. Now, one might object: even if Nature lacks independent agency, its agency in the form of transformation is certainly admitted even by the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*). Why, then, should this verse not be intended for that purpose? To this he says: "Modification," etc.

Although agency in the form of a modification of *prakṛti* has been accepted, this verse is not intended for that purpose. This is because here it is stated that all actions are performed by *prakṛti* alone. Furthermore, if this were its meaning, the word "in every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*) would result in a loss of its proper sense, since the actions of the Supreme Lord and others are not modifications of *prakṛti*. To the question, "Why is the action of the Supreme Lord and others not a modification of *prakṛti*? he says: "Inert... (verse 30).

It is not sufficient merely to know that the Blessed One is the impeller of all; rather, it is stated that one must also know His state as the substratum of all, beginning with the words "When... Since the meaning of that [verse] is obscure, he explains it by means of an authoritative scriptural statement: "One... By stating that the differentiation of beings resides in the Supreme Self, it is intended that those who are differentiated reside in Him.
That very point is what is expressed here. || 31 ||

Since the Supreme Self consists of both the sentient and the insentient, how can there be a separate existence of the elements from Him? To this it is said: "Because of beginninglessness. In that context, in order to refute the notion that the Supreme Self is not an agent, he explains the term "dwelling in the body" (*śarīrastha*). As for the question of why the word "dwelling in the body" denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), he demonstrates its connection to that [Supreme Self] by means of the phrase: "by means of dream" (*svapnena*).

Now, one might object: since the Lord also resides in a body just like the individual soul (jīva), why is it that only the jīva is denoted by the word "tat" (That)? To this, he says: "Residing in the body. Even Viṣṇu possesses the conceit, "This was created by me," and "It is dependent on me. Therefore, how can there be an absence of such conceit in Him? To this [he replies]:

He says: "Of those pertaining to that" (*tadgatānām*). If the term "situated in the body" (*śarīrastha*) denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), how is the construction to be understood? To this he says: "Because of beginninglessness" (*anāditvāt*). The word "thus" (*iti*) is to be supplied [as the conclusion]. Since the individual soul is also beginningless, why is this [attribute] specified for the Lord alone, such that it might serve as the reason for precluding His identity with the individual soul? To this he says: "The body... (*śarīra...*). Even in the absence of possessing such qualities as having a beginning, how is there a distinction of the Supreme Self from the individual soul? To this he says: "Of the individual soul... (*jīvasya*). The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

[Objection: But how can the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) be the reason for His difference from the individual soul (*jīva*), given that the reason is unestablished because qualities such as being the creator of the world exist in the Lord? To this, he says: "Sattva... etc. Here, by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), qualities such as being the creator of the world are not intended; rather, it refers only to [the qualities of] *sattva* and so forth. The point is that while there is no connection with those [qualities] in the Lord, there is such a connection in the individual soul; thus, it serves as the reason. "He acts but is not tainted"—this is another reason for the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord. He explains that: "All... etc.

It should be understood that the individual soul (*jīva*) does not act, yet it is indeed tainted; and this tainting occurs through the fruit of those actions. Now, one might ask: since the non-difference of the soul and so forth has not been previously established here, how is a negation of it appropriate? To this he says: "The proponent" (*vādī*). Just as the doctrine of emptiness as the cause is negated by such passages as "On this point, some say," because it is established by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), so too the negation of non-duality is appropriate, because it is accepted by all proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*).

Just as the negation of the attainment of human goals such as heaven through mere ritual action—arising from a failure to understand the intent of the *karma-śruti* that one must worship the Lord alone through actions for the sake of liberation by means of knowledge—is made by the passage beginning with "sacrifices and public works" (*iṣṭāpūrtam*), so too it is logical that there should be a negation of non-duality (*advaita*) arising from a failure to understand the intent of the *śruti* passages such as "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), which state that the Blessed One pervades everything; this is the underlying sense.

To the objection, "Why might this meaning not be merely conventional (prātītika)? he states the agreement of other scriptural passages regarding the point already explained: "kurvāṇa" (while acting), etc. By the phrase "free from death and so forth," the word "avyaya" (imperishable) is explained. Furthermore, he cites the agreement of scripture regarding the Lord's being distinct from both the sentient and the insentient: "sa eṣa" (this very one), etc. (Verses 32–34).

The meaning of the chapter is summarized: "In the Field," etc. Therein, the phrase "the state of liberation from the material nature of beings" is explained because its meaning was obscured: "of the individual souls," etc. Liberation, as well as the means to liberation—humility and so forth—have been stated. (35)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words, "The Field," etc. By means of the subsequent chapters, the means [of liberation] itself is primarily taught. In that regard, the practice of the means for its liberation is appropriate only when there is a thorough understanding of the manner of bondage. And bondage consists of the three *guṇas*. Therefore, the intention is that by means of this chapter, [the Lord] demonstrates the state of the transformations of the three *guṇas* and the means for transcending them, preceded by an exposition of what was stated in the verse beginning, "As long as [it] is produced."
Since the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) were mentioned briefly in such passages as "For one is made to act helplessly by karma," the word "having analyzed" (*vivicya*) was used.

"What I promised when saying, 'I shall speak further,' is now being stated: 'My womb' (mama yoniḥ). In this context, he provides an authoritative statement to refute the perception that the word *yoni* means "cause" and to establish that it means "wife" and so forth. [The text says: "The womb. This refers to a place, specifically a secret place. Granted that the word *yoni* has multiple meanings such as "wife," for what purpose is it used here? To this he replies: "In this [context]. Since the word *yoni* has many meanings, how can this specific meaning alone be intended? To this he replies: "In that... (verse 3).

When the three *guṇas* have been described in detail, a doubt might arise that the *guṇas* themselves are the supreme of all, and that there is nothing else superior to them. That doubt is refuted by the words, "not another" (*nānyam*). Here, [the Lord] says "from these" (*etebhyaḥ*) to dispel the misconception that agency belongs to the *guṇas* alone and not to the Lord. Furthermore, since even an ignorant person possesses the nature of a *puruṣa*, one might ask what the distinction is for the knower; to this he says, "bound" (*baddhaḥ*). If such were the interpretation, the statement "he attains my own state" (*madbhāvam adhigacchati*) would be rendered meaningless.

Since the sentence would be complete even without that [qualification], he demonstrates its purposeful significance by asking: "How so? The status of being a *puruṣa* belongs only to one who is fit for attaining devotion (*bhāva*) toward the Blessed One; this is established by such scriptural passages as, "In the state of *puruṣatva*, the Self [is revealed] at length. To the objection, "Why should the meaning not be simply what is perceived [in the literal sense]?", he explains it by means of the Smṛti passage beginning with "My womb," namely: "Mahālakṣmī. She is *parā*, meaning superior to the six [categories].

Because it possesses nine qualities, it is *sat*; and because it is of the nature of light—derived from the verbal root *tviṣ* meaning "to shine"—it is *tvam*. Thus, the meaning is that it is *sattva*. For through creation, there is indeed delight (*rañjana*). To the question, "Is this the well-known deity Earth? he says: "That which... The verbal root is *tam*, meaning "to weary. Wearying means the cause of exhaustion by means of *saṃsāra*. By the phrase "those who have not attained liberation," the meaning of the verse "the embodied one [is bound] in the body" is expressed. To the question, "Of whom is what the binder? he says: "All..."

By this passage beginning with "sattvam" (the quality of goodness) and so forth, the scope of the threefold bondage described according to its gradations is demonstrated. Thus, one should not think that these [qualities] are the most excellent because of their supreme power as universal bondages; regarding this, he says: "etābhyaḥ" (from these). Since one is liberated only by knowing Viṣṇu as the most excellent of all, therefore He alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣa). Consequently, the meaning is that one who knows "there is nothing higher than these" is a mere beast among men. (16–19)

Regarding the statement, “The fruit of *rajas*, however, is suffering,” the author says [the following] to dispel the misconception that the word “suffering” (*duḥkha*) here refers to suffering alone. He says: “Of *rajas*. To the question, “How can the word ‘suffering’ denote pleasure mixed with suffering? he says: “Suffering. To the objection, “Why could it not denote suffering alone here? he cites a traditional authority (*smṛti*) regarding the mixed nature of the fruit of *rajas*: “Of action... [and so forth].

Thus, by the phrase "born of ignorance" (ajñānaja), "ignorance" (ajñāna) itself is explained. By this, it is indicated that the statement that pure suffering is the fruit of darkness (tamas) serves as a refutation of any other [interpretation]. || 20-21 ||

The answer to the question regarding the means for transcending the qualities (*guṇātiga*) and so forth is stated as: "He does not desire light" (*prakāśam*). In this context, he does not desire the light within himself; he does not hate the delusion inherent in himself; his equanimity toward suffering and the like is merely the absence of longing and such; and his renunciation of all undertakings is indifference toward everything. To dispel any contrary understanding, he explains this by means of another authority: "In the world... (*loka...*). The meaning is that he does not favor the light and so forth residing in other persons, nor does he desire the delusion and so forth residing therein which are unfavorable.

Since He has attained self-luminosity and is free from delusion (*moha*), one might ask: why would there not be an absence of desire and so forth even toward Himself? To this, he says: "Himself" (*svayam*). It should be understood that He also hates delusion. By the phrase "and Him also," the meaning previously stated as "and me" is implied. Regarding the phrase "pleasure, pain, etc.," the meaning is: even though pleasure exists when one abandons devotion to Viṣṇu, and pain exists otherwise. By the phrase "for the sake of wealth, etc.," the meaning of what was said in "equal toward a clod of earth, etc. is expressed.

By the term "non-Vaiṣṇava," the meaning previously stated by the phrase "in all undertakings" is expressed; by the phrase "goes to Viṣṇu," the intended purport of the passage beginning with "those possessing qualities" (saguṇa) is stated. || 22 ||

Furthermore, the phrase "one who has abandoned all undertakings" does not denote mere indifference. This is because the preceding statement, "as if indifferent," already expressed the absence of mere indifference; and since the preceding statement, "he does not stir," expressed the absence of action, one might ask how there can be an absence of mere indifference. To this he says: "He does not stir. The meaning is that "he does not stir" is not a prohibition of all activity, but rather a prohibition specifically of the Lord's indifferent activity.

[Objection: In that case, since the non-performance of non-Vaiṣṇava actions has already been stated by the word "neṅgate" (does not move), the phrase "sarvārambhaparityāgī" (one who abandons all undertakings) would be redundant. To this he says: [the words] "thus he speaks" is the ellipsis to be supplied. It should be understood that "neṅgate" is a general statement. By "neṅgate," the absence of minor non-Vaiṣṇava activities is expressed; by "sarvārambhaparityāgī," the absence of extensive non-Vaiṣṇava activities is expressed. Thus, there is no redundancy. With this intention, he provides the authority for the words "movement" (iṅganā) and "undertaking" (ārambha) having the meanings of "minor" and "major" actions respectively: "Movement... (23–25).

[Objection: Since by the word *guṇa* (qualities) Lakṣmī and the others are intended, how can their transcendence be spoken of in the passage, "Having completely transcended these qualities"? [Response: Because it would be impossible, he says: "By Lakṣmī and the others. Here, *lakṣmī* is said to mean *śrī*. Having restated the meaning as taught in the *Smṛti*, he states another meaning with the word *tat*. He shows the usage in both cases with the words: "Just as..."

The meaning is as follows: just as one who travels by passing beyond the bond established by the gatekeeper is said to "go to the king" after having passed the gatekeeper, and just as one who goes to the king is said to go "having passed the gatekeeper," so it is here. To dispel the misconception that the term *brahmabhūyāya* means "for the state of becoming Brahman," he says: "*Brahma*"—because in the passage, "My womb is the Great Brahma" (*mama yonir mahadbrahma*), the Great Lakṣmī alone is the subject referred to by the word *brahma*, she alone is intended here as well.

He establishes this point even by means of the designation used in another authoritative source (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the word "having transcended" (*atītya*): for one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*), it would have been appropriate to state only the attainment of the Lord (*bhagavat*) and so forth; since the attainment of the Lord occurs through the attainment of Lakṣmī, the mention of her [attainment] would otherwise be inconsistent. Therefore, he states the underlying intention with the word "me" (*mad*); the words "in her abiding" (*tatsthatve*) are to be supplied as the remainder. If there is no separation between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, then it should simply be said that "one who has transcended the qualities attains me. Why, then, is there this indirect statement? To this he replies: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

The meaning is that although there is no separation between those two, nevertheless, having approached Lakṣmī and with her permission, the attainment of the Blessed One occurs; thus, the statement regarding the succession is logical. He explains [the term] because its meaning was obscured in the phrase "of exclusive happiness" (*ekāntikasya sukhasya*): "Of exclusive" (*ekāntikasya*)—that which stands at the end in a calculation where nothing else is superior to it is "exclusive. The point is that this refers exclusively to liberation (*mokṣa*).

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. || 14 ||

This indicates the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter: "Thirteen. That which was described as the nature of the world in the thirteenth chapter is presented here in detail for analysis, because that very [world] is the nature of saṃsāra, and because its true nature must be known by one who desires to abandon saṃsāra. Furthermore, the means for transcending saṃsāra which was set forth there is also shown here; such is the meaning. To eliminate non-comprehension and misconception regarding that [subject], the chapter is explained by the Śruti itself.

"Distinctly" (*pṛthak*): the meaning of "with its roots above" (*ūrdhvamūla*) in that context is "distinctly. If Hari were the root of the world-tree, then he would be merely a part of that world; therefore, it is said to be "distinctly. The meaning is that just as the earth is the root of a well-known tree while being a part of it, so it is here. He shows another way in which it has its roots above: "sattva, etc. "Like the portion of the root" means that the root is like the root of a well-known tree, which constitutes a single part of it.

By the phrase "endowed with sattva and the rest," it is stated that the tree of the world has three roots; thus, the intended meaning of the expression "increased by the qualities" (guṇapravṛddha) is also explained, for branches grow from roots. Now, one might object: since the world is insentient, its root must be the insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) alone; consequently, it would follow that this [Self] undergoes transformation into the form of the world, because in the world we observe that portions of earth and other elements are subject to transformation. To this, he says: "Earth... and so forth.

In that regard, Hari is the root of the world-tree merely as its instrumental cause (*nimitta*), like the deity Earth is the root of a well-known tree, but not as its material cause (*upādāna*) like clay; this is the meaning. If that is so, one might ask: what then is the root in the sense of being a transformative material cause? To this he says: "Like clay. This refers to the insentient primordial nature (*prakṛti*). If the world-tree thus has Viṣṇu and others as its root, how can it be said to have its roots above? To this he says: "Because of its excellence."

Because Viṣṇu is the supreme among all, Śrī is the highest among those dependent on others, and the insentient primordial nature (acit-prakṛti) is the highest among insentient things, that which has its roots above—meaning its roots are Viṣṇu and the others—is called "ūrdhvamūla. The meaning of "adhaḥśākha" is "nīcā" (low). That which has branches such as Mahat and the rest—which are lower than the Lord—as its branches is "adhaḥśākha"; this is connected with the phrase "of the world-tree. He explains how the Vedic meters (chandas) constitute the leaves: "kāma... [etc.].

The sense is that, just as in the world one observes the appearance of fruit immediately after the emergence of leaves, here too, because they are the cause of the fruits, the desires are called "leaves. By this, it is stated that since dharma and artha exist for the sake of kāma and mokṣa, the tree of the world has two fruits known as kāma and mokṣa. The meaning of the phrase "below and above" is "mutually. By this, it is stated that the branches situated below extend into those whose roots are above, and the roots are continuous within the branches below. The justification for this is expressed by the words "in the causes."

Since the effect resides within its causes, the extension of branches into the roots is logical; since the cause pervades its effects, the continuity of the roots into the branches is logical—this is the meaning. Since only a general similarity to a tree has been stated, one might ask how there is a specific mention of the *aśvattha* (holy fig tree) in the passage beginning with "They call it the *aśvattha*"; to this he says: "The world. The meaning is that it is called *aśvattha* because it stands like a horse (*aśva*). If it is so fickle, why is it not completely cut away? To this he says: "Inexhaustible" (*avyaya*).

What follows from this if the world is thus a tree? To this he says: "By the sword of knowledge accompanied by detachment" (*svaśakti*); that is, by the sword of knowledge conjoined with freedom from attachment. Why is there a distinctness (*pṛthaktvam*) from this Viṣṇu, and what is the purpose of knowing that? Explaining this, he says: "Beginning with the unmanifest" (*avyaktādi*). By means of the knowledge of distinctness through such [scriptural passages] as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), there occurs the search for the Blessed One. For the intention is that once the world's difference from the Blessed One is known, his true nature can then be known.

By this, the phrase "him alone" (*tameva*) is explained. The words "for the purpose of cutting down the tree of the world" (*vṛkṣacchedārtham*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, one might object: "The cutting down of the tree of the world occurs even through the realization of Brahmā and others; therefore, why is it restricted to 'him alone'? To this he says: "That which... (*yaditi*). Since Brahmā and the others are merely partial manifestations of the Lord and are thus incapable [of this task], the intention is that one should take refuge in the Lord alone for the purpose of cutting down the tree of the world. (1.4)

If it is asked, "Why could it not be merely a part (aṃśa) [of the Lord]?", we say no, because they are distinct. Then, as to how there can even be an absence of parts, he says: "Something" (kiñcit). By this, the meaning of the phrase "of Me alone" (mamaiva) is established. Furthermore, with the intention that even the soul's impelling of the senses toward objects and so forth is dependent upon the Lord, and thus devotion to Him is the means for cutting down the tree of the world, he demonstrates the greatness of the Blessed One. By the word "enjoys" (bhuṅkte), the meaning of the word "ear" (śrotra) is explained.

By the term "auspicious" (śubha), the meaning previously stated as "qualities" (guṇas) is intended. Since the Lord is full bliss (pūrṇānanda), one might ask: what is the use of enjoyment of sense objects? To this, he says: "Full... (9-12).

The meaning is that He is called Vaiśvānara because of His connection with the essence of all beings (viśvanara) by virtue of being their source of sustenance. *Kṣaraṇam* means destruction; this is from the root *kṣara*, which signifies both destruction and continuous flow. Here, by the use of the word *ātman*, it is stated that the word *puruṣa* in the passage "These two Puruṣas... has the sense of a conscious being (*cetana*). Consequently, there is no contradiction in Śrī possessing the nature of a *puruṣa*. (13–20)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter [with the words] "O Deva": The sense is that since the characteristics of the deities, such as fearlessness and so forth, are the causes of liberation, they are to be attained; whereas the characteristics of the demons, such as hypocrisy and so forth, are opposed to that [liberation], they are to be abandoned. Therefore, both of these are described in this chapter.

In this regard, the text states "and [they have] arrogance," "I am the lord," "They say the world is without truth, without foundation, and without a Lord," "produced by mutual union," "Hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others," "therefore they go to the lowest state," and "This threefold [path] is of hell," and so forth; thus, the nature of the Cārvākas as non-gods (asuras) is declared. To dispel any contrary impression, he explains: "He who... [is not born from others], because he is born of delusion alone. To the question, "Why are these [Cārvākas] non-gods? he says:

He says: "It does not perish. If everything—including the perception that "the earth exists," the scripture that "the universe is true," and the inference based on being perceived by valid means of knowledge—were false, then since the falsity of all things would itself result in being false, there would be a contradiction with your own statement, "everything is you. He states that it is not only the Asuras who think "I am the Supreme Lord" and so forth, but whoever else asserts what is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, they too are all Asuras. Thus he says: "In this way."

He states the characteristics of the gods (*deva*): "But those who... By this, the passage beginning with "the practice of the yoga of knowledge is [the highest] charity" is explained. To the question, "Why do such individuals possess godhood?", he says: "Perceptible... By the phrase "they go to the state of liberation," the meaning of "goddess" (*devī*) is already expressed.

[Objection: Since it will be stated later that "therefore they go to a lower state" (*tato yānty adhamāṃ gatim*)—meaning that the demonic nature (*āsura-sampat*) is a cause for blinding darkness (*andhatamasa*)—how can it be said here that it is "considered a cause of bondage" (*nibandhāya asurī matā*)? To this, he says: "For bondage, the lowly [nature]. The point is that what is being stated here is not merely its being a cause of *saṃsāra*, but rather specifically its being a means to the most base blinding darkness. [Objection: Since the creations of beings (*bhūta-sarga*) are of exceedingly many kinds, how can it be said that "there are two creations of beings" (*dvau bhūta-sargau*) and so forth? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the creations" (sargāṇām): although there are a great many creations, it is possible to speak of them as being "two," because the intention is to emphasize the predominance of auspicious and inauspicious results. One might ask: since even Gandharvas, humans, and those lower than them possess a predominance of auspicious and inauspicious results, what is the distinction regarding Devas and the rest? To this he says: "Gandharva... The meaning is that they exist within the range of both those types of results. He explains this further: "those going to liberation" (muktigāḥ). In the same way, it should be understood that "those going to darkness" (tamogāḥ) are likewise included.

If that is so, one might ask: what is the distinction between these [beings] and the gods and others, since they too attain liberation and so forth? To this he says: "The gods," etc. In the same way, it should be understood that the asuras alone are those who go to the most terrible darkness.

Regarding what was stated—that because liberation is of many kinds, the superior liberation belongs only to the gods and not to others—in order to establish that statement, he says [in the verse], "for the sake of liberation," indicating that this is also known from the *Gītā*. Now, one might ask: since we observe the rejection of godhood and so forth through specific causes, how can it be said that there are "two natural creations" (*nisarga*)? To this, he says, "the gods... The meaning is that because they are natural, it cannot be otherwise.

[Objection: But since we observe that Prahlāda and other asuras attained the state of gods, how can there be no possibility of change? To this he says: "The gods... The meaning is that Prahlāda and others were already gods by their very nature, and their state as asuras arose solely due to a particular cause; therefore, it is logical that they abandoned that [state] and returned to their godhood. [Objection: But even in that case, their state as asuras was indeed destroyed. To this he says: "Due to the cause. Since the state of being an asura was merely adventitious (aupādhika), its destruction is entirely logical.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the doctrine that the destruction of one's inherent asura-nature does not occur through that [means]. One might object: "Let it be that the asuras do not attain divinity; however, the gods have attained asura-hood by abandoning their divinity. To this, he says: "Nor..."—meaning that there is no state of being an asura [attained by the gods].

The intention is this: [the curse] removes the divine nature of Prahlāda and others because it is adventitious (aupādhika), just as redness does not remove the whiteness of a crystal. If one then objects that [if their divinity is gone] curses and the like would be rendered useless, he refutes this with the words "But... (kiṃ tu). Because of that, the gods no longer possess the state of being Asuras. Even though their divinity has not departed, why are they not to be pitied? To this he says: "Because of liberation... (mokṣa...). He explains that further with: "Of Hari... (hareḥ). By this very statement, the intended meaning of the phrase "Do not grieve" (mā śucaḥ) is also explained. (1.24)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.

He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words "The good" (sat). Since only good action is to be performed as the means for attaining the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), and since bad action is to be abandoned as being contrary to that, and because performance and abandonment are impossible without a clear discrimination between them, the meaning is that good and bad actions are here explained by way of such a distinction. (1-2)

The answer to the question, "Those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures... is stated as: "Threefold... In this regard, performing sacrifice by casting aside the scriptural injunctions out of ignorance is not an indicator of whether one is *sāttvika* (of the nature of goodness) and so forth; rather, faith (*śraddhā*) becomes threefold according to the distinctions of *sāttvika* and the rest. Thus, it has been said that the knowledge of such a person is determined by their faith alone, and for the purpose of establishing that, it was stated: "In accordance with the *sattva* [nature]..."
