In this regard, since it has been stated that faith conforms to the nature of the *sattva*, how does this establish the principle that "whatever one's faith is, that indeed one is"? To answer this, he says: "The *sattva*... The fact that the word *sattva* denotes the individual soul (*jīva*) has already been established previously. If this is so, what follows? To answer this, he says: "Therefore... The meaning is that because faith conforms to the individual soul, the soul's true nature is known through that faith. Why is faith the very nature of the individual soul? To answer this, he says: "Consisting of faith (*śraddhāmaya*)."
In this regard, since the word *mayaṭ* has multiple meanings, he states the meaning relevant here: "Faith," etc.

The promise, "Listen to that," is stated by way of an elaboration on the verse beginning with "Whatever one's faith" (*yo yacchraddhaḥ*). Regarding the word "they sacrifice" (*yajante*): since the internal mental modification of faith (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti-śraddhā*) also exists there, its true nature (*svarūpa*) cannot be distinguished [from the individual soul]; therefore, how can there be knowledge of the soul's true nature through it? Furthermore, since all [beings] worship a deity, how is it that [the text speaks of] "Yakṣas, Rākṣasas," and so forth? And how is it that the Tamasic people emaciate the eternal and non-emaciated Lord? To resolve such doubts, [the text states] "according to their nature" (*sattvānurūpa*), and so on.

He explains this by means of an authoritative statement: "Faith" (*śraddhā*). Is faith merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the self], or does it also exist as something distinct? To this he says: "The essential nature" (*svarūpa*). If that were so, since faith as the essential nature itself would be impossible to know, there could be no discernment of the individual soul’s (*jīva*) true nature through it. To this he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). It is manifested within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). In this way, one should understand that even the *rājasa* [faith] may occasionally become *sāttvika* or *tāmasa*. What follows from this? To this he says: "On account of its predominance" (*bhūyastvāt*).

Thus, since the nature of faith itself can be known through its predominant manifestation, the meaning is that the true nature of the individual soul (jīva) is discerned by means of that faith. || 3 ||

To the question, "How is there a discernment of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) through faith? he says: "Through faith. By this, the meaning of the statement "they sacrifice" is established. "Sacrificers of mixed offerings" refers to those who sacrifice out of sequence; the meaning is that they consider the entire world to be illusory (mithyā). By this, it is stated that although all sacrificers are equal in being sacrificers of deities, the expression "the gods," and so forth, is used with the intention of referring to the enjoyer (bhoktṛ).

By the phrases "designated as the knowledge of the presiding deity" (*adhyakṣavidyākhyā*), "due to wretchedness" (*dīnatvāt*), and "Śiva, Skanda, etc. (*śivaskandādi*), the rationale for such statements in certain instances has been explained. He states the fruit of the worship of those three types [of deities] as follows: "Liberation" (*mokṣa*). This refers to a conceptual heaven (*sāṅkalpika-svarga*) imagined as a substitute for [actual] heaven. One might ask: according to the method described, is liberation attained by the *sāttvika* [worshippers], whether they know the scriptural injunction or not? To this he says: "Having abandoned... (*tyaktvā*).

By this, the underlying intention of the statement—that faith alone is the motivator, having rendered the injunctions and prohibitions of the scriptures non-motivating—is also described. He establishes that for those characterized by *tamas*, the state of being "born of the elements" (*bhūtādi*) is merely a secondary result, whereas *tamas* itself is the primary one. The phrase "by the unscriptural" (*aśāstra*) serves to clarify the meaning of what was stated in "know them" (*tān viddhi*). The phrase "by foods" (*annaiḥ*) expresses the purport of the passage beginning with "food" (*āhāraḥ*).

Since faith is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva), knowledge of that [soul] is established through it. To the question, "How is that [knowledge] attained through food and so forth?", he says: "Those who are characterized by sattva" (*sāttvikāḥ*). Here, it should be understood that the "sattvic-ness" and so forth of living beings refers to their excellence and so on. He says "Om" in order to prescribe a further internal state for sacrifices and other acts performed with sattva. By this, the meaning of such passages as "Om tat sat" is explained. To the question, "For what reason is 'Om' the name of Viṣṇu?", he says: "The Brahmins... (*viprāḥ*).

Therefore, O Blessed One, because the syllable *oṃ* is a name [of the Lord], the word "having uttered" (*omityuccārya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "They proceed" (*pravartante*) means "they cause [the rites] to proceed. By this, the meaning previously stated regarding the Brahmins and so forth is established. Since there exist other names of the Blessed One, one might ask how there is such a restriction to the utterance of this one; therefore, he states its distinction: "that which is not preceded by *oṃ*" (*anoṅkṛtam*). With the intention that the utterance of *oṃ* must be performed only after first knowing its meaning, he says: "but that which is preceded by *oṃ*" (*oṅkṛtaṃ tu*).

To the question, "For what reason is that name of Viṣṇu [called 'consisting of that']?", he says: "The fruit. By this, the meaning of the word "that" (tat) becomes explained. Now, since the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sole sense of "modification," how can there be an explanation of "consisting of faith" (*śraddhāmaya*) as "having the nature of faith" (*śraddhāsvarūpa*)? To this he says: "The suffix *maṭ*. Why is it that the description of the intention behind the explanatory statement—that "faith alone is the efficient cause, and not [the factors] such as following the injunctions of the scriptures"—is made? To this he says: "The scripture... and so forth.

The point is this: since the Blessed Lord himself has stated that even one who follows the injunctions of the scriptures is merely a non-sentient being (*asattva*) in the absence of faith, it is understood that faith alone is the motivating factor and nothing else. Thus, it is established that in the case of the word "offered" (*hutam*), it is according to the scriptural injunctions. This is mentioned in connection with the discussion of those injunctions. Furthermore, this was said while granting for the sake of argument that such a person exists; however, in the absence of faith in the Blessed Lord, there is no conformity to the scriptural injunctions either. Therefore, with the intention that faith alone is the cause of being *sāttvika* and so forth, he says: "In the Blessed Lord... (*bhagavad-*) and so on.

To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Because of devotion to Viṣṇu. The meaning is that since scripture is understood to have been composed solely for the purpose of enjoining devotion to Viṣṇu, in the absence of that [devotion], one does not act in accordance with the injunctions of the scripture. To the objection—"If the injunctions of the scripture are not the motivating factor, how can it be said that acting contrary to the scripture is the cause of being tāmasa?"—he says: "Because of the Lord... [and so on].

Regarding the statement that foods are "succulent, unctuous, and stable," what is meant by their "stability," and for which [beings] is this said? To this he says: "stable. This means they provide their qualities over a long period of time. Regarding the statement that pungent, sour, salty, and so forth are *rājasa*, that is not fixed; sometimes they may even be *sāttvika*. To this he says: "of the pungent and so forth. *Rasa* here refers to elixir (*rasāyana*).

Thus, regarding the qualities such as "palatable" (*rasya*), "smooth" (*snigdha*), "firm" (*sthira*), and "heart-pleasing" (*hṛdya*)—which were described as being *sāttvika*—their status as *sāttvika* is not fixed; for sometimes they may even be *rājasa*. To this he says: "Palatable... [and so on]. One might ask: why should there not be a rule that pungent (*kaṭu*) and other such qualities are exclusively *rājasa*, while occasionally they are *sāttvika*? To this he says: "...due to suffering... (*duḥkhaiḥ*).

The meaning is as follows: since it has been stated that things which bestow suffering and so forth are *rājasa*, one understands that pungent substances (*kaṭu*) and the like—which are causes of health and so on—are *sāttvika*; therefore, there is no fixed rule (*niyama*) that they must be *rājasa*. Furthermore, regarding the lack of a fixed rule for *rasa* and the others being *sāttvika*, one should cite [the verse] beginning with "longevity, strength... (*āyuḥ-sattva*). He says "sattvam" because the word *sattva* is not significantly different in meaning from the word *bala*, and thus [the former] avoids the charge of tautology.

In this context, the meaning of the word *sattva* is not "goodness," because that [goodness] lacks the quality of being produced here; therefore, he says: "it exists" (*bhavati*). To dispel the notion that the words "increasing pleasure and joy" (*sukhaprītivivardhanāḥ*) and "heart-pleasing" (*hṛdya*) have the same meaning, he says: "heart-pleasing" (*hṛdyam*). That which captivates the mind so that one desires it even after having served it is "heart-pleasing. That which bestows happiness at the very time of its use is "dear" (*priya*). That which, once used, bestows happiness for a long duration is "giving happiness" (*sukhada*).

The meaning is that only that which has been enjoyed many times is pleasant and provides happiness. (8) Since the word *rūkṣa* has multiple meanings, he states the intended meaning here: "Rūkṣam" [is...]. To establish the pungency of the food, he says: "Tīkṣṇam" [is...]. (9) Since it is well known that the food left over from a person who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) is *sāttvika*, how can it be *tāmasa* as "stale" (*yātayāma*)? Therefore, he explains it by another method according to authoritative evidence: "Yāmam" [is...]. (10)

The term *yāmya* refers to that which is to be restrained (*niyamyam*), meaning the portion that has been consumed; the sense is that its essence (*sāra*) has been expected [but is now gone]. If one objects that this is a tautology with the word *gatarasa* (devoid of flavor), he says: "Previously. The point is that there is a difference in meaning: whatever its flavor may have been, once that has departed, it is *yātayāma*; whereas when its palatability (*svādutva*) has departed, it is *gatarasa*. Alternatively, he says "previously" to address the question: since that which is called "dry" (*rūkṣa*) was described as being *rājasa*, how can it now be said to be *tāmasa*? Thus he says: "Previously."

The meaning is that there is no fault in [the food] being "lacking flavor" (*nīrasa*)—that is, dry (*rūkṣa*)—because it was originally savory but later became otherwise, thus losing its flavor. It is difficult to understand how the state of having lost its savor constitutes *tāmasa* nature, since the presence or absence of savor in a single object can vary according to different persons, leading to uncertainty regarding what is "savorful" and so on; therefore, he says: "Pure," etc. As for the statement that heaven is merely conceptual (*sāṅkalpika*) due to the sacrifice of a passionate person (*rājasa*), that is not tenable.

Regarding the phrase "but with a view toward the fruit," he addresses the doubt that because one acts there with a desire for a fruit—since some scriptural statement says that through a *rājasa* sacrifice the world of the gods, such as Indra, becomes heaven—he refutes this by means of another traditional text (*smṛti*). [The text says: "From sacrifice... [He asks: Since one engages in that [sacrifice] with a desire for heaven, how can there be an absence of that [heaven]? To this he replies: "In Viṣṇu... On the contrary, by desiring heaven, only hell results, not heaven.

The sense is that for those who are fit for heaven due to the presence of faith in Viṣṇu, the desire for that [heaven] is not appropriate [for them]. As for how the desire for the unattainable and so forth can be the cause [of hell] when there is an absence of sacrificial rites performed with desire by the *rājasa*—even though such rites exist—the author says: "Without... He provides the explanation for the occasional observation of hell by saying: "That which is forbidden... Here, it should be understood that by the statement regarding the abundance of the hellish world, the *madhyama* (middle) *rājasa* types are intended, and not the *nityatraividyā* (those eternally devoted to the three Vedas).

If hell were to result from rajasic action, then since sattvic persons might also perform such actions, they too would incur hell; therefore, he says: "Sometimes" (*kadācit*). Although sattvic persons may perform rajasic and tamasic actions, rajasic persons may perform sattvic and tamasic actions, and tamasic persons may perform sattvic and rajasic actions, nevertheless, these occur only occasionally. Their primary state remains fixed in their own natural (*svābhāvika*) actions. Furthermore, because a greater [disposition] overcomes the lesser, there is no confusion of results—this is the intended meaning.

He says [the following] because there is no confusion of results (*phala-saṃkara*), since it is possible for one's natural disposition (*svabhāva*) to overcome others through its own nature—whether that nature be of great fruit or of small fruit. Regarding the word "one's own" (*svam*): if the performance of actions were merely natural or unnatural for those characterized by *sattva* and so forth, then how could one know, "This is a natural action; this is not"? To this he says: "abundance" (*bāhulyam*).

The meaning is that among the *svābhāvika* (innate) and other types of actions, that which is predominant is *svābhāvika*, while that which is minimal is *asvābhāvika*; thus, this serves as an indicator for determining predominance and so forth. || 10-15 ||

Regarding the phrase "serenity of mind, gentleness, and silence" (*manaḥprasādaḥ saumyatvaṃ maunaṃ*), he says "silence" (*maunam*) in order to dispel the notion that the word "silence" has some other meaning here. The sense is: how else could this be considered mental austerity (*mānasaṃ tapaḥ*)? Regarding the phrase "by those disciplined (*yuktaiḥ*) and desiring no fruit," he asks what is meant by "disciplined" and answers with "by those disciplined. Now, one might ask: why is the dedication to the Lord not mentioned for Sāttvika sacrifice and charity, but only for austerity? To this he replies: "by those disciplined."
The meaning is that this is not stated only with regard to austerity (*tapas*), but rather it should be applied to sacrifice (*yajña*), charity (*dāna*), and austerity as well.

This has been explained by the other statement: "The designation is *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*. By means of the exposition of that statement, he explains this present statement [at verses 16–22]. Regarding the word *sat*: What follows from that? To this he says: *oṃ*. For it is precisely because actions and so forth are connected with *sat* that they possess existence (*sattva*). And that term is Brahman itself, because the names *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat* are well-known to refer to Viṣṇu. Therefore, the sense is that action and the rest are *sat* only insofar as they are connected with Viṣṇu.

By this, the statement "Oṃ tat sat—whatever belongs to Viṣṇu" becomes explained. For it is well known that what is not preceded by Oṃ would be demonic (*āsura*); thus, the established fact of the demonic nature of that which is un-ornamented by Oṃ is stated as the reason for its utterance. To the question "What is that [Vedic basis]? he says: "It flows," etc. And regarding the meaning already stated in "But even when preceded by Oṃ," he cites the Śruti: "One who does not know the meaning," etc. "Nirartha" means purposeless. Why? Because it is precisely through knowledge of the meaning that the mantra protects the knower; for such is how the mantra is described.

Now, one might ask: "In this chapter, the discrimination between existent and non-existent actions ought to be performed; setting that aside, what is being said by [the words] 'Oṃ tat sat' and so forth? To address this, he states the underlying intention: "Because it has that as its purpose. For here, having first recollected the meaning of the syllable *oṃ* and having uttered it, that which is performed with devotion, for the sake of the Lord, and without desire, is indeed [what is intended].

Action is said to be of another kind—namely, *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and so forth. Therefore, the point is that such action alone is "good action" (*sat-karma*) while other action is "bad action" (*asat-karma*); thus, good and bad action have already been distinguished and described. Nor should it be argued that here the goodness of this kind of action and the badness of the other are being stated by the words themselves; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the description] not being consistent with the context, since terms such as "good" (*sat*) and so on carry the meaning of *sāttvika* and the like. By this, the connection of the chapter is also indicated in the same way for the passage beginning with "by those who do not desire fruits" (*aphalākāṅkṣibhiḥ*).

Now, one might ask: "Having described sattvic action with the words 'And action for that purpose is this,' and without mentioning rajasic action, why is only tamasic action described by the verse beginning 'Offered without faith'? To this he replies: "Of the rajasic... The sense is that here the word *asat* (unreal/evil) does not denote only tamasic action, but rather rajasic action as well. Why is this so? Because the characteristic of *asat* mentioned in the phrase "without faith" (*aśraddhayā*) exists in rajasic action too; thus he says: "In the case of Viṣṇu... etc.

By the verse, "And that [fruit] exists neither hereafter nor here," the fruit of rājasa and tāmasa actions which was mentioned is shown by the Smṛti after having analyzed it: "That which is characterized by sattva... and so forth.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He shows the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter with the words "All," etc. Whatever means for achieving the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) have been stated scattered throughout all the previous chapters, that is now set forth concisely in this chapter for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect. The meaning is that the threefold nature of the qualities (traiguṇya), which was not mentioned in the fourteenth chapter and elsewhere, is also being described here. 1–2.

In order to determine the true nature of renunciation as previously stated—namely, "the renunciation of the fruits of all actions"—an apparent contradiction among the views of the learned is raised by means of the word "to be abandoned. Here, some hold that sacrificial, charitable, and ascetic acts are not to be abandoned, but must indeed be performed; others, however, hold they are to be abandoned like defects because they contradict the Lord’s teaching. To dispel this erroneous perception, He says: "by the wise" and "therefore."

Just as in the verse, "Action alone must be performed," the renunciation of action is described through the abandonment of attachment to its fruits rather than through the abandonment of the action's essential nature, so too can the meaning of "that which is to be abandoned" (tyājya) be explained. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Blessed One’s doctrine. If one asks, "Why then should another meaning be imagined? the intention is that this is precisely because the word "wise ones" (manīṣiṇaḥ) has been used. || 3-4 ||

The promise "Listen to the certainty" is now stated: "In sacrifice," etc. To this, one might ask: since ascetics and Śūdras and others lack the qualification for sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and for gifts of gold and the like, and since householders and others lack the qualification for austerities such as celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*), how can sacrifice and so forth be prescribed for everyone? To this, he says: "By means of wealth," etc.

In this context, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, the giving of gold and other gifts, and ascetic practices such as celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) are not prescribed for all; rather, it is sacrifices such as the sacrifice of material goods (dravyayajña), gifts such as knowledge (vidyādāna), and ascetic practices such as truthful speech that are prescribed. Since these are appropriate even for ascetics (yati) and others, the sense is that it is logical for them to be prescribed for everyone. Regarding the statement "no fire, no sacrifice," etc., [the author] says "Viṣṇu... because those outside the three varṇas have no entitlement to any sacrifice whatsoever.

Even in the absence of sacrifices involving material substances and the like, they certainly possess the qualification for the sacrifice of self-study (svādhyāya-yajña). Nor does their lack of qualification for the Vedas imply a lack of qualification for that [self-study], because qualification for the sacrifice of self-study consisting of the names of Viṣṇu is possible; this is the sense. To the question, "What is their austerity? he says: "Truth," etc. (5–6).

The statement "For renunciation... is now elaborated upon with the words "of that which is obligatory. Since the renunciation of action is itself being praised there, one might ask: how can it be said to be caused by delusion? To this he says: "Attachment... Why is even the renunciation of the essential nature [of action] caused by delusion? To the question of how this meaning could be so, he says: "One's own..."

Now, one might object: "Even in an action that accomplishes the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), since it is said to be *rājasa* because its nature is abandoned through the false cognition that 'it is a means to suffering,' how can it be *tāmasa*? To this he says: "Delusion" (*moha*). [The phrase] "without delusion" means without the false cognition that "this is a means to suffering even in another [life]. To dispel the misconception that the word "suffering" refers merely to physical exhaustion, he says: "Suffering," etc. [He adds: "Merely," etc.

The meaning is that [the goal] is not attained through the exertion of the body. To the question, "Could it not be that the exertion of the body itself is the goal? he says: "kārya... (as the result). It is not only because otherwise there would be the fault of tautology that the word *duḥkha* here signifies mental suffering; rather, he says "duḥkham" because it is so stated [in the scripture]. This should be understood as being intended when a specific meaning is desired to be expressed; in its absence, both [types of suffering] are denoted by the two words. || 8-9 ||

The renouncer of the *sāttvika* type is further defined by the words "he does not hate" (*na dveṣṭi*). In that regard, one might ask: how can the absence of hatred toward unwholesome actions and non-attachment to wholesome actions be predicated of the *sāttvika* renouncer? This would seem to contradict the statement "merely because it is duty" (*kāryam ity eva*). Therefore, he explains this through another means of knowledge: "He does not hate," etc. "In merit" (*puṇye*) means, in other words, in its fruit. He praises him [the renouncer] with the word "who" (*yaḥ*). By the word "properly" (*samyak*), the meaning previously stated in the passage beginning with "not seeking reward" (*amoghavī*) is established.

By the phrase "by offering that," the meaning of what was stated as "the renouncer" is established. By the word "of that," the intended sense of the term "undesirable" is expressed. To the question, "Is action that is in every way binding not conducive to bondage for him? he says: "If it is abundant. If it is abundant, it causes even a very slight defect for those who have renounced everything; to the question "To what extent? he says: "As long as... (10–11).

Regarding the phrase "undesirable, desirable, and mixed," the author says [the following] to dispel the misconception that the fruit of action which binds is desired by the renouncer (*tyāgin*). He says: "Of others. To the question, "Why might it not be desired even by the renouncer? he says: "Of this one. The fruit of action that binds is not desired by the renouncer; for the very reason that he is a renouncer, it is stated that only one who has abandoned the desire for the fruit of action is a renouncer, as in the verse: "But he who renounces the fruit of action" (Gītā 18.11). This is the intended meaning.

This would indeed be so if, in the phrase "unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed," the fruit of binding karma were intended; however, this is not the case, as there is no contradiction in including the fruit of non-binding karma as well. Therefore, while for one who renounces there is the absence of the very fruit of binding karma, for one who does not renounce—

He states the authoritative proof for the existence of the fruit of the action of renunciation: "Of knowledge and so forth" (*jñānādeḥ*). This refers to the mere act of relinquishing, such as knowledge, devotion, and the like. For one who has realized the Truth through that very [renunciation] by means of direct perception, there is a superior bliss to be enjoyed in liberation. "Without that" (*tadṛte*) means without knowledge and the rest. By this, the meaning of what was stated in the verse "it happens for those who do not renounce" (*bhavatyatyāginām*) is established. Since it says, "It happens after death for those who do not renounce, but not for those who renounce," the term "those who do not renounce" must be understood as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to "those who renounce. To the question, "Why then are renunciants (*saṃnyāsinaḥ*) mentioned? he replies:

Regarding the word *kevala*: the mention of renunciants (*saṃnyāsika*) as those who do not abandon [even obligatory duties] is not inconsistent. For even in the absence of desire for a result for one's own sake, there are those who abandon [desire] (*tyāgin*) who perform purely optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, for the sake of benefiting others. Since renunciants (*nyāsin*) do not possess even that [motivation], they are distinguished from those who merely abandon [desire] by this much alone; this is the meaning of the statement that renunciants are superior to those who abandon. If this is the only distinction, then what is their similarity, given that renunciants are mentioned while those who abandon [desire] ought to have been discussed? To this he says: "The state of being a renouncer" (*tyāgitvam*).

The meaning is that the absence of desire for the fruits of action is equal for both. To the question, "From what [source] is this specific distinction stated for renunciants (nyāsins) as compared to those who merely renounce (tyāgins)? he says: "Because of the other," etc. (12).

With the intention that even the renunciation of egoism regarding action is *saṃnyāsa*, the causes of action are stated as "five. In this context, by the term "the final conclusion of Sāṅkhya" (*sāṅkhyakṛtānta*), it is precisely the supreme Sāṅkhya doctrine that is meant, and not merely the well-known [classical] Sāṅkhya.

Since the word *daiva* (fate/divine) here refers to Īśvara, and because the Supreme Sāṅkhya is theistic while the well-known Sāṅkhya is atheistic; and since it is possible for the Supreme Sāṅkhya to be included here due to its Vedic character, whereas the other cannot be so included due to its non-Vedic character—it is with this intention that he states the proof for their theism and so forth: "It has been stated" (verse 13).
He states the intended meaning of the term "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) here: "The substratum," etc. (14–16).

That knowledge is praised in the verse beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*). And since this [knowledge] is common to all who possess egoism and the like, he explains it by means of another statement in order to dispel any other [mis]conception: "Sovereignty" (*svātantryam*). [The phrase] "of the Self, within the Self" (*ātmana ātmani*) is supplied; and it is understood that one knows the sovereignty of the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth. [An objection is raised: "If that is the purpose, then it is sufficient for him to be born simply for the sake of destroying the world; what is the use of knowing the sovereignty and other attributes of the Lord? To this he says: "The ignorant one" (*ajñaḥ*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "if he destroys the worlds."

In that case, knowledge alone would suffice; what is the need for being "born for that purpose" (jātatva)? To this, we present a refutation through a distinction based on the destruction of worldly life, even for those possessing both indirect (parokṣa) and direct (aparokṣa) knowledge who have not yet been born for that purpose. Regarding the verse beginning with *aparokṣa*: the meaning is that if one possessing indirect knowledge, though born for that purpose, destroys the worlds, then he is tainted by some degree of fault. By the use of the term *aparokṣa*, it is indicated that knowledge must also be direct (*aparokṣa*) [for such a claim to hold].

[The author] says this [verse] because it might be argued: "Is it not enough that he has arisen for that purpose? What need is there for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)? Regarding the phrase "immediate," it should be understood here as "one who has arisen for that purpose. Now, since all [beings] are non-independent and thus possess the nature of being "slayers" (*ahantṛ*), why is it stated specifically that "he alone does not slay"? To this he says: "Because of non-independence. The connection is to be made as follows: the distinction that "he does not slay" is logical on the grounds that he lacks the state of being [an agent], whereas others possess that state. Thus, there is no tautology in saying "he does not slay."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the non-destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*) means the abandonment of the conceit of independence? Therefore, [your statement] is redundant. To this, he says: "The intellect... This would indeed be so, provided there were a difference in meaning between the two [verses], "He whose state is not characterized by egoism" and "His intellect is not defiled," such that both the conceit of independence and the passion resulting from it were equally causes of bondage. Why is that so? To this, he says: "Independence... (17)

By the phrase "and indeed destiny" (*daivaṃ caiva*), it is stated that the Lord is the impeller of actions. The nature of that impelling is now defined as "knowledge" (*jñāna*). He establishes this through a traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "of the impeller. Since impelling is an attribute of the Blessed One, one might ask how it can be [described as] "knowing-ness" and so forth; to this he says: "that [impelling]. The meaning is that because impelling is identical with the very nature of the Blessed One—consisting of knowledge and the rest—it is logically consistent for it to be such.

To the question, "How can that which arises at various times as an impulse (preraṇā) possess the nature of the Lord's own form (bhagavatsvarūpatva)? he says: "By its very nature" (svarūpeṇa). It is not the case that the impulse is produced at each respective time; rather, existing eternally as the very nature of the Lord, it is manifested in a manifest form. Therefore, the sense is that its being the nature of the Lord is logically established.

One should not suspect that this particularity (*viśeṣa*), which is the manifestation of the impulse (*preraṇā*), is also non-eternal; for, since it is of the nature of an eternal impulse, it arises as a particularity precisely because it is already eternally present. Thus he says: "The particularity also... In this way, there might be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—that there is a further particularity of the particularity, and so on. To this he says: "...self-establishing" (*svanirvāhakatā*). There would be an infinite regress if one were to admit a particularity distinct from the impulse, and yet another for that one as well. But it is not so.

That impulsion itself brings about its own nature as something qualified—that is, as a specific distinction—because it is accepted that even that distinction is likewise [of the same nature]. He establishes this by means of an illustration: "as in the case of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭavat*). He explains that very point: "of the qualified object" (*viśeṣyasya*). There is, first of all, an undisputed non-difference between the qualified object and the qualification; for even by one who maintains a difference between attribute (*dharma*) and substrate (*dharmin*), that non-difference is admitted. Yet, there is no non-difference devoid of distinction between the qualified object and the qualification.

If that were the case, it would follow that the words "knower" (*jñātṛ*) and "Devadatta" would be synonyms. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress by admitting particularities even for the substantive (*viśeṣya*), because the substantive entity and its particularities are self-sustaining. Thus, the point is that there is no fault whatsoever in admitting a particularity of God’s impulsion and a further particularity of that [impulsion], provided that the identity between the substantive and its qualifier is established. To the question, "How is that very identity established? he says: "Of the knower... (*jñātuḥ*).

The point is that there is no experience of difference between the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) and the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*), and because there is indeed an experience of non-difference, there is no distinction. Furthermore, he demonstrates another experience regarding the non-difference of the qualified object and the qualified by saying: "I see. Here, "I" refers to the qualified object; "a particular has arisen" indicates its state as the qualified.

That which is joined with a qualification is the "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*). He defines that qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) by saying: "the qualification. This is called a "particular," such as the existence of an entity or the blueness of a fruit.

Thus [it is said]. A staff and so forth are absolutely distinct from this [object]. Why, then, is it said that both of these are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)? To this he says: "The particular" (*viśeṣam*). That is, it makes one understand (*gamayet*). Now, one might object: while a qualifier such as a staff makes one understand the particularity of "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) in the object, what particularity could [the object] itself make one understand? To this he says: "By the particular" (*viśeṣeti*).

The causes of action mentioned previously are stated here in brief as "the instrument" (*karaṇam*). To the question, "In what way is this statement of the summary of action useful?", he explains it by restating that [term], with the intention that this is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopisamāsa*). He says: "The summary. To the question, "How can the fivefold set beginning with the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) constitute the threefold set beginning with the instrument? he says: "Of the locus," etc. Now, since an action not previously mentioned is being discussed here, one might ask how this could be a summary of them; to this he says:
"Karma" [is the subject]. || 18 ||

The distinctions among the *guṇas* are stated for the purpose of practicing the means such as *sāttvika* knowledge and so forth—beginning with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). To dispel the misconception that the term "enumeration of *guṇas*" (*guṇasaṅkhyāna*) refers here to the well-known Sāṅkhya system (in which *guṇas* are enumerated therein), he says: "Thus" (*evam*). [An objection is raised: Why should this not simply be the well-known Sāṅkhya system? To this, he replies: "Thus."

Thus, it is stated here that the knowledge of the omnipresent Lord regarding objects such as difference and so forth from all things is *sāttvika*, and so on, as described in the enumeration of the qualities (*guṇasaṅkhyāna*). And this is only possible upon accepting the supreme Sāṅkhya scripture, not upon accepting the atheistic Sāṅkhya; such is the intended meaning. || 19 ||

Therein, the threefold nature of knowledge previously promised is stated: "all" (*sarva*). To dispel misconceptions such as non-perception of that [knowledge], he explains it precisely through the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "because of its existence" (*astitvāt*) up to the end of the phrase "as distinct" (*pṛthaktvena*). By this, the intended meaning of the locative case in "in all beings" (*sarvabhūteṣu*) is also expressed. By the words "of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ*) and so forth, the meaning of the term "undivided" (*avibhaktam*) is clarified. By the phrase "in a state of gradation" (*tāratamyena*), the expression "among the divided" (*vibhakteṣu*) is explained in two ways.

Now, having considered that by the word *bhūta* (being) both "that which exists" and the "insentient" (*jaḍa*) are denoted, the meaning of the phrase "among the distinct" (*vibhakteṣu*) is stated: "from the insentient" (*jaḍebhyaḥ*). By this expression "from those insentient ones," the sense of the locative case is expressed. Regarding the word "properly" (*samyak*): the meaning is that Viṣṇu is the supreme among all, while the individual souls (*jīva*) possess knowledge and other qualities dependent upon Him, whereas the insentient is devoid of them; thus, there is a distinction between Viṣṇu and the others. By this, the intended meaning of what was said [in the verse] as "one" (*ekam*) is established. (20)

By the phrase "of Viṣṇu," the intended meaning of [the word] "separately" is expressed. Since even Sāttvika knowledge is stated to be true regarding what is other than Viṣṇu, one might ask: how can this [knowledge] be Rājasa? To this, he says: "If... This means that one who knows the principles in a mixed way knows the nature of the Lord with uncertainty. By the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*), the meaning expressed by "but whatever" (*yattu*) is conveyed. Furthermore, it should first be understood as: "he knows some single thing as the whole.
By the end of the passage ending with "knows," the intended meaning of the statement "attached to the effect as if it were the whole" is expressed.

The meaning is: "just as [the world] perceives Brahman as being full of qualities such as being entirely uncreated (*akāryatva*), so too [it perceives it] as Brahman. By the phrase "that very same," having accepted that the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) in the expression "attached to the entire effect" refers to the whole universe, a different interpretation is stated. By the word "one" (*eka*), the intended sense is that it is attached to one particular effect as if it were the whole. By the word "reasoning" (*yukti*), the meaning is that it considers even what is irrational to be rational (*yuktivat*).

By the word *alpa* ("small"), the meaning "insignificant" is expressed; that is to say, it refers to limited correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because even one who is deluded possesses correct knowledge regarding the objective basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth. By the phrase *atattvārtham* ("not having reality as its object"), the meaning "that which possesses what is not the true object" is expressed; that is to say, it has a form contrary to the actual mode of existence. [The phrase] *tattvārthajñānavarjanāt* means "due to the absence of knowledge of the form as it actually exists."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very knowledge which [perceives] all beings as distinct is what is called "diverse states" (*nānābhāvān*) and "of various kinds" (*pṛthagvidhān*)? Therefore, there is the fault of tautology. To this, he says: "As distinct" (*pṛthaktvena*). The intention is that because of the relationship between the explanation and the thing to be explained, there is no fault of tautology. [Objection: Since the object of the knowledge of distinctness regarding all beings has been stated to be *sāttvika*, how can its *rājasa* nature be stated here? To this, he says: "All... (*sarva...*).

It is not only that sattvic knowledge regarding the distinctness of all beings has been described; rather, it is that which takes as its object the Lord residing within them, perceiving Him as non-distinct and as the supreme of all. The sense is that even though this king’s knowledge concerns the distinctness of beings due to the absence of that [realization of the Lord], his possession of *sattva* is appropriate. By this, the *smṛti* verse beginning with "yadi" (if) is explained.

However, as for the claim that "knowledge which is attached to a single effect as if it were the whole is causeless, being devoid of the true object and joined with a small amount of real knowledge," this would necessarily result in a tautology if stated again; therefore, explaining [the meaning], he says: "Of one... This is the commentary on the previously stated meaning up to the word "does not exist. It is not the case that the qualifiers such as "causelessness" and so forth are being predicated of what was already mentioned before, such that there would be a tautology.

However, the intention is that the aforementioned qualifiers are stated in order to demonstrate the extreme tamasic nature of those who are themselves tamasic, by virtue of their association with such qualifiers as "causelessness" (ahetukatva) and so forth. The meaning is that [the doctrine] is joined with the fabrication of non-existent forms, such as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent (sadasadvailakṣaṇya). Thus, having accepted the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of these words and thereby avoided redundancy, he avoids it again by means of their having multiple substrata, stating: "In one... (ekasmin).

The phrase "the entire world" is to be construed with "in every effect," and the phrase "the entire world" is to be construed with "attached to a single effect"; thus, it is rightly understood that there is no tautology. Now, one might ask: since such knowledge does not exist anywhere [in its pure form], how can it be described as being characterized by *tamas*? To this, he says: "It is *māyā*. (21–22)

The threefold nature of action is stated according to the distinction of its qualities, beginning with the word "niyatam" (obligatory). To dispel the misconception that the term "niyata" there refers merely to that which is appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), he says: "mayi" (in Me). Here, only that action performed with the knowledge of Viṣṇu’s supreme excellence, preceded by devotion to Him, and with the intention of offering it to Him, is called "niyata. It does not refer merely to what is appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life.

Why? Because, having prescribed the performance of action with the intention of offering it to Him—preceded by the knowledge that the Blessed Lord is supreme over all, expressed in the words "All actions in Me"—the text states in the verse "Those who follow this My view" that this constitutes a means to liberation. Furthermore, in the verse "But those who... it is stated that there is sin (pratyavāya) for its non-performance. The sense is that whatever, when performed, leads to the attainment of the fruit, and whose non-performance results in sin, that alone is what is mandatory (niyata). Let it be granted that action performed with the intention of offering it to the Blessed Lord is mandatory.

From what source is it known that this [practice] is preceded by the knowledge of the Lord’s supremacy over all? It is because that is not mentioned in the verse beginning with "all actions in Me" (*mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi*). To this, he says: "Adhyātma... etc. "Adhyātma-cetas" means the mind directed toward the Supreme Self, who is superior to all; it is understood as being required [for the practice]. This might be so, provided the word "adhyātma-cetas" were intended for the purpose of knowing the Lord's supremacy over all. Why is that very point established? To this, he says: "But those who... etc.

Regarding the phrase "in me all" (*mayi sarvāṇi*), which serves as a restatement of the meaning of the verse: since in this verse beginning with "all," the word *adhyātmacetasā* has been explained as having the purpose of knowing and remembering the Lord’s absolute supremacy through the words "devoted to Me" (*matparāḥ*) and so forth, the sense is that this word indeed serves that purpose. Those for whom I am the supreme, the highest of all, are "devoted to Me" (*matparāḥ*). Nor should it be asked why this verse is a restatement of that [previous] verse.

Since it is appropriate for the Blessed One to provide a reply in that very manner when questioned by Arjuna through the restatement of the previously mentioned mode—namely, "those who are thus constantly disciplined"—and since this status as a restatement of the meaning of the present verse is understood from the force of the title [of the chapter], [Arjuna asks]: "Is this state of being fixed (niyatattva) the sole determinant for the sattvic nature of action, or does it apply to knowledge and the other factors as well? To this he says: "Thus... (evam). And here, the offering to the Blessed One and so forth should also be understood. (23–25)

The threefold nature of the agent is stated according to the distinction of qualities—namely, "the liberated. To the question, "If the agent there does not speak of 'I,' how is that so? he says: "Of everything. Even as an agent, one who is characterized by *sattva* does not say, "I am the doer"; for the reason is that he has ascertained that everything, including his own agency, is dependent upon the Lord. (26–27)

Now, one might object: since procrastination and long-windedness exist even in the *sāttvika* type, how can these be said to belong exclusively to the *tāmasa*? To this, he shows the meaning of those two terms by recalling the traditional authority (*smṛti*). [He says: "The Lord," etc., and "remembering," which means "contemplating. Since the thought "I shall do it later" is common even to the *sāttvika*, he says: "Having arrived," etc.

The meaning is that one who, even when the time for a particular action has arrived, thinks "I shall do it later," is a procrastinator (*dīrghasūtrī*). By this, his distinction from the merely indolent (*alasa*) is indicated; such a person simply neglects the action at the proper time. Now, if this is so, since the procrastinator is superior to the stubborn and others, why are they counted among the *tāmasa* (dark-natured) types? To answer this, he classifies them specifically among the *tāmasa* by means of an authoritative statement: "The indolent... and so forth.

"Unfit" means devoid of yoga such as dedication to the Blessed One and so forth. "Arrogant" means not bowing down anywhere due to self-conceit. "Deceitful" means one who performs base actions. "Hypocritical" means one who harbors secret malice. He states the fruit of these three types of *tāmasa* [actions] as follows: "the state of being a wicked man. (29–30)

The proposition stated as "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*) is now explained by the words "activity" (*pravṛttim*). Since the two types mentioned there—namely "by which one [perceives] dharma and adharma"—are of a single nature, how can they possess the qualities of *rājasa* and *tāmasa*? Therefore, he shows their distinction through another sentence: "something" (*kiñcit*). By this, it is implied that "not as it truly is" (*ayathāvat*) is a restrictive rule meaning "not as it truly is. Regarding the word "by means of yoga" (*yogena*), in order to dispel the notion that it refers to a small degree of effort, he explains it through another sentence: "Vaiṣṇava" (*vaiṣṇava*).

By this yoga, [the requirement] "by means of reasoning" is fulfilled. If *dhṛti* (steadfastness) is indeed free from deviation, then why is it specifically qualified as "non-deviating"? To this, he says: "Enjoined," etc. It is not...

The meaning here is that "infallibility" (*avyabhicāritvam*) refers to being unerring (*askhalitatvam*). To dispel the notion that the *tāmasī* [type of fortitude] is that which does not let go of what is merely called "dreaming," he says: "Dreaming. The sense is that everything prohibited by the elders, such as hatred toward the Lord, is *tāmasa* because hatred toward the Lord and so forth is forbidden by the elders; therefore, the fortitude directed toward such objects is also *tāmasa*. To the question, "Even if it is forbidden by the elders, why is it *tāmasa*? he says: "That... (referring to the verse).

Now, one might object: "Since hatred toward the Lord and the like have been prescribed by certain elders, how can they be censurable? To this he says: "The great-souled ones" (mahātmānaḥ). Those who prescribe hatred toward the Lord and so forth are not true elders; rather, it is those who worship the Lord alone who are so called. This is because it has been stated thus. (35–36)

That which was promised as "happiness" is now stated: "from practice. In this context, in order to dispel the misconception that the phrase "born from the clarity of self-awareness" means "born from the clarity of one's own mind," he states the meaning by means of a traditional authority (smṛti). [He says] "of Viṣṇu"; the word "arisen" is to be supplied. What is called "clarity of mind" is generally the mind's lack of engagement with sense objects even when they are present. (37–39)

The threefold nature of all living beings is also stated by way of their qualities—namely, "not that" (na tat). In that regard, since *sattva* itself is a specific quality (*guṇa-viśeṣa*), how can it be said to be bound by the qualities? To this, he says: "*Sattvam*" (Sattva...). Now, one might object: since the statement is already complete by the fact that there is no *sattva* beyond the qualities, what is the purpose of the specific mention of "on earth" and "in heaven"? To this, he says: "*Muktānām*" (Of the liberated ones).

The meaning is that since liberated beings lack the state of being bound by the *guṇas*, it might be argued that there is no *sattva* beyond the *guṇas*; however, because that [state of being beyond the *guṇas*] would then logically apply to them as well, the specific qualification "in the earth," and so forth, is rightly stated in order to exclude them.

Anticipating the objection—"How can this [verse] exclude them, given that even liberated souls wander through these worlds, assuming forms at will and moving about on the earth and so forth?"—the author dispels this doubt by showing, through another scriptural passage, how they are divided manifoldly according to distinctions suited to their individual nature. He says: "As they desire. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because of the absence of connection with the defects inherent in those [lower states]. Thus, it should be understood here that by stating that those bound by the *guṇas* remain situated on the earth and other such realms, the exclusion of the liberated ones is established.

Since it was asked how those who are bound by qualities can be unliberated, he explains this by dividing them: "Among men... etc. Living beings are of three kinds: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. Among these, the *tāmasa* are themselves of three types, who are described as "the lowest of men. Having thus stated the divisions among the *tāmasa*, he speaks generally of the *rājasa*: "The *rājasa*... etc. Men are superior, middling, and inferior; they too are of three types. Among them, those from the Brahmins down to the *pulkasas* are *rājasasāttvika*.

He describes their manifold variety according to the distinction of caste: "In that regard" (*tatra*). Among those Brahmins—whether *rājasasāttvika* or *sāttvika*—he describes their manifold variety according to the distinction of *āśrama*: "Among those situated there" (*tatrastha*). [This refers to] those who are *śuddhasāttvika* among the *rājasasāttvika* and *sāttvika* [Brahmins].

This is the meaning. The *paramahaṃsas* are devoid of the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), and carry a single staff (*ekadaṇḍin*). One who has abandoned the sacrificial thread and carries a single staff while being devoid of the topknot is a *haṃsa*. One who carries three staves (*tridaṇḍī*), possesses the topknot and the sacrificial thread, stays for only one night in a village, and is a *bahūdaka*. One who carries three staves, possesses the topknot and the sacrificial thread, and eats food provided by his sons for as long as he lives is a *kuṭīcaka*. The word "furthermore" (*adhikam*) is to be connected with "respectively" (*kramāt*). To the question, "Is that [same] common even to the *paramahaṃsas*?", he says: "The duties" (*dharmāḥ*).

The meaning is that [qualities] such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) are described as the duties of Brahmins (*brāhmakarma*). [An objection is raised: since the gods and others also possess a great abundance of ritual actions (*karma*), they too would be of a passionate nature (*rājasatva*), just like the *haṃsa* birds and others. To this, he says: "Of the gods and others... [He asks: Why not? To this, he says: "For not... Whether the mind is active in ritual action or not, there is nonetheless an abundance of action; therefore, the gods and others must be of a passionate nature just like the *haṃsa*s. To this, he says: "Of others..."

Even in the case of actions such as those of swans and the like, action does not indicate *rajas* by its very nature; rather, it does so solely by being a cause for the agitation of the mind. The point is that since divine actions lack this [agitation], they do not serve as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of *rājasa* nature. To the question, "Why should action not indicate *rajas* by its very nature? he says: "If... The point is that since an action caused by the remembrance of the Blessed Lord is seen to indicate *sattva*, action does not indicate *rājasa* nature by its very nature.
For this very reason, he said, "It would generally be so" (*prāyaḥ syāt*).

He shows, by way of a brief analysis, the increasing abundance of ritual duties (*karma*) that has been described in sequence for those from the *paramahaṃsa* down to the householder (*gṛhastha*). [The verse begins with] "Dharma... etc. This sequence of the increasing abundance of ritual duties among the *haṃsa* and others is to be understood as not limited [to these alone]. For the student (*brahmacārin*), who is one of the four types of ascetics (*yati*), the specific duties are the cutting of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and so forth, the worship of the fire, and the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*). For the householder, compared to the student, the specific duty is the taking of a wife.

The meaning is that the forest-dweller (vanastha) is distinguished from the householder by the non-production of offspring, the absence of service to village-dwellers and worldly objects, and the non-injury of animals. By the mention of the renunciation of village life, it is implied that even for the forest-dweller, there is a reduction in ritual activity compared to the celibate student (brahmacārī). Other duties, such as sacrifices and the like, remain appropriate to his own stage.

Among the *bhāgavatas* who are *rājasasāttvika*, the nature of the *vipra* has been described according to their various classes. Now, by means of another statement, he shows the nature of the *kṣatriyas* and others, as well as the nature of those who are *rājasarājasa* and so forth: "The *sāttvikas*," etc. It should be understood that this refers to those among the *rājasasāttvikas*. "Those who are *sattvarājasa*" means those in whom *sattva* and *rajas* are equal. "By virtue of a slight excess of *sattva*" means that *sattva* is predominant in such a way that even *tamas* is extremely minimal.

To the question, "Why is the status [of the devotee] thus restricted only to the Kṣatriyas and so forth?", he says: "He who... To the question, "If the Bhāgavatas are outside the [four] castes, what then?", he says: "In Sattva... The meaning is that even a Pulkasa who is a Bhāgavata possesses a greater degree of *sattva* than those characterized by *rajas*. Having described those who are *rājasasāttvika*, he now speaks of those who are *rājasarājasa* and so forth: "Those who possess the three Vedas... He distinguishes the Bhāgavatas from those born at other times: "Only those who possess the three Vedas... [And finally: "In all respects superior..."

It should be understood that this refers to superiority in every respect. He states the subdivisions of the *sāttvika* type: "The ancestors (*pitṛ*), Gandharvas," and so forth. By the phrase "only the superior ones," it is meant that those preceded by the ancestors and Gandharvas are *sāttvika-tāmasa*, the sages (*munayaḥ*) are *sāttvika-rājasa*, and the gods (*devāḥ*) are *sāttvika-sāttvika*.

Having distinguished the gods, he says: "The gods. Regarding "those who are progressively higher": among those who are predominantly *sāttvika*, Bṛhaspati and others are *tāmasa*, Indra is *rājasa*, and those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Rudra are said to be *sāttvika*. Having distinguished [the group] beginning with Viriñca, he says: "Śiva. Regarding "those who are progressively higher": among those who are predominantly *sāttvika*, it is stated that Rudra is *tāmasa*, Sarasvatī is *rājasa*, and Brahmā is *sāttvika*. If this is so, then what is meant by "Viriñca"? To this, he says:

Regarding the word "sattva": since, according to the manner stated, their gradation is based solely on the *guṇas*, why is this so? To this he says: "In liberation (*muktau*). The sense is that even in the absence of the *guṇas*, the gradation is established by the very sequence of the dissolution of the body as described above. It has been said: "The lowest among men are among the *tāmasas*; the *sāttvikas* [are higher]. As to what kind they are, he explains that by saying: "In Viṣṇu... and so forth.

It has been stated: "But the *rājasa* brāhmaṇas there, O brāhmaṇas, are *rājasasāttvika*. In that context, by the force of another statement—"those who are *bhāgavata* castes"—it is indicated that one should understand the status of being a *bhāgavata* to belong to those who are *rājasasāttvika*. Thus, in order to dispel the misconception that *bhāgavata* brāhmaṇas are exclusively *rājasasāttvika*, he completes what was not explicitly stated [in the previous verse] with the words: "Of the *rājasa* ones. Having mentally accepted the distinction of castes mentioned regarding the *rājasasāttvika* through the two statements, he demonstrates it for the sake of clarity.

Regarding the phrase "rājasasāttvikāḥ": by this, what was previously stated in the manner of "the Brahmins are rājasasāttvika" and so forth is explained. It is not ordinary Brahmins and others who are rājasasāttvika, but rather only the Bhāgavatas; thus, in accordance with another statement, he provides a further reason: "sattva... etc. Indeed, all beings from those characterized as rājasasāttvika up to Hiraṇyagarbha are fit for liberation. However, among these, it is only the Bhāgavatas who possess the fitness for liberation due to their predominance of *sattva* relative to the other *guṇas*.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that all those characterized by *rājasa-sāttvika* and other such temperaments are indeed *bhāgavatas*. To the question, "Even if *sattva* is predominant, why is there fitness for liberation? he says: "From *sattva*. Since it has been stated that when *sattva* prevails—overpowering *rajas* and *tamas*—it bestows its own fruit, then through the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas* and *tamas* are subdued, making possible the knowledge that is the means to liberation; thus, when *sattva* is in excess, liberation occurs.

The intended meaning is that it has been stated that knowledge has goodness (*sattva*) as its fruit. Here, he states another verse for the sake of clarity: "One in whom *sattva* predominates," etc. One in whom *sattva* predominates refers to those characterized by *rajas* and *sattva*, and so forth. One in whom *tamas* predominates refers to the lowest of men, and so forth. One in whom *rajas* abounds is the possessor of the threefold knowledge (*traividya*). "Equal" means one who possesses all three qualities in an equal measure and is ignorant. (41)

What was stated as "the Brāhmaṇa" is now elaborated upon: "Tranquillity (śama)," etc. Therein, he explains that by means of another authority in order to dispel the misconception that tranquillity and the other qualities belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone: "Tranquillity," etc. By this it is meant that the mention of these in the Brāhmaṇa is intended to show their preeminence. Austerity (tapas) consists of celibacy and so forth. Purity (śauca) is cleanliness. Forbearance (kṣānti) is the non-arising of anger. Rectitude (ārjava) is the absence of deviation in the actions of mind, speech, and body. Knowledge (jñāna) is general; specialized knowledge (vijñāna) is specific.
Faith (āstikya) is the conviction regarding dharma and so forth: "This indeed exists for me."

The meaning is: "This is the purpose. To the question, "How can this be so, given that among Kṣatriyas such as Kārtavīrya, these qualities are seen even more abundantly than in Brāhmaṇas?", he says: "Or superior. The sense is: it is true that among Kṣatriyas there exist tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities in greater measure than among Brāhmaṇas; nevertheless, there is no contradiction with what was stated before. This is because those [Kārtavīrya and others] were sages (*ṛṣi*), whereas it is other Kṣatriyas who are intended here. *Śaurya* is fearlessness; *tejas* is bodily luster; *dhṛti* is fortitude; *dākṣya* is skillfulness.

One who possesses the qualities of a Brāhmaṇa, such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, which are inferior to those of a Kṣatriya, is described as such. [If he is] from a Vaiśya, he is a *śuśrūṣu*, one who lives by service. This restriction is not logical, because even a Śūdra may be seen to possess superior qualities; therefore, he says: "But if they are superior. "A Brāhmaṇa, etc."—this should be understood to mean "one possessing qualities such as tranquility equal to those of a Brāhmaṇa," and so on. The phrase "only a Śūdra" is an illustration; it should be understood that this applies to anyone who possesses qualities equal to those of the respective [higher caste].

To the question, "How can the status of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth be conceived based solely on qualities while disregarding birth?", he says: "Even a man... (the word "as" is to be supplied as the remainder). Having thus stated that the practice of tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues exists even among Kṣatriyas and others through other means of knowledge, he establishes this further by the force of the supplementary portion of the text: "By their own duty... (*svakarmaṇā*). Here, it is said that for all [castes], the worship of the Lord alone is prescribed, and not merely tranquility and so forth; therefore, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

When the worship of the Blessed One alone is prescribed for all, then tranquility (śama) and the rest have already been implied; the sense is that without those, complete worship is impossible. To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Properly" (samyak). For "proper worship" and "complete worship" mean worship performed with tranquility and the other qualities. [An objection: Why should it not be intended here as mere worship, accomplished through the perfection of means even without tranquility and the rest? To this he says: "And not... (na ca).

In this context, "worship" (abhyarcana) is intended to mean worship through tranquility (śama) and the other [virtues], and not anything else apart from tranquility and so forth; for it is heard that this worship leads to liberation, and such [liberation] is impossible in the absence of tranquility and the rest—this is the sense. He states, "By sacrifice," etc., to show that by the force of the opening statement, the persistence of Brahminical duties among Kṣatriyas and others is understood. To the question, "Why is there an absence of liberation in the absence of tranquility and the rest? he says, "Tranquility," etc.; for devotion to the Lord and so forth is indeed what is meant by tranquility and the rest.

The sense is that it is well-established that in the absence of the culmination [of practice], there can be no liberation. Furthermore, since there is no prohibition [against them], tranquility (*śama*) and the other [requisites] must be accepted for Kṣatriyas and others; thus he says: "And not... A prohibition occurs only in the context of teaching the duties of those [specific classes]; this has been stated extensively regarding their respective duties. For this reason as well, tranquility and the rest must be accepted by Kṣatriyas and others; thus he says: "For it is fitting... Tulādhāra was a Vaiśya. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of Śūdras such as Daṇḍadhāra and others is intended.

The word "hi" indicates what is well-known from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources. If this is so, one might ask: how can there be a distinction between one's own duty (*svadharma*) and the duty of another (*paradharma*)? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that, according to the reasoning already stated, these [duties] are common to others as well. Thus, agriculture and so forth are for the livelihood of a Vaiśya; service is for a Śūdra; and officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts are to be understood as the means of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa. He states the duties of another: "But those two... (*tau tu...*) and so on.

Even though tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are common to all, why should not all qualities such as valor (*śaurya*) be the specific duties (*viśeṣadharma*) of the Kṣatriya? Why should the Brāhmaṇa’s own duty (*svadharma*) consist merely of teaching and so forth, and the Śūdra’s merely of service (*śuśrūṣā*)? To this, he demonstrates their commonality by means of authoritative evidence: "Valor," etc. By this, it is also stated that the mention of valor and so forth in relation to the Kṣatriya refers to its predominance (*ādhikya*). The connection is: "teaching the virtuous" and "service."

To the question, "What is meant by saying that for a Śūdra there is [duty] other than teaching? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because service (*śuśrūṣā*) is the duty common to all. The word "of the good" (*satām*) is to be connected [with this]. To the question, "If bravery and so forth are common [to all], what are the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the Kṣatriyas and others? he says: "These. The meaning is: those other than those stated as being common, such as not fleeing in battle, sovereignty, and so forth. They are innate (*naisargika*), meaning they are uncommon.

One might ask: "Are these qualities exclusive to men by necessity? To this he says: *syāt* ("it may be"). Furthermore, one should not suspect that because these are exclusive, they must necessarily be practiced; to this he says: *balāt* ("by force"), as for example, the officiating at sacrifices and so forth for the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, one should not consider them to be things to be abandoned simply because they are not exclusive and thus not inherently one's own; to this he says: *anisarga* ("not innate"), as for example, teaching and so forth for the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa.

He states an exception to what was previously said: "By officiating at sacrifices," etc. The meaning is that even auspicious qualities that are not innate should be cultivated only when they are common [to all], but not those such as officiating at sacrifices and so forth, which are specific to Brahmins and others. By stating that heroism and the like are not common, it is implied that non-retreat from battle and sovereignty are the specific duties (*viśeṣadharma*) of a Kṣatriya. He states an exception to that: "Non-retreat," etc. By the specific mention of "for the sake of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas," it is established as a general rule for the Kṣatriya alone;
therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated before.

Just as non-retreat from battle—though stated as the specific duty of a Kṣatriya—may also apply to others due to particular circumstances, might sovereignty likewise be the duty of others? To this, [the author] first defines its essential nature and then demonstrates by means of authoritative evidence that it does not apply to those other than Kṣatriyas. Regarding the word "prasahya" (forcibly): since it is asked "of whom? in reference to the seizing of wealth and so forth by force, he states "sarve" (all) to exclude those for whom the Kṣatriya's duty of not failing in his task is intended. Thus, he specifies those who are excluded from the phrase "not failing in his task by those other than Kṣatriyas."

If one asks, "In that case, should Brāhmaṇas and others not perform the instruction of those who follow different dharmas? he says: "Aṅga, etc. To the question, "What kind of person is called a disciple (śiṣya)? he says: "And the disciple... If one then asks, "Does this not lead to the undesirable consequence that sons and others would not be subject to instruction? he says: "The son... The sense is that such a person is a disciple by nature, not merely by birth. He further states that it is not only disciples who are to be instructed by Brāhmaṇas and others, but teachers and others as well: "Teachers... [This refers to] "among the things to be taught."

The meaning is that this refers to the subject matter concerning those who are to be instructed. He states [the following] to show that not only teachers and others are to be disciplined, but even those who are ignorant: "Sin," etc. Here, in all cases, the specific rule—that punishment for failing to perform the constituent parts [of the rite] falls upon the disciples, while teachers [are punished] according to place and time—should be understood as distinguishing them from Kṣatriyas. It has been stated that those practicing sin are to be restrained; however, if they should commit a great sin known as "opposition to one's own superior," then what should be done? To this he says: "That," etc.

To the question, "Should they be abandoned immediately? he says: "Just as... To the question, "Should those who oppose one's superiors, such as gurus and others, be abandoned altogether? he says: "In Viṣṇu... He describes the manner of instructing them: "While instructing... To the question, "What should be done if one who is a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu commits a sin other than opposing his superiors? he says: "The great ones..."

In this context, he shows by means of the Smṛti the duties for Brahmins and others in times of distress (*āpad*). Regarding the phrase "in times of distress": he states the specific rule for a Kṣatriya when practicing the duties of a Brāhmaṇa with the words "the Kṣatriya. The meaning is that he may become a solicitor of alms or an acceptor of gold and other such gifts. This is connected with the statement, "he should practice the duty of a Śūdra. It has been stated that a Śūdra, however, should not practice the duties of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya; so, what duty should he resort to in times of distress? To this, he says: "the Śūdra."

He states the specific rule regarding the Śūdra’s adoption of the Vaiśya’s dharma: “The Śūdra,” etc. This means that he must not engage in hearing the syllables of the Veda and so forth. It has been stated that a Kṣatriya may follow the Brāhmaṇical [dharma] in times of distress, and that in his own distress he may practice the dharma of the Vaiśyas. To the question of what should be done even beyond that, he says: “In extreme distress,” etc. This means that while practicing the Śūdra’s duty of service toward Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, he does not incur fault. Not only is the Kṣatriya not defiled by practicing the Śūdra’s dharma, but rather—[he says the following].

Regarding the phrase "in those [tasks]": if a Kṣatriya encounters misfortunes while performing his own duty, then—even if his master is superior in strength—he must not overcome him for the sake of dharma; rather, he should be requested by the master to perform those tasks to which he is appointed. Even if these are Śūdra-like tasks performed for the sake of wealth and so forth, it is better dharma for him to subsist on the dharma of Brāhmaṇas and others than to remain idle. This is the meaning.

In this regard, he says "by the master" (*prabhuṇā*) to show that being requested by the master is especially a cause for merit, even because of the non-overpowering of the master’s ownership. [An objection is raised: Since there is no dependence on others when one resorts to the duties of a Brahmin and so forth, whereas such dependence exists in the duty of a Śūdra, how can his state be superior despite the presence of the master’s continuous connection and superior strength? To this, he says "of the arms" (*bāhvoḥ*). The sense is that because everything belongs to him, there is no dependence on others. 48.

An alternative state of the very person described by the statement, "One who is devoted to his own duty attains perfection," is now stated: "unattached" (*asakta*). Therein, he states the meaning in order to dispel the notion that the term *naiṣkarmya-siddhi* (attainment of actionlessness) refers to liberation (*mokṣa*): "By *naiṣkarmya*... The word "all" (*sarva*) refers to everything except for those karmas whose fruits have already begun (*prārabdha*). (49)

With the words beginning with "unattached" (*asakta*), the author first makes a formal promise to explain the means for attaining the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*), and then states its subsequent result: "perfection" (*siddhim*). In that context, in order to dispel any misconception, he says "to be described" (*vakṣyamāṇa*)—namely, the method by which one attains the Supreme Brahman immediately after the perfection of actionlessness; learn that manner.

Here, the meaning is simply this: "Understand that method"—namely, the manner in which one, existing in the way that will be described, having attained *naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, reaches *Mahālakṣmī*. It does not mean, however, that after *naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, one should understand the means for attaining the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). To the question, "Why is the word *brahman* used here as a synonym for Lakṣmī?", he says: "My... [referring to the verse beginning with *mama*]. To the further objection, "Why should the word *brahman* here not refer to the Supreme Brahman itself?", he says: "*Brahman*... [referring to the definition of *brahman*].

One might ask: "Could this not be the Supreme Brahman itself even immediately after attaining this [lower] Brahman? To this, he says: "Brahman... The meaning is that even immediately after attaining this Brahman, because of the scriptural mention of the attainment of devotion (*bhakti*) and so forth, this is indeed the reality of Lakṣmī, and not the Supreme Brahman. This would be the case if it were established that the attainment of devotion and so forth occurs for one who has reached the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*) even after attaining Lakṣmī, but not after attaining the Supreme Brahman. Why is that? To this, he says:

"All" (sarva) refers to the term "sin," meaning those undesirable actions that have not yet begun to bear fruit (*aprārabdha*). Now, it may be argued: since the state of being established in actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*) belongs to one who possesses immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*), how can there be a further attainment of knowledge and so forth immediately after that? If this were the case, it would follow that such attainment would occur even in liberation (*mukti*). To this, he says: "Immediate" (*aparokṣa*). Prior to the abandonment of the body, the increase of knowledge and other qualities may indeed continue even after immediate realization. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for the point is that in liberation, the absence of such increase is established in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 50-52 ||

It might be argued that when it was said, "Learn the means for achieving freedom from action (naiṣkarmyasiddhi)," only that was being stated, and not that the means for attaining Brahman follows immediately after. This is incorrect; for after stating the means beginning with "with a purified intellect," it is said, "he is fit for becoming Brahman. Otherwise, one would have had to say, "having attained freedom from action. Anticipating this objection and in order to dispel any other possible misconception regarding the term "becoming Brahman" (brahmabhūya), he states the meaning as follows: "Being liberated... (vimucya).

The sense is that, since there is no necessity for further means once prosperity is attained immediately upon the dawn of knowledge, it is precisely this state of having attained perfection through actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*) that is intended here. (53–55)

The statement "from which [action] proceeds" is further specified as "all. In that context, to dispel the misconception that one who takes refuge in Me might attain the eternal state while performing all actions—whether prohibited or unprohibited—according to one's own will, He explains this by saying: "prescribed" and "taking refuge in Me. "Taking refuge in Me" means surrendering everything to Me alone. To the question, "Why should it not be taken in its literal sense? He replies: "For indeed..."

One should not assume here that the intent is the performance of prohibited or permitted actions according to one's own will; for if that were the case, it would follow that the intent here is even the non-performance of prescribed duties by one who has taken refuge in the Lord, since the commission of a prohibited act and the non-performance of a prescribed duty would be equivalent. To address the objection that there must indeed be an intent toward the non-performance of prescribed duties even for one who has taken refuge in the Lord, he says: "Me... (mām).
