The sense is this: if the intention here were that even the non-performance of what is enjoined applies to one who has taken refuge in the Blessed Lord, then for Arjuna himself—who has taken refuge in the Blessed Lord—a prior transgression would have been stated in such passages as "Remember Me and arise" (*māmanusmara yudhya ca*) regarding the non-performance of the enjoined battle, and in "But if you do not perform this righteous [duty]" (*atha cettvamimaṃ dharmyam*), etc. This would result in a contradiction.
Furthermore, if the literal meaning were not accepted, the word *api* ("even") would be redundant; therefore, he says: "*Api*. (55)

If liberation were to accrue to one who performs prescribed duties while depending upon the Blessed Lord, then it would also accrue to the possessor of the three Vedas (*traividya*). For even he, having performed his prescribed duties, is not distinct from one who depends upon the Blessed Lord due to the existence of the spirit of offering them to Him. To resolve this doubt, the author introduces the verse beginning with "bhagavad-". [The meaning is: Even though there is equality between the one who depends on the Blessed Lord and the possessor of the three Vedas regarding the performance of prescribed duties and so forth, the presence and absence of liberation are nonetheless established as possible.

The sense is that one who has performed all prescribed duties, having surrendered them mentally to the Blessed Lord, acts while taking refuge in the Blessed Lord; it is not so for the one possessed of the threefold knowledge (*traividya*). Thus, the distinction between the two exists precisely through the mind. By the phrase "having Me as the supreme goal" (*mat-para*), the superiority of the devotee (*bhāgavata*) over the one possessed of the threefold knowledge is stated. In that regard, if the meaning were taken to be "one who has intent (*tātparya*) toward the Blessed Lord," that would be common even to the one possessed of the threefold knowledge.

Alternatively, if one accepts the position that "I am the other," meaning the supreme one among all, such conceptual constructions are untenable; therefore, since that [objection] is equal for the three Vedas as well, he says: "That very same [one]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the other in every respect. It should also be understood as "always" and "in all states."

If it were [merely] "my mind," it would be a tautology. To dispel the doubt that there is no state of being His (the Lord's) mind other than the fact of the Lord's supreme excellence, he says "therein" (*tatra*) for that purpose. "Therein" means in the Lord; the ellipsis is "the devotee's (*bhāgavata*) distinction [arises] from the threefold knowledge (*traividya*). In that case, it would again be a tautology to say "resorting to the yoga of the intellect" (*buddhiyogam upāśritya*), because the "yoga of the intellect" is simply the application of the intellect toward the Lord. Therefore, he says "intellect" (*buddhi*).

The meaning is that the "yoga" of the intellect—that is, of knowledge—is the means consisting of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, this has been stated on the assumption that you accept [the self] as being of the nature of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). (57–58)

It is said that "it is impossible for you not to do what has been stated"—this is expressed by the word "yadi" (if). In this context, the term *prakṛti* might be understood as referring to inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth; therefore, to dispel such a misconception, he says: "*prakṛtiḥ*" (the primordial cause). If it is asked why the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) is denoted by the word *prakṛti*, he replies: "*prakṛtiḥ*" (the primordial cause). In this connection, he extends the point already made here to other instances as well: "*eṣā*" (this). If it is asked why the word *prakṛti* here denotes the will of the Supreme Lord and why it might not instead mean inherent nature and the like, he says: [the following].

"Of that very [nature]" (tasyā eva). In the verse "Nature (prakṛti) will impel you," it is stated that Nature is the impeller of the individual soul (jīva). However, since that [impelling] primarily belongs to the will of the Lord (īśvara), it is His will alone that is meant here; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "How can this not be so, given that in the subsequent verse—which serves as a commentary on the phrase 'by your own nature' (svābhāvajena)—the word *prakṛti* is understood to mean 'inherent nature' (svabhāva)? To this he replies: "Inherent nature," etc. The word "the individual soul" (jīvam) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

This "prakṛti" (nature/material cause) is not what is later referred to by the term "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature); rather, the sense is that because this [Ishvara's will] serves as the means for the governance of the individual soul (jīva), it is later called "svabhāva" and so forth. For this reason as well, he states that here the meaning of the word "prakṛti" is simply the will of Ishvara: "That very same... Since in the subsequent verse, which serves as an explanation of this, it is stated that the will of the Blessed Lord alone is the governor of all, the sense is that the word "prakṛti" here has that [will] as its meaning. By the term "māyā," it is Ishvara's will itself that is being expressed. (Verses 59–61)

In passages such as "The Lord of all beings," since the Blessed Lord Īśvara is indicated in the third person (parokṣeṇa), the author says "ascertained" (*niścita*) in order to dispel the notion that this Īśvara is different from the Blessed Lord. The sense is that because the statement is made in the third person, there is no other possible explanation [for the usage], and therefore one should not assume on that basis alone that the Īśvara is distinct from the Blessed Lord. Furthermore, he states "me" (*mad*) to show that such an assumption should not be made.

In this context, because the attainment of refuge in the Lord is intended—by means of excluding others through the instruction "take refuge in Him alone"—and because at the conclusion there is the teaching on attaining refuge in Himself through the words "be intent on Me" (*manmanā bhava*) and so forth, this Lord is none other than the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). The implication is that otherwise, there would be a contradiction. To the question, "What is this 'eternal abode' (*śāśvataṃ sthānam*) mentioned in the phrase 'you shall attain the eternal abode'? he says: "The eternal. [To the objection: Since all abodes perish at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), how can Vaikuṇṭha and the like be eternal? To this he says: [the following].
"Śrī herself," thus [ends the verse]. || 63 ||

Having made the promise, "But this which I shall declare to you is the most secret," that reality which was described as the most secret through such terms as "knowledge" (jñāna) and so forth is here stated once again as "the most secret of all. To dispel the misconception that this might be something else, he says: "That reality... One should not understand here that there is a conclusion [of the topic] based on the supplementary phrase "thus [it is] the most secret. If so, what is declared here as the most secret? To this he says: "In this regard..."

[Objection: But since it was stated, "Having understood this, one would be wise," the essence of the means has already been summarized; how then can that [essence] be mentioned here? To this, it is said: "The reality... The point is this: in that [previous passage], which takes the form of a summary of the essence of the means, there was no praise for the knowledge of the Lord's supreme excellence as such. Rather, the intention is that because liberation exists through the mere knowledge of Him, what need is there to describe His greatness? Thus, it is solely for the purpose of praising the Lord.

To this, he says: "They are my measures" (*manmānāḥ*). Since the *Sādhanasāra* was previously mentioned, the sense is that [this work] is justified as being "more" (*bhūyaḥ*) in comparison to it. If one were to object that this would then result in a redundancy, he states that this is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *Sādhanasāra*.

[Objection: But surely, since the worship of oneself has been taught here in passages such as "Fix your mind on Me" (*manmanā bhava*) by means of the exclusion of others, the Lord's status as the supreme of all has been stated; so why is it not a statement of the essence of reality (*tattvasāra*)? To this he says: "In meaning" (*arthataḥ*). It is true that the superiority of Viṣṇu is stated here; nevertheless, it was stated only because otherwise the instruction to worship oneself—preceded by the rejection of the worship of others—would be inexplicable. It was not stated explicitly (*mukhataḥ*). Therefore, the sense is that there is no statement of the essence of reality here. (Verses 64–65)

To the objection—"Since no other deities are excluded here because [the Lord] has not been made so, how can Viṣṇu’s superiority be stated even by implication?"—he says: "Not... The statement "having abandoned all duties" (sarvadharmān parityajya) exists as a supplement to what was said in "be devoted to Me alone" (manmanā bhava), in the form: "having abandoned all other attributes. Therefore, the sense is that the worship of Him alone is indeed taught here, preceded by the exclusion of others.
One might ask: "Could it not be that here, by saying 'abandoning all duties' and so forth, and 'take refuge in Me alone,' the teaching is simply this? To this, he says: "Me," etc.

The sense is that by the statement "Come to Me alone as your refuge," the very meaning previously expressed in "Fix your mind on Me" and so forth is being explained; otherwise, if one were to imagine a different meaning, there would be a contradiction in the teaching, as it would result in saying "abandon fixing your mind on Me and so forth, and instead practice [something else]. To address the objection that this explanation of what was already said is redundant, it is stated that it serves as a conclusion (*nigamana*). One should understand that the passage beginning with "Fix your mind on Me" functions as an explanation of the statement "Come to Me alone as your refuge."

This might be so if taking refuge in the Blessed One, the mind, and so forth were itself *śaraṇāgati*; but why is that? To this he says: "Because of being the supreme of all. Here, one should see the identity of meaning with the previously stated sense of "fixing the mind on Me" (*man-manāḥ*) and so on, as applicable. [The service] is threefold, arising from mind, speech, and body. It is by its very nature, not in expectation of any other fruit. By the phrase "granting the fruit of liberation,"...

The meaning is that you shall come to Me alone; this is how it should be understood as an explanation of the phrase "all dharmas" by "Me alone. The sense of "I [am] all" is that I am everything. Now, one might raise the objection: "Arjuna has not yet accepted what he himself said; so how can the Blessed One conclude his instruction of him? Anticipating this doubt, the Lord dispels the misconception that He is merely granting permission for Arjuna to act according to his own desire by saying, "Do as you wish," and thus provides the following rebuttal: "As... (yathā).

The sense is that since it has been stated right here that Arjuna acted in accordance with what was spoken by the Blessed One, it is therefore logical that the Blessed One—who already knew this—should have ceased instructing him prior to that point. (73–78)

Now, this venerable teacher, having completed his work, pays homage to Vāsudeva in the very manner he has set forth. Regarding the word "namaḥ" (salutation): since even the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature is the cause of all human goals, such as liberation (*kaivalya*), he says "yasya" (of whom) while offering the service consisting of the composition of this treatise to Keśava. Then, with special reverence, he praises that very Hari once more with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). Here, *bhūti* refers to Mahālakṣmī.
May the Lord who delights Indirā, who is the stainless abode in the hearts of the venerable Ānandatīrtha, and who is devoted to compassion for the wretched, attain my affection.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Nyāyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmadbhagavadgītātātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya, written by the sage Jayatīrtha. 18.
